Stratigraphic trap in Lower Cretaceous Coracle Sandstone Member, sealed by Hauterivean mudstones. Reservoir facies are deep-sea turbidites sourced from the north-west. Top and lateral/base seal provided by combination of Hauterivean mudstones and some pinchout against the BCU. Basin modelling suggests prospect is underlain by hydrocarbon generating Mid-Jurassic, Late Jurassic and Devonian intervals. Migration via faulting likely to have taken place during the Early Cretacoues/Tertiary. Amplitude response similar to that seen on Norfolk prospect (cp12_16_7). No parameters provided - entered cf. 'Norfolk' prospect.

The crest of the Western Coracle Amplitude prospect is at 650m. The reservoir consists of older Coracle sands than the Norfolk Amplitude prospect. The trapping mechanism is entirely stratigraphic, with again reservoir being formed by deep-sea turbidite sands sourced from the north west. Top and lateral/base seal are provided by a combination of intra-Hauterivian mudstones and some pinchout against the Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU). Basin modelling suggests this prospect is underlain by hydrocarbon generating Mid Jurassic, Late Jurassic and Devonian intervals. Migration is likely to have been via faulting set up in the Early Cretaceous and/or the Tertiary. The seismic amplitude response of this prospect is similar to that at the Norfolk Amplitude prospect and has a similar PCOS (16%). Stochastic volumetrics give a STOIIP (P90/P50/P10) of 61/ 91/ 137 mmbbls, and a recoverable range of 12/ 22/ 38 mmbbls.

Local wells show relatively low NTG, however prospect is updip and may be closer to sediment source. Lateral/base seal provided by KCF, top seal provided by transgressive muds at top of Valanginian interval. No parameters provided - entered cf. Norfolk prospect (cp12_16_7).

description:
The Juniper lead is part of the most proximal terrace of the south eastern UK Rockall Trough, immediately adjacent to the main basin-bounding fault. This greater terrace area is approximately 220 km2, with the Juniper lead in the north, being about 70 km2. This is one of the shallowest leads in the inventory, located in approximately 140 m of water, with the crest around 2,400 m below mudline.
Juniper is interpreted as a Lower Cretaceous clastic reservoir, charged by Jurassic marine (Type II) source rocks and preserved within a Jurassic ‘back-basin’ (Figure 5.1). As the actual top reservoir pick in this back-basin is unresolved, trap configuration may be described as either a low-side fault dependent trap (likely when reservoir is deeper, with the ultimate updip seal against the basin bounding fault) or as a sub-unconformity trap (if top reservoir is shallower and therefore truncated by the Albo-Aptian unconformity before reaching the basin margin).

Updip seal to NW is provided by truncation of the Sgiath reservoir beneath the BCU. Seal to the NE & SW is provided by juxtaposition against upthrown Triassic mudstones or Zechstein anhydrites and tight carbonates.

The Marshall North structure is a NW-SE trending Jurassic tilted fault block. Target reservoirs are the Sgiath sandstones. The structure is dip-closed to the south-west and south-east. The Sgiath reservoir is upthrown against Kimmeridge Clay shales to the north-east. Mapping shows reservoirs are downthrown against either Triassic mudstone or Zechstein evaporates to the nort-east.

Charge modelling indicates that Marshall South is the lowest risk structure as this fills first, oil then  migrates to the northwest into the Greater Marshall truncation edge – only if this seals can you then back-fill into the Marshall North structure.

Marshall North is the further prospect away from the known source rock in the Greater Marshall complex

Curly is an Upper Jurassic 4-way structure or possibly several smaller structures located in block 16/1a on the East Shetland Platform in 120m of water depth. The confidence of the structure varies due to the subtle nature of the structure and because it is sensitive to the depth conversion and seismic interpretation due to tuning with the Cretaceous package. The eastern boundary of the prospect coincides with a NNW-SSE trending fault that separate it from the nearby 16/1-1 well. The spill of the structure is to the northwest. The Curly Upper Jurassic Prospect is sealed by overlying Lower Cretaceous calcareous claystones, chalk and Kimmeridge Clay. Migration modelling suggests that oil could have migrated up the main boundary fault towards southern Viking Graben and along the Curly complex high into the main Curly prospect.

Originally defined as a prospect, Curly has been redefined as a cluster of leads following the drilling of the Tiger Lily well and update of the licence velocity model.
The prospect was defined as a subtle 4-way closure at the Base Cretaceous Unconformity with limited volume potential and high risk. The prospect was proposed to have an Upper Jurassic Piper Fm reservoir, charged from mature Kimmeridge Clay Formation in the South Viking Graben to the east and sealed by Cretaceous calcareous claystones and chalk. Updated mapping and post-drill depth conversion of the Curly prospect, and a review of risk, in light of semi-regional studies, indicate that the prospect is likely to be broken into several smaller closures and at best offers a low volume, high risk opportunity with low resource density. Given the Tiger Lily well outcome, the Curly cluster is of no further interest to the partnership.

During drilling of the Tiger Lily well the Paleozoic succession was found to be extremely tight with ROP <3m/hr and the Paleozoic succession is interpreted as granitic basement. Unlike the Cairngorm discovery wells, no losses were observed in the Tiger Lily well and the Paleozoic succession penetrated in the well is believed to be tight with no flow potential. Shows were observed to a depth of 2420m TVDss, 25m shallow to the likely OWC observed in the Cairngorm structure. Whilst the Tiger Lily Paleozoic penetrated at the well location does not constitute a reservoir rock it seems likely that it is part of the Cairngorm granitic complex and that the encountered shows could relate to a mega-closure at OWC level. This would assume a working lateral seal, as well as competent top seal, which is unproven by the well. The extent of the Cairngorm complex is uncertain, albeit somewhat constrained by the presence of Devonian sub-crop in the near-by 16/02a- 2 well and the seismic character at Top Paleozoic level. An attempt to quantify the in-place volume in a potential Tiger Lily granite segment (Figure 8 and Appendix C) has been made, yielding a potential, but highly uncertain, mean in-place volume of approximately 128 mmbbls. The apparent lack of fractures in the Tiger Lily basement suggests a significant risk on producibility and hence low recovery factor. The Tiger Lily well went straight from Kimmeridge Clay Formation into very hard granitic basement with low ROP (~3m/hr). Sampling in the granite is limited to cuttings, based on which there is no evidence to suggest the presence of a conglomerate or significant weather zone at Top Paleozoic level.

Edzell prospect is a 3-way dip closure mapped at BCU level on the SE flank of the Fladen Ground Spur. Anticipated reservoir is U. Jurassic Glamis sandstones. Prospect is located at the tip of the South Viking Graben, where the graben bounding fault terminates. The preferred interpretation is that shallow marine sandstones were deposited via a relay ramp in the bounding fault, rather than Brae-type conglomerates deposited against a steep fault scarp. Main risks are reservoir presence (as distribution of U. Jurassic is irregular) and trap effectiveness. P50 recoverable of 4.7mmboe stated, but no other parameters provided.
A small structure abutting the South Viking Graben bounding fault. Relies on proximal Brae-type sandstones for reservoir potential.

The Tinker Bell prospect is a combined structural and stratigraphic trap divided into three segments; South, Mid and North. The postulated reservoir is the Upper Jurassic Piper Formation, and the AVO attributes have led to increased understanding in the definition and extent of this reservoir. The AVO attributes support the presence of hydrocarbon in the southern prospect segment. Tinker Bell is located in a position favorable for migration from the South Viking Graben. The main risk is the trap seal.

The Estella South (aka Tinker Bell South) prospect is a structural-stratigraphic trap situated along the eastern edge of the Fladen Ground Spur. At the time of application, the definition of the prospect outline relied heavily on the AVO attribute and an apparent depth conformancetowards the east. 
Trap-seal was, and is, the key risk to the Estella South prospect as the updip stratigraphic pinch-out of the reservoir sand can no longer be mapped with confidence and is further 
compromised by the presence of Piper Formation sandstone in the updip 15/10- 1 well. The updip sealing potential may benefit from the presence of small-scale faulting, however, these faults cannot be mapped in detail and appear unlikely to form a continuous barrier. 
A revised prospect outline has been defined assuming the presence of an updip structural-stratigraphic seal, albeit considered extremely risky, and dip closure towards the east. The presence of Piper Formation sandstone within the redefined prospect outline is considered relatively low risk. However, the presence of Piper Formation sandstone deposits forming a continuous carrier bed downdip of the prospect is not supported by the sand-flag attribute, nor the downdip 16/6a- 1 well and hence effective migration into the prospect is very risky.
North Star is a Tertiary lead and is an amplitude bright south of the Dalmore discovery. There is a high risk on reservoir presence for this lead as the amplitude bright could be cemented sandstone.

Dalmore is a Tertiary discovery, a structural closure combined with a stratigraphic trapping component. Although fully covered by 3D seismic data, seismic imaging is slightly disrupted above the prospect by the presence of a gas chimney. A series of east west tending normal faults are interpreted within the Tertiary section. The main reservoir interval on the discovery is the Eocene age Skroo Formation. Sands were deposited by southeasterly trending submarine channels fed from uplifted areas to the northwest. The discovery was made by well 16/6b-6, which targeted the crest of a differential compaction mound at Top Skroo sandstone level. Well 16/6b-6 encountered 33 m of net oil pay in Eocene sandstone, but was suspended without testing. Well 16/6b-7 (1997) targete a stratigraphically younger channel sandstone lobe similar to that penetrated by the discovery well (16/6b-6). It was located 1 km southwest of 16/6b-6, and proved oil shows. Appraisal well 16/6b-9 (1999) also proves oil.

Top seal is provided by the overlying mudstones of the Horda Formation.

Duffield T38 is a subtle 4-way dip closure identified below Base of Balder, in the T38 prograding clinoforms. The trap formation is related to Neogene inversion. Top seal relies on a basal T45 flooding event (seen in Balder in 204/17-1). Despite the absence of HC shows in 204/17-1 or 204/22-2 wells at this level, presence of gas chimneys above indicates migration either along the faults or vertically. Reservoir is expected to represent clinoform topset to foreset environment, represented by shoreface and outer shelf storm deposits, which are preserved in a sand-rich interval in 201/22-2, getting more heterolithic towards 204/17-1. Stratigraphic interval within closure is dim, which may be  a reflection of shallow gas above masking true amplitudes. Locally, however, the dim spot is conformable to structure. Top seal is the main risk for the prospect.

Duffield T36 is a subtle 4-way dip closure with a fault bounded upside with a reservoir in the  'Kintail' and 'Cuillin? turbidite aprons  of T36 ? T35 age.  The turbidite deposits are amalgamated at this location and therefore presence of an intra-formational seal is unlikely. An analogous 204/19-3A 'Cuillin' well penetrated 42m net T36 reservoir beneath the Kettla Tuff with an 8m oil column. Nearby 204/18-1 and 204/22-2 had shows at T35 level. Charge is assumed via underlying and/or bounding faults, and possibly also laterally within the sequence. The top seal is provided by Kettla Tuff or late T36/T38 mudstones. Stratigraphically equivalent turbidite sandstones found in 204/17-1 and 204/22-2 were silty and often thin-bedded, however, seismic attributes indicate more axial environment for the prospect. The closure is mainly seismically dim, but lithological variation within Kettla tuff masks potential fluid expression. Seal is the main risk.
Duffield T36 is a small four-way dip closure with limited volume range.

Chatsworth is a subtle 4 way dip closure with a minor fault-bounded component, developed in the turbidite fans of T36 ? T35 age. It is uncertain whether a working seal is likely to exist between these two intervals. Currently, the prospect is assumed to have one reservoir-seal pair, but a deeper brightening against a bounding fault at T35 level suggests a possibility of stacked pay both in T36 and T35 sands. There is dimming in amplitudes observed at T36 level, but not conformable to structure, probably reflecting  lithological variation. Good quality reservoir sandstones were found in T36 in 204/18-1 well, showing thinning towards 204/17-1. Seismic mapping, however, suggests the prospect is located in the axial position of a channelized fairway. The top seal is provided by Kettla Tuff or late T36/early T38 mudstones (seen in 204/18-1 well). Charge is assumed via underlying and/or bounding faults, or laterally (shows seen in 18-1 at T35 level). Top seal failure is the main risk.

Chatsworth and Cruachan are four-way dip closures, both carry significant seal risk due to

Cruachan T40 is a subtle structural four-way dip closure. Top seal relies on a basal T45 flooding event (204/18-1 drilled shales and coals at the base Balder). A fluvial to paralic reservoir sequence is expected, based on a regional mapping of an incised valley and wells which typically found 70-160m sand-rich T40 sequences. The underlying muddy foresets of the T38 clinoforms might have hindered charge migration into the structure, as indicated by absence of shows in T50-T38 levels of 204/18-1. However, the deep seated faults underneath likely acted as a charge conduit, judging by gas clouds above the crest of the structure.  These may, on the other hand, indicate top seal breach, or partial leakage of gas across the T40/Balder boundary. No amplitude conformance with structure or other DHIs were observed. Amplitude dimming occurs below the gas clouds. Top seal is the main risk for the prospect, and because of its shallow crest, there is a risk of biodegradation if oil is encountered.

A combination trap defined by a T35 canyon fill and an updip fault offset, separating it from a dry well 204/23-1. Several faults offset the reservoir interval, but reservoir self-juxtaposition is likely. The trap is defined by a fault with the largest throw. The top seal is provided by a thin shale developed above T35 sandy sequence. Unlike the good-quality T36 reservoir in the updip 204/23-1 well, T35 is a cemented conglomerate there, likely causing the very strong amplitude with a hard leading edge. This amplitude response remains unchanged along the extent of prospect. Brightening is also present at the soft loops below the hard top, suggesting development of reservoir quality sand below a hard abandonment surface. Downdip part of the closure is relatively dim. Charge is expected via deep faults intersecting the channel. Gas chimneys are present both downdip and updip in the overburden. Main risk is the top seal erosion by overlying T36 channels and updip fault seal integrity.

MacDui is a rotated fault block forming a 4 way closure filled with an opaque seismic pack of pre-rift stratigraphy.  The current assumption informed by nearby wells is that it contains Triassic sediments that have been draped by a KCF and Cretaceous sequence. Column height is likely top-seal constrained with concerns around presence of seal and effectiveness of seal at the crest.  Assuming the top seal is effective, the column would exist within an unknown arrangement of Foula and Otter Bank sediment.  Regional work shows a correlatio between lithostratigraphy and rock quality with the productive rock existing within the Otter Bank. Based on basin modelling the prospect is expected to be gas filled and it is lily that the degradation in rock quality due to depth of burial will result in a dependency between phase discovered and chance of developability. Alternatively the prospect could be Clair Group however the current well interpretation and seismic data do not support this.

Cruachan T38 is a fault-bounded three-way dip closure identified at the top of the lower part of T38 sequence. 
Its crest is approximately coincidental with that of the shallower T40 closure, indicating trap formation related to Neogene inversion. 
Unlike T40, the interval is faulted, which contributes to closure definition.  
Despite the absence of HC shows in 204/18-1 well at this level, presence of gas chimneys above indicates migration either along the fault or vertically. 
Top seal is assumed to be provided by muddy clinoform foreset deposits of upper T38 (204/18-1 drilled significant amount of silty shales at that level). 
Reservoir is expected to represent basal turbidite toeset deposits of T38, seen in 204/18-1 and 201/18-2b. 
Stratigraphic interval is very dim in the closure and no DHIs were observed. 
Top seal and reservoir presence are the main risks for the prospect, and because of its shallow depth, there is a risk of biodegradation if oil is encountered.

Cruachan T32 is an subtle-relief four-way dip closure identified at the top of the T32 sequence. Its crest is approximately coincidental with that of the shallower T38 & T40 closures, indicating trap formation related to Neogene inversion. T32 represents the uppermost sequence of a very sand-rich, 100s m thick amalgamated succession without significant muddy drapes that could provide seal (as seen in 204/18-1, 18-2b, 13-1, 17-1).  Elsewhere, T32 is overlain by a channelized T34 fan, which appears to bypass the area, allowing for the development of a potentially working seal below base of T35.  Presence of gas chimneys above the structure may indicate migration either along a fault or vertically. Reservoir is expected to be a very sand-rich basin-floor turbidite fan system (lack of heterogeneity indicated by low amplitude seismic facies).  Stratigraphic interval is very dim in the closure and no DHIs were observed. Top seal and charge migration are the main risks for the lead.

Sgurr nan Gillean is a fault dip stratigraphic combination trap in an embayment to the West of the Westray Ridge.  
It is filled with a Lower Cretaceous stripy seismic package. 
The trap is reliant on faults that seal and, in the larger cases, a stratigraphic edge.  Seals are regarded as the critical risk as shows are seen in the overburden. 
When mapped the stripy response has a fan like shape, which can be seen clearly on SNA extractions, this appears to be sourcing from the south and entering the embayment at a saddle point between the Westray Ridge and the Macdui structure. 
The prospect is down dip and across a fault from the 204/19-1 well which penetrates the same stripy seismic package and encounters a high NtG Lower Cretaceous section.  
This section was cored and has good properties for the depth (15% poro & circa 200 mD), sedimentology suggests a sub-marine flow and is very well sorted. 
Charge appears to have reached the well and leaked into the overburden; the key risk is seal.

The remainder of the Mesozoic portfolio consisted of potential Jurassic and/or Cretaceous sands pinching out against the Westray/Macdui Highs. 
Further seismic interpretation downgraded the lateral and seat seals of these previously identified leads. 
These leads required a Kimmeridge seat seal and/or lateral seal against the Westray High.

A combination trap consisting of a stratigraphic pinchout of slope channels and a lateral/updip fault offset. The closure is identified at the top of the lower part of T38 sequence, in a succession interpreted as toeset turbidite aprons  at the base of prograding clinoforms. Nearby 204/13-1 (Tornado) discovery encountered gas in good quality sands in the same setting, in a slightly younger T38 clinoform. Lower T38 sands were also present in 204/18-1, 18-2 and 14-2 wells. T38 sands are relatively thin and typically low amplitude when brine filled, brightening significantly when gas filled. Charge is possible via deep-seated faults downdip of the closure, and laterally. Top seal is assumed to be provided by muddy clinoform foreset deposits of upper T38 (204/18-1 drilled significant amount of silty shales at that level). Top seal and charge migration are the main risks , and because of its shallow depth below mudline, there is a risk of biodegradation if oil is encountered.

The Ard Lead is represented by a 4-way closure at base Balder Fm level.  This closure was formed by the pattern of deep incision of the T45 shore face sand by channels of the Balder delta.  Muds and coals drape this surface followed by tuffs and shale of the Balder Fm. which create the seal.  The lead is adjacent to and above a thin oil sand at T38 level found in 204/19-5 demonstrating the migration of oil to this level. Company CoS = 10%.

Two additional small and high risk leads were identified in Block 204/19c, namely the Ard and the
Ech leads. Both leads are mapped at the T45 level and are thought to have been
developed on a deeply incised Top Balder landscape creating structural and partly stratigraphic
features that lie to the north and south of the well 204/19-5.

Am Basteir is a strat, fault dip feature in a thickened section of Upper Jurassic sediment.  The adjacent 204/15-2 well penetrates a similar section a finds a thick J70 KCF equivalent with thin sands suggestive of the Solan system in Quad 205. Fionn Choire is a fault dip combination trap filled with a seismically opaque package below the BCU.  The package is not penetrated and seismic correlation into nearby wells is challenging due to intensity of faulting and presence of sills.  Best interpretation and visual comparison with penetrated packages nearby in the AOI (204/15-2, 204/19-9 and 204/22-1) suggests that the target is pre-rift Lower Jurassic alluvial to shallow marine however; it could equally be thick Middle Jurassic or Triassic.  The pre rift interpretation is supported by indications that the top of the package is truncated which would mean it was older than the Middle Jurassic uplift event. The prospect has a small four way component however significant volume relies on fault seal to increase the bulk volume.  This is likely challenging due to the nature of the underlying sediments (typically high NtG Triassic or Clair Group).  The top seal is likely Upper Jurassic KCF which has on-lapped the erosion surface.

Buxton is a faulted 3 way dip closure in the  'Kintail' and 'Cuillin? turbidite aprons  of T36 ? T35 age. Very little sand of T36 age was found in 204/22-2 well, although basin floor turbidites were encountered deeper at T35. Amplitude maps, however, suggest toe-of slope fan present in the area at T36 level, whose axial part was missed by the offset wells. Presence of reservoir is also suggested by hints of DHI?s, although lithological variation likely masks the potential fluid expression.  The top seal is provided by Kettla Tuff or late T36/early T38 mudstones, although those are likely to be thin. An analogous 204/19-3A 'Cuillin' well penetrated 42m net T36 reservoir beneath the Kettla Tuff with an 8m oil column. Nearby 204/16-1 well had gas shows throughout Paleocene, while oil shows were seen in T34 in 204/22-2. Charge is assumed via underlying and/or bounding faults.  No shallow gas anomalies were observed. Seal and charge are the key risks.
Buxton T35/T36 is a fault-dip closure – again small and with limited column upside.

The Bedlington prospect primary target was the Palaeocene T31 Lower Sand unit, with secondary targets of sand units within the Palaeocene T10 to T35 intervals. The Bedlington structure is compartmentalised by a series of E-W and SW-NE faults. The compartments in the NW are fault/dip closed while those of the SE margin require a stratigraphic sand onlap edge for closure against the regional dip. The well was designed to test significant amplitude anomalies, believed to indicate gas, observed downdip of the crestal area.

Mam Tor is a down-faulted 3 way dip closure with a lateral stratigraphic pinchout component in the amalgamated  'Kintail' and 'Cuillin? turbidite aprons  of T36 ? T35 age. T36 amplitude maps indicate the prospect is located in a proximal channelized base of slope environment. Intra-formational seal between T35 & T36 is not likely. The top seal is provided by Kettla Tuff or overlying Flett T40 mudstone (analogous to 204/22-1). The updip 204/22-1 well has a very sandy T35-T36 succession, potentially penetrating shoreface sands. Because of this abundance of sand recorded nearby, top and fault seal are key risk. Charge is assumed via underlying and/or bounding faults, or laterally.  No HC shows were present in the updip 204/22-1; while oil shows ocurred in T34 in 204/22-2. There are no shallow gas chimneys in the vicinity. No DHI?s were observed, but there is brightening against the fault, especially deeper in T35 (without structural conformance).

The Mam Tor T36 lead has a very small four-way dip closure. Larger volumes would depend on fault seal to the south and a stratigraphic pinch-out to the east. 
The fault seal component is problematic, as the well up dip (204/22-1) records a very sandy T35/T36 succession making fault seal less likely. 
No clear seismic amplitude shutoff at a potential contact was observed. 
The 204/22-1 well had no shows in the Palaeocene.

Mam Tor is a structural/stratigraphic trap defined by the thinning and pinchout of the T10 basin floor turbidite fans onto the Westray ridge, assisted by the offset along intersecting fault trends (NE-SW, NW-SE and E-W). Lateral and up-dip seal for the T10 relies on fault seal juxtaposition against mud-prone Upper Cretaceous, or alternatively Middle Jurassic or basement seen in 204/22-1. Top seal is provided by a thick shale below the T20 sequence, as in 204/22-2 well. Based on the analogy with other T10 penetrations in the area (204/22-2, 204/16-1 and 204/16-1z), porosity of 10%-15% and permeability from 5-200mD can be expected. The main risk is seal and trap definition. Reservoir effectiveness and migration are also issues; boundary faults are deep seated and igneous dykes may also act as conduits.  No DHI support, dimming over the crest of the structure is probably related to thinning of the reservoir. The downdip 204/22-2Z recorded gas shows and residual oil in parts of T10.

The Lathkill Lead is interpreted as a large fractured basement block. There is a possibility for a thin reservoir drape of Jurassic (Rona) or Lower Cretaceous age sands, but due to the shallow nature of the crest (1200m TVDSS) and the lack of internal reflections in the seismic section, these intervals are assumed to have been eroded. Seismic data suggests evidence of extensive faulting, thus invoking a fractured basement play. The shallow crest of the basement structure poses a risk with regards to hydrocarbon quality. The current seismic quality results in large uncertainty associated with presence of any syn-rift reservoir draped on top of the basement high. The basement age is uncertain, it may be Lewisian in nature given its shallow location, but similarly it may also contain pre-rift strata of Devonian to Triassic age. Kimmeridge Clay source rock may exist along the down-faulted flanks of the basement high.

The Hawk prospect is interpreted as a syn-rift reservoir onlapping and downlapping on to the pre-rift Jurassic and older sequences. The trap is a combination stratigraphic-structural trap. The current 3D seismic (the BP963F survey) only allows for coarse mapping of the prospect with large uncertainty associated with trap geometry. The prospect trap is defined by onlap on underlying Jurassic, with well 202/3a-3 suggesting onlap onto Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation shales which act as the base seal. Top seal is formed by overlying Cretaceous shales. It is suggested from analogues that the underlying Kimmeridge Clay in the adjacent basin will be within the onset of the oil window. The reservoir package, characterized by a stripy seismic facies, may also contain Rona sandstone towards the base of the section.

It is suggested by analogues that the prospect is overlying Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay modelled to be within the onset of the oil window. The reservoir package is characterized by a stripy seismic facies and may also contain Rona sandstone towards the base of the section.

The Black Rock Colsay Lead is a low relief 4-way dip closure identified at Palaeocene T40 (Colsay) level with potential upside in a speculative stratigraphic trap to the south. The Black Rock Lead is currently mapped as part coincident with Cambo North Lead and the possibility exists that the same Colsay unit extends through both leads, but there is potential that there are separate/additional Colsay units within the two leads.  The volumes invoked for the Black Rock Lead assume an additional Colsay sand to that in the Cambo North Lead. Company CoS = 14%.

There is much uncertainty on the thickness and presence of the pre-basalt units at this location due to tentative well ties and the impossibility of seismic facies characterisation or modelling on current data. Company CoS = 8%.

The main Hearach prospectivity is located in block 209/14a. The Hearach prospects were identified on the TGS Non-Exclusive 3D survey (Northern Lights 2014) reprocessed seismic data and became the primary prospect for the P2044 licence during 2017. Prospectivity was identified at the Flett and Lamba levels. The Tertiary prospects have been delimited by Class IV AVO responses and represent structural/stratigraphic traps with interpreted Flett aged (T45) channel fill sands pinching out onto basement and Lamba aged (T38) shelfal sands. Rock physics well studies have identified that both high porosity and gas filled sands can produce Class IV AVO responses and it is interpreted that the lack of sealing capacity indicates a strong possibility that the sands are brine saturated. Seismic reconditioning work was undertaken in an attempt to improve the conformance to structure, following a work programme of gathers
conditioning the amplitude response showed the same poor conformance to structure and as such could not be incorporated into Nexen's DHI risking matrix. The uncertainty in the amplitude response and lack of containment resulted in the overall size of the prospect being significantly reduced.

The package is further divided into three sub-packages (Megan A, B and C) which are each defined as turbidite channel complexes and are expected to contain a significant portion of turbidite channel sands. The Megan prospect is a stratigraphic trap defined by the onlap of Upper Jurassic sands onto the southeast flank of the Margarita spur/Manet ridge. Top seal is provided by Cromer Knoll shales and base and side seal requires the presence of a shaly Brent/Dunlin section below. 
Base and side seal are the highest risk elements of the prospect. 
The reservoir at Megan is interpreted to be Upper Jurassic sand, deposited as part of the channelized feeder system to the Magnus fan to the South. 
Hydrocarbons are sourced from organic rich Kimmeridge Clay Fm and Heather Fm shales.

Tatties is a downthrown Brent Gp fault block to the east of well 210/30a- 2, which had oil shows within the Brent and Upper Jurassic. The lead requires fault seal along the western bounding fault as Brent-Brent juxtaposition occurs towards the south of the prospect. Full fault seal is considered unlikely based on other Brent fields. Reservoir quality is considered the main risk. The 210/30- 1 discovery well to the east encountered a 200ft oil column at a similar depth, but reservoir quality was poor. The nearby Pelican Field achieves only 5% recovery without injection. No volumes or risking provided.
Troilus South Brent lead. Fault terrace. Relies on fault seal between lead and updip well 210/30a-2.

Glendullan is located in the Faroe-Shetland Basin, extending across the Flett High and SE margin of the Flett Sub-Basin. Contained within a stratigraphic trap, Glendullan demonstrates a distinctive sedimentary morphology, apparent on a number of seismic amplitude extractions, and interpreted as a slope channel and channelised lobe system.  The reservoir objective is interpreted as an intra-T35 Vaila sandstone, mapped as a low-impedance 'soft' event on 3D seismic data. Top, base and lateral seal is provided by T35-aged Vaila mudstone and the source rock is proposed as Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation. The prospect is identified by a DHI signal, derived from intercept and gradient seismic volumes, and is comparable to the nearby Laxford discovery anomaly. The Talisker prospect is a four way dip closure at top volcanic level and is attributed to have formed due to the formation of seaward dipping reflectors following continental breakup around 55 Ma. The two plays are 1) base volcanic Early Paleocene marine sandstones which are equivalent to the Egga Formation offshore Norway and 2) Mid-Late Cretaceous marine sandstones equivalent to the Springar, Nise and Lysing Formations offshore Norway. The recoverable resource prognosed in the Talisker prospect was 73 MMboe (P10), 200 MMboe (P50) and 556 MMboe (P90) and the hydrocarbon type was modelled to be predominantly oil.
For each play, the primary source rock is considered as Late Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation which is present elsewhere along the UKCS. The nearest hydrocarbon accumulations in the area are in the Tobermory/Erlend discovery well 214/4-1 and in the Tulipan discovery offshore Norway (6302/6-1).
Following the drilling of the Lagavulin exploration well, a reappraisal of the license was completed. This resulted in a downgrading of the recoverable resource in the license, housed in two separate prospects, Talisker East and West (Figure 5). The recoverable resource in Talisker East is 10.26 MMboe (P10), 31.88 MMboe (P50) and 99.15 MMboe (P90). The recoverable resource in Talisker West is 2.99 MMboe (P10), 9.71 MMboe (P50) and 30.88 MMboe (P90).

The Dungeons lead was originally evaluated as a carbonate play comprising a thickened section of what is
interpreted to Zechstein carbonates located on a structural high and having a component of 4-way dip closure
with potential for additional stratigraphic trapping. Limestones and dolomites of the Halibut Formation form
secondary reservoirs on the Auk and Ardmore (Argyll) and Innes Fields and are the reservoir for the Carnoustie
Field, which lies beneath the Montrose Field adjacent to Block 22/18c. Montrose well 22/18-T2 encountered
135 ft of dolomite which flowed 3,439 bopd (42.1oAPI) and 12 mmscfg/d on a 1/2' choke from a test interval of
100 ft. The field has produced intermittently, recovering approximately 0.4 mmboe during 2005 / 2006 and
again during 2013. Well 22/18-4 drilled Zechstein limestone and dolomites from 10,570 to 10,855 ft md.

Well 29/20-1 was drilled relatively low down the northern flank of the 4-way dip closure and the bulk of the mapped structure lies to the south of the discovery well, with potential for Rotliegende reservoir sands above the oil/water contact.

Lead Q29-A is a shallow gas accumulation, trapped in a 4-way dip closed structure within Pleistocene aged sediments. The lead straddles the boundary between blocks 29/23b and 29/28. The structure has been mapped at the strongest of a series of stacked amplitude anomalies, resulting in a closure at that level defined by a closing contour at 1,110 ft, with an area of 16 km2 and a maximum relief of 70 ft. The reservoir consists of stacked unconsolidated sands, probably deposited in a channel system and sealed by mudstones. The gas is most likely to be of biogenic origin.

The reservoir comprises unconsolidated Plio-Pleistocene aged channel sands in broad, low relief structural closures, sealed by extensive mudstones, containing biogenically derived gas. The identification of these gas charged sands is strongly dependent on the interpretation of seismic amplitudes and other DHI’s.

Defined by seismic ampltiude anomalies overlying the Skiddaw Cretaceous and Jurassic leads. The seismic amplitude anomalies are typically Class III AVO gas anomalies (comparable in type to the nearby Nuggets 2 and 3 gas fields) but are small and in places appear disconnected. The gas anomalies sit within overbank/splay deposits from the Eocene Frigg turbidite system crossing block 3/17. Company CoS = 34% with res quaility the key risk.

Skiddaw 'Eocene' prospect - The Skiddaw prospect is comprised of three target intervals including the Tertiary Frigg Member sandstones, the Early Palaeocene Ekofisk Formation and the Middle Jurassic Broom Formation. The Frigg Member sandstones were deposited as over-bank and levee type deposits along the margin of a high net to gross channelised turbidite system. The Tertiary target consists of stratigraphically trapped hydrocarbons within these over-bank and levee deposits and is identified by clear class III AVO gas anomalies along the Frigg Member seismic pick, comparable to the seismic response of the down-dip Nuggets gas fields

Faun remains the only other prospect defined on the licence. It is interpreted to be a Frigg Member stratigraphic trap that is observed to show possible gas bright spots. Regionally, Frigg sandstones are characterised by a hard top and there is a clear polarity reversal where gas charged which gives Class II to Class III AVO anomalies depending on sand thickness and porosity. The Faun prospect is defined by a series of Class III anomalies which are interpreted as overbank deposits associated with the main Frigg channel fairway which feeds the Nuggets Field.

Boltmaker is a well-defined, fault modified four-way closure at the base Upper Jurassic/Top Triassic stratigraphic level. The reservoir is located within the Triassic Cormorant Formation (Lewis Member), proven by a nearby well. The oil mature Kimmeridge Clay Formation acts as source rock to the Beryl Field, situated approximately 20 km north-east of the prospect, and a fill-spill route from this field is the anticipated hydrocarbon charge into the Boltmaker prospect. A potential breach of the relatively thin Upper Jurassic shaly top seal represents the key risk to the prospect. The calculated mean recoverable volumes of oil in the Boltmaker prospect amount to 81 mmbbls, with an upside (P10) of 145 mmbbls. A geological chance of success of 38 % has been assigned.

The main objective of the Bigfoot well was to test the Bigfoot prospect, targeting a well-defined, fault-modified closure identified at the Base Jurassic/ Top Triassic level.
The Bigfoot well (GB 16/22a- 4A) was drilled with the West Phoenix semi-submersible rig between the 22nd January and 13th February 2019. The well encountered the prognosed Triassic reservoir, but no hydrocarbons.

The Goose Eye prospect is defined as a downfaulted three-way dip closure to the East against the Beryl Embayment Fault. The identified reservoir package is interpreted to be the Upper Jurassic turbidite sandstones of the Bruce Fm. The Top Seal lithology is considered to be Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay, with ultimate seal from the Cromer Knoll in the Chalk Group. Fault juxtaposition seal across the fault with Triassic shales is also required. Hydrocarbon migration is considered as a fill-spill route through the Boltmaker prospect. Prominent signs of hydrocarbon leakage are seen above this fault and support this being a migration pathway.

Three high risk leads were identified in the licence at the time of application; Greyhawk, Ram Tam and Goose Eye. The Ram Tam and Greyhawk leads are located on the edge of the East Shetland Platform in the footwall of the Beryl Embayment Fault, whilst the Goose Eye lead lies in the hangingwall of the same fault. 
Predrill these leads were considered to be situated in a good location for migration if a viable migration pathway to the southern part of the Beryl Embayment could be confirmed by the Bigfoot well. 
In light of the Bigfoot well outcome, and migration failure, no uplift can be applied.
The volume potential of these leads was never considered to be significant enough to make them viable drilling candidates in their own right.

The Ram Tam prospect is identified and confidently mapped on a decrease in acoustic impedance that is proposed as the top reservoir. The trap is defined by a dip closure to the West against the Beryl Embayment Fault, and fault bound to the North-West. The identified reservoir package is sitting directly on the Palaeozoic crystalline basement and is therefore interpreted to be Devonian in age. From the regional understanding of the Devonian the reservoir is predicted to be fluvial sandstones, with intra-formational lacustrine shales providing the sealing lithology as penetrated in GB9/16-3. Hydrocarbon migration is anticipated from the Beryl Embayment relay ramp and across the Beryl Embayment Fault into the reservoir. Prominent signs of hydrocarbon leakage are seen above this fault and support this being a migration pathway.

The Ram Tam and Greyhawk leads are located on the edge of the East Shetland Platform in the footwall of the Beryl Embayment Fault, whilst the Goose Eye lead lies in the hangingwall of the same fault. 
Predrill these leads were considered to be situated in a good location for migration if a viable migration pathway to the southern part of the Beryl Embayment could be confirmed by the Bigfoot well. 
In light of the Bigfoot well outcome, and migration failure, no uplift can be applied.

The Greyhawk prospect is defined as a subcrop to the Base Cretaceous on the East Shetland Platform, in the footwall of the Beryl Embayment Fault. The reservoir interval is uncertain as no confident tie can be made across the Beryl Embayment Fault from the wells down on the relay ramp, but it is suggested Jurassic Bruce Fm. in combination with Triassic Cormorant Fm. is likely. Hydrocarbon migration is anticipated from the Beryl Relay ramp and across the Beryl Embayment Fault in to the structure. Signs of leakage are prominent along this fault, and this is seen as a positive indication of migration towards the prospect. The sealing lithology is the Cromer Knoll shales of the Chalk Group. Approximately 25% of the maximum closure of the prospect is located outside the application area.

Elongate Lower Eocene (Sele/Balder sands) prospect, north of Gryphon Field. Proj 06/04: COS downgraded (trap presence since based on old mapping of 2D).

The Silver Shadow prospect is located in blocks 16/1a and 9/26 and is a Upper Jurassic 3-way structure dependant on fault seal or stratigraphic elements in the deepest contact case. It is an intriguing prospect as excellent reservoir properties and hints of hydrocarbons are found in a nearby well and the prospect has a very strong AVO anomaly, although not perfectly conforming to structure, associated with it. The predicted reservoir is Upper Jurassic shallow marine sandstone. The proposed seal for the Silver Shadow prospect is the overlying Lower Cretaceous calcareous claystones, Upper Cretaceous chalk or Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay.  Laterally the prospect depends on up-dip fault seal against tight interbedded Devonian sand and shales. The updip fault seal is supported by an AVO shut off.

The structural map for the Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) (Fig. 5.9) shows a gentle dip from the northwest to the southeast with one isolated structure to the northeast of the licence. This structure extends to the north into licence P2315 and defines Silver Shadow, which is a prospect that was identified as part of the licence maturation work.
The Silver Shadow prospect is a combined structural and stratigraphic trap of Upper Jurassic age with a strong AVO anomaly.

Sunray Shadow is a robust structure that can easily be mapped on seismic data. However, while the structure is well defined laterally, the up-dip part of the trap was shown to rely on stratigraphic pinch-out as the structure is subtle, which makes Sunray Shadow likely to be in communication with sands up-dip. 
No indications of hydrocarbons were detected in the AVO analysis, and this was taken as further evidence of trap-seal risk.
Due to the high geological risk, Sunray Shadow was not considered robust enough to be put forward as drilling candidate at this time.

Bunsen East is a four-way dip closed structure located midway between the Bentley and Bressay fields in Block 9/3c.  Closure is at the Upper Dornoch formation (now regarded as Lower Eocene age), with top seal being provided by the Eocene Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.  The closing contour is slightly deeper than Bentley Field at 3,750 ft TVDSS.  It is considered likely that Bunsen East will be charged with oil as the structure lies on the migration route for oil spilling from Bentley into Bressay, however the slightly deeper spill point increases migration risk somewhat.  Oil is likely to be of very similar quality to that found in Bentley and Bressay with an anticipated API of between 10 and 11 degrees.  Bunsen East measures approximately 1.0 km by 0.5 km, with the structural crest estimated at 3,715  ft TVDSS.

The Bunsen, Bunsen West and Bunsen East prospects (the “Bunsen Prospects”) are elongated fourway dip closed structures located midway between the Bentley and Bressay fields in block 9/3c.
Closure is at the Upper Dornoch formation (now regarded of Lower Eocene age), with top seal being provided by the Eocene Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.

The Brunel Prospect is located 2.5km southwest of Bentley and consists of two interconnected four-way dip closed structures.  The crest has been mapped at a depth of -3,590 ft TVDSS and the spill point at -3,690 ft TVDSS.  Closure is at the Dornoch Formation sandstone, with top seal being provided by the Eocene Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.  The main closure covers an area of 2.5km.sq.
This is an extra prospect in their Promote application which is mainly in 9/3b. Parameters taken from the adjacent Bessemer leads.

Lead B (Xcite, 21 Round, Promote) - 4-way dip closure of Dornoch Formation, slightly deeper than 9/3-1 & 9/3-4 heavy oil accumulations. High charge risk - not on obvious fill and spill route from known accumulations. Lies W of main wedge of Dornoch reservoir. Gas cloud above lead.
HIGH RISK. An elongate anticlinal structure. Migration and biodegradation are the main risks. Replaced by a company prospect in Dec 2003. cp9_3_4

The Brindley Prospect is situated 4.5 km southwest of Bentley.  It consists of a number of interconnected small faulted four-way dip closures produced by mounds of Dornoch sand and covers an area of approximately 2.7 km.sq.  Brindley has a crest at 3,606 ft TVDSS, with a spill to the west mapped between 3,642 and 3,658 ft TVDSS.  Closure is at the Dornoch Formation sandstone, with top seal being provided by the Eocene Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.

Bessemer prospect comprises a series of 5 separated four-way dip closures within the Upper Palaeocene, with slightly different spill points, which collectively make up the Base case for the prospect.  Top seal is provided by the Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.  Large upside may exist if a trap can be mapped to the southwest but this is not possible on the current dataset so has not been assumed.   Some uncertainty exists whether the reservoir would be Bressay formation or Dornoch but this has minimal impact on either chance of success or volumetrics as both are excellent reservoir quality with multi-Darcy permeability.  This structure may be on a hydrocarbon migration shadow, similar to the 9/3-3 structure, hence it carries a higher risk than Bunsen.  The possibility of an alternative migration route from the south, coupled with the presence of oil in the Kraken field to the west, mitigates this risk. The Base Case in-place volume is 8 MMbbl.

The Bessemer prospect (subsequently renamed Brindley) was located just to the WSW of the Bentley Oil Field, both within the uppermost Palaeocene, lowermost Eocene Dornoch sandstone reservoir. Bessemer was interpreted to have a chance of success (CoS) of 25% and relatively low in-place volumes (8 MMstb). However, it had the potential for a stratigraphic upside volume (not mapped) in the order of 100 MMstb, but which required additional seismic to investigate.
The Bessemer prospect was mapped as a series of separated four-way dip closures within the Upper Palaeocene, with slightly different spill points, which collectively made up the Base Case for the prospect. Top seal was provided by the Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales. Large upside may exist if a trap could be mapped to the southwest but this was not possible on the dataset at the time of application so was not assumed. This structure may be on a hydrocarbon migration shadow, similar to the dry well 9/3-3 structure, hence it carried a higher risk and lower CoS than the Bunsen prospect to the north in block 9/3c. The possibility of an alternative migration route from the south, coupled with the presence of oil in the Kraken field to the west, mitigated this risk.

The Lybster Field, which received field development status on the 31st August 2010, was reached from the onshore PEDL 158 via extended reach drilling of the Lybster well and five sidetracks from 21st June 2008 to the 23rd January 2011. 
A mixed vintage 2D/3D dataset was amassed over the acreage and ten leads were identified. However, no further wells were drilled within the licence.
There is a potential Volgian fan prospect which could be quite big (~50 mmbbls recoverable). Target at Beatrice level also. No parameters provided; entered cf. Cp11_25_1.

The Forse lead consists of a series of seismic anomalies, interpreted as submarine channels within a larger fan system, that intertwine at different levels underneath the Near Top Volgian horizon.
The play type envisaged for Forse is similar to offset fields such as those in the Brae area (Viking Graben of the North Sea) where Upper Jurassic turbidite fans build out in the hangingwall of the main graben bounding fault. Updip seal is provided by an increasingly heterolithic channel fill as the bounding fault is approached, which results in little or no reservoir quality when compacted.

The Grampian prospect (subsequently renamed Manuel) was targeting stacked Upper and Middle Jurassic sands in block 11/29, approximately 10km west-southwest of the Beatrice Alpha platform.
The Manuel well 11/29-1 was drilled to the west on the prospect in February 2008 targeting stacked reservoirs in the Upper and Middle Jurassic. The well failed to find any significant sand in the Volgian, and Kimmeridgian sand was absent. In the upper Oxfordian, 40 ft of oil-bearing Lower Brora sand was found to be separated from an overlying 90 ft water bearing Upper Brora sand by a 15 ft shale. The MDT pressure tool demonstrated the water sand had good permeability of about 950 mD, whereas the oil-bearing Lower Brora sands was found to be tight.

The Echo Prospect was primarily targeting the Beatrice Formation A and B Sands on an upthrownfault block, 5 km southeast of the Beatrice Field that straddles blocks 11/26c and 11/30a. The western two thirds of the structure lay outside the P1392 licence in block 11/30a, operated at that time by Talisman Energy. The A and B sands have been observed in the adjacent 11/30a-A29 and 12/26-3 wells, with oil shows in the A sand. The structure, mapped on limited 2D seismic data, was a footwall 3-way dip closure against a SW-NE trending fault (Figure 10). The 3-way dip closure of -6,378 ft TVDSS yielded an estimated STOIIP of 4.7 MMstb and corresponding reserves in the range 0.7 to 1.0 MMbbls.
Proposal to appraise 11/30-6 discovery in horst block trap dip closed to NE; A & B reservoir sands absent in 11/30-6, probably due to faulting.

The 11/30-6 discovery was drilled by Mesa in December 1977 on a poorly defined upthrown fault block, 12 km southwest of the Beatrice Alpha platform. The well encountered 11.5 ft of reservoir quality oil bearing sands in the Brora Coal Formation. A well-defined oil-down to (ODT) was observed at a depth of -4,413 ft TVDSS and a water-up to (WUT) at -4,434 ft TVDSS. The gross depth structure is illustrated in Figure 12, which shows a triangular shaped fault block at Top Beatrice Formation that is fault sealed to the west and east and dip closed to the north. The structure straddles blocks 11/30b, 11/29, 17/4a and 17/5a.
The Beatrice Formation A and B sands interval was found to be about half the thickness off that seen in the Beatrice Field with very poor reservoir quality. It was speculated that the thinner and poorer quality interval in 11/30-6 could be the result of a fault intercepted by the well which had faulted out a better reservoir quality section.

The Kappa-Asland Permian Lead has upthrown fault closure to the east, downthrown closure to the north and mainly dip closure to the south and west. The Kappa - Asland Permian Lead requires fault seal along its eastern boundary (the East Deemster Fault). This is because the throw on this fault exceeds the Cumbrian Coast Group top seal thickness (500ft to 600ft thick) - so leaving Collyhurst sandstone juxtaposed against the Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group. Imaging is poor and interpretation difficult along the eastern-most section of the South Deemster Fault which forms the northern closure for the lead. This makes the throw of the fault and the juxtaposed stratigraphy in the footwall uncertain. The main risk is around the efficacy of fault seal along the on the eastern boundary East Deemster Fault. Trap mapping is also a significant risk particularly with respect to characterising the fault and downthrown closure along the South Deemster Fault to the north.

Lower Cretaceous Punt Sandstone stratigraphic trap. Small 4-way dip closure with structural crest at 1000m. Biodegradation is a critical risk.

The Punt Channel is a relatively small four way dip closure with stratigraphic upside in the Punt Sandstone member, and a structural crest at 1000m. Upper Jurassic Claymore Sandstone stratigraphic trap based on intra-KCF amplitudes. No company volumetrics. Company CoS = 10%.

Girraween lead - large dip-closed elongate dome - transpressional fold on the corner of the Smith Bank High; the boundary fault of the High is a major strike-slip fault. Volgian sands proved locally are highly likely in closure, with intraformational seals. 
Potential for additional closure in the Upper Jurassic sequence, reliant on the fault for side seal - high risk as the footwall comprises Devonian & Triassic fractured sequences. 
Main risk is late Tertiary structure deformation cracking the trap, without replacement of oil from Devonian and/or early Jurassic source rocks. CoS = 34% (reservoir effectiveness reduced 100>50%; seal reduced 100>50%).

Volgian lead in fault bounded anticlinal trap, with J66 (Early) and J73/74 (Mid) sands expected to be present from nearby well info. Reservoir quality is main risk. CoS = 10% (downgraded due to high play risk). Duplicate of larger, better defined prospect cp12_17_1; not recommended for YtF.

Ridgewood is interpreted as a four way dip fault related roll over structure with the maximum closure, at Volgian level in Upper Jurassic, measured as 1236 acres.  The Volgian sandstone was deposited as turbidites from a provenance area to the north and potential reservoir sand is related to strong amplitudes.  
The prospect has a bounding fault dipping to the south-west and a vertical well was designed to cross this fault at a depth of 2046 MD BRT (-1896ft TVDss).
Unnamed Middle Jurassic lead in fault-bounded trap (below stacked Ryazanian channel target). Parameters entered cf. cp12_16_1.

Middle Jurassic fault block. Note that SE fault coincides with limit of 3D seismic (must be based on 2D). Updip seal provided by two faults, dip closure to south. Top seal provided by Heather Fm mudstones. Critical uncertainties with respect to top seal integrity related to mapping of faults.

Eugenie is a tilted fault block lead at Beatrice Formation level mapped on the 1986 Western Geco data, owing to poor signal to noise ratio on the First Oil data set at this depth. Updip seal is formed by two faults which in most places do not appear to go to surface. The lead is dip closed to the south. Top seal is provided by Heather Formation mudstones. The critical uncertainties with this lead are associated with the mapping of faults and top seal integrity, related to faults. The chance of success was set at 27%, but recoverable volumes are relatively low (P90/ P50/ P10: 4/ 9/ 20mmbbls).

Libra South lead - 4-way dip closure along E-W Punt channel; closure developed over N-S L Cretaceous structural nose, with stratigraphic component in pinchout at channel margins. Strong evidence of compactional drape over sand body. Area increased 1000>1177 acres to match Arc polygon. Trap presence reduced 60>25% due to poor seismic coverage over lead.

Libra East lead - flank closure (adjacent to 12/18 high) interpreted as containing attractive wedge of Punt Sandstone. Heavy biodegraded oil possible due to shallow depth of target. Reservoir effectiveness reduced 100>50%. Area increased 2000 > 2975 acres to match Arc polygon

Libra lead - Volgian pinchout trap on S flank of 12/18 high, with well defined strike closure. Several reservoir levels possible down dip from sand-free section in 12/18-1. Up dip seal risk - Volgian silty in well.

Dunaverty lead - Pinch out trap within J60 sequence downdip and towards basin axis of 12/18-1 (oil shows in tight sandstones within valid dip/fault closed trap, interpreted to be in lower part of J60 sequence). Presence of trap is main risk. CoS = 12% (downgraded by high play risk). Duplicate of prospect cp12_18_4; not recommended for YtF.

MJB1 - large stratigraphic prospect on N edge of Smith Bank High; Beatrice sands target, predicted to pinch out laterally into deepwater shales. Associated with acoustic anomaly. Source/migration are key risks - Middle Devonian lacustrine shales may be most likely source. CoS = 22% (trap presence reduced 80>50%; reservoir presence reduced 100>50%).

A single large stratigraphic prospect (MJB1) has been identified in the Middle Jurassic Beatrice Formation on the northerly edge of the Smith Bank High. The prospect is predicted to have Beatrice Formation sands as the reservoir. These sands are predicted to laterally pinch out by facies change into deeper water shales. The prospect has been identified as an acoustic impedance anomaly on several lines. Company CoS = 11%.

A single large stratigraphic prospect MJB1 (subsequently renamed Sunset Prospect) was identified for the 26th Round in the Middle Jurassic Beatrice Formation on the northern edge of the Smith Bank High. The prospect was identified on 2D seismic data with the sands predicted to laterally pinch out by facies change into deeper water Heather Formation shales. The prospect has been identified as an acoustic impedance anomaly on several lines. Reservoirs, seals and source rocks were assumed to be the same as those found at the Beatrice Field. The nature of trapping however is significantly different with the Sunset Prospect interpreted to be a stratigraphic trap created by a change from typical Beatrice shallow-marine sandstone facies into deeper water Heather Formation shales.

The prospect is contained within the Zechstein aged Bosies Bank Formation and located on the eastern flank of the Smith Bank High. The reservoir is predicted to consists of fluvial sands capped by 300ft+ of shales in the upper portion of the Bosies Bank Formation. The prospect has been identified using reprocessed 3D seismic data in the frequency domain. Trapping is provided by antithetic faults which are rooted in a listric fault developing on the Smith Bank High.

The Bravo prospect is a combined structural stratigraphic trap. The change from clatic rich sediments in the Bosies Bank Formation southwards into anhydrites of the Turbot Anhydrite Formation sets up the potential for a large stratigraphic trap

The acoustic impedance values for sands and shales are very similar at the depth of the prospect and so cannot be discriminated on the available seismic data, making prospect definition a challenge.

The prospect is located due south of the Neo gas discovery, 12/27-1. The trap is mapped at Beatrice Fm. level as a simple tilted fault block with a single main NE-SW oriented normal fault combined with 3-way dip closure. Well 12/27-1 encountered reservoir quality Triassic reservoir c. 300ft deeper to the Beatrice Fm. and this unit represents a stacked secondary target. Subject to communication, the Triassic reservoir might have a shared GWC with the Beatrice Fm. target or an independent contact. In the upside case, it is also possible that the Neo discovery area and Trinity prospect may form a single feature. Company CoS = 21%.

The Sati lead is located SE to the Neo/Trinty prospect area. The lead is set up by a faulted embayment on the northern edge of the Buckie Ridge, in an area where Late Jurassic Burns Sandstone Member reservoir is mapped to extend and pinchout into the embayment. The mapping at this stage is immature. The trap requires downthrown fault seal on two sides as well as stratigraphic pinchout requiring effective bottom and side seals. Top seal is provided by KCF shales. The down dip well 12/27-2 proves the presence of reservoir but quality is sub-optimal at this location and reservoir quality in a distal location at the pinchout represents a key risk as well as trap integrity. The lead is mapped at c. 3000 ft TVDSS placing some uncertainty on oil quality due to risk of biodegradation. Company CoS = 7%.

Punt lead - small dip-closed compartment in E-W trending Punt channel system crossing 12/28 - probably formed by compaction over high net:gross sand unit. Petrcanada consider this best lead in block. All parameters, Cos (8%) provided - seal risk 20>35 (20 seems pessimistic)

L. Cretaceous, Punt Sandstone Member Lead
A Punt channel system traverses the block, orientated broadly east-west. Within this channel system a small dip-closed compartment can be identified that is likely formed from compaction related relief due to the high net:gross sand content of the channel fill. 
Additional upside reserves could be generated if a hanging wall fault seal could be effected by the small NW-SE orientated normal fault that transects the channel, (Figure 6). There is very likely to be sand-on-sand contact across this fault which introduces a high risk on the cross-fault seal integrity.

The Windsor prospect is located on top of the Halibut Horst and is defined as a heavy oil Lower Cretaceous reservoir sweetspot trap that has potential for lateral tar mat and/or stratigraphic trapping based on a minimum reservoir thickness cutoff (8 m net). 8 m of oil stained Lower Cretaceous reservoir potential was confirmed on the Halibut horst top by the 13/24a-2A well (1981), At a large scale the Halibut Horst can be defined as a large four-way closure at Base Chalk level. The Windsor prospect is seismically defined within this large scale four way closure through the detailed mapping of the Top Chalk. Laterally the Windsor sweetspot is interpreted to seal through a combination of; 1. lateral facies change within the Lower Cretaceous interval to a non reservoir facies forming a lateral stratigraphic trap (the resolution of the current seismic does not allow us to definitely define this boundary), and/or 2. lateral heavy oil 'tar mat' trapping in a poor quality, thin Lower Cretaceous interval (again the resolution of the current seismic does not allow us to definitely define this boundary).

The acreage contains the Fat Cat prospect which was drilled by Amoco in 1981, (13/24a-2A). The well encountered a potentially prospective interval between the Cretaceous Chalk Group and Basement section containing drilled oil shows. Evaluation of the limited dataset available led to the interpretation that this interval was oil bearing. Consequently, the work programme was directed towards reducing technical and commercial risk on the interpreted discovery that might have concluded with the justification to drill an appraisal well. 
This objective was addressed in part through the acquisition of new high resolution 2D seismic data, in order to map the internal architecture of the Base Chalk to Top Basement interval in more detail.

The prognosed reservoir was deposited in a confined channel system which can be mapped with confidence on good quality 3D seismic. However, given the shallow depth of the prospect and the thick, highly porous sand within the prospect, an amplitude versus offset anomaly would be expected if the prospect is gas-charged. The prospect is therefore considered to be high-risk for gas, and specific work programme is proposed to assess this risk. Alternatively, the prospect could be oil-charged, as well 13/26b-2 also discovered oil at three intervals on the adjacent fault block, downdip of Boonie. Company CoS = 13%.

The Walmer prospect is located on top of the Halibut Horst, and is defined as a heavy oil Lower Cretaceous reservoir sweetspot trap that has potential for lateral tar mat and/or stratigraphic trapping based on a minimum reservoir thickness cutoff (8 m net). The prospect is defined by detailed seismic mapping of the Top Chalk, Base Chalk and Top Granite/Base Mesozoic seismic horizons over the Halibut Horst. 8 m of oil stained Lower Cretaceous reservoir potential was confirmed on the Halibut horst top by the 13/24a-2A well,

Casquets is interpreted as a channel with sand fill, stratigraphically trapped with lateral and up-dip pinch out of the reservoir. Seal is again provided by surrounding mudstones. A 'top channel' and 'base channel' pick can be made defining the gross geometry of the feature. Seal is again provided by surrounding mudstones.

Coquet Lead, which sits within the Palaeocene, is interpreted as a low relief structural four way dip closure of an east-west channel with sand fill. Stratigraphic upside exists with lateral and up-dip pinch out of the reservoir. There is no seismic amplitude anomaly associated with Coquet, rather it is defined by an apparent zone of differential compaction between a 'top channel' and 'base channel' pick beneath the volcanic section and above the Top (Upper) Cretaceous. Seal is provided by surrounding mudstones. Similar features are productive in the North Sea (e.g. the West
Brae oil field).

The Wolf lead is seismically defined as an onlapping package interpreted as stratigraphically trapped deep water mass-flow sandstone (turbidite) enclosed within Upper Cretaceous mudstones. Upper Cretaceous Cenomanian sands are proven in the up-dip 132/15-1 well. This is an untested play in the Rockall Basin, however Cretaceous reservoirs are proven elsewhere along the Atlantic margin (Faroe-Shetland and Voring Basins, along with multiple locations in West Africa). Wolf is represented by a'soft' peak or positive amplitude which equates to a decrease in acoustic impedance, however the limitations of the available 3D data did not allow for offset gather analysis and an AVO classification could not be attributed to the anomaly, as such this has not allowed it to be fully assessed.
Eocene basin floor fan above volcanics, identified by amplitude anomaly. No parameters provided. Company in-place volumetrics: 95 - 192 - 303 GIIP assuming dry gas.

Pendeen is along strike from Godrevy at the same stratigraphic level and is represented by an anomaly of identical seismic character. However, the limitations of the available 3D data did not allow for offset gather analysis and an AVO classification could not be attributed to the anomaly, and as such the anomaly could not be fully assessed.

The Godrevy lead, is interpreted as a turbidite fan sand, consists of an amplitude anomaly with stratigraphic pinch-out laterally and up-dip, with seal provided by surrounding mudstones. The amplitude anomaly is a bright peak or positive amplitude which equates to a decrease in acoustic impedance. Down-dip of the 'bright' the seismic character varies somewhat in comparison to the surrounding units. An analogue was drawn with the Tormore oil and gas field with the bright amplitude representing a gas cap and the mapped down-dip portion potentially being oil-filled. Such bright low impedance anomalies may be typical of gas-filled sands. However, the limitations of the available 3D data did not allow for offset gather analysis and an AVO classification could not be attributed to the anomaly, and as such the anomaly could not be fully assessed.

Homer is a structural/ stratigraphic lead developed against the SW bounding fault of the Jura Basin. The Homer lead is based on the development of thin but reservoir quality sands, age equivalent to the main Scapa field reservoir (Scapa SD), down-dip in well 14/12-2 (8,433-8,518 ft TVDSS). This section and the underlying Lower Cretaceous are interpreted to thicken into the southern Jura Basin bounding fault. The same appealing seismic geometries are observed at Homer that appears to be similar to the geometries that contain the Scapa debris fans in the Scapa field area. There are no secondary targets associated with the Homer lead. The lead is highly immature as only 2D seismic is available for its definition. 3D seismic is required in order to mature the lead to prospect status.  Estimated Tecgnical Chance of Success: 11%.   Source: 60%.   Migration: 95%.   Reservoir: 80%.   Trap: 80%.   Seal: 30%

The Olive lead (Figure 19) was generated from an observed increase in thickness of the Lower Cretaceous section in the north-western end of the Jura Basin, up-dip from the Homer lead. This thickened interval is broadly correlated with two thin sandstones penetrated in the down-dip well, 14/12-2. The play is based on the premise that these sands, believed to be Aptian aged Captain sands, (or possibly slightly older Coracle sands), thicken up-dip towards the basin margin. To the west of the margin no sands are seen within the equivalent section in well 14/11-1. The crest of the Olive structure lies at approximately 6,500 ft TVDSS against the Jura Basin bounding fault and the lead is contained wholly within block 14/11.  The available 2D seismic data is of quite poor quality at the reservoir level.  Estimated Technical Chance of Success: 4%.   Source: 60%.   Migration: 70%.   Reservoir: 50%.   Trap: 70%.   Seal: 30%

cross-fault seal against potentially sand-bearing strata of Jurassic age within the foot-wall. 
As such it is considered to be very high risk.

The Caedwalla Lead s the turbidite fill to a feeder canyon, which supplies turbidite sands to the submarine fans seen within the Jura Basin to the north. The canyon is a fault-controlled feature, which is cut into already largely compacted sediments. As a result, the prospect does not have a positive topography, but forms a stratigraphic pinchout within an erosive low. The reservoir presence is inferred from seismic response and a corresponding thick sand package within the receiving basin. The prognosed sands are probably laterally equivalent to the surrounding shales or marls.

Lobate Lead - mounded lobate feature on terrace forming western part of 14/18-7 high. Main risk is seal to separate it from U Scapa sands. CoS = 20%. Net thickness (and GRV) reduced 300/250/100 to 230/110/60 ft so that deterministic reserves approx operator estimate. GRV increased 33600/16230/4950 > 67620/28567/12600 acre feet to match area/net reservoir data.

Leith lead - large 4-way dip closure (closure to S betond limit of interpreted 3D data) at top Chalk - potential for onlap trap for Muareen Sands, 4-way dip closure of Andrew Sands. 14/19-11 & 14/18-5 drilled on flank of structure (below mapped spill point) encountered additional reservoirs in Jurassic & Devonian. Principal risk is hydrocarbon source/migration. CoS = 22% (downgraded by play risk; reservoir effectiveness reduced 100>75%; migration reduced 50>25%). Lies above Permian prospect cp14_18_11. Net reservoir reduced 116>35 m so that deterministic reserves approx. operator estimate.

Halibut East - lower, relatively small of 2 targets defined on base Cretaceous map. Well defined, fault-bounded trap. CoS = 20%. Trap presence reduced 75>50%; source effectiveness reduced 50>25%. RF amended to match reserves data.
