Lower Cretaceous A lead - feeder canyon in 14/23S for L Cretaceous depocentre to SE in Halibut-Renee Trough; Kopervik Sandstone target not imaged clearly on seismic data, and currently unclear whether trap in 14/23 might be isolated from main depocentre. Trap integrity, seal and migration are all significant risks. P10 only parameters provided; other parameters entered cf. cp14_23_1. CoS = 4% (downgraded by high play risk).
Application to develop 14/24-1 discovery (Skye) in  Promote Application (Midmar, 21 Round) - simple upthrown fault closure. Digitized blob is 4658 acres.

Prospect A - 4-way dip top Paleocene closure with 14/24a-4 on closing contour. Similar closure tested by 14/24-1 (14 ft heavy oil at top of thick Paleocene sand. All parameters, reserves, net CoS (23%) provided; closure to S poorly constrained.

Lead B - large 4-way dip top Paleocene structure (but closure to S, if any, lies outside limit of 2D data interpreted - very high trap risk. All parameters, reserves, net CoS (20%) provided. No closure to S indicated on prospect map; not recommended for YtF.

Macdonald Prospect - hanging wall trap adjacent to basin boundary fault (high seal risk) with Piper Sandstone target. GRV but no other  parameters, reserves, CoS provided; entered cf. Petronella. Reserves, CoS (18%) provided in PetroCanada Fallow Sept 06 CD.
Scapa lead - Scapa Sandstone pinchout trap, constrained by 14/25a-3 (dry).

The Scapa Lead is a structural-stratigraphic trap located between wells 14/25a-3 and 14/25a-6A. 
The objective reservoir is of Lower Cretaceous age comprising intercalated sandstones. The lower Scapa sand interval shows significantly better reservoir properties than the overlying interval. Cementation is the main control over reservoir quality. Good quality Lower Cretaceous sands in the lower Scapa sequence were encountered in the 14/25a-3 well although they were water-bearing.
The sands are interpreted to pinch out up-dip to the west and are not present in the 14/25a-6A well, where the Scapa interval represented a secondary target to the primary Jurassic Piper objective.

Finn lead - step terrace between Rob Roy/Ivanhoe area and East Halibut Spur with Carboniferous (Namurian) target cf. 15/21b-41 and oil sands in 15/21a-7 (700 bopd). Juxtaposed against tight Devonian strata of Halibut Horst. Possible Piper/Sgiath sands may occur as target instead cf 15/21-5. CoS 11%; downgraded by play risk.
CB1 Lead. Tay Sst (ORS) Lead updip of 15/21b-45.

Finn Shallow lead pinchout trap of Beauly Sands against delta front to W & dip closure to E. Beauly oil leg (21 ft) in 15/21b-45; mapped spill point updip from well (depth conversion problem/local stratigraphic variation). 
CoS 25%; downgraded by play risk, likely seal risk.

The Beauly Formation accumulation discovered by Well 15/21b-45 is interpreted as likely to extend onto Block 14/25. Petro-Canadas previous mapping has been compared with a new interpretation by Stavanger Petroleum and this has highlighted prospectivity that requires further technical evaluation to determine confidence levels of chance of success (COS) and potential resources. The Beauly sand is present in all wells drilled to the west on the Halibut Horst as well as on the northern and southern flanks of the Horst.  The map on the Top Beauly Sand shows that the  Discovery cannot be closed to the west at the Block 15/21e border, but extends further west into Block 14/25.  All well drilled on either side of the Halibut Horst have found thick Beauly sands, most with hydrocarbon shows or columns.  No well has been drilled on the continuation of the Finn Fan discovery up structure on the Halibut Horst.

The Perth West prospect is a potential extension of the Perth Field into Block 14/25. This extension of the field contains 13% of the field GRV as currently mapped, but it may be partially isolated from the field by a SW to NE fault mapped at Rattray level.

The Scapa Lead is a stratigraphic trap, formed by a hanging wall fan in the North Halibut Trough. The trap geometry is subtle, and is identified by a thickening of the BCU to SA interval and a structural nose at SA (Valanginian) sandstone level, (just west of 14/25a-6a).

J1 lead - Ettrick Sandstone target cf. thick section encouneterd in 14/26-2 in fault-bounded container - hanging wall on N, E sides; high seal risk. No parameters, reserves, parameters provided; entered cf. 14_27_2.

The Sheaf lead lies in the north-west part of block 14/26b and lies in the hanging wall immediately south off the main bounding fault of the Halibut Horst. It also lies downthrown to the ?bald? well 14/26-4, which encountered neither Cretaceous nor Jurassic Sandstones. It is upthrown to the 14/26-3 well.  Lying immediately downthrown of the Halibut Horst, the lead is also downthrown of the unsuccessful number 4 well. However, Ardent Oil believes it is possible that reservoirs may exist in Punt fan sandstones, possibly Jurassic Sandstones, and also within granite wash sediments within the overall envelope of structural closure.
Punt Sandstone target that may or may not connect to Golden Eagle - planned well will also drill Kopervik, Ettrick & Buzzard targets - all proved to be water wet.

Upper Jurassic wedge downfaulted to the south of the Halibut Horst, combined structural and stratigraphic trapping. Additional potential in overlying Lower Cretaceous wedge (not quntified). Culzean is a potential thick Upper Jurassic combined structural (down-thrown 3-way dip) / stratigraphic (lateral seal towards the 14/26b-4 well where the Upper Jurassic is absent) trap in the graben immediately adjacent to the main Halibut Horst southern bounding fault.

At the time of licence application it was inferred that a sealing Kimmeridge Clay Formation (KCF) shale would be present between the Upper Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous segments, not visible due to the lack of seismic resolution. A Lower Cretaceous prospect segment was defined between the BCU horizon and the Base Chalk horizon (Figure 5.8). The Lower Cretaceous segment was defined as a secondary, downthrown, three-way dip closure located up-dip of well 14/26b-4.
Subsequent mapping on the new ST15M03_ Q14_PSTM 3D seismic survey with a seismic well tie to well 14/28a-5z on the EC04Q14_3D seismic survey, located to the east of Pevensey in a more basinal setting, resulted in identification of a potential Upper Jurassic Burns Sandstone (top reservoir) reflector which could be mapped into the Pevensey prospect.
Untested embayment setting analogous to Blake Field

K3 prospect - Punt/Coracle Sandstone targets in narrow fault terrace, dip closed to SE; in contact with Jurassic shales, basement across N boundary fault. Principal risks are migration, trap validity, seal to N. All parameters, reserves, CoS (14.7%) provided; trap reduced 70 > 50%; seal reduced 60 > 25%; res effectiveness 100 > 90%. Gas & oil cases provided; oil entered.

Four-way dip closure with Upper Jurassic Burns Sandstone reservoir. Bungo is considered to have stratigraphic upside potential based on the J73 to BCU isochron. This requires further work. As currently mapped, it is a lookalike to the BlackJack Prospect which has been tested by the partnership in April 2014. The BlackJack well is still under evaluation. Reservoir is risked at 50% due to initial results from the BlackJack well which indicate that the Burns Sandstone local depositional model needs to be modified. Trap and containment are both risked at 60% due to the relatively shallow structure, the uncertainty associated with depth conversion and the potential for Punt channels to erode the topseal.
Proposal to appraise Scapa Sands component of 14/26b-5 Thunderball discovery.

Bumblebee lead (ExxonMobil) = Octopus lead (Amerada Hess & BG) - Lower Cretaceous stratigraphic trap. No description, parameters, reserves, risking on fallow CD. Limited/no sandstone in adjacent wells. Parameters entered cf. cp14_30_1.

Zante Prospect is a combined structural / stratigraphic trap. The primary reservoir targets are Zechstein marine carbonates, equivalent to the Jarvis Field reservoir, approximately 15 km to the southeast in the Ettrick Sub-Basin. Charging into the Zechstein from the younger source rocks is one of the critical risk factors for this play, especially when thick Triassic sequences are present, forming a lateral barrier between mature source rocks and reservoir.

Zante is a combination trap in which Permian Zechstein carbonates terminate up-dip against the Halibut Horst to the north. 
It is located approximately 12km north-east of the Golden Eagle field, in blocks 14/27a and 20/02b. 
Water depth is 400ft. Depth to crest of prospect is 7000ft TVDss and depth to contact is 7400-9800ft TVDss.

Mermaid is a faulted 4-way dip closed structure on a well-defined terrace, which Ardent also believes was visible on a recent viewing of modern TGS 3D data. The Lower Cretaceous Sandstone objectives remain unproven in block 14/27 to date, although the only drilling here has occurred in the south. Postulating the presence of Punt Sandstones in hanging wall settings seems reasonable in the north, but for the Mermaid prospect, in the centre of the block and in a footwall setting, Jurassic targets are considered more likely.

K2 prospect - Punt/Coracle Sandstone targets in small faulted 4-way dip trap. Principal risks are reservoir presence on high, migration, trap closure to NW.  All parameters, reserves, CoS (22.7%) provided; trap reduced 60 > 50%; reservoir presence reduced 70 > 50%; res effectiveness 100 > 90%; seal 90>50%. Gas & oil cases provided; oil entered.
J1 prospect - downfaulted terrace immediately updip of small Thunderball discovery. Parameters, net CoS (20%) but no details of prospect provided. Risking entered cf. cp14_27_5..

Touque is a 4-way Upper Jurassic prospect which lies 18km north-east of the Golden Eagle field and was evaluated as a potential tie-back opportunity. 
The crest of the structure and most of the volume down to the P50 HWC is located in block 14/27a, in licence P2155, whilst the upside of the prospect and much of the volume below the P50 HWC extends into block 14/27b to the north, outside of the licence. 
Water depth is 340ft, depth of crest is 4100ft TVDss and depth of spill point is approximately 4350ft in the P50 case.

Formerly known as Colonsay Deep, the Penny Prospect is a large faulted 4 way closure at the BCU level. Downdip parts of the structure have been drilled previously by the 15/11-1,2 & 3 wells. All 3 wells had excellent quality Piper sandstone reservoir and the structurally shallowest well, 15/11-3, had significant residual oil shows. Company CoS = 29%.

The Dyer structure represents the highest culmination point of the local overall structure tested by the 15/11-1, 15/11-2 and 15/11-3 wells. It is dip closed to the north, east and south and fault bound to the west. The target reservoir is the Piper Formation shallow marine sands with top seal being provided by the overlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation and carbonates of the Upper Cretaceous Chalk Group.

Penny prospect is an up thrown Piper fault block in the footwall of the bounding fault to Fynn (cp15_16_18). This fault block appears to have been tested by 3 wells all of which encountered water bearing Piper Formation. However, the first well (drilled with 2D seismic) missed the main part of the structure, and seems to be situated in a slump zone. Well 15/11-2 was situated too far down-dip. The new 3D seismic data indicates that well 15/11-3 was drilled in a separate compartment of the structure, The principal risk on Penny (Jurassic) is top seal effectiveness (top seal breach) along the major bounding fault.

Prospect B is the Base Cretaceous structure already drilled by 15/11-1, -2 and -3. There is an area of closure updip from 15/11-3 (dry) that could still be worth testing as a secondary objective to a shallower target. CoS =  0.18 (downgraded as based on 1 line only). Duplicate of cp15_11_7; not recommended for YtF.

Cortez Lead is potential missed pay associated with 15/11-3 well. Cortez is bounded to S by a normal fault. To the N, E and W, there is mainly dip closure. Closure on Base Cretaceous above the well (i.e. to 6100 ft tvdss) if the well has residual saturations; if oil bearing then the lowest closing contour could be as deep as 6300 ft tvdss. Key risk is potential fault breach at the crest where Piper Sst may be juxtaposed against permeable Tertiary sands. The oil in 15/11-3 suggests any breach must have occurred post-oil emplacement. CoS = 25% (trap presence reduced 50>25%).

Deep Colonsay prospect - Piper Formation target in 4-way dip trap. Piper (KCF absent over crest). Missing parameters entered cf. cp15_11_7. CoS = 23% (trap presence reduced 50>25%). 
Duplicate of cp15_11_7: not recommended for YtF.

The only prospectivity recognised by Talisman at the time of application for Block 15/11a was a four-way dip closure reservoired in Upper Jurassic Piper sandstones, informally known as Deep Colonsay.

CoS = 0.25 (downgraded due to probable heavy oil).

Lead D is a broad structurally high area at Base Cretaceous level. U Jurassic lead - related to thickening of U Jurassic section into North Piper Basin; chaotic seismic facies tentatively correlated with J71 Galley Sands. No CoS provided. Net reservoir reduced 236.2/164/105 > 190/131/84 feet to allow calculated reserves to approx opeartor estimate.

The prospect is a downthrown trap in the Lower Cretaceous Valhall Fm.  Dependent on CSEM data. No L Cretaceous sand in adjacent 15/11b-5. Parameters entered cf. cp15_24_17.

The Roger prospect is targeting the Palaeocene Upper Balmoral and Andrew sands in a 4-way dip closure on the distal part of the southern arm of the east-west trending channel axis. The prospect straddles the 15/10 and 15/15 blocks as well as partially extending outside the P1771 licence into 16/11. Roger was identified on 2D seismic and a strike line from the WG822D001 2D seismic data set across the structure can be seen in Fig. 5.18. 
The key risks are charge and reservoir, with the Balmoral member being absent in down-dip wells 16/11a-2, 16/11a-4 and 16/11a-5.
The 15/15 lead is mapped at 1.71/5.21/30.1 mmbo.

The Denslow Prospect consists of a downthrown truncation trap associated with the hanging wall side of the main Witch Ground Graben bounding fault. Top reservoir is defined by the Base Creatceous Unconformity with dip closure to the south and west and either a pinchout of sands or downthrown faulted closure to the north and east. The target reservoir is the Upper Jurassic Claymore Sandstone Member turbidite sands with top seal being provided by the encasing Kimmeridge. Containment and closure are the dominant risks.

Ranger Main is a drill ready AVO based prospect from the Balmoral Sandstone Member. The prospect was initially identified using far offset reflectivity volumes but was later verified using simultaneous impedance inversion techniques calibrated to wells. The anomaly is on an established Balmoral fairway and is up-dip of similar impedance anomalies that correspond to discoveries in 15/12-1, 15/18b-11 and 15/18a-12.
Ranger Main is contained within a structural closure and the AVO response conforms to structure. Upside potential in overlapping stratigraphic traps Ranger East (cp15_16_20), South (cp15_16_21), and Southeast (cp15_16_22). Combined STOIIP for all Ranger prospects is 314mmbo.

Amity is a drill ready 4-way dip closed prospect stratigraphically above the Ranger prospect. Amity contains a DHI in the form of a clear flat spot that is coincident with the lowest closing contour of the structure, is consistent at all azimuths through the prospect, is the expected hard kick response and is analogous to the flat spot seen at Macculloch. The reservoir is considered to be the Upper Forties Sandstone Member. Sitting above Amity are a number of Eocene amplitude anomalies that are considered to be heavy oil deposits. Amity would be fully evaluated with the firm well commitment to drill the Ranger prospect.

Roberts is an Andrew sandstone amplitude reflectivity and CI (Colour Inverted) anomaly identified within an onlapping sandstone. The trap geometry for the prospect is dip closure to the east, west and south; therefore providing a 3-way dip closure. To the north the sandstone either pinches out or is sealed by a small fault that has formed in response to the topography produced by the underlying regional graben bounding fault. Reservoir presence can be correlated to the 15/16b-18 and 15/16b-21 wells where the Andrew Formation is evident. The overlying seal is the Balmoral Tuff Member and its associated shales. Hydrocarbon source is the underlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation, and charge into Roberts is likely up the bounding graben fault or vertically through fracture networks. Roberts COS is determined to be 24%.

Kidd is an Andrew sandstone amplitude reflectivity and CI anomaly identified within a play fairway orientated approximately N-S on the western edge of the block. The strength of the CI anomaly is greater than that encountered at Roberts, perhaps indicating increased likelihood of hydrocarbons or increased porosity. The prospect?s trap is a combination of dip and stratigraphic closure. To the east there is clear dip closure, while to the west a trap is provided by pinch-out or possibly fault seal. To the north and south the trap is more ambiguous and while some structure exists to provide dip closure, a stratigraphic component is also thought to be evident. The overlying seal is the Balmoral Tuff Member and associated shales. Hydrocarbon source is the underlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation, and charge into Kidd is likely laterally along the regional Andrew fairway. Kidd?s COS is determined to be 24%.

Ward is an Andrew sandstone amplitude reflectivity and CI anomaly identified within the same play fairway as Kidd. The prospect?s trap is a combination of dip and stratigraphic closure in the same configuration as Kidd. However, the stratigraphic trapping element of this prospect makes it slightly more risky than Kidd. The overlying seal is the Balmoral Tuff Member and its associated shales. Hydrocarbon source is the underlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation, and charge into Ward is likely laterally along the regional Andrew fairway. Ward?s COS is determined to be 22%.

Trap is a combination of dip closure and either pinch-out or fault seal to the north. Hydrocarbons are likely sourced vertically up the regional graben bounding faults.

NW Hoy prospect.  3-way dip closure against the southern bounding fault of Piper Terrace III. It is updip of wells 15/16-18 and 21 which found shows in the Upper Jurassic. Piper/Sgiath sands of similar reservoir quality to Lowlander are expected. The key risk at NW Hoy is fault seal. CoS = 30%.

The Birnam prospect (formerly known as North West Hoy) is located in the north of block 15/16e and comprises one or more fault terraces downthrown from the Piper Field to the northeast. Primary reservoir targets are Piper and Scott sands with possible secondary targets the Paleocene and Claymore/Galley sands. The Claymore interval was oil-bearing in 15/16-18Y but absent in 15/16-21. The Claymore oil is probably stratigraphically-trapped. Only the primary targets are included in hydrocarbon volume estimates. 15/16b-18Y and 15/16b-21 wells encountered moderate quality down-dip water-bearing Piper and Scott Sandstone. The trap is entirely dependent on across fault seal, but potential exists for an oil column in the Piper/Scott up-dip of the two wells.  The geological chance of success is estimated at 0.3. The main risk is on across-fault seal, reservoir extent (reservoir may be missing in the upper terrace) and access to migrated hydrocarbons (trap risk:1.0, seal risk: 0.5, reservoir risk 0.7, source risk: 1.0, timing and migration risk: 0.8). Reservoir quality is proven in the down dip wells. See Appendix B for details. Prospect parameters listed are for entire prospect: 27.7 MSTBO lies inside block 15/16e, reminder lies outside block to the west.

The most likely interpretation is that the well was drilled outside the structural closure at top Piper.

This structure is complicated by its location on a zone of fault transfer that runs from NE to SW through the 15/17-24z well location

Taransay lies 2km N of Saltire. It is a dip and fault bounded structure at Galley level. There is dip closure to the E and upthrown fault closure to the N,S & W. The primary reservoir targets are the Galley and Piper sands which are present in down-dip 15/17-20, drilled in 1988and encountered a gross interval of 78ft Galley sands at 9,677ft and 131ft gross Piper sands. N:G was 0.87 and 0.84 respectively. The sands were water bearing. The 15/7-19 well drilled to the west in an adjacent fault block also encountered water bearing Galley and Piper sands. With two nearby dry holes, hydrocarbon charge is considered a major risk in Taransay as the prospect may lie in a migration shadow. Parameters cf cp15_17_5.

At Galley level Tiree has dip closure to the S and upthrown fault closure to the N, W and E. Like cp15_17_12 the main reservoir targets are the Galley and Piper sands. The 15/17-19 well, drilled on an adjacent fault block to the W encountered 155ft gross Galley sands at 9,022ft TVDSS and 233ft gross Piper sands. N:G was 0.81 and 0.91 respectively. Both sands were water bearing. Hydrocarbon migration is considered the key risk due to the nearby dry wells. Furthermore the Galley is eroded towards the crest of the structure where it is directly overlain by the Valhall, thus vertical seal may be an issue. Parameters cf cp15_17_5.

Ailsa prospect lies approximately 2 km S of Iona Field. It comprises a  complex cut and fill channelised mounded feature within the Forties turbidite sandstone. Maria discovery in adjacent 15/18a is considered a good analogue. On seismic there are indications of
brightening due to gas above the prospect and shallow gas features at Frigg level. The top Forties surface indicates that Ailsa comprises two lobes, fed from a channel feature to the NW. These sandstone mounds occur at the shelf edge margin with top seal interpreted as the pro-delta mud prone toe-sets. Given that the top Forties sand has shallow burial depths (~5,000ft) sand quality is expected to be excellent. The north lobe carries additional risk due to the presence of a fault which intersects the top seal. A loss of high amplitudes is also recognised over the north lobe which, when combined with the brightening effects above, suggests that the seal may have been breached. The high amplitudes are preserved over the southern lobe. Parameters entered cf cp15_17_7.

On seismic data, the Scroo Sandstone has a mounded facies interpreted as compactional drape over a sand-filled depression. The primary Dirk Sandstone target has a gross thickness of 113ft. description: Bowmore is an elongate fault and dip-closed gas-condensate discovery mapped at Base Cretaceous level with a crest at approximately 13,800ftTVDSS, bounded to the N by a fault and to the S and SW by dip-closure. Bowmore is proven by the 15/24a-4 and 15/24a-9 wells. An easterly thinning of the Upper Jurassic across the structure results in pinch-out of Upper Jurassic Claymore and Galley turbidite sandstones onto the underlying tilted fault block, thereby providing a combination stratigraphic-structural trap, overlying deeper shoreface Piper Sandstone. Wireline log analysis confirmed all three sandstones as hydrocarbon-bearing.  The Galley Sandstone was thinly-developed in 15/24a-4 but thickens markedly down-dip in 15/24a-9. Core data indicates modest but effective reservoir quality. Logs and RFT data in 15/24a-9 confirmed a hydrocarbon contact at 14,342ftTVDSS. Mean recoverable reserves for the Galley Sandstone are calculated at 11.7mmbbls condensate and 41.4bcf gas.

The Bowmore Terrace prospect lies to the north of the Bowmore discovery in a down-thrown terrace setting. Dip closure is present to the south, an additional pinchout is required to close the P10 area which is down dip of the Bowmore discovery. A total relief of 290m is present from the top of the Galley horizon to the deepest contour. Trap integrity does not rely on the fault seal with Bowmore as this structure has been shown to be charged, though clearly this has implications for the maximum trap fill. Combination structural stratigraphic trap (3 way dip with updip strat pinchout), Balmoral Sandstone reservoir with AVO anomaly. The bright amplitudes from the extracted maximum positive attribute on the far minus near envelope volume define the prospect. A stratigraphic pinch-out edge is identified surrounding the prospect. The edge matches with the AVO anomaly extent and with an interpreted change in depositional facies from a submarine turbidite channel to basin plain deposits.

Combination structural stratigraphic trap (3 way dip with updip strat pinchout), Balmoral Sandstone reservoir with AVO anomaly.  Sealed by Sele shales, source - Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Dunscaith lies over a positive AVO anomaly. The bright amplitudes from the extracted maximum positive attribute on the far minus near envelope volume define the prospect. The N & S edges are marked by a change in seismic character and the lateral limits are defined by the extent of the AVO anomaly and a change in reflection character associated with a change in depositional facies. Hydrocarbon migration modelling has highlighted that there is a limited drainage area for  Dunscaith. However, there may be potential for migration from the Jurassic level with direct fill from beneath the prospect.

Downthrown fault closed BCU structure with Jurrasic Piper Sandstone Reservoir.  Source and seal provided by Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Seismic mapping of the Piper and Claymore sandstones in the Jurassic levels and the Kimmeridge Clay Fm would have to be undertaken in order to fully address the key risks and uncertainties.

Stratigraphic trap with reservoir of Grid Sandstone sealed by Horda Formation shales and sourced from Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Bright seismic amplitudes are observed on RMS amplitude map (in a 200ms window beneath the Top Grid) in both full stack and far minus near offset data. It is postulated that whilst hydrocarbons migrate up-dip through the Balmoral Fm sourcing Palaeocene plays, an alternative migration pathway facilitates migration into shallower stratigraphic intervals. This is supported by the presence of hydrocarbons in the Grid Fm in some offset wells. Eocene conical sand injectites have been interpreted down-dip of the Rowallan Lead during an in-house geological study in the area. During this study, several large sand injectites have been mapped. Some of these injectites are truncated by shales and could have the capability to form reservoirs, whilst others are observed to reach the base of the Grid Fm thus potentially acting as migration pathways into the Grid sandstones.

Seismic amplitude supported stratigraphic trap, Cromarty Sandstone Member reservoir  Geological chance of success is 29%.   Volumes calculated probabilistic. It is difficult to recognise and pick on traditional seismic, but becomes more evident on inversion volumes. It forms a narrow channel above the Forties sequence analogous to but significantly smaller than the Rubie Cromarty feature. The channel feature is interpreted to form possibly discontinuous sandstone pods ('string-of-pearls') of Cromarty Sandstone age.
The 15/28a-A prospect lies within the Ruby Palaeocene channel complex, just to the north of the Ruby Field which contains gas and oil within Cromarty sandstones.

Seismic amplitude supported stratigraphic trap, Forties Sandstone Member reservoir  Geological chance of success is 10%.   Volumes calculated probabilistic. Comparison of the Forties Sandstone top structure map with SVI images of the same interval suggest that this lead lies alongside a channel structure but has no 4-way closure in its own right. The structure forming the Melle lead could therefore be interpreted as a levee or crevasse splay system flanking a turbiditic channel system which no longer contains significant sands, or that the feature could be a continuation of the channel system that appears to join the 'Mulligan' channel in the vicinity of well 15/28a-8. Whatever its origin, it is clearly displayed on SVI and REI images.
Melle, the down dip extension of the Mulligan channel is the secondary Lead for appraisal.

Seismic amplitude supported stratigraphic trap - small feature located on the outer curve of the 'Mulligan' channel, Forties Sandstone Member reservoir. The feature is defined on the presence of an REI anomaly on the flank of the channel and does not itself have any significant topographic expression. The location of the REI relative to the channel axis suggests that it represents a leve or crevasse splay formed where there is an abrupt change of direction of the 'Mulligan' channel.

Seismic amplitude supported stratigraphic trap, Balmoral Sandstone Member reservoir. This large feature is defined on the presence of an REI anomaly on the flank of a younger Forties channel and but does not itself have any significant topographic expression, forming a broad low relief structure. The location and shape of the REI anomaly relative to the younger channel axis suggests that it represents a leve or crevasse splay which formed adjacent to an older late Balmoral Sandstone age channel that developed along the same orientation as the younger Forties 'Mulligan' channel. There is no evidence for such a channel in well 15/28a-5 to the east, but hints of the presence of such a channel can be seen in the uppermost interval of the Balmoral Sandstone in well 15/27-10

trap_type_comment: Three way hanging wall structure with over 2300 feet of mapped closure. Similar traps have been proven successful elsewhere in the Witch Ground Graben and also in the South Viking Graben to the North. Closure to the south is provided by fault seal against the Rattray High while top seal is provided by Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation mudstones. Excellent seals are provided by shale intervals within the Upper Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous sequences. The Temple Wood prospect is interpreted to lie within the Alder Field pressure cell. Abundant RFT pressure data defines the aquifer gradient for this pressure cell at 5400 psi of overpressure. This data suggests that at Temple Wood column heights in excess of 4,000ft can be supported in the Temple Wood trap. This is more than sufficient to hold back the expected column height of 2,355ft, crest of the structure to the spill point.

description: ConocoPhillips has identified the Temple Wood gas-condensate prospect which extends over 15/29c, 15/29b and open Block 15/30c.  The reservoir objective is the Upper Jurassic Galley Sandstone Member which is dip closed to the north, west and east.  The reservoir sands are interpreted to have been deposited as mass flow deposits within the Witch Ground Graben and are a proven reservoir in a number of nearby fields. The depositional system is characterized by thick sequences of sheet sands with excellent reservoir properties. Field analogues include Scott, Tartan and Lowlander within the Witch Ground Graben and Thelma, Brich and Brae within the South Viking Graben. A condensate yield of 110 - 200 - 280 STB/MMSCF was used in the evaluation. Britannia and Alder have variable CGRs of 60 to 180 STB/MMSCF, with an average of 110 STB/MMSCF. Pre-drill, the prospect had a Ps of 42% with a technical resource distribution of 24/148/405 MMBOE (P10/P50/P90)

description: The Kilmartin Prospect comprises a three-way dip closure sealed updip by a combination of stratigraphic pinchout and lateral seal against the impermeable footwall of the Renee Ridge. Sealing lithologies are present in updip wells 15/29b-4 and 15/29c-16. The adjacent basin is fully charged by mature Kimmeridge Clay source rock. The nearby Alder Field (well 15/29a-8) provides the reservoir parameters, which have been adjusted to expect lower net to gross and porosity in this deeper setting (5,400m vs 4,500m at Alder).

Black Ghost is defined as a stratigraphic trap of Upper Jurassic Piper equivalent clastics that infill a local intra-cratonic depocentre on Top Devonian. The mudstones and chalk of the Lower and Upper Cretaceous respectively would act as top seal, with the Devonian tight sands as bottom and lateral seal.

At the time of licence application, the concept behind the Black Ghost and Black Argus leads was that Upper Jurassic Piper Formation-equivalent sands could form traps beneath the Base Cretaceous Unconformity. 
These traps would be formed by either pinch-out or truncation of the sands in an updip direction, with a topseal formed by Cretaceous mudstones and chalks, and bottom and lateral seals provided by tight Devonian or Triassic sediments.

The Aston lead is a Middle Jurassic Hugin Formation down-thrown trap. The concept for the lead stemmed from the observation that the formation pressure gradients in the 16/23-4 and 5 wells on the structural high, within the Hugin Formation, were offset by approximately 600psi when compared with the Hugin Formation in wells 16/18-2 and 16/18-1. This change in formation pressure suggests some form of compartmentalisation of the reservoir unit and the potential for a structural or combined structural/stratigraphic trap to exist in 16/23b. The current interpretation suggests that minor faulting west of the 16/23-4 and 5 wells could act as a lateral seal creating the Aston trap.

The reservoir objective for the Aston prospect is the Hugin Formation sandstone, which comprises shallow-marine and marginal-marine sediments deposited during the overall transgression and southward retreat of the ‘Brent Delta’ systems. Interpretation of the new seismic data has increased the principle risk of lateral seal as only a flexure is seen rather than a significant fault on the easterly updip edge of the prospect. The prospect trends from south-west to north-east across 16/23b and extends into the southern end of 16/18c, similar to the 28th Round application mapping.
This flexure may be the result of a lineation of small faults. It is probable that these faults will be discontinuous along the length of Aston and because of their minor offset and discontinuous nature, they are unlikely to be an effective seal for trapping. 
The optimal place to test the prospect is in 16/23b where the overlying Alcedo (Heather Formation) prospect can also be tested. However, the overall geological chance of success is considered low due to trap risk and reservoir presence.

The Hugin Formation reservoir encountered at the 16/23-4 Wrasse Discovery well is thin and fairly poorly developed (gross Hugin Formation thickness of 23.3m). The reservoir is characterised by coaly sandstones and heterolithics that have been deposited in coastal plain to shoreface marine depositional environments. Azinor Catalyst have undertaken petrophysics on the discovery well and has the following petrophysical calculations; 12.2m Net Pay, 18.2% average porosity and 52% average NTG. The well tested gas and 47 API condensate at rates of up to 4 mmscfpd and 2,190 bcpd.

description: The Palaeocene Kidd Discovery was made by well 16/23-3. The accumulation has been mapped as a small low relief 4-way dip closure at top Heimdal Member level and is on trend to the Kinnoull Field which shares the same reservoir age sands. Top seal is provided by the shales of the Palaeocene Lista Formation. The discovery has been mapped up on 3D Mega Survey seismic data.  The Heimdal Member reservoir encountered by the discovery well comprise stacked turbidite channels. Petrophysical analysis of the Heimdal Member sands estimates porosity to 24% and oil saturation to 70%. Permeabilities are typically measured in the hundreds of mD but may range up to several Darcies. An oil-down-to has been established at 2,484 m TVDSS and a water-up-to at 2,492 m TVDSS, coincident with the mapped spill point of the structure to the southwest. An oil sample recovered to surface confirmed a 33 deg API oil.

The Bermuda Prospect is defined as a sub-unconformity trap in the Hugin Formation. The trap is delineated by structural dip to the south and east, by the erosion of the reservoir to the west-northwest and partially by faulting to the north.The reservoir target is the Hugin Formation shallow marine sandstones, with top seal provided by the overlying mudstones of the Heather and Kimmeridge Clay formations. It is crucial for the Bermuda Prospect that the upper part of the Pentland/Sleipner Formation is an effective base seal since the Skagerrak and thin Pentland/Sleipner Formation sandstones present in Well 16/23-3 are water bearing. The lack of base seal is considered to be the primary risk for the prospect. Another key risk associated with the Bermuda Prospect is charge.

The Prospect is seismically well defined fault block, bounded by narrow grabens to the south, west and north. Hugin Formation shoreface sands, top sealed by the overlying mudstones of the Heather and Kimmeridge Clay formations. A key risk associated with the Burnt Island Prospect is charge. The local grabens adjacent to the prospect are believed to have generated insufficient volumes. The contribution from the area to the north and east is potentially larger but with more uncertain migration because Hugin is faulted to the northeast. Another important risk factor is containment. Other structures in the area appear to have leaked the hydrocarbons vertically through the chalk (e.g. Nor 15/12-1). The Burnt Island Prospect may be at less of a risk for vertical leakage since Upper Jurassic shales are draping over the crest. The area to the west is more exposed, as the highest structural area is over a buried volcano with probably no Upper Jurassic shales present at all. The Kinnoull Paleocene Field is positioned directly above this volcano.

The Burnt Island Prospect straddles the UK/Norway median line with the crestal part of the prospect on the UK side. The principal target is the Hugin Formation shoreface sands, sealed by the overlying mudstones of the Heather and Kimmeridge Clay formations. Additional reservoir intervals are the Triassic Skagerrak Formation and potentially thin sandstones within the Sleipner/Pentland Formation. 
The prospect is located in a seismically well-defined fault block, bounded by narrow grabens to the south, west and north. The prospect is believed to be charged by short distance migration from local kitchen areas to the south and south-east.

The undrilled Wildcat prospect is a tilted fault block structure at Middle Jurassic level, located about 5 km east of the Kinnoull field and 10 km north of the Maureen field. A small Paleocene 4-way closure to the east of the Kinnoull Field. It directly overlies the crestal area of the Burnt Island Hugin Prospect. Top Heimdal sandstone cannot be mapped with any confidence on the MegaSurvey, and top Heimdal is constructed by adding 20 m of shales below top Lista. There is a very pronounced anomaly in the Miocene section which abruptly changes exactly above the mapped Lista spill point. If this anomaly is causing velocity changes, it may easily change the level of the spill point by more than 10 m either way relative to the crest which is outside the anomaly. Such a change will have a significant effect on the potential volumes for the prospect. Tthe primary risk factors are the validity of a trap, considering the low relief structure and potential velocity variations in the overburden, and the risk of being in a migration shadow.

Bay Island is mapped as a 4-way closure at the Near Base Lista level, down-dip and separated by a saddle from the Maureen Field. The principal target is the submarine fan sandstones of the Maureen/Ty Formation top sealed by Lista shales. A new depositional model suggests that extensive remobilisation of the original Maureen sandstone bodies occurred in some areas shortly after deposition. The porous, unconsolidated Maureen Formation sands were in part liquefied and subsequently injected into the overlying sediments, and more importantly extruded on the palaeo sea floor. These extruded sandstones are believed to form the main reservoir of this prospect. The main risk is considered to be the presence of quality reservoir above the spill to the Maureen Field.

FLETT FORMATION LEADS - The Cumberland are defined at T40 seismically, partially on 3D data but the critical up-dip fault closure is not fully covered by fully migrated 3D. The seismic pick used is the Top T40, which corresponds to the top of the Colsay Mbr., lava sequence, within which is siliciclastic sandstone in 164/25-1z
and 164/25-2. The tie to these wells is on good quality RR14 2D data and is robust.
No direct mapping of the reservoir interval is possible. Siliciclastic sandstone is present down-dip in 164/28-1A in the same seismic interval. Top and base seal is interbedded volcaniclastic claystone and is considered robust. The fault seal is juxtaposition of the Colsay Mbr., sequence and the sealing fault up-dip which is a significant risk, although
sealing faults in such sequences are proven (see Walker et al., 2013). The trap is formed by normal faulting in the Eocene, for which the downthrown block to the west is the Cumberland leads. Tilting from the Eocene to present formed the dip component, which dips westwards. 
Both leads are substantially the same, separated by a ~E-W trending normal fault. Migration is prognosed to be from the NERB to the west, where oil shows were encountered in 164/28-1A. 
There is no mapped stratigraphical or structural break between 164/28-1A and the leads.

The Buzzard-aged reservoir is regionally present within the Moray Firth. A Top Buzzard equivalent reflector has been mapped from the Buzzard licence area across the P.2101 licence area where 2 Buzzard-age equivalent leads are highlighted. The reflectors pinch out in a north westerly direction onto the tilted fault block with the Nash structure at its crest. However, westwards from the Buzzard Field, Buzzard-aged sands pinch out down dip of well 19/10a-1 creating an effective and proven seal for the field. Therefore the up-dip locations for Leads A and B probably represent an area of sediment bypass or non sandstone deposition. The seismic thickness of the Buzzard-aged unit also halves from 19/08-1 well to the Lead A location and is even thinner at the Lead B location.

Lead C is a Lower Cretaceous pinchout trap. The Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) in this area is a very erosive event and east of the 'pinch out' on-lapping events and amplitude variations have been observed that could correspond to reservoir facies. The target is the Punt Fm. No amplitude dimming on the Base Cretaceous Unconformity horizon has been observed to indicate a clastic depositional environment, akin to the Golden Eagle Punt Field. However, once Nexen have acquired new 3D seismic data and reprocessed the existing data sets, it is possible that amplitude extractions may illuminate reservoir facies within the C lead. No parameters provided; entered cf cp19_5_9.

CretaceousNumerous Lower Cretaceous leads over P.2101 were defined by the western most stratigraphic pinch out of the Punt age-equivalent sandstones. The up-dip offset well, 19/08-1 contains Punt age-equivalent sandstones that are interpreted to be shoreface sandstones that have been reworked by wave action. The key horizons used in these Lower Cretaceous lead evaluations are the BCU and the Top Valhall Marl. The Top Valhall Marl has been identified in the 19/10-1 from a synthetic well tie and was mapped across the P.2101 licence area where it represents an approximate Punt-equivalent age reflector. A thickness map between the Top Valhall Marl and the BCU shows the main westerly pinch-out can be separated into a number of scalloped shaped features, as shown in Fig. 5.7. The event at the BCU appears highly erosive in this area and is followed by sediment infill. However, down-dip offset well data does not indicate that Punt age equivalent sandstones are present and as a result has placed a high risk on reservoir presence.

The Carrickarede Lead is located in the NE corner of Block 2/15b, and extends into adjacent Block 3/11a. 
The lead was originally identified as a low relief dip closed time structure at Top Palaeocene (Heimdal Sandstone) level. 
Subsequent examination, using additional 2D seismic data, showed that it does not close structurally to the NW. 
The lead is therefore no longer considered as having potential. 
Furthermore, it is not underlain by any structures of interest in the Jurassic or older section.

Portrush lead. Emerald fault trap formed by east-dipping Middle Jurassic andstones, lying directly on basement, which are trapped to the east by fault seal against the footwalls of the platform boundary faults. 
Lateral fault seal against crystalline basin rarely works, even in the best of circumstances, and the seal-failure risks for the Cushenden lead is compounded greatly by the possible juxtaposition of sandstones across the fault, especially in those places where the throw is small. 
Other risks for the play include: reservoir continuity and quality; the risks of longdistance lateral migration from the mature Kimmeridgian source rocks in the East Shetland Basin; and the risk of degradation of the oil at the shallow depths (1600m) of the target. CoS

The Cushenden and Portrush leads lie along the western side of Block 2/15b, at the faults that separate the Transitional Platform from the East Shetland Platform. 
The concept behind both leads is a trap style formed by east-dipping Middle Jurassic Sandstones, lying directly on basement, which are trapped to the east by fault seal against the footwalls of the platform boundary faults.

Due to the significant risks of reservoir presence as well as the shrinking of the structure post- seismic reprocessing, Unicorn is regarded by the partnership as unprospective.

The principal prospect identified on the blocks was Dragon, a fault bounded high with dip closure to the north east. 
The prospect was first mapped using the un-reprocessed British Sun Oil data with the assumption that Brent Sands would be present. However after remapping, using both reprocessed 2D surveys and re-working of the well correlation, it is clear at the Base Tertiary that the Dragon Prospect is part of the same large fault block that well 2/3-1 drilled and the Brent sands are absent. 
This well was dry, but with strong oil shows in the Palaeocene Sands. The Dragon prospect therefore appears unprospective.

Cello is a Carboniferous lead located in blocks 20/11 and 20/12 in the south of the P2283 licence. The lead was identified on the basis of minor residual oil shows in well 20/12-3 immediately down-dip of the lead.
The well penetrated multiple reservoir intervals including the Zechstein Halibut Dolomite, Lower Carboniferous sands of the Buchan Formation and the underlying Devonian sands. No shows were indicated within the Carboniferous or the Devonian, however minor residual oil shows where recorded within the Zechstein, possibly related to thinner algal rich shale beds of the Kupfershiefer Formation. 
The lead is trapped by stratigraphic pinchout to the northeast and southwest of the Lower Carboniferous sand drilled in the well onto the Peterhead ridge and is defined on 2D. 
Re-interpretation of the top Zechstein interval using new 2D data does not reveal any clear trap at this stratigraphic level.

Linnet is a three-way dip-closure prospect at the Tay Mbr level, supported by an AVO amplitude which shows a strong class 3 signature and good conformance to structure. The Marten Discovery is in Block 20/3c and was discovered in 1984 by the 20/3-4 well drilled by Amoco and encountered an oil column in Buzzard aged sandstones. 
Marten is a three-way dip closed structure to the north, south and west, with a stratigraphic pinch-out component to the east.
The reservoir for Marten comprises four stacked sandstones: three relatively thin oil-bearing sands of J66 - J64 Buzzard age above a thicker, J64, water bearing Buzzard main sand.
Mapping suggests there is a spill point at around 10,750ft which is where the 20/3-4 well penetrated the J66 section, however the CPI (Fig. 13) suggests that the ODT is 10,951ft TVDSS and the WUT is 11,007ft TVDSS.

Lower Cretaceous Punt Stratigraphic Trap on the northern margin of the Ettrick sub-basin. The potential reservoir is interpreted as a confined turbidite channel-fan sandstone that extends from north to south and appears structurally controlled largely by northeast-southwest and east-west trending rift topography. It has a mounded expression due to four-way differential compaction of Valhall shales over the Punt channel, These provide a vertical and lateral seal. The seismic architecture is very similar to the Golden Eagle Punt discovery. It also appears seismically similar due to the effect of BCU amplitude dimming that was caused at Golden Eagle by the presence of low impedance Punt sands that directly overlie the Base Cretaceous unconformity.

The Badger Prospect is a downthrown hanging wall block located to the north of the 20/4-1 ridge.

The lowside Badger case is a three-way dip closure to the north, east and west and fault closed to the south against an east-west trending down to the north normal fault. This fault forms the northern margin to the central horst structure in Block 20/4a.

The Polecat oil discovery comprises a stratigraphic trap in Upper Jurassic deep-marine J62a-66a age Lower Buzzard sandstones. Polecat was discovered in 2005 by Nexen's 20/4a-8 well. 
Oil was present in 29.5 feet of net pay but a southerly appraisal sidetrack of this well found the upper oil sand missing, and a thickened equivalent of the thin lower oil sand. 
An additional sand was also present towards the base of the sequence but all sands were water-wet. 
A successful appraisal well, 20/4a-9 was drilled to the east in 2010, with hydrocarbons present in two sands, both were tested and flowed at potentially commercial rates.

The 20/4a-8 Polecat discovery well drilled in 2005 found oil in two Upper Jurassic Lower Buzzard Sandstones of J66a - J62a age, with 31.5ft net oil pay. The well was sidetracked
down-dip to the south to delineate the oil water contact. The upper oil sand found in the original well was missing in the sidetrack and there was a thickened equivalent of the lower
thin oil sand and an additional sand package towards the base of the sequence. However, all sands were water bearing.
The commerciality of the accumulation is the greater risk with this discovery.

description: The Verbier prospect comprises of a Upper Jurassic submarine fan complex that has accumulated in the hanging wall of the Buchan trough. The deep-water sands are interpreted to be the Burns Sandstone (J64 in age) based on observations from the 20/05a-10 & 10Y wells. The sands are charged directly from the surrounding Kimmeridge Clay Formation which is mature at the prospect location. The Verbier prospect has a Pg of 1 due to the 20/05a-10 & 10Y wells location within the 'base case' polygon outline. The well encountered a ODT within 16m of Burns sandstone which flowed at 4804 bopd.

The Meribel lead was originally introduced in the 28th Licence Round application, with the sandstone being Upper Jurassic Burns Sandstone Member. It was originally interpreted on the CGG VerQ21 3D seismic data on a strong seismic reflection interpreted as submarine fan sandstones, and the trap was considered combination structural-stratigraphic. The dry wells 20/05b- 12 and 20/05b- 2 were considered to have been drilled on fault isolated compartments. The imaging was very poor and did not allow an accurate definition of the faults in the area. Subsequent to the licensing the PGS 3D seismic data, the lead was re-evaluated, and it was noted that the amplitude on the feature is much dimmer than what originally stood out on the CGG 3D seismic data.

Stratigraphic Trap with Zechstein carbonate reservoir. Flute Lead is located in the hangingwall roll-over structure to the northeast-trending Peterhead Fault which downthrows to the northwest. The rollover dips to the east, imparting dip closure to the Flute Lead but is cut by east-trending normal faults of the Ettrick Sub-basin trend that predominantly downthrow to the north. The roll-over does not have a structural closure in the vicinity of Flute, where the combination trap is caused by the
Zechstein carbonate facies belt, which trends slightly oblique to the eastwards dip of the roll-over structure, passing up-dip (westwards) into non-reservoir anhydrites, imparting a strong up-dip stratigraphic element to the trap

The primary lead on licence is Flute, which is a Permian Zechstein carbonate prospect.
Flute is a combination trap delineated by seismic amplitudes.

The most likely containment failure mechanism is that the southern depositional edge, continued further up-dip to the south-west, providing a potential thief zone for hydrocarbons to migrate along and away from the prospect area.

Pure stratigraphic trap somewhat resembling to the Mustard North prospect in the East Solan Basin; Solan turbidite sands target. Jackson is a down-thrown fault bounded 3-way dip closure located to the south of the Nuevo High. The closure has been identified at intra-Cretaceous level, but additional closures exist throughout the Early Palaeocene section as well as the deeper Cretaceous. The relief of the structure at Cretaceous level is approximately 1100m. Several shale units acting as seals are thought to be present in the Cretaceous to Early Palaeocene stratigraphy.

The main reservoir is the uppermost T36 sand - the same reservoir as at Handcross South. The lead exhibits a strong AVO anomaly that brightens immediately up-dip of well 204/14-2, which found high quality water bearing T36 sand. Company CoS = 39%.

The lead has been mapped at T35 level, is associated with possible hydrocarbon tuning effects, and exhibits hydrocarbon indicators similar to those seen in the Suilven discovery. The seal is formed by the T35 shale unit overlying the T35 sand unit. The Pemberton lead has been modelled to have a gas cap similar to that of the Suilven field. Company CoS = 22%.

was characterised as a clearly defined lateral pinchout/shale out into a fan neck in the T36 level.
The feature is defined by an extensive amplitude anomaly which is mapped at the top T36 seismic
event and calibrated to dry wells 204/14-2 and 204/18-1.

The reservoir for the Handcross prospect is expected to be the same stacked T36
sandstones penetrated by the 204/14-2 well beneath the T36 Kettla tuff. These
sandstones wedge out in an easterly direction such that they are absent a short
distance to the East at Suilven. The pinch out edge of these T36 sands can be
mapped out on a NE-SW azimuth. Top seal is provided by the Kettla Tuff (which
thins to the East) and overlying shales.

The Ech Lead is represented by a 4-way dip closed T45 shore face sand unit, sealed from the SE by the deep incision by channels of the Balder delta. Additional volume in the closure is formed by the cut out of the T45 sand along the up-dip side adding a stratigraphic element to the trap beneath the 4-way closure. Muds and coals drape this surface followed by tuffs and shale of the Balder Fm. which create the top seal.  The lead is adjacent to and above a thin oil sand at T38 level found in 204/19-5 demonstrating the migration of oil to this level. Company CoS = 11%.

Two additional small and high risk leads were identified in Block 204/19c, namely the Ard and the
Ech leads. Both leads are mapped at the T45 level and are thought to have been
developed on a deeply incised Top Balder landscape creating structural and partly stratigraphic
features that lie to the north and south of the well 204/19-5.

BP/Shell's discovery Suilven Segment 3 in applicaton for blocks 204/14&15. 10% chance of success. P50 oil in place 58 mmbl; recoverable 18 mmbl; gas in place 12 bcf; recoverable 6 bcf. No parameters or trap details in report.

NL: "Small amplitude anomaly that suggests small gas accumulation less than 5 BCF of recoverable reserves. Alnwick lead - T34 sands target onlapping acoustically transparent unit proved to be mudstones in 204/26-1A. BG downgrade lead due to 'absence of side seal, no amplitude anomaly, no valid stratigraphic closure'. Parameters entered cf. cp204_21_2.

Blyth lead - T 35 sand target originally defined by amplitude anomaly, abutted to N by later intra-T35 sand-filled channel - seal risk. Onlaps shale-prone unit to SE. Effectively tested by 204/16-1A well; amplitude anomaly disproved - not recommended for YtF. Parameters entered cf. cp204_21_2.

Bedlington extension prospect - stratigraphic trap relying on pinchout of T31 sands up dip to E - lies up dip of Bedlington prospect in 204/21, possibly associated with flat spot. All parameters, reserves, risking in application.

The Glas Maol Prospect appears to be very similar in nature to the nearby SW Foinaven Discovery, being a T31.3 (Palaeocene) channel with a clear seismic amplitude anomaly.  The reservoir is expected to be a high-quality deep-water turbidite sand.  The prospect is split by a fault into North and South segments.  The prospect is stratigraphic, with most of the edges defined by sand pinch-out within a channel.  The up-dip pinchout within the channel is the riskiest element of the trap.  Calibration of amplitudes with SW Foinaven suggest that Glas Maol North has oil and gas, whereas Glas Maol South has oil.  The prospect on its own is likely to be uneconomic, but could be considered for development as part of the larger inventory of opportunities in this application.

Glas Maol South is a lookalike for the SW Foinaven Discovery. Glas Maol last examined in 2008. BP still trying to track down all the relevant work. Glas Maol North is small (3 mmboe resources) and expected to be mainly gas. Glas Maol South is a lookalike for the SW Foinaven Discovery

Glas Maol lead - a poorly defined N/S turbidite slope channel system segmented by minor down to the S normal faults; requires up dip strat pinchout of southern segment. Clear Class III AVO. CoS = 34%, with seal as principal risk; trap definition (reduced 85>50%) & hydrocarbon phase are also risks.

The Tarsuinn Prospect is a four-way dip closure defined at Base T40 (Palaeocene).  The structure has a well-defined flat spot and seismic rock property modelling suggests that the structure is likely to be oil-bearing.  The reservoir is anticipated to be shallow-marine T38 sands and the seal is assumed to be T45-T60 mudstones and coals.  The Kimmeridge Clay source rock is mature in this area, but the low temperature of the reservoir (40-50degC) means that oil biodegradation is likely (hence low assumed recovery factor).  The prospect on its own is likely to be uneconomic, but could be considered for development as part of the larger inventory of opportunities in this application.

The Rona Sandstone discovery, named Tempest, directly overlies the basement high and controls the ultimate 4-way dip closure for the structure. The prospect is associated with heavy oil, however there is the potential for lighter oil away from a gas chimney which has been identified close to 204/28-1 and may have been responsible for bleeding off some of the lighter hydrocarbon fraction in its vicinity. Unit 1 is comprised of localised alluvial fans / conglomerates, Unit 2 is comprised of gravity flow sands and Unit 3 is comprised of shelf sands. HP/HT prospect is a fairly well defined 4-way dip closure (~60km2 max, 25km2 mode) at Pre-BCU, located on the "Flett ridge" between the Clair field and the Laggan-Tormore-Edradour discoveries. This deeply buried object (>4000m) is evaluated for dry gas at both Jurassic sands pinch-out on the flanks and at Devono-Carboniferous (iso-Clair formation) objective. Talisker is interpreted as an HP/HT, deeply buried, robust 4-way dip closure (up to 60 km2) at BCU level located on the southwest of the Flett Ridge. It is located 20 km to the northwest of the Clair Field and straddles blocks 205/10 and 209/9a. The water depth over the crest of the structure is 450 m TVDSS.

Sanda prospects have a very similar morphology to the Schiehallion and Foinaven Fields, but with lower amplitudes. This could be due to thinner reservoir, or the slightly
greater burial depth at Sanda, or indeed a product of the seismic processing. Sanda is interpreted as an up-dip pinch out of Sullom/ Lower Vaila Formation turbidites. This play
has been successfully tested in Quadrants 204 and 206, but between these two areas there have only been a few wells that have tested this play, most unsuccessfully. Oil and gas shows were recorded in wells, 205/8-1 and 205/10-2b, but the reservoir was poorly developed in these wells, which are situated outwith the 205/13 anomaly. Identification of Vaila/ Sullom pinch out traps is generally only possible from seismic attribute analysis. All the neighbouring discoveries show a clear amplitude response due to fluid fill (oil and/or gas) and down-dip amplitude shut off at the oil or gas water contact. This amplitude response is complicated by the reservoirs being channelized, resulting in significant changes in reservoir thickness and therefore amplitude response in the hydrocarbon column. The presence of gas caps above oil can further complicate this amplitude picture. However, in all the neighbouring discoveries the Vaila reservoir sands are seismically invisible unless hydrocarbon bearing. Amplitude driven: Amplitude to be checked by a geophysicist. Trapping towards Sanda N & S? Oil scenario 50/50%. New modern broadband 3D seismic is required.

Company CoS = 9%.

Upper Jurassic dip closed structure The structure is faulted, particularly along the northwestern flank and is underlain by a fault plane contact with basement. Over 300 m, 985 ft of mid Jurassic sands and shales are present at 206/5-1 and 206/5-2.(due to reservoir quality risks, these are classed as secondary targets). The reservoir for Craster is the Kimmeridgian mass flow sands of the Solan Formation. Lead A - defined by strong brightening at top Vaila Fm in trap controlled by updip fault cf, Schiehallion. Seal likely to be significant problem. No parameters, reserves, CoS provided; entered cf. Schiehallion. 'Reservoir is the fatal flaw' according to BP
A tilted fault block has been identified at Top Albian (K50) and Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) levels, which straddles Blocks 205/16c and 205/16b. This lead has been called Ghlo Deep.

The Dunrobin lead is as a combined structural and stratigraphic trap within Lower Cretaceous strata. It is defined by an area of strong amplitudes and located within a regional three-way closed structure. These amplitudes are interpreted to represent a package of sand within a shale dominated section of Albian age.  Probabilistic input parameters used.  Those shown are P90, P50 and P10..   Gas condensate assumed to be the most likely hydrocarbon phase. It is recognised that reservoir presence is a key risk for Dunrobin, particularly as downdip well 205/16-1 failed to find any
significant sand. This well drilled on the fringes of the bright amplitudes and may lie on the distal edges of a turbidite fan system. In addition the immediate zone around 205/16-1 is characterised by lower amplitudes and indications of faulting. This may be the reason why no significant sand was encountered, and updip potential remains.

A further amplitude anomaly was identified within Lower Cretaceous stratigraphy (Dunrobin
Lead) at the application stage, mapped on mid-1990's vintage full offset data. Results of the
work carried out on the reprocessed 3D dataset and the long offset 2D, indicate that
the seismic amplitude anomalies are unlikely to be caused by the presence of hydrocarbon filled
sands.

The Ghlo Core lead is seismically defined on far offset data (1993 data, reprocessed 1999) as a broad meander belt of a T31 slope turbidite channel system. The lead does not exhibit a clear class III AVO response on seismic data as can be seen within the Schiehallion T31 interval. The lack of clear AVO response can be explained by the presence of thiner sands (~25m) than at the Schiehallion field (~100m), and the 9Hz low cut to the seismic data making it lower resoloution than the modern seismic data over Schiehallion. The	 Ghlo	 Core	 lead	 relies	 partially	 on	 stratigraphic 	pinchout	 and 	fault	 closure, 	the 	latter	 being 	poorly	 defined 	due 	to 	the	 presence	 of	 an 	updip	 gas 	chimney.

Reservoir presence is seen as a fatal flaw, with considerable additional risk on trap due to the poor updip imaging at a gas chimney. At this degree of risk, the P2041 JV does not see Ghlo Core as a prospect.

The Ghlo Core Lead was recognised as a combination stratigraphic/structural trap defined by the seismic amplitude anomaly at T31 reservoir level. Amplitudes suggest channel edges on two sides of the trap and possible conformance with the Schiehallion OWC down-dip. The up-dip portion of the trap was poorly imaged due to the presence of a gas chimney that disrupts the seismic data.

Lead B - defined by strong brightening at top Vaila Fm in trap controlled by updip fault cf, Schiehallion. Seal likely to be significant problem. No parameters, reserves, CoS provided; entered cf. Schiehallion.

The Ghlo East Lead is less well defined than the Ghlo Core Lead, visible on far offset seismic data (1993 data, reprocessed 1999). The amplitude anomaly associated with the Ghlo East lead is areally extensive but cannot be attributed to any known depositional fairways.  The lead does not exhibit a clear class III AVO response on seismic data as can be seen within the Schiehallion T31 interval. The lack of clear AVO response is thought to be caused by the sands being thinner (~25m) than in Schiehallion (~100m) and the 9Hz low cut to the seismic data making it lower resoloution than modern seismic data over Schiehallion. 
The Ghlo East	lead	is likely to be compartmentalised into a series of terraces and reliant on fault closure	and unlikely to require stratigraphic pinchout. Given the immature status of the Ghlo East lead, trap definition is seen as one of the key risks.

The Ghlo East Lead was less well defined on the available 3D seismic data. Amplitudes associated with this lead were seen to be areally extensive, but lacked conformance with structure and were broken up by faults. Recoverable volumes were estimated at 44-87-91 mmboe (P90-Mean-P10) with a chance of success of 18%. Key risks were thought to be trap presence and charge access.

Probabilistic volumes were generated.  Min refers to P90, ML to P50 and Max to P10.
Oil/gas reserves refers to producable volumes at stock tank conditions, MMSTBO.   STOOIP(MMSTBO) P10 934, P50 1036, p90 1146.

Lower Clachaig prospect is a stratigraphic trap mapped at T35.4A sandstone level The trap is developed along the SE pinch-out of the T35.4 depositional fan system onto the Tormore (Flett) high. The prospect is defined on the basis of a high amplitude/low impedance event at T35.4A Sandstone level, taken to represent the channel axis of a high density turbidity current, which shows lateral pinchout to the east. AMS data suggests the T35.4 depositional system runs from a NE-SW direction through the 205/9-1 well where no closure is mapped. The overall structure dips to the north-west with updip pinchout to the east. A critical element of the trapping mechanism is provided by an E-W trending fault that provides part of the updip seal. The fault appears to be sealing, with significant changes in the amplitude response between the footwall and hangingwall. Fault displacement across the E-W fault is estimated to be 30m.

description: The Lady prospect was initially identified by Faroe in the 2015 Relinquishment report of Licence P2045 and has been re-evaluated. The Lady Prospect is located in the south of 208/21 and the north of 208/26, 12km Northeast of the Glenlivert Discovery. The Lady prospect is identified by a strong amplitude anomaly indicating a reservoir is within the V1 and V2 unites of the Palaeocene Vaila Fm and has a majorly stratigraphic closure with three dip-dominated closures and an up-dip pinch-out required in an area of poor data quality. The 208/22-1 well identifies an entirely shale dominated V1 and V2 units of the Vaila Fm and so we can identify that the north eastern trend stratigraphically pinches out. The Lady prospect is charged by the Kimmeridge Clay Fm. and is suspected to lie within the Gas window directly above the source. Migration is proven by the similar Glenfarclas Field but a risk is proposed due to the down cutting of the V3 unit of the Vaila Fm.

The Glenfarclas Prospect is a large structural and stratigraphic trap of Palaeocene age, located around 12km north-east of the Glenlivet gas discovery. Mean recoverable resources of 394Bcf were calculated, with P90 of 26Bcf and P10 of 940Bcf.
Risk is distributed between trap, reservoir and seal, with the overall geological risk considered to be high.
This view is largely driven by the rock physics study, which concluded that the seismic response observed at the Glenfarclas Prospect is inconsistent with what would be expected if hydrocarbon bearing sandstones were present within the trap.

Fettercairn straddles blocks 209/12, 16 and 17 on the original licence. The Fettercairn prospect was
identified on Dong proprietary 3D merged seismic data (see section 4) and the potential reservoir target was the
Upper Cretaceous shoreface sands of the Kyrre Formation, mapped as a high amplitude hard seismic event. The main risk for the prospect is reservoir presence and quality. The uncertainty on reservoir presence and trap and the low volumes reduced the prospects commerciality.

Lead 209/15-M comprising blob only - no description, parameters, reserves, CoS on Rd ppt. Target comprises Mesozoic sands (?Jurassic) in tilt block. Parameters entered cf. cp219_21_1. DONG consider hydrocarbon phase uncertain, but favour gas cf. Q214 to SE.

NW-SE downthrown fault closure against basement high, with dip closure to the NE.  Sparse 2D seismic data preclude fault mapping, and seismic image is degraded by proximity to igneous intrusions to the south and west.  Amplitude brightening distinct from that associated with sills indicates interbedded sand/shale within the Early Cretaceous, pinching out against a basement high to the east, an effective base seal.  Mature Kimmeridge Clay source beds present to the north are unproven at depth within the block.  A dominantly vertical migration pathway facilitated by faults is most probable.  Reservoir is a significant risk factor and remains largely untested by local well penetrations. The prospect ranges in depth from approximately 3200mSS to 5450mSS. Reservoir quality is at risk in the deeper portions of the structure.  Chance of Success:  10%.   (Charge: 70%, Reservoir: 40%, Seal: 60%, Trap: 60%).   .   Hydrocarbons in place and reserves are probabilistic estimates.  .   .   Volumes are for total prospect, approximately 44% in 209/4 and 44% in 209/5.

The Mardyke prospect is located in the south of block 209/05 and covers an area of approximately 26km2. It lies outside the area influenced by overlying basalt flows, and can therefore be mapped with relative confidence. The prospect sits within a downthrown fault terrace, and is interpreted to consist of a series of stratigraphically trapped Early Cretaceous deep water sands, ponded within the terrace. The sands pinch out to the south against the underlying BCU, and the prospect is dip closed to the north, east and west. Additional upside is recognised in an alternate scenario, by invoking a structural trapping element. In this case, a fault seal is required between Early Cretaceous sands juxtaposed against the basement footwall to the south. The crest of the prospect is at 3,850m below sea level.

N-S trending fault splays from the main bounding fault have the potential to compartmentalise the structure. Deterministic estimate of best technical case.   .   Chance of Success 10%

The Topper Prospect is an Eocene Cromarty Sandstone Member slope turbidite play.  The Topper Prospect lies in blocks 21/1aS and 21/01b. Two prospective plays have been identified in Block 21/01b immediately to the south of the Buchan Field: the Palaeocene-Early Eocene, Forties Sandstone, basin-floor fan play and the Eocene Cromarty Sandstone slope turbidite play within the Sele Formation.  The Eocene Cromarty Sandstone is the primary target for the Topper Prospect. Exploration potential is recognised within both the slope and basin-floor facies of the Cromarty Sandstone Member, particularly where subsequent claystone-rich clinoforms have downlapped, creating the potential for lateral and vertical seal. Where contemporaneous slumping of the slope has occurred, mounded features such as that of the Topper prospect in 21/01b are observed.

The Topper Lead is a potential structural and stratigraphic trap related to a channel-like, or slump, feature within the Tertiary sequence. Some structural conformance is supported by potential 4-way dip (P90 closure within block 21/1a) while larger closure relies on stratigraphic trapping. The P1 closure extends across blocks 21/1a and 21/1b with ca. 40% mapped within 21/1b. The objective reservoir likely relates to the Forties depositional system but has also been interpreted as possible Lower Eocene, Cromarty Sandstone. Sele Formation shales are interpreted to provide top and lateral seal. Hydrocarbon migration into the Tertiary could be vertically, via faults, or by longer distance migration. There is a risk of biodegradation based on the relatively shallow depth of the target reservoir interval.

Stratigraphic prospect, being a submarine fan of late Jurassic (J64) age located on the terrace northeast of Buchan field that debouched onto the basin foor towards the north and east. It is a seismically visible feature recognised as a series of progradational reflectors in the North Buchan Trough immediately updip and NW of the tight sandstones of J64 age that were penetrated by 21/1a-18. These sands pinch out basinward and were not penetrated by the Tweedsmuir North and Tweedsmuir South wells in the northeastern part of the block. To the south, these sandstones truncate against normal faults that bound the northern flank of the Buchan Horst.
Jurassic blob only.

The Bunty leads are a series of  4 Upper Jurassic (J62-J72) mounded features probably representing episodic deep marine fan development. They are combined structural/stratigraphic traps. The sands pinchout  and are laterally sealed (and sourced) by the Kimmeridge Clay Fm but to the south they rely on lateral fault seal against the Devonian? of the Buchan Ridge. Anomalies with similar AI expression on inversion data to Burns sand are imaged at J62 & J66 level.  These are also coincident with the 4 way closure that forms part of the lobate, fan-like forms.

Stratigraphic trap of Balmoral Sst target.

Fulmar Sst lead E of 21/11-1. The trap is located on the flank of a Zechstein salt wall. The Fulmar Sandstone pinches out stratigraphically onto Smith Bank mudstones to the S, W and NW.

Migration up the Esk Basin bounding fault is possible; if as suspected patches of the basin are oil mature. Other migration paths into Astute are difficult to map out. 
It is also difficult to prove conclusively that Fulmar Sandstone is present given the difficulty of mapping Top Fulmar. CoS 22%.

The flat spot represents a fluid contact in the Balder sands that could have an associated oil leg up to 10 square miles in size. It is an elongate faulted closure, interpreted to lie along the Dornoch shelf slope boundary. Topseal is reliant on the mudstones and tuffs of the Sele and Balder Formations. Hydrocarbons sourced from the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation in the Central Graben are anticipated to have migrated via Fulmar sand carrier beds from the east and then up the major faults which define the prospect.

The Pigweed Discovery (fully evaluated) is a Fulmar stratigraphic trap (inter-pod).   The inter-pod was penetrated by the 21/17-3 discovery well (Shell 1986) to test 1) a small 4-way dip closure (Wagtail) and 2) a stratigraphic trap upside. The Henbit prospect is a Fulmar Fm stratigraphic trap within an inter-pod setting.   There are a number of very small four-way dip closures mapped at Fulmar Fm level but with a small cumulative recoverable resource of <2mmboe.  For this reason, the volumes and risking presented for Henbit are for the pod/inter-pod geological concept only.   There are currently no wells within the Henbit inter-pod, with the nearest wells being 21/18-7Z and 21/18-8 which are offset from the Henbit prospect by 1300m and 3200m respectively, both of which intersected Smith Bank Formation mudstones directly overlain by Kimmeridge Clay shales.  These wells prove discontinuity of Fulmar sandstones between individual inter-pods and as such discovery wells within other/adjacent inter-pods (e.g. 21/19-2) cannot de-risk the Henbit prospect. The Henbit prospect lies between the producing Kittiwake Field and the Tumbleweed prospect.

Chinook is a stratigraphically trapped Andrew Sandstone Member prospect. It is defined by both a minimum amplitude and isopach anomaly. 
Lista Formation mudstones provide top, base and lateral seal. 21/1c and 21/2b are located above and adjacent to Kimmeridge Clay in the mature oil window. 
Migration into the Palaeocene could be via vertical migration paths (e.g. faults) or by longer distance migration through Tertiary carrier beds. 
Immediately updip of Chinook oil shows occur within the Andrew sands of well 21/1b- 17, which is a positive for migration of hydrocarbons into the prospect. 
However this also suggests that perhaps the Chinook seal has failed.

description: The Bligh Discovery was drilled by Enterprise in 1995. The structure is defined by mapping the Top Pentland event which has good reflectivity due to the presence of the coals. The Puffin Sand reservoir lies immediately above this surface with the top of the sand being approximately 42ft above the Top Pentland which was hydrocarbon bearing. The well tested 2766 bcpd and 15.4 mmscfd of 47.6 API crude with a CGR of 188. No contact was encountered and an ODT of 14376ftTVDSS was defined. 21/20d-8 was later drilled by Centrica in 2012 with an aim of appraising the extent of the Puffin discovery.  An equivalent section was found of similar thickness, reservoir quality and hydrocarbon saturation but the interval failed to flow significant volumes on DST.

The Bligh discovery, proven by exploration well 21/20a-5 (Enterprise, 1995), constitutes a HPHT gas condensate accumulation reservoired in sandstones of the Puffin and Pentland Formation. A DST flowed 15.4 MMscfg/d & 2,750b/d of condensate on test. The Bligh discovery was further appraised by the down-dip 21/20d-8 well, located on the NW flank of the structure (Centrica, 2012). 
The appraisal well found 63’ gross hydrocarbon bearing reservoir, however, the well test flowed gas and condensate to surface at extremely low rates. 21/20d-8 was plugged and abandoned following testing.
