The Lindens lead is a channelised Tay Sandstone stratigraphic trap entirely within unlicensed Block 21/18b. The lead has been identified as an anomaly on proprietary seismic inversion products generated by PGS for E.ON, namely Vp/Vs, Amplitude versus Angle (AVA) Stack Lithology & Fluid and Acoustic Impedance (AI) volumes and extractions. Being a stratigraphic trap in a play with limited regional extent and trapped entirely in marine mudstone makes hydrocarbon migration into the trap extremely tortuous. This is further compounded by the Lindens lead being lateral offset (west) of the mature Kimmeridge Clay line. The stratigraphic trap has been identified on seismic inversion products as an anomaly. There is difficulty in discriminating between lithology and fluid response on these products and the anomaly could be a water bearing lithology response.

Owel is a low-relief structural closure with potential for stratigraphic upside within the Eocene Tay Member. It does not appear to be on trend with any channel like feature on regional seismic attribute maps. In seismic cross section it looks to be a broad feature with some bright seismic amplitudes with complex geomorphology.  A possible interpretation is for Owel to be a channel feature with sand in the central areas.  Another is that it is a sand injectite feature with the steep shapes being the ?wings? injected upwards from a sandy central base. Injectites are interpreted to provide significant connectivity between the Tay Sandstone units in the producing fields to the south.  Reservoir where encountered is generally good quality reservoir with up to 30 pu porosity and 1 Darcy permeability.  Seal for the Tay Member is provided by the overlying thick, regionally extensive, Upper Eocene and younger Tertiary marine shales.

Initial rock physics modelling and synthetic AVO modelling suggest this is what would be expected with a hydrocarbon bearing sand.

The Crinan & Dandy Discoveries are considered to comprise combination trapping mechanisms reliant upon dip closure and stratigraphic pinch-out. The proven reservoir in each case is the Eocene Middle Tay Member sandstone within the local Fyne trend. Both located within Block 21/28b, these discoveries were previously considered too small for conventional development solutions by the previous operator (i.e. marginal/stranded).

The Dandy Discovery Well, 21/28a-6, drilled in 1990, reached a total depth of 5,200ft in Tor Chalk having encountered 4ft net gas pay and over 47ft net oil pay in the Lower Eocene Tay Sand.  The well flowed 20.3º API gravity oil at 1,016 bopd and 2.4 mmscfd from the interval 4,110 - 4,158ft MDRKB.  In 1998, Dandy appraisal Well 21/28a-8 and sidetrack 21/28a-8Z were drilled reaching total depths of 5,216ft and 5,029ft in Tor Chalk and Sele Formation, respectively.  The sidetrack encountered the OWC at 3,964ft TVDSS and flowed 21.4º API gravity oil at 1,080 bopd from the Tay Sand interval.  The porosity ? permeability cross-plot below demonstrates the excellent reservoir quality with permeabilities in the range 0.1 ? 10 Darcies and porosities in the range 34 ? 40%. The sole water-wet well in the Block, 21/28b-7 drilled in 1991, encountered the thickest section of Tay Sand of any of the wells drilled thus far in Block 21/28b with over 300ft of high net/gross and 30+% porosity sand.

Grasshopper is a 4-way dip closure mapped in the Paleocene near top Forties Member. Down dip is a well, 21/29b-1 drilled in 1978 by Mesa to target the Forties, which encountered thick good quality Forties sandstone but water bearing. No core was taken in this well so there are no measured permeabilities but petrophysical analysis estimates porosity 28-32 pu.  It is possible that the well was drilled too far down dip on the flank of the trap as the depth of the reservoir encountered is well below the lowest closing contour. It would have required significant stratigraphic lateral seal to have a hydrocarbon column down to that depth.  It is possible that that there is a stratigraphic component to this trap with the Forties sandstone pinching out up dip.  The whole Forties sequence pinches out onto the West Central Shelf up dip of the Grasshopper structure and is overlain by Late Paleocene/Early Eocene deep marine shales, which act as a seal in the neighbouring producing fields.

The Cyclone prospect is a Upper Palaeocene Cromarty Formation prospect, with a gas cap and oil rim lying in 21/6b and the majority of the down dip oil lying in 21/7b. It has a convincing AVO anomaly which is comparable with similar AVO anomalies recently drilled in the adjacent block to the East (21/8). Sands transported down the slope have ponded against mappable paleo relief, setting up a fill-spill-fill mechanism for material moving down slope. The trapping mechanism is primarily stratigraphic, relying on up and down dip pinch outs across mappable by pass zones, with a differential compaction expression evident over the sand lobes. The applicant group plan to test the down dip oil leg in 21/7b, with an expected spud date in Q3 2012.  COS for the Cyclone prospect has been estimated by combined geological and geophysical risks via the SAAMs workflow (Seismic Anomaly Analysis MOdule, Rose Associates). The final COS for a well targeting the oil leg is 40% (for a well targeting the gas cap the COS is 47%)..   . The Precious Prospect is a four-way dip closure at the Home Sand level located within Block 210/24c, just to the north-west of Hudson. It is defined by a structural closure at BCU coincident with a high amplitude Upper Jurassic seismic anomaly, which defines an Upper Jurassic Home Sand channel.
Prospect 210/24B based on 3D seismic mapping by JE Cavill 2003.

The Mordor Play concept is a seismically mapped Lower Cretaceous feature which pinches-out into Block 210/24c. Isochore maps show the package to be a broadly confined channel-like feature located between the ESP and Hudson Ridge. The play would evoke a stratigraphic pinch-out within the package as a trapping mechanism.

Originally mapped as a Brae Fm fan, Dana's interpretation is conglomeratic rock fall and fault plane debris deposited against the basin bounding fault. Structure pinches out to the east. Lateral limits along strike of the fault are unclear. Top and lateral seal are significant risks due to the presence of U. Jurassic 'Home Sands' above the prospect, and uncertainty that an effective lateral seal exist. Oil typing has concluded that charge to this structure is highly unlikely. STOIIP and Reserves provided, but no other parameters - entered cf. B0505042.

Flannan lies approximately 3km northwest of the Hudson Field and is an Upper Jurassic wedge directly abutting the basin bounding fault. The structure pinches out to the
east but its lateral limits along the strike of the fault are difficult to pick. Due to its proximity to the major basin bounding fault there is a high risk that the fill will be conglomeratic rock fall and fault plane debris which will be poor reservoir quality. Top and lateral seal are also a significant risk due to the potential presence of Upper Jurassic ‘Home Sands’ above the prospect and uncertainty that an effective lateral stratigraphic or structural trapping mechanism exists.

The Tulla prospect is a conventional faulted dip closure at Middle Jurassic Brent Group level with fault closure to the north-west. It is located approximately 8 km southwest of the Tern Platform. The north-western bounding Pobie Fault defines the western limit of the Tern-Eider Ridge. A period of post Jurassic structural compression has effectively inverted the southern end of the Tern Horst and has contributed to the dip closure that defines the Tulla prospect. The inversion has induced local reverse movements on a fault to the east of the Tulla structure but well beyond the spill point.

The Home sands are a sequence of Upper Jurassic turbiditic sandstones which form in erosive channel features oriented perpendicular to the East Shetland Basin margin. The channels lie within the Kimmeridge Clay, which provides top and base seal to the sands.

The Canyon Play Concept is an identifiable seismic feature which has been interpreted as an erosive canyon with major incision and erosion of Mesozoic strata down to the Basement, later infilled with sediment. 
Hydrocarbon charge would rely on migration up the main East Shetland Platform bounding fault.
Cressida Triassic lead. Stacked below cp210_29_4. Drilled by 210/24a-13 in Feb 2009.

Troilus North Brent lead. Fault terrace on the hanging wall of the main N-S fault. Drilled by 210/30a-2 which found residual oil in top 2m of Brent. This well has proven the presence of hydrocarbons but ruled out large oil volume in this terrace although a substantial volumes can be present up dip from the well. Comparison made with architecture of Rinnes West discovery.
JU1 lead - Home Sand channel mapped on amplitude anomaly cf. Bowstring East 210/29-1,2. Same as Cladhan South 1 advertised at Prospex 2010.

Mastiff is a Paleogene stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of Margarita?s Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits sourced from the west or southwest. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with an invoked vertical migration pathway to the Paleogene. The top seal is formed by Paleogene mudstones. The nearest wells are wells 210/5-1 and 210/4-1 which targeted Jurassic and Triassic reservoirs. These wells penetrated a low net to gross section at the same stratigraphic interval as the Mastiff Lead. However, the wells were drilled on stratigraphic highs updip of the interpreted pinch-out of reservoir sands at the lead. Well 210/5-1 had shows in the Paleogene indicating vertical migration to the Paleogene works in the area.

Mastiff is a Palaeogene stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of the Margarita Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits sourced from the west or southwest. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with an invoked vertical migration pathway to the Palaeogene. The top seal is formed by Palaeogene mudstones. The nearest wells are wells 210/5-1 and 210/4-1 which targeted Jurassic and Triassic reservoirs. These wells penetrated a low net to gross section at the same stratigraphic interval as the Mastiff Lead. However, the wells were drilled on stratigraphic highs updip of the interpreted pinch-out of reservoir sands at the lead. No positive AVO anomalies were observed (Figure 25) and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the lead was downgraded and not matured.
Troilus South Triassic lead. Stacked below cp210_30_1.

The Upper Jurassic ?Deep? Play was identified as a seismic package within the Upper Jurassic section in the mature basin to the east of the area. The lead follows the same concept as the Thunder prospects in the basin to the north with Upper Jurassic turbiditic sands, similar to those that fed the Cladhan system, extending into the basin and occupying the available accommodation space.

The Balder Lead was identified as a bright amplitude directly below the Top Balder reflector. The lead is located at the extremities of the Palaeocene Dornoch deep water turbidite fan system. Although the bright amplitudes do not correspond to the structure at the Top Balder, they appear to form a linear-type shape which could be indicative of a channel and could allow stratigraphic trapping of hydrocarbons at this level.

The Heimdal Lead was identified to the south of the license area as a seismically mappable package, with downlapping internal geometries, which can be tied to the 002/5-12a well up-dip. 
The lead is located at the northern edge of the northern Heimdal fan which is interpreted to comprise fault-scarp slumps and channelised slope sands, and the pinch-out of this system can be seen on the seismic line. The Lead would rely on stratigraphic pinch-out.

Saluki is a Paleogene stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of Margarita?s Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be comprised of deep-water coarse clastics charged by the Kimmeridge Clay and sealed by a Paleogene top seal. The closest well to the lead is the 210/5-1 well 11.5km to the southeast that penetrated thin sands on a high above Margarita?s Spur. Shows were encountered in the Balder Formation. On 2D seismic, the Saluki Lead is only identified as a single cycle event that dims both updip and downdip of the lead. Reservoir thickness is therefore deemed to be below seismic resolution. No clear updip pinch-out is observed, however, this may be due to the single cycle nature of the seismic reflector.

The Saluki Lead identified at the time of the 28th Round application was Paleocene in age and was a stratigraphic onlap trap comprising sands that pinched out onto the northern flank of the Margarita Spur. Subsequent mapping on the 3D survey resulted in the identification of two stacked leads at Saluki which were Paleocene and Eocene in age. However, the absence of seismic facies and positive AVO anomalies suggesting sand presence and hydrocarbons resulted in the downgrading of this opportunity.

Alsatian is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of Margarita?s Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay and the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. Within the prospect there are multiple zones/targets with varied amplitude responses. The nearest wells are wells 220/26-1 and 220/26-2 which are ~5km to the east. Cretaceous sands were observed in well 220/26-1 but not in 220/26-2. Shows in the Cretaceous were observed in both wells.

The Alsatian Prospect is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of the Margarita Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastics. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay and the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. Within the prospect there are multiple zones/targets with varied amplitude responses. The nearest wells are 220/26-1 and 220/26-2 which are ~5km to the east. Cretaceous sands were observed in well 220/26-1. Shows in the Cretaceous were observed in both wells. However, no positive AVO anomalies were observed on the 3D survey and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the prospect was downgraded and not matured.

Landseer is an undrilled Mesozoic structural high. The reservoir sands are interpreted to be Jurassic shallow water or Triassic fluvial sands in a combination trap, with a top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. There is evidence of faulting in the Triassic which separates the Landseer Lead from both down dip and up dip wells, which both have shows in the Triassic (220/26-2 and 210/5-1 respectively). The Jurassic was absent in both wells and the Triassic was sand-rich but tight. The key risk at Landseer is therefore reservoir presence (Jurassic is most likely absent) and reservoir quality of the Triassic. There is considerable uncertainty surrounding trap presence at the Landseer lead as it is reliant on fault seal separating the lead from both up dip and down dip wells, both of which were dry in the Triassic.

Landseer was identified in the application work on 2D seismic as an undrilled Mesozoic structural high. The reservoir sands were interpreted to be Jurassic shallow water or Triassic fluvial sands in a combination trap, with a top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. On 2D data during the licence application work, there was thought to be evidence of faulting in the Triassic which separated the Landseer Lead from both down-dip and up-dip wells, which both have shows in the Triassic (220/26-2 and 210/5-1 respectively). The Jurassic was absent in both wells and the Triassic was sand-rich but tight. 
However, further mapping on the 3D data has shown there is limited to no compartmentalisation between Landseer and the down-dip and up-dip wells and therefore the lead was down-graded and not matured due to high trap and reservoir risk.

Deerhound is an Upper Jurassic lead on a Mesozoic structural high with a combined structural stratigraphic trap. The high is likely to expose Permo-Triassic/Devonian deposits with potential for Jurassic shoreface sands to develop on the high. The analogue to this lead is Johan Sverdrup. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. The nearest well is Well 210/4-1 which penetrated the high 10km to the east, but did not encounter any Jurassic deposits.

Deerhound is an Upper Jurassic lead on a Mesozoic structural high with a combined structural stratigraphic trap. The high is likely to expose Permo-Triassic/Devonian deposits with potential for Jurassic reservoir sands to have been preserved on the high in isolated lows. The analogue to this lead is Johan Sverdrup. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. The nearest well is Well 210/4-1 which penetrated the high 10km to the east, but did not encounter any Jurassic deposits. On 2D data the lead had a low geological possibility of success and more detailed mapping on the 3D seismic led to a further downgrading of the lead due to the absence of seismic facies indicative of Upper Jurassic sands as well as the absence of a well-defined trap.

Alano is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. Alano is updip of the Cretaceous sands penetrated by the 210/10-1 well in a stratigraphically younger sequence. This well penetrated a thick, high net to gross interval of sands which were dry. There are similarities between the seismic facies of the sand-rich interval penetrated by well 210/10-1 and the seismic facies at the younger Alano Prospect.

description:
Alano is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. Alano is updip of the Cretaceous sands penetrated by the 210/10-1 well in a stratigraphically younger sequence. This well penetrated a thick, high net to gross interval of sands which were dry. 
However, no positive AVO anomalies were observed on the 3D survey and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the prospect was downgraded and not matured.

Greyhound is an Upper Jurassic lead on a Mesozoic structural high with a combined structural stratigraphic trap. The high is likely to expose Permo-Triassic/Devonian deposits with potential for Jurassic shoreface sands to develop on the high. The analogue to this lead is Johan Sverdrup. Charge is interpreted to be from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. The nearest well is Well 210/13-1 to the south of the Greyhound Lead. This well did not encounter any Jurassic sequences and was plugged and abandoned dry after no hydrocarbon indications were observed.

Broholmer is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap to the west of the Alano Prospect in a stratigraphically younger sequence. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. Similar to the Alano Prospect, the Broholmer Prospect is updip of the Cretaceous sands penetrated by the 210/10-1 well in a stratigraphically younger sequence. This well penetrated a thick, high net to gross interval of sands which were dry. On 2D seismic lines, the Broholmer Prospect is identified as a number of bright, single cycle reflectors which onlap onto the slope margin of the East Shetland Platform.

Broholmer is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. The key risk is seal; seat seal is deemed high risk due to the potential of onlap onto Triassic sands and fault seal is deemed high risk based on potential late fault movement after charge. No positive AVO anomalies were observed and the seismic facies did not show any evidence for coarse clastics. As a result, the prospect was downgraded and not matured.

Shepherd is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap to the south of the Manet Ridge. The reservoir is interpreted to be shallow water coarse clastics charged from the Magnus Basin by the Kimmeridge Clay, with the top seal formed by Cretaceous mudstones. Updip of the Shepherd Prospect, 211/2-1 penetrated younger Cretaceous deposits which did not encounter shows. The well was plugged and abandoned as dry. On 2D lines, the Shepherd Prospect is generally observed as single cycle and more rarely, multi-cycle bright seismic events. On a number of 2D lines, downdip amplitude dimming and/or cutoffs can be observed.

Camus is interpreted as the syn-rift fill of an Upper Jurassic half-graben. The reservoir is interpreted to be both shallow-water and genetically related deep-water coarse clastics. Charge is from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Upper Jurassic/Cretaceous mudstones. The trap is defined by both stratigraphic pinch-outs and fault seal. Updip of the Camus Prospect are two wells; Well 211/1A-1 to the west did not penetrate any Upper Jurassic, but penetrated sands in the Lower to Mid Jurassic and Triassic with shows in the Lower Jurassic. To the east, Well 211/2-1 also did not penetrate an Upper Jurassic sequence, but shows were observed in sands in the Lower Jurassic and Triassic. In both wells, the Lower Jurassic and Triassic are interpreted to be tight whilst the Upper Jurassic is interpreted to have pinched out downdip.

The Camus Prospect is a combination trap in an Upper Jurassic half-graben. The reservoir is interpreted to be both shallow-water and genetically related deep-water coarse clastics. Charge is from the Kimmeridge Clay with the top seal formed by Upper Jurassic/Cretaceous mudstones. The trap is defined by both stratigraphic pinch-outs and fault seal. The key risk is seal with the prospect seal dependent on reservoir sands juxtaposed across faults with Triassic sands and on onlap on to Triassic sands. The absence of seismic facies and positive AVO anomalies to suggest both porous sand presence and hydrocarbons, as well as the high risk trap, resulted in the downgrading of this opportunity.

This lead is defined by a pinch-out to the north west, west and south east with the down-dip closing contour arbitrarily at 4000m. This lead lies within another remnant Upper Jurassic basin in block 211/1. There is no clearly identified fairway that could source sand into the basin. It is believed that there is a very high risk on the presence and quality of the reservoir. The mapped area is 35kmÂ² from spill down to the 4000m closing contour, the apex at 3525m MSL results in a column height of 475m. The column height is large so the mapped area was taken as the P10 case. The P50 case was a 30kmÂ² area. The P10 reservoir thickness was taken as 25% of the average thickness of the Magnus Sandstone Member of 200m.The P90 case was thin, only 5m, so the P50 case was 27.5m. Net to gross, porosity, oil saturation and recovery factors were taken from the Magnus field data.

Broholmer is a Cretaceous stratigraphic onlap trap to the west of the Alano Prospect in a stratigraphically younger sequence. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits charged from the Kimmeridge Clay in the Magnus Basin with Cretaceous mudstones forming the top seal. Similar to the Alano Prospect, the Broholmer Prospect is updip of the Cretaceous sands penetrated by the 210/10-1 well in a stratigraphically younger sequence. This well penetrated a thick, high net to gross interval of sands which were dry. On 2D seismic lines, the Broholmer Prospect is identified as a number of bright, single cycle reflectors which onlap onto the slope margin of the East Shetland Platform.

The prospect comprises Early Cretaceous submarine fan sands in a stratigraphic trap on the northern edge of the Magnus Basin. The reservoir is located at depths of 5500-6000 m TVDSS. Hydrocarbon charge is from Late Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay source rocks in the Magnus Basin. Hydrocarbon type is likely to be gas condensate based on the depth and temperature of the reservoir. Early Cretaceous sands of K30 age are present in the Magnus Basin wells 210/10-1 and 210/15b-4 to the southwest. The sands in 210/10-1 display a similar mounded geometry to the prospect facies. The Moluag fan sands are interpreted to have a north-eastern provenance. Reservoir presence is viewed as low risk. K30 sands in 210/10-1 and 210/15b-4 are poor quality at depths of 5000 m TVDSS with porosities which average 4Ã¢â‚¬â€œ6% (range 3Ã¢â‚¬â€œ12%). Factors which could lead to improved reservoir quality for Moluag include different provenance and cleaner sands, early charge and over-pressures. Reservoir effectiveness is currently assessed as high risk.

The prospect comprises Early Cretaceous submarine fan sands in a stratigraphic trap on the northern
edge of the Magnus Basin. The reservoir is located at depths of 5500–6000 m TVDSS.
Hydrocarbon charge is from Late Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay source rocks in the Magnus Basin.

The Lead comprises potential Middle to Late Jurassic sands preserved in a small basin on the Manet High, northwest of the Magnus Basin. The sediments are stratigraphically trapped beneath the BCU with Cretaceous mudstones forming a top seal. The depth of the reservoir is 3800?4300 m TVDSS. Hydrocarbons are charged locally from the Late Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation, which is part of the reservoir interval. The hydrocarbon type is likely to be oil.

Structural dip provides closure to the S, up dip seal to the N is provided by stratigraphic pinchout beneath the BCU. Lateral seal to the W and E is provided by pinchout of the sands. As the lead is located where the shale prone Brent/Dunlin has been totally removed by erosion, base seal is dependent on sealing capacity of Triassic sands and shales, and thus carries additional risk. The age of the interval constituting the lead is outside the area where the U. Jurassic can be mapped with confidence. It is oriented N - S and is clearly controlled by N - S trending faults. It is thus likely that the anomaly forms a channelized slope feeder for the greater Magnus depositional system, thus the sands were sourced from the NNW and fed into the basin towards the basin floor in the Magnus area to the S.

A single prospect had been identified, named the Tiger Prospect, in Upper Jurassic Magnus sands, deposited as a separate lobe to the submarine fan sandstones developed in the Magnus Field less than 5km to the west. Petrophysical analysis in the Magnus field shows that the sands are of excellent quality with porosities in the 18% to 24% range (average 21%) and permeabilities of up to 950 mD. The Upper and Lower Kimmeridge Clays were postulated to provide top, bottom and lateral seals to the prospect as well as the source rock for the petroleum system.

Mossat is an upthrown trap in which the primary reservoir is Brent Group and secondary reservoir is Banks Group. The prospect is located within an actively generating hydrocarbon kitchen. The Fjellrose closure is defined at Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) level. It is a simple fault block with a robust structural closure, sealed by overlying Cretaceous shales.

The highest risk is the quality of the reservoir, using 6201-11-1 as the closest analogue, Charge would also be medium to low risk as the 6201/11-1 well had a 203m oil column from a similar source area. The area of mapped closure is 3.7km², with the apex at 3434mMSL and the spill point at 3510mMSL. This gives a prognosed column height of 76m. 
The mapped prospect area was used as a P50 case in the volumetrics. Porosity range (P10-P90) was 10 - 20% based on analogues, the net to gross range used was 40 - 60% and a shape factor correction range of 0.4 - 0.6 was used. Water saturation values of 0.2 - 0.5, and formation volumes factors of 1.2 - 1.4 were also used in the volumetrics input, along with recovery factors of 20 - 40%.

The trap consists of a wedge, interpreted to be U. Jurassic and containing significant sand content, onlapping onto the SE flank of the Margarita Spur. Steep dip provides structural closure to the SE, up dip seal to the NW is provided by stratigraphic pinchout between underlying Brent/Dunlin shales and the BCU. Lateral seal to the SW is provided by a combination of pinchout and shale out of the sands, and to the NE by shale out of the sands associated with a N - S trending cross basin fault. The proposed U. Jurassic reservoir sands are interpreted to have been deposited as a more proximal
equivalent within the overall greater Magnus depositional system. They are likely to have been deposited in a submarine environment by turbiditic flows. The abundant internal geometries seen within the interval point to a highly variable facies distribution, poorly understood at present, but with improving data quality and greater regional geologic understanding, becoming better defined.

Sybil is a stratigraphic trap defined by Upper Jurassic sands on lapping onto the southeast flank of the Margarita spur/Manet ridge. The extension of Sybil to the northeast is poorly defined due to poor seismic data quality and there is a possible up dip connection to Basil. Top seal is provided by Cromer Knoll shales and base and side seal by the shaly Brent /Dunlin, Heather and Kimmeridge clay section. The reservoir at Sybil is interpreted to be Upper Jurassic sand, deposited as part of the channelized feeder system to the Magnus fan to the south.

The Hammerhead prospect is located 3km north of the 214/30-1 Laxford gas discovery well which was drilled near the crest of a mud mound high, onto which the Hammerhead prospect on-laps. The Laxford well (214/30-1) contains a condensed (or non-complete) Vaila Formation sequence (55ft) which is much thinner than surrounding wells (which can extend to >500ft). However due to the nature of the high, the sands penetrated on the mud mound are younger and thinner than those interpreted at Hammerhead and therefore are not a direct analogue.
Hammerhead sits in a stratigraphic low created through differential loading of turbidite flows onto mobile shales which created mud-mounds. This deposition was also disturbed by igneous intrusions and possible reactivation of deeply seated faults. The prospect dips to the north-west where it is interpreted to shale-out onto a localised mud high and potentially spills and fills deeper lying ponds. Up-dip, the prospect on-laps onto a prominent mud high that appears to have grown during turbidite deposition. This mud high separates the Hammerhead fan from feeder channels on the south-east of the high.

description: The Basking prospect is located in the south of block 214/30b. The prospect targets the T34 Vaila sands similar to the Sandvoe prospect. First analysed by Centric in 2014, the identified high amplitude anomaly suggest hydrocarbon presence due to conformance. Well 206/5-4 encountered 25-100m of overlying limestone above the Vaila sandstone reservoir and this can be predicted to seal the Basking prospect along with the cruiser Fm Shales above. Sourced by the Kimmeridge Clay, the prospect is within the oil window, and hydrocarbons are migrated into the basin by carrier beds and extensional faults in the cretaceous. During basin modelling, it is possible that the Basking and Sandvoe prospects are located within a migration shadow and therefore, the prospects would need considerable and extensive further modelling. Well 214/29-1 located 5.5km SW of the basking prospect encountered thick clay beds with interbeds of silts which do not confirm but indicate the Vaila Fm.
The Basking prospect is located between Top Commodore and Top Royal Sovereign Formations.

Cnut prospect. Mostly in Norwegian waters (total area = 67,731 acres). Palaeocene turbidite fan sands in closure at Top Balder Tuff. CoS = 18%. Relinquishment: the results of chemostratigraphy and heavy mineral analyses did not validate GDF SUEZ hypothesis that sands sourced from East Greeland could reach the Cnut structure. The Shetland platform and Western Norway are today seen as the most likely sand supplies for the area. Clear geometries supporting sand presence have been observed on some 2D lines. This does not however apply to the large Cnut Prospect where sub-parallel reflectors are mapped at the location of the 4-way closure. Hence res effectiveness downgraded.
The Early Palaeocene Sullom sandstone was the primary reservoir target for the Cnut structure and the nearby leads.

The COTN prospect was initially interpreted as an extensive Lower Eocene fan complex with an amplitude supported up-dip stratigraphic closure (see Figures 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3) with estimated in place gas volumes of 5.1Tcf. 
The results of the seismic reprocessing and inversion, and rock physics analysis have clearly indicated the absence of gas saturated reservoir sands within the Eocene. 
Detailed seismic to well ties and event mapping attribute the identified amplitude anomaly to the presence of Balder formation volcanics. A subsequent ‘exotic reservoir study’ has determined that the Balder Formation volcanics are likely to be of non-reservoir quality.

opportunity_comment: The Eowyn lead is located in UKCS blocks 219/23, 219/24, 219/27, 219/28 & 219/29, licence P1936. The licence was awarded as a 6 year frontier licence in January 2013 following the 27th licensing round application. It has since been part relinquished as per frontier licence obligations. The trap is defined by a stratigraphic pinch-out in all directions. The reservoir is thought to be analagous to the Flett Formation deep marine sandstones of the Faroe-Shetland Basin. The intial interpretation of the reservoir was conducted on 2D seismic, driven by anomalous amplitudes identified within the Balder Formation.
hc_case_comment: Current risking focusses on the amplitude anomaly as defined on recent 3D seismic data, therefore discarding the original (27th Round) Eowyn lead concept
shape_file: Shape file name: Eowyn lead_post-Balder amplitude anomlay
trap_type_comment: Based on the 2016 evaluation, the Eowyn trap is still largely stratigraphic in nature and in all directions, with Eocene shales expected to form top, lateral and base seals to the reservoir interval. The exception is the presence of a small four-way-dip (4WD) closed structure ~2km2 within the northern part of the anomalous amplitude, of which is described in more detail below.
key_evaluation_comment: The thin sand encountered by 219/28-2Z was later confirmed by biostratigraphy as being within the Balder T50 interval. During 2015Ã¢â‚¬Â16 an evaluation of the area benefitted from new 3D seismic data (TGS Brendan Basin 2014) across the licence and full integration of all the studies undertaken in the area, including several new studies. The new interpretation provided an improved understanding of depositional environments and revealed that the Eowyn lead outline was in fact an isopach thick (Top Balder - Top Lamba) resulting from incision of a muddy shelf/slope. Accommodation generated by this incison was infilled by Eocene shales. Remaining potential for the lead is restricted to anomalous amplitudes identified above the Balder seismic marker, which display a class III AVO response. Given the extensive work carried out regarding the imapact of volacanic activity on the petroleum system in this area, the anomalous amplitudes are interpreted to be related to hydrothermal vent complexes, where the vents act as gas/fluid conduits to the Early Eocene (Balder level). However, caution is applied to this interepretation as reservoir facies of this age have not been encountered by any offset wells.

description: The view taken by GDF at the 27th Round (2013) was that Eowyn was a large stratigraphic trap of ponded sediment within a depositional low. Deposition of a tectonically controlled fan system was interpreted to infill palaeo-Â?topography controlled by sill emplacement. A gas influx into well 219/29-Â?2(z) was detected from thin sand interpreted to be within the Flett Fm deep marine sands, resulting in an interpretation of missed pay.

description: The facies prediction of the Arwen lead went from sands, to incision of a muddy and shaly slope. However, it was also recognized that it could also be a feature caused by hydrothermal activity, being the surface imprints due to magma activity below. Analog features to Arwen and Eowyn caused by magma tectonism are observable in the Norwegian Vøring Basin at the Top Balder Formation level. No matter which of the two models the conclusion was the same that Palaeocene reservoir presence is considered unlikely.

Bernard is a Paleogene stratigraphic onlap trap that pinches out onto the northern flank of Margarita?s Spur. The reservoir is interpreted to be deep-water coarse clastic deposits sourced from the west and / or southwest. The Oxnard and Newport prospects are three and four-way dip closed structure mapped at both Base Cretaceous and Top Skagerrak levels. The maximum spill for the Oxnard prospect is constrained by data availability on licence, however, may have greater extent in the P10 case. The top sealing mechanism for both prospects are the shales and chalk of the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll and Upper Cretaceous Chalk Group respectively, which are proven regional seals. Consistent with elsewhere in the CNS, the source of oil is the mature Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation. The dominant migration route into the Oxnard and Newport prospects are via lateral charge from the mature Upper Jurassic depocenter to the east in the East Central Graben.

Stratigraphic pinchout trap with Lower Cretaceous Kopervik Sandstone reservoir. The mapped seismic package lies directly above the Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) and is defined by pinchout of the top Lower Cretaceous pick (Valhall Formation) onto the BCU. Deep water submarine fan sequences are likely to form the reservoir sequence in this prospect. A sediment entry point for a 'channel complex' is interpreted to be present at or near the prospect crest and is possibly controlled by active Jurassic - Early Cretaceous faults that intersect the main east - west channel boundary fault. Petrophysical evaluations of the 22/21-4 and 22/21-7 wells have interpreted the intervals in the Sola Formation to be marly sands containing hydrocarbons with levels of 60-65% hydrocarbon saturation. The main risk for this play is reservoir presence and quality and there is a high risk of trap failure along the combined pinch out and fault edge towards the northwest and north.

The lead is delineated by AVO extraction at the Upper Palaeocene level as described in the previous section. There is a series of strong AVO anomaly patches, however each one is small ranging from only 1 to 3 km2, associated with the structural nose continuing towards Arbroath Field with probably 3-way dip closure and stratigraphic pinchout or shale out towards the NE, where the edge is limited at 22/22a-1 which was dry at Forties Sand but encountered no Cromarty Sand. This setting is similar to Adgestone Lead particularly the 'core area', however, the AVO anomaly is rather patchy. 
Biddenden Lead is defined with an area of 17.4km2 at the maximum closing contour of approx 2665m, providing a vertical column of 30m in the maximum case. The strongest AVO anomaly is roughly concordant with a small 4-way dip closure (core area), with an area of 2.9km2  and a 10 to 20 m vertical column.

The Tenterden Lead is a four way dip closed anticline at Top Lower Cretaceous level. It has, however, not been possible to identify the presence of any sand development within the Lower Cretaceous here so it is not considered a viable target. Offset to this anticline is a major fault with hanging wall closure induced by Zechstein salt upwelling at depth. Closure is probable at Jurassic level but the current 3D seismic data is poorly imaged in this area due to faulting, presence of salt and inversion with steeply dipping beds within the Upper Jurassic section. There is likely to be an upside element of stratigraphic closure against the main bounding fault to the east. Stacked Jurassic sands pay is possible although the most likely reservoir target within the Jurassic here is thought to be the Volgian Ribble and/or Freshney sands as seen in nearby well 22/22b-2y. Depth to top reservoir is estimated at approximately 4,250m.

The Adgestone Lead is delineated by AVO extraction at the Upper Palaeocene level. There is a strong AVO anomaly associated with the structural nose continuing towards Arbroath Field with probably a 3-way dip closure and a stratigraphic pinchout towards the NE and potentially NW. This favourable combination of AVO anomaly and the structural setting, the Ã‚Â¿Core AreaÃ‚Â¿ of the Adgestone Lead is located in Block 22/22d and defined with an area of 3.2km2 at the maximum closing contour of 2700m, providing a vertical column of 40m in the maximum case.  The AVO anomaly continues towards the E/SE to form the Adgestone Extension Lead and suggests the potential for much larger reserves. However, the magnitude of the anomaly weakens and is not related to a structural component suggesting the anomaly may be related to lithology and or an increase in isochore of the Sele/Cromarty. It will be necessary to reassess the anomaly and the well results after the award of the block.

description: The Culzean N/NW prospect consists of two stacked prospective reservoir intervals. The deeper of the two prospective intervals is the regionally extensive Pentland Formation (mid Callovian-mid Oxfordian in the Culzean area) coastal plain which underlies an Upper Jurassic interval with potential for shoreface and deepwater sand reservoir development. The trap for both intervals is a 2-way fault, 1 way stratigraphic pinch out, which in part relies on a salt ridge to the west, and dip closure to the east. The Pentland trap is more extensive than the Upper Jurassic trap. The Pentland interval relies on a base seal of the Triassic Jonathan mudstone interval, a proven pressure seal at the Culzean discovery. The base seal for the Upper Jurassic would be intra Heather Formation shales. The top seal for both segments is a combination of intra Heather Formation shales and the Cromer Knoll Group marls. The charge route into the prospect is from the Lomond deep to the east where the Kimmeridge, Heather and Pentland Formations are all mature.

configuration, but is not without precedent. The figure from the Millenium Atlas illustrates an analogous occurrence of sealing faults on the Conoco-Phillips operated Judy Field (UK block 30/7).
The remaining play elements are considered low risk, with the presence of high quality Skagerrak sandstones proven down dip of Seagull by the 22/29-7 Janus well, and ubiquitous hydrocarbon charge along the west-east chain of structures extending from Seagull to Commander. 
The Seagull flank prospect is likely to be gas-charged.

The Bass Prospect is a stratigraphic updip pinch-out trap within the Maureen Sandstone, with potential upside in the Mey Sandstone. The hydrocarbon distribution in Everest suggests an initial oil charge, displaced by gas as the source matured to leave a small oil rim. The Bass prospect is situated in an intervening saddle region above which the Maureen thinned through attenuation or non-deposition of the 'M1 Lower' unit. However, high net to gross reservoir sections are developed in 22/5a-11 and 22/10a-8z; the wells immediately north and south of Bass respectively. Hence, there is a high probability of encountering Maureen reservoir at Bass. There is a risk of reservoir degradation, principally through incorporation of non-reservoir, often chalky material which slumped off the Jaeren High. Such intervals are common in East Everest.
The Bass prospect is located close to the pinch-out edge of the Mey Sandstone. This is a significant, secondary reservoir in East Everest but not developed in Fleming and therefore represents potential upside in Bass.

The COTN prospect was initially interpreted as an extensive Lower Eocene fan complex with an amplitude supported up-dip stratigraphic closure (see Figures 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3) with estimated in place gas volumes of 5.1Tcf. 
The results of the seismic reprocessing and inversion, and rock physics analysis have clearly indicated the absence of gas saturated reservoir sands within the Eocene. 
Detailed seismic to well ties and event mapping attribute the identified amplitude anomaly to the presence of Balder formation volcanics. A subsequent ‘exotic reservoir study’ has determined that the Balder Formation volcanics are likely to be of non-reservoir quality.

This well is interpreted to have penetrated the interval outside of the fan complex associated with the Dalmatian Prospect.

Trap: 100%, Seal: 80%, Reservoir: 40%, Migration: 70%, Total: 22%.   .   EnQuest uses a probabilistic method for the calculation of resource estimates in exploration targets. Usually input variables are entered as normal distributions, except GRV which is entered as log-normal, and except where offset data indicates otherwise. Blenheim Prospect is a Paleocene synclinal pinchout trap with fault seal on the northern side which exhibits strong amplitude and AVO anomalies. Thin sands found within the Paleocene at well 29/16-1are seen as an indicator of a nearby sand fairway. The postulated "Blenheim-Watling" fairway differs from those proven and postulated to the North in that it is believed to overly and infill the topography created by a series of Early-Mid Paleocene Mass Transport Complexes. These MTCs are clearly visible in seismic across the application area and tie with Early-Mid Paleocene slump deposits in 29/16-1. Later input of Paleocene turbidite sands flowing from the South West off the shelf are postulated to have ponded immediately above these MTCs, with turbiditic flow possibly influenced by the slump scar. The Pilchard structure is a fault-bounded Triassic prospect, located west-northwest of Puffin. As the seismic is of poor quality in this area only a rather poor interpretation of top Skagerrak and top Smith Bank has been possible and DHI indications were not visible. Where present, the Skagerrak reservoir is expected to be of good quality. Key risk are lateral fault seal and top seal, the latter because several substructures of the neighbouring Puffin structure were identified as blown traps. Furthermore, another key risk could be presence of reservoir, although at the moment this is not captured in the POS definition for this prospect. Company CoS = 52%.

The Kite prospect is a grounded out and eroded Triassic fault block, analogous and on trend with the Puffin discovery. The primary risks identified with this prospect are hydrocarbon charge and reservoir presence / effectiveness. The primary reservoirs for this prospect are sandstones of the Triassic Skagerrak Formation. Differentiation on seismic data of the Skagerrak and the Smith Bank Formations is currently very uncertain and so the reservoir thickness is uncertain. The trap is a robust 4-way dip closed Triassic fault block or 'pod'. If Jurassic sands of the Pentland and/or Fulmar Formation directly overlie the pod, then these may act as thief zones that leak towards the Puffin Field or limit column height within the underlying Skagerrak Formation.

Puffin Deep structure is a Triassic prospect, located west of Puffin. The structure has been partially tested by well 29/9A-1, which drilled through a fault into the Smith Bank shales and did not encounter the Skagerrak. Uncertainty exists in the presence of sufficient Skagerrak reservoir due to the fact that the seismic is of poor quality over this structure and therefore no DHI indications are visible. Key risk is seal, since several substructures of the neighbouring Puffin structure were identified as blown traps (likely related to faulting in the overburden and creation of leak paths). The Regan Lead is located right in the downthrown block of the Cordelia Prospect, slightly North-West of the Puffin field and of well 29/9a-1. 
A roll over closure against the Cordelia bounding fault, this lead is sealed by both Jurassic and early Cretaceous mudstones and possibly charged via the same sources as the Puffin Field. 'it is very difficult, from a structural standpoint, not to expect reservoir presence in the lead.'. 
However, no Skagerrak reservoir has been encountered by well 29/9a-1, less than 5Km from the lead: this is not surprising considering the heterogeneity of lithologies and structural complexity of the Puffin Field. 
The main risks for the Regan Lead are : trap effectiveness (0.60) and reservoir presence (0.55), both factors linked to the seismic data quality.

Well 29/9a-1 discovered 120 ft of light hydrocarbons in thick Mey sands (in excess of 300 ft gross thickness) and well 29/4a-1 encountered 90 ft gas shows in 465 ft Mey Sands. Looking closer at the log characters the Mey Sandsare generally much thicker than the Cromarty sands but with overall less porosity. They are interbedded with Paleocene silts and claystones representing periods of non-deposition and tectonic quiescence. Hence, these sands have been interpreted as sand sheets or slope apron fans composed by sand lobes and intraformational sealing units. Regional isopachs, DECC Promote UK 2014, suggest the Lista thickens to the south west away from the 29/9a-1 and 29/9a-5 wells, across and beyond the mapped four-way dip closure. It is thought the thickening of the gross interval is related to presence of a thickened Mey sequence. Reservoir quality is seen here as key risk as the sands are likely to become more silty laterally towards the edge of the sand sheet as verified by well 29/9a-5  where poor quality Paleocene sands where encountered.

The lead is located at the very distal end of the Forties Sandstone fairway and as a result sands, where developed, are thin. Throughout the area of the license requested, the Kimmeridge Clay is in the oil window and actively generating hydrocarbons at present. The prospect is not based on a structural or stratigraphic concept, as we are in a graben and the mudstone is present over the entirety of the area.  Our strategic plan, technical and other work to date suggests that the acreage requested is optimally located to facilitate an effort to cause the initial testing of the economic viability of unconventional oil production from the Kimmeridge by drilling a minimum 5,000' lateral wellbore that is subjected to a "multi-frack" completion procedure.  License 1 is not as sand rich as license 2.  It is comparable to license 3.  The average temperature is between that of License 2 and 3.  If initial test wells are ultimately drilled on all three licenses, the impact of the subtle differences in temperature and sand richness will start to be understood.  As we are not applying for licenses in pursuit of conventional oil and gas prospects, the above lead prospect new play discovery volume format may not be the best way to set forth information relating to volumes for producible oil from unconventional shale.  We have attempted to fill in the information, but encourage that the reader refer to Appendix B for a more detailed discussion of volumes (in place and recoverable) and the technical chance of success.

The 3/2-7 prospect is a 3 way dip closed structure with an eastern boundary defined by the Hutton/Ninian boundary fault. It lies half way between Hutton and Ninian, southeast of NW Hutton. It is penetrated on the flank by the 3/2-7 well, drilled in November 1984. The well encountered oil stained Ness sands, with the Tarbert and uppermost Ness eroded. Seismic imaging of the prospect is poor resulting in an uncertain structure and volumetrics.  Fairfield's detailed work on NW Hutton, 8km to the NW, has increased confidence that the prospect can be developed and tied back if further work confirms the base case volumetric estimate of 34mmbbls STOIIP. Appraisal uncertainty remains on the STOIIP due to possibly a reduced GRV as a result of a more complex faulted crestal structure, as observed on Ninian, or a long transition zone across the Brent and reduced reservoir pressure, affected by production from Ninian and Hutton. These uncertainties could reduce STOIIP from 34 to 20mmbbo.  Four vertical wells drilled in the 3/2b prospect could recover around 14mmbbls. Two producers could each recover 7mmbbls from a base case STOIIP of 34mmbbls.   Subject to appraisal, current estimates show that this four well count could be reduced to 3 wells recovering almost the same volume although further data is required to gain confidence in this development scenario. Facilities design would be minimal with a tieback to either Ninian (16km to the south) or the planned Darwin facilities (8km to the NE). The risk of the 3/2-7 prospect is considered to be low, with the 3/2-7 well in the block de-risking the prospect.

Heimdal target with good CoS but possible heavy, viscous oil. However, the sedimentological model and seismic interpretation imply that the Heimdal reservoir target pinches out immediately updip and therefore may not have access to meteoric waters, reducing the risk of heavy oil. The Heimdal Sand can be split into three lobes, L1, L2 and L3. The L1 basinal sands on-lap from the east and are poorly represented on the block.
The L2 and L3 sands were deposited from a medium scale submarine channel-fan system seen on seismic as a discrete lobe with a 'bird's foot'? morphology. 
The feeder channel crossed the East Shetland Platform and spilled onto the Transitional Shelf near well 3/27-2. This access point is at the intersection of a re-entrant fault at the edge of the platform. On the shelf-slope the sediments form braided mid fan channel lobes that shale out to the east and south east. The lobes can be separated out on well data and mapped on the 2D seismic as distinct intervals. The proximal L2 and L3 Heimdal sands have net to gross ratios in excess of 80%, porosities of 30% or more, and excellent permeabilities in the order of 20D. Parameters entered cf cp3_22_1 to _3.

Throughout the area of the license requested, the Kimmeridge Clay is in the oil window and actively generating hydrocarbons at present. The prospect is not based on a structural or stratigraphic concept, as we are in a graben and the mudstone is present over the entirety of the area.  Our strategic plan, technical and other work to date suggests that the acreage requested is optimally located to facilitate an effort to cause the initial testing of the economic viability of unconventional oil production from the Kimmeridge by drilling a minimum 5,000' lateral wellbore that is subjected to a "multi-frack" completion procedure.  This license area is sand poor and has a lower burial/temperature profile when compared to the other two licenses.  As we are not applying for licenses in pursuit of conventional oil and gas prospects, the above lead prospect new play discovery volume format may not be the best way to set forth information relating to volumes for producible oil from unconventional shale.  We have attempted to fill in the information, but encourage that the reader refer to Appendix B for a more detailed discussion of volumes (in place and recoverable) and the technical chance of success.

description: The Ockley reservoir is an intra-unit of the Lower Cretaceous Hod Formation comprising of chalk with varying degrees of clay content from 5 to 30%. It is a very low permeability (0.005-0.05mD) and uniform reservoir with an average porosity of 12% in the hydrocarbon interval. There are 9 distinct successions within Ockley that correlate over large distances to the regional wells. The chalk is interpreted to be in-situ with deposition in a slope/basin setting. There is no evidence of remobilisation.

Ockley is a discovered resource in the same UK Licence block P2455 in Quadrant 30 (see Figure 2). It overlays the Oakwood discovery at approximate burial depth of 12,500ft TVDSS. The field was discovered by BP in 1983 with the 30/01c-2 exploration well and the well abandoned afterwards due to very low-test rates. Between 2008 and 2012 Maersk Oil drilled three appraisal wells (30/1d-10, 30/1d-12 and 30/1d-12z) to further access the viability of the field. Tests in two of the wells (30/1d-10 and 30/1d-12z) failed to achieve stable economic rates. However, the test performance of the 30/1d-12z well following propped and acid fracture stimulations with approximately 70% of the total 4MMscf/d well test rate coming from the one failed propped hydraulic fracture stage, gave some room for optimism for a possible development route for the discovery. 
Ockley is a high pressure (11,000psi) and high temperature (310 degF) gas condensate Hod chalk discovery with extremely low porosity (10 - 12%) and matrix permeability (10 to 50?D). This re-evaluation work covered subsurface re-assessment of the Ockley accumulation to provide Harbour Energy a view on the In-place and recoverable volumes. The work scope also explored available well drilling, completion and stimulation technologies/techniques that would allow better performance success to the prospective wells. The results and lessons learnt from the Maersk 30/1d-12z well formed the basis for the well performance improvement studies undertaken.

The undeveloped Jacqui field tested oil and gas condensate in Upper Jurassic mass flow sands. The different fluid types at different pressure regimes suggest the field is horizontally and vertically compartmentalised due to the presence of multiple sand fans and faulting. Despite this complexity, the field is seen as having siginifcant upside potential due to having only encountered HDT in all 3 wells, with recently processed PreSDM data showing undrilled sand fans, fault compartments and that the gas condensate 30/13-4 well has not drilled the crest of the Northerly Fan structure.

The Baffin discovery is situated in the Jacqui sub-basin, in an inverted Upper Jurassic feature that is dip closed against a principal east-west fault system. The basin has three existing discoveries, all testing hydrocarbons within the Jacqui Sandstone Member of the Heather Formation (primary target).  The structure is a faulted anticline with five main compartments that are defined on the basis of fluid type and PVT data. The discovery has been tested by 3 wells, the 30/13-4 and the 30/13-6 wells, and the 30/13-3 well that was drilled in a separate fault block and encountered a restricted hydrocarbon column. The main risk is reservoir connectivity as each discovery well has shown different PVT and pressure data. Compartmentalisation is considered to be both stratigraphic and structural. The 30/13-3 West compartment, is located directly to the west of the compartment containing the discovery well 30/13-3 tested oil, which tested oil with a GOR of 858 scf/bbl.

The Janis prospect is identified as an amplitude anomaly within the Palaeocene located in the north of block 30/13b. The prospect is seen as stratigraphic pinchout of the Andrew sands southwest onto a palaeo-high with dip closure to the northwest, northeast and southeast.   On the PGS Mega Merge dataset, the absolute maximum peak and minimum trough have been derived for a window between the top Sele and top Ekofisk. When the Andrew Sandstone shows are superimposed they show a general conformance with the amplitudes.  There also appears to be amplitude cut-off conformance with dip.

The Primary Target is the Triassic Joanne Sandstones which forms a series of stacked fluvial channel and sheet flood sandstones, interbedded with overbank shales. This unit is the main Pre-Cretaceous reservoir in the adjacent Judy Field, and is widespread in it's distribution. The deeper Middle Triassic Julius Claystone seismic marker allows mapping of the Joanne reservoir over block 30/13b  Well 30/13-3, which tested oil in Upper Jurassic, drilled the downdip flank of the structure and encountered the Triassic Skagerrak sandstones with good shows at TD.  No clear top seal could be identified in the well, however 30/13-1 to the south of Jennifer tested oil in the Triassic Joanne Sands. Company CoS = 16%.

The fill and spill of a Palaeocene aged palaeo-anticline with the growth of the Orion diapir may have resulted in the trapping of hydrocarbons against the northeastern flank of the Orion structure. The palaeo-anticline is formed by differential compaction around a Jurassic and Early Cretaceous NW-SE trending fault or small late stage movement of the same fault. However, the end Palaeocene anticline may be a seismic artefact resulting from pull-up from a high velocity Palaeocene lineament. Iris also overlies a gas chimney and can also be explained by direct charging from a Jurassic age fault.

Tommeliten Alpha is a chalk discovery drilled in 1976, in Block 1/9, Norwegian North Sea. The main reservoirs are the Ekofisk and Tor Formations.  
In 2003, appraisal well 1/9-7 T3 was drilled to further appraise the Tommeliten Alpha discovery and test a Jurassic exploration target. The well confirmed the western extension of the chalk discovery but the Jurassic was dry. New geological and reservoir models confirmed the development feasibility of the discovery. 
Development was put on hold because of capacity constraints at Ekofisk.  
In 2012 an alternative facility concept was identified and development evaluations were restarted.

The Devonian/ Permian discovery well, 30/25a-4, lies within a three way dip closure north of the Ardmore/ Argyll Field and flowed 500 bopd, although, the reservoir quality is described as marginal.  New Chalk Play: The overlying Cretaceous Hod, Tor and Ekofisk Formations have a log signature indicative of allochthonous chalk units. Hydrocarbon shows are observed on the mudlogs. Petrophysical calculations indicate hydrocarbons. The blocks are located in an area of faulting and the trapping mechanism at Permian/ Devonian level is tilted fault blocks. It is anticipated that during post hydrocarbon charging of Devonian and Permian compartments periodic movement and faulting occurred allowing hydrocarbons to breach reservoir seals. Gaian was originally defined on legacy 2D data and was a large structural closure at Top Palaeozoic with primary
reservoir being Permian Rotliegendes sandstones. Interpretation of the new 3D seismic has resulted in Gaian
being split into two distinct east and west structures with similar properties to Blodwyn. The proximity of Gaian
to proven Kimmeridge Clay source kitchen and favourable migration pathways has partially derisked
hydrocarbon charge for these structures. The overall chance of success for the Gaian structures have
increased, but they still remain volumetrically challenged are are likely to be sub-economic.

Wyvern is a structural ridge surrounded locally by sub-basins of Jurassic origin, which contain only early mature source rocks. Charge into this structure to fill the Permian closures therefore requires a fill and spill route from the fields of the Argyll Ridge or potentially from Iris. However, complex charge histories are required to maintain a charge route that allows oil to either directly or indirectly (i.e. by top down filling of the trap from closure in Jurassic reservoirs) fill reservoirs at the Permian level. However, the Wyvern Ridge was a sub-regional high at end Cretaceous and into the Early Tertiary, thus opening up the possibility that an early charge from the Central Graben could have been directly trapped and preserved in Wyvern. The primary reservoir is the Rotliegend aeolian sandstone. The trap is well defined on modern long-offset 3D seismic data. The dip closure occurs at the 8550 ft contour as mapped at the top Palaeozoic level. The trap geometry is robust both in time and depth

The original interpretation of Wyvern had reservoirs in the Upper Jurassic Fulmar sands, Zechstein carbonates and Rotliegendes sands. The prospect comprised two segments, an upthrown three-way fault dependent trap in the north (segment 1) and a downthrown faulted structure in the south (segment 2).
It was always recognised that there was considerable containment risk on the downthrown segment 2, and following re-interpretation on the reprocessed TOMO ML seismic, it was considered that segment 2 was no longer viable due to lack of fault seal. This re-evaluation was also applied to the southern bounding fault of segment 1, which was judged as unlikely to seal below the juxtaposition of the downthrown Jurassic/Zechstein against upthrown Permian reservoirs.

ProspectThe Basilisk Prospect is mapped as a structural trap at the Palaeozoic level, and comprises a NW-SE trending linear footwall high with two structural sub-crests, which are additionally fault-bounded to the south and east. Murcar Fulmar lead - 4 way dip closure of base Cretaceous down dip from Fergus Field - reservoir may thin from Fergus. Stacked above cp31_27_2. CoS = 40% (trap reduced 75>50%; reservoir reduced 71>50%). RF increased 30 > 36% to match company estimate reserves. Review April 2006 - resr eff 100 to 50; trap/seal 75 to 50.

Murcar Rotliegend lead - tilted fault block bounded by large N-S fault and to N by Epsilon Fault. To E and S structure spills into Fergus Field, though migration considered to have been from E rather than N as in Fergus. Reservoir presence/quality main risk - reservoir potentially Carboniferous rather that Rotliegend. CoS = 20% (downgraded by high play risk; trap reduced 70>50%). Net reservoir increased 50/40/20 m > 68/55/27 m to allow calculated reserves to approx operator estimate. Review April 2006 - outside Rotl Fairway.
Shale gas or tight gas sand play in Carboniferous Coal Measures or Namurian/Dinantian organic-rich shales.

C2 prospect - Yoredale Fm sandstone target in rift basin cf. Stainmore Trough, in heavily-faulted intra-Dinantian trap. All parameters, reserves, CoS (14.1%) provided; downgraded by source 70 > 50, migration 80 > 50%, trap 90 > 50%, seal 80 > 50%. Renamed Rockcliffe Prospex 2007 poster.

Cranesbill prospect - 4-way dip closure of top Scremerston Fm mapped on poor-quality seismic data (possibly now reprocessed). No parameters provided; entered cf. cp34_30_1. Risking based on relinquishment report.
Four way dip closure at Top Scremerston and Top Fell Sandstone levels.

Babburgh prospect - - 4-way dip closure of top Scremerston Fm mapped on poor-quality seismic data (possibly now reprocessed). No parameters provided; entered cf. cp34_30_1. Risking based on relinquishment report.

C3 prospect - Yoredale Fm sandstone target in rift basin cf. Stainmore Trough, in fault-bounded 2-way dip trap. All parameters, reserves, CoS (10.3%) provided; downgraded by source 70 > 50, migration 70 > 50%, trap 80 > 50%, seal 75 > 50%. Renamed Bamburgh Prospex 2007 poster.
Fault closed high at Fell Sandstone and Scremerston Coal levels.

Delaval prospect - well-defined 4-way dip Variscan anticlinal trap with 300 m relief; main risk is presence of good intraformational Dinantian seal. Potential reservoirs in Fell Sandstone, Scremerston Group. All parameters, 18.9% risk provided; downgraded byhigh source risk.

Lead A: This region does not have potential for Rotliegendes Leman reservoirs. Reservoirs will be either Carboniferous or Devonian in age. The closest well to the BPU closure situated on the licence has Tournaisian Cementstone Formation directly beneath the BPU; this is a very low net to gross, very tight and cemented formation with interbedded mudstones and carbonate cemented sandstones with very poor reservoir potential. Coal measures and shales within the Scremerston Formation are not present within the licence so there is a need for long range migration.
3-way fault bounded, fault block with a Lower Dinantian reservoir Fell Sandstone target. Company CoS < 10%.
Very longe-range migration from S required.

The trapping mechanism in this area is considered to be closure at the Base Permian Unconformity as seen in the majority of Carboniferous fields in the SNS. This region does not have potential for Rotliegendes Leman reservoirs as this stratigraphy was not deposited over the Mid North Sea High where this licence is situated. Reservoirs will be either Carboniferous or Devonian in age.
Anticline 4-way closure on Top Fell Sandstone mapped on new 2D 2011 seismic. Net reservoir, Porosity, HSC, RF, Prospect CoD copied from nearly cp36_27_1 at same horizon level.
Horst block trap; closure to W poorly constrained by contours; long-range migration from S required.

Complex low-amplitude faulted trap; long-range migration from S required.

Anticline 4-way closure mapped on Top Fell Sandstone on new 2D seismic. Porosity, HSC, RF, Prospect CoS copied from nearby cp36_27_1 prospect. Net reservoir has been downgraded.

Anticline 4-way closure mapped on Top Fell Sandstone on new 2D seismic. Porosity, HSC, RF, Prospect CoS copied from nearby cp36_27_1 prospect. Net reservoir has been downgraded.

Fault-bounded intra-Dinantian compartment; closure of northern boundary fault very poorly constrained by seismic data. Long-range migration required and high risk of topseal and boundary fault seal failure.

Kiwi lead - 4-way dip closed trap mapped at Base Zechstein, with large upside in potential stratigraphic trap provided by syn-sedimentary movement on faults on N flank of Mid North Sea High - down-dip and downthrown closure invoked. Parameters entered cf. F1212072. Net reservoir reduced 150/100/50 > 85/45/25 ft to allow calculated reserves to approx operator estimate.
Tui lead - secondary play comprising hanging wall trap on N flank of Mid North Sea High. Parameters entered cf. F1111023.
Top Rotliegendes closure, intra-Carboniferous reservoir.

The main reservoir target is the Rotliegend Leman Sandstone, although the two dry wells (37/10-1 & 48/1-1) do not contain any Rotliegend sandstones because they drilled two highs,
implying that the Rotliegend sands were deposited in the structural lows. 
A secondary reservoir target is the Dinantian sandstones of the Fell Sandstone Formation.

Audley End is a combined structural/stratigraphic trap located within a major N-S trending salt withdrawal syncline.. The structural component is composed of a high saddle area within the syncline. Therefore, the proposed Lower Cretaceous reservoir plunges to the north and south to provide closure along the axis of the syncline. Lateral seal to the east and west is interpreted to be entirely stratigraphic with pinch out on to the flanks of the syncline.

the lead is derived by trapping hydrocarbons within a north-south trending linear body with stratigraphic pinchout to west and east, and structural closure to the north and south. The traps shown have additional dip closure to the north and south, within the sand fairway. In order to charge Troubadour, long range lateral migration from the mature Kimmeridge kitchen area in the Central Graben is required, a distance of approximately 75km to Troubadour. This is the key risk. The palaeogeography for the latest Ryazanian to Early Valanginian time is not well understood, but the Devil's Hole Sandstone is thought to represent a shallow marine, shelfal sand deposited on the flanks of the Central Graben. A Lower Cretaceous lens-like package can be mapped into the application block area. It is believed that this represents a continuation of the shelf sand to the north-east (in blocks 29/18, 29/19 to 29/30 and 30/26, although there are no well penetrations in the area to confirm this.
The Troubadour Lead was targeting Lower Cretaceous sands in the Devil's Hole sandstone.

Black Creek, a combination structural stratigraphic trap of Upper Jurassic sandstones onlapping a central Permian high, capped by Jurassic and Cretaceous shales, and sub-cropped by older Jurassic (Oxfordian) and Smith Bank (Triassic) shales, sourced by long distance migration by Upper Jurassic shales within the Central Graben. Map below is BCU Depth.

Black Creek straddles two blocks, 37/15 in the P.2208 Licence and 37/10 in the P.2207 Licence. The Black Creek prospect was identified, along with Lindisfarne in P.2207, as a key play type for this region of the basin margin. The reservoir target is the Jurassic Fulmar sands.

Cragganmore lead - directly overlies Dogger granite with possibility of patch reef development with good reservoir facies cf. 30/24-3. Principal risk is presence of high quality Devonian marine source rocks downdip from the lead; likely to be dry gas play. CoS = 10% (downgraded by play risk; reservoir reduced 100>50%). Net reservoir reduced 180/60 > 110/35 m to allow deterministic reserves to approx operator estimate. 
Proj 06/04 - COS downgraded to less than 5% (trap presence 100 to 80 since based on interpretation of 2D data)
