description:
The post-well interpretation of the Corbenic structure suggests it is a large basement high feature, with the Devonian Kyle Limestone only present on it’s northwestern edge.
This results in a Statigraphic (3-way closure) trap of the Kyle Limestone abutting the basement to the south. However, from the 37/25-1 well results, there is no top seal or any indication of a working hydrocarbon system. Nor is there any seismic evidence of “reefal” character. 
The pre-well interpreted “karsted reefal” character is now interpreted as eroded basement.
Fault/dip closure at Fell Sandstone level requiring downthrown fault seal. Hanging wall closure to N (Fell Sandstone absent to N).
Faulted anticline with crestal unconformity; Scremerston Formation target. Hanging wall closure to N (Scremerston Fm absent to N).
Fault/ dip closure at Scremerston level
Faulted anticline at Scremerston level. Hanging wall closure to N (Scremerston Fm absent to N), and appears to subcrop base Permian to E
Unconformity Trap; ?Yoredale Fm at subcrop?
Zechstein Reef - play concept for a shelf margin fringing or barrier reef system along the Northern margin of the Southern Permian Basin from the Darach area into the southwest corner of Quad 37.
Fault/dip closure at Fell Sandstone level requiring downthrown fault seal.
Long-range migration from S required.
Anticline with Unconformity; Scremerston Formation target
Downthrown Fault and Dip Closed, Fell Sandstone target; unconformity trap to S (Fell Sandstone absent to S).

37/3-A lead (renamed Sherriffmuir in relinquishment) - base Zechstein 3-way dip/ fault-bounded trap, Rotliegend most likely target, but if thin underlying Carboniferous sandstones provide secondary target. Main risks are quantity of source rock, trap (defined by only 6 2D lines) and migration. 
All parameters, reserves, CoS (14%; 25% in relinquishment) provided; downgraded by reservoir quality (100>50%); migration (100>50%).
Small satellite trap to Snizort cp29_28_2 prospect. Parameters entered cf. cp37_3_1.

37/4-A lead - base Zechstein tilted fault block trap (currently poorly constrained by seismic), Rotliegend most likely target, but if thin underlying Carboniferous sandstones provide secondary target. Main risks are quantity of source rock, trap (defined by only 4 2D lines) and migration. All parameters, reserves, CoS (14%) provided; downgraded by reservoir quality (100>50%); migration (100>50%).
Small satellite trap to Snizort cp29_28_2 prospect. Parameters entered cf. cp37_3_1.
Top Rotliegendes closure, intra-Carboniferous resevoir.

The main reservoir target is the Rotliegend Leman Sandstone, although the two dry wells (37/10-1 & 48/1-1) do not contain any Rotliegend sandstones because they drilled two highs, implying that the Rotliegend sands were deposited in the structural lows. 
A secondary reservoir target is the Dinantian sandstones of the Fell Sandstone Formation.

Brinkburn is a structural trap consisting of a 3-way closure. The eastern margin of the closure is defined by fault contact with the major basement involved normal fault that defines the footwall  of the 37/10-1 early Permian mesa horst to the east and northeast . The southern margin of Brinkburn is defined by poorly constrained up-dip stratigraphic termination of the reservoir horizon and overstep of the younger bajada sealing formation. This trap is defined on a relatively sparse lattice of 2D data. Source rocks for Brinkburn are the Lower Carboniferous Scremerston Coals in the Devil's Hole Basin kitchen.

Ribstone is a stratigraphically trapped Fulmar reservoir charged from the basin to the north. The lead is mapped on 2D seismic and forms a north-south trending linear body
with stratigraphic pinchout onto the eastern flank of the Zechstein thick in the west, and dip closure to the east. The northern and southern edges mark the boundary between the pinchout and the dip closure. Long range lateral migration from the mature Kimmeridge kitchen area in the Central Graben is required, a distance of over 70km. Therefore the 'Charge' element is the key risk. Reservoir presence is also a significant risk.
The Ribstone Lead was a stratigraphic pinch-out of the Jurassic Fulmar sands.

LeadCreemore is a 4-way dip-closed structural trap mapped at the base of the Zechstein salt. The primary reservoir is expected to be the Permian Rotliegend sandstone. The main risks associated with this lead are the Carboniferous source, charge and presence of reservoir. The presence of a local Carboniferous (Scremerston Formation) source kitchen in the southern half of Quad 29 has been inferred from the Hay et al. (2005) EUPP report.
The Creemore Lead was targeting the Permian Rotligendes sands in a four-way dip closure in Block 37/9.

Lindisfarne is a combination structural/stratigraphic trap consisting of a major 213 km2 3-way closure extending over the three blocks,. Located in a salt-withdrawal syncline on the NE margin of the Mid North Sea High. Reservoir section is of probable upper Jurassic age, representing a palaovalley estuarine infill sequence. Migration is postulated along a long-distance route from the Central Graben.

The Lindisfarne Prospect, a 3-way truncation trap within Upper Jurassic Fulmar Formation-equivalent
rocks located to the south-west of the main Central Graben Kimmeridge Clay source-rock kitchen
Figure 2.2, was identified from mapping on regional 2D seismic data.

Permian (Auk Sst.) downfaulted 3-way closure bounded by faults to the east and south, dip closure to the west (into syncline) and closing contour along basement high to the north. The nearest plausible kitchen area is the centre of the Devil's Hole Basin to the north-west.

Padar is a 4-way dip closed structure with a component of fault closure at the BCU level and with an Upper Jurassic sandstone reservoir target. Padar lies approximately 35 km from the edge of the mature Kimmeridgian Clay source kitchen. Therefore, long distance migration would have to have taken place to charge Padar. The key risks are reservoir presence and hydrocarbon migration.

Iguana is faulted dip closure at the BCU and top Zechstein horizons. It is bounded on the north and east by faults which appear to tip out at the BCU horizon and to the south by a fault which appears to tip out within the Chalk. The western side of the trap is a dip closure. Iguana has 3 reservoir targets: Upper Jurassic (but this part is duplicate of cp38_1_1), Zechstein Dolomite and Rotliegendes sandstone. Iguana requires long distance migration in order to have received charge from the source kitchen to the east or north.
Upper Jurassic Stratigraphic Trap. Company CoS = 18%.

Paleocene closure on NAM/Shell company maps, but only 10-20 ft uppermost Paleocene sand encountered in nearby 38/18-1; very high risk reservoir & migration risks - lies well outside Forties-Andrew play fairway; no available seismic data - no QC carried out.

Komodo is a large relatively flat lying four-way dip-closure, as currently mapped on vintage 2D seismic data. A dry well, 38/1-1, is present to the southwest of the Prospect, which means that an additional trapping mechanism is required to separate Komodo away from that well. NW-SE trending, down to the southwest faults are observed on 2D data across the south central part of the structure which may allow trapping of such a column. However, their trends and linkages cannot currently be constrained on 2D data and hence the need for 3D seismic to enhance trap definition. The primary reservoir is prognosed to be Carboniferous to Devonian Buchan Formation, with secondary potential for Permian (Rotliegend) sandstones. The Lower Cretaceous, Jurassic and Triassic sections onlap the flanks of the Komodo structure, where there is potential for additional reservoirs to develop.
Source is mid-mature, gas-prone Carboniferous. Reclassified as Devonian play from Carboniferous (April 2006).

The P.2050 licence was awarded with a contingent commitment to drill a well on the Komodo prospect to 2150m or 50m beneath the Base Zechstein, whichever is the shallower.
The original interpretation of Komodo was based on 2D seismic data which identified a large low relief structure with primary prospectivity in the Carboniferous to Devonian Buchan Formation.
The acquisition of new 3D seismic in 2012/2013 allowed more detailed and regional mapping and identified the Zechstein carbonates as an additional reservoir target on the Western flanks of the Komodo structure. Zechstein reservoir presence was also supported by a regional well and literature (e.g. publications on the Auk and Argyll fields) study undertaken in 2013 that suggested the Komodo high (an extension of the Auk Ridge) was the site of shallow water carbonate deposition in the Late Permian.

Ryu was originally defined on legacy 2D data and was a combined structural/stratigraphic trap at with updip
pinchout/truncation towards the Komodo High and dip closure to the north, east and south. Primary reservoir
was prognosed to be Upper Jurassic Fulmar sandstones. Further evaluation has been unable to reliably map a
competent base/lateral seal as any Fulmar reservoir is likely to unconformably overlie permeable Palaeozoic
sediments, and this package would be juxtaposed against older Palaeozoic sediments in the Komodo high.
Petroleum systems modelling has also suggested that hydrocarbons are unlikely to charge this structure.
Updip from well 38/25-1 which is drilled within the lower part of the closure - no shows. Company CoS = 17%.
Unnamed lead based on 4-way dip closure at base Zechstein, assumed to have Dinantian target. No parameters provided; entered cf. G1326057.
Large low-amplitude footwall trap; long-range migration from S required. Possible Fell Sandstone within closure.

A couple of low relief base Zechstein leads are present but, even with the aid of additional data, these are unlikely to firm up into prospects of sufficient size to warrant drilling given the inherent geological risks.

A further lead, named Mansell, which is primarily located in Block 38/4 also extends briefly into Block 30/29.

Mansell prospect: Interpreted as a fault-bound structural closure, it is bound by both upper Jurassic N – S and Triassic NW – SE trending faults. It is sealed by shales of the Triassic Smith Bank Formation. 
The spatial extent of the Mansell prospect is restricted by the throw of the bounding faults as the faults are not expected to be sealing where reservoir rocks are juxtaposed against one another. 
This is the case at the analogous Ardmore field to the north where reservoir rocks are in pressure communication with each other across faults which intersect the field.

A 13 km2 fault-bound structural closure, within a primary Rotliegend sandstone reservoir with a minor contribution from the overlying Zechstein dolomite where it  as not been eroded. 
Top seal is provided by the upper Cretaceous Chalk Group. 
Depth to top reservoir is calculated as 2,000 m. CoS = 19%.

Button prospect: Interpreted as a fault-bound structural closure, it is bound by both upper Jurassic NE – SW and Triassic NW – SE trending faults. 
The upper Jurassic NE – SW trending faults are influenced by the older underlying structure which can be mapped from the mid Devonian limestone which is a prominent reflector on seismic lines. 
The Button prospect is sealed by the upper Cretaceous Chalk Group although it is very thin over the prospect and may be eroded in places in which case Palaeocene shales will act as a seal.

Dulcy was originally a lead defined as a structural trap at Top Palaeozoic level with potential reservoir targets in the Zechstein carbonates and Rotliegendes/Carboniferous/Devonian sandstones. 
With the new 3D dataset the whole of the Dulcy structure has been clearly mapped and the primary reservoir target is prognosed to be Devonian sandstones as the Permian and Carboniferous are only present on the flanks of the structure.
Petroleum systems modelling has shown that the Dulcy structure is well placed to receive any charge that may come from the north (via Wyvern) or east (Edgware embayment), and analysis of fluid inclusions from drill cuttings suggests that the Zechstein carbonates in nearby well 38/3-1 may have been on a migration pathway.
As several factors have been derisked, leading to an improved Pg of 32% (from 20%), Dulcy was upgraded to a prospect, and at ~25km2 with 500ft-plus of vertical relief it is the largest of the remaining prospects.

Aldgate (Auk) Lead (Tullow, 21st Round) - tilt block mapped at top Zechstein, top Rotliegendes with potential reservoirs in Halibut Formation dolomite and Auk Formation sands, both sealed by Turbot Fm anhydrites. Hydrocarbon charge possible from Blackfriars structure to W. Reclassified as Devonian play from Carboniferous (April 2006).
Source is Kimmeridge Clay Fm. Review (April 2006) - OK.
Pair of adjacent footwall closures with same closing contour; mapped at base Zechstein. Source is Kimmeridge Clay Fm. Replaced by a company prospect in Dec 2003.

Blackfriars (Auk) Lead (Tullow, 21st Round) - tilt block mapped at top Zechstein, top Rotliegendes with potential reservoirs in Halibut Formation dolomite and Auk Formation sands, both sealed by Turbot Fm anhydrites. Hydrocarbon charge less likely than in Aldgate structure to E, lies in its migration shadow. Reclassified as Devonian play from Carboniferous (April 2006).

Blackfriars (Fulmar) Lead (Tullow, 21st Round) tilted fault block with closure at base Cretaceous, base Jurassic. Seal provided by Kimmeridge Clay/Chalk. Migration probably required updip from Central Graben. Most of structure is low relief (c 250ft) though locally 350 ft. Fife Sandstone target - though possibly paralic or fluviodelatic here. Mature source rocks 10-20 km to NW. Migration and reservoir presence are key risks. Edgware South - Largely stratigraphic pinch-out/truncation, but with some dip closure to the East and fault closure to the West. 
Targeted by 'Edgware 2 & 3' well locations

This bid is on a play concept. As a result of sparse 2D seismic data coverage no prospects have been defined yet but the wide line spacing allows sizeable opportunities to exist. The main play considered in this area is a Rotliegend reservoir charged by a Carboniferous source. The thick Zechstein is considered to be an adequate seal for this play. Faults propagate up into the Rotliegend, indications are that structuration is present, either rotated fault blocks and/or anticlines/roll over, but more data is required to map full trapping configuration

Lead 1 - stratigraphic trap to E of prominent N-S horst and S of Permian high tested by 39/1-1; dip closed to E & S, stratigraphically and fault closed to N & W. Fife Sandstone target oil-bearing in same sub-basin by 31/26a-9A (Fife). Key risks are presence of sufficient mature source rock, reservoir sand, and trap presence. CoS = 20% (downgraded by play risk; reservoir reduced 90>50%; source effectiveness reduced 80>50%). GRV reduced 294750/120000/43200 > 73070/37500/32305 to match area/net reservoir data. Key risk is that this is unproven play in area - reservoir sand and trapping mechanism are major risks. Jurassic sands at pinchout could provide thief zone. CoS = 16% - downgraded due to unproven play. Net reservoir reduced 200/75 to 45/20 ft to allow deterministic reserves to approx operator estimate. Proposal to appraise 4/26-1A Sween discovery - 21 ft Oxfordian Sands net pay tested 40 mmcfd gas, but interpretation of test indicates pich outand/or faulting within 300-600 ft of well. Large pinchout trap mapped - sand absent in N30/10-1x & -5. All parameters, reserves provided.

The reservoir is a stratigraphically trapped Brae sandstone equivalent. There is considerable upside in the fact that the gas-bearing sands encountered in well 4/26-1A would thicken away from the well accompanied with increasing net-to-gross.

The 4/26b-1 well discovered gas in mid-Oxfordian sands. Reservoir thickness was 9m and associated volumes are at this stage too small to be economic. 
The depositional model is currently using a shoreface reservoir, with a possible updip thickening of this sand. 
An alternative model with a deep water turbiditic setting is possible.

The current evaluation of the Sween prospect is based on the 3D seismic PGS 2012 NVG-11 merged PSDM. 
The 7m Oxfordian sandstones penetrated by well 4/26-1 are below seismic resolution and detection. 
High amplitude markers are visible down dip of the 4/26-1A well. Seismic modelling has indicated that these high amplitudes could correspond to thick and porous turbiditic lobes. The amplitudes indicate a sediment source from the west (East Shetland Platform).

Strati-structural trap consisting of Oxfordian turbiditic sands - 4/26-1 tested pinch out of upper of 2 sand units.. The seismic amplitude map indicates turbiditic sand fairway possibly sourced from the W and initially moving to the E across the North Viking Graben, later on trending towards NE to N. 4/26-1A encountered this sand fairway at its fringe in the SE. Wells 3/30-2A and 9/5a-1, SW of 4/26-1A well did not encounter sands in the Oxfordian level, thus defining the S boundary of the Sween fairway. The S boundary can be explained by the tilting and deepening of the graben to the N, causing the fairway to eventually extend towards N along the graben axis. Stacked lobe complexes form the multi-layer reservoir system.

The Sween prospect was defined as a strati-structural trap within Oxfordian sandy turbiditic lobes running eastwards across the Viking Graben towards the Frigg high (Lobe A and Lobe B). The trap was expected to be filled with dry gas and minor condensate.

The Bison Blocks represent a new play within the Southern North Sea. The unconventional resource potential currently being identified onshore UK can be directly mapped to the Bison Blocks. The Carboniferous sequence drilled in Well 41/01-1 is over 4,700 ft. The shales and coals of the Lower Carboniferous section act as both a source of dry gas and also a reservoir as the gas will adsorb onto the surface of organic matter and pool within the intergranular porosity and porosity created within the organic matter as it breaks down during gas generation. The sandstones and limestones will also act as reservoirs and can be further used as carrier beds. This means that horizontal wells could be drilled within these brittle facies and then fractured. It is more efficient to initiate a fracture within a brittle facies and propagate the fracture into a more ductile shale. Using carrier beds in fracture design leads to higher recovery rates for individual wells.

The Fell Sandstone was considered to be a high-risk, high-reward play in the P2270 licence and surrounding area and also formed the basis for a number of other successful licence applications including the P2126 (‘Aurora’) and P2327 (‘Jazz) licences. 
The key geological risk associated with the Fell Sandstone play was the requirement for the Scremerston Coal Formation (SCF) to function as an effective top seal to any underlying Fell Sandstone accumulation. At the time of application, the Fell Sandstone was believed to be the thickest and highest quality reservoir interval likely to be present in the P2270 licence and indeed
the surrounding region - hence the significant exploration interest. 
Although this remains the case, confidence in the Scremerston Coal Formation acting as a top seal to any Fell Sandstone accumulation was significantly reduced following the most recent technical evaluation thus effectively eliminating this play concept.

The Braeburn Prospect was mapped at the time of the original application, as a large structural closure, with prospectivity, at Yoredale and Fell Sandstone levels, extending across both the P2126 and P2270 licences. 
For the Braeburn Prospect, volumes at both Yoredale and Fell Sandstone levels are interpreted to be limited by spill on a major fault between the Braeburn Prospect and the Crosgan Discovery. The reduced column height at both levels has resulted in a significant reduction in calculated volumes compared to those calculated at the time of application.

The Gasta Lead is defined as a closure on the Base Namurian depth map, with Visean reservoir being sealed by overlaying basal Namurian shales (Pendleian). Namurian deltaic sands form a secondary shallower target, sealed by intra-Namurian shales (marine bands).The event picked is taken to be topographically representative of the Upper Carboniferous over this lead, even if the event picked is not precisely the Base Namurian. The structural trap forming the Gasta lead trends NNW-SSE and appears to be an example of a Visean hanging wall inversion. 
Based on the current mapping it is anticipated that there is no erosional truncation of the Visean reservoirs section over Gasta by the Base Permian Unconformity, so the younger, better-quality reservoirs seen in Zone 1b in the Breagh Field should be preserved. 
The anticipated top seal to the Visean will be the basal Namurian shales (Pendleian), which in this area are anticipated to be around 100m thick.

The key to exploring the Hyskeir Discovery is identifying zones of better quality reservoir ('sweet spots'), preferably inside structural closure, although stratigraphic closures work. The other key to unlocking the prospectivity is identifying early structural movement enabling early charge, preventing later illitization due to the Tertiary inversion, although associated fractures will enhance deliverability.

Darach is dependent on mapping a structure that combines dipping Base Namurian/Intra Carboniferous events that subcrop the Base Zechstein across the BPU (Figure 10). The Base Zechstein shows very weak low relief closure but this is enhanced beneath the Base Zechstein where the Base Namurian rolls over and subcrops the Base Zechstein on the flanks of the structure to the NE and SW. However in a NW-SE orientation (inline) on the 3D dataset the trapping mechanism is more difficult, with minimal dip closure shown on the PreSTM beneath a benign overburden.

The main prospectivity has been mapped at Top Z2 Hauptdolomit. The Top Hauptdolomit to Base Zechstein isopach map clearly demonstrates a pod like geometry of this prominent structural feature, which may represent a reef complex. It can be clearly seen that the Zechstein build-up identified at Top Hauptdolomit overlies a prominent eroded Carboniferous anticline mapped at Base Namurian. It is quite likely that a post Carboniferous residual paleo-high would have existed at the time of Z2 deposition. Any such high would form the focal point for reef development in a shelfal depositional environment. Top Hauptdolomit is a high amplitude event on both flanks of the Z2 build-up, but over the crest it is much weaker and less continuous.

The Andromeda South Prospect lies within the licence P2128 and is located on the southern side of the CM fault, separated from the Andromeda North discovery by that lineament. 
It is defined as a 3-way dip closure, bound to the North by the CM fault and at least partly traversed by a subsidiary WNW-ESE trending fault that may have the potential to compartmentalise the prospect. Both the primary and secondary play of Andromeda South have been identified as prospective. The main risk element for the primary play opportunity is the CM Fault Zone and whether it provides an effective seal. If the fault is open, such that Andromeda North and South are in communication, no accumulation can exist in the Andromeda South prospect, as the Andromeda North free water level (FWL) lies close to the level of the Andromeda South crest. The secondary play is seen as very high risk due to the lack of gas in the same intervals in the Andromeda North discovery.

The Delta Lead is mapped on sparse legacy 2D seismic data. The lead is a truncation play in which the Ketch reservoir section is preserved in an outlier formed by Carboniferous faulting and folding prior to erosion at the Base Permian Unconformity, and subsequent deposition of the Rotliegendes section.  The reservoir section is not interpreted directly, but isopached up from a Westphalian A/B reflector, correlated to the Amaliae marine band.  Key sealing elements of the trap include the Base Permian Unconformity (where no significant closure is mapped), a basal seal beneath the Ketch reservoir unit, and a crossfault seal against older presumed Carboniferous strata to the north. The Carfax Prospect lying within Block 43/14b is mapped on 3D data at Intra-Carboniferous Marker II level (intra-Namurian).  The prospect is mapped as a three-way dip closure, with downthrown fault closure ( the normal fault juxtaposes reservoir sandstones against older Carboniferous units) to the north.  A number of potential reservoir units have been identified in the offsetting wells, suggesting the possibility of stacked pay zones, but the key risk on the prospect is the nature of the fault seal given the high net-to-gross within the Namurian and the likely juxtaposition of reservoir against porous units across the fault.  Key uncertainties include the possibility of juxtaposing reservoir in the trap against porous units across the fault, thereby providing a conduit for leakage from the trap; and whether or not the fault itself could provide a seal. The prospect is an untested 3-way dip closure structure approximately 5 km east of the Tyne platform and between the Tyne North and Tyne South hydrocarbon accumulations. The only well available in the area (44/18a-5) has failed to fully evaluate the potential of the structure. 44/18a-5 was drilled in 1997. At the well both main targets, the Caister Sand and Lower Ketch were water wet. A gas accumulation occurs in the Transition Sequence above the Lower Ketch, but this was not tested. Petrophysical interpretation of the logs give a Gas Down To (GDT) of 12311' (TVDSS) and a Water Up To (WUT) of 12417'(TVDSS). The RFT plot shows an intersection between the water and gas gradients close to the WUT (cc 12400' TVDSS).  The gas accumulation in the Lower Ketch is still unproven. There is no base Permian closure, and any trap will require a top seal in the shale-prone Upper Ketch. This is similar to the trapping mechanism in the Tyne Fields, but not identical. In Tyne, the top seal is provided by a combination of both Upper Ketch shales and Silverpit Formation shales, the base of the latter truncating the Carboniferous section. There is no base-Permian truncation over the 44/18a-5 area. The fundamental issue is: can a GWC from the Transition Zone accumulation be extrapolated into the Lower Ketch?.   .   Within the Transition Sequence, the low net to gross ratio suggests that connectivity is likely to be poor. A recovery factor of 15% and 25% have been used for Min and ML Case, respectively. Only Max case includes some GIIP in the Lower Ketch with a GWC at 12417'(TVDSS). At present, all GIIP estimates in the Lower Ketch, although demonstrating potential, have to be treated with caution.

The Carboniferous Wheatsheaf Lead is a combined structural and stratigraphic trap. It is a major NW-SE trending horst block closure bounded to the north by erosional truncation of the Westphalian C/D reservoir sandstones and to the south by a sealing cross fault. Lateral seal would be provided by the abundant and continuous intra Carboniferous coals and shales of the Westphalian B.  The reservoir target is the Lower Ketch sandstone. The sandstones are developed on-block in wells 44/27-1 and 44/27-2, where they were found to be thick and well developed. The sandstones had a gross thickness of 750 to 1020 ft and 33-35% Net to Gross. Porosities were approximately 10% on average; even at depths of 13,120 ft. Regional data on porosity-permeability relationships indicate that the Westphalian C and D sandstones would have good permeability at the predicted porosities and reservoir depths for the identified prospect.

Garnet was discovered in 1986 by LASMO with exploration well 44/27-1. The well was drilled to a TD of 16,500 ft MD. A DST was run at between 13,426 ft - 13,442 ft and 13,280 ft ? 13,314 ft MD. The well tested at a disappointing 2.43 mmscf/d. An evaluation of the test suggested that the poor flow rates was either the result of formation damage as a high positive Skin (+25) was recorded over the upper tested interval; or salt plugging porosity.The Garnet structure is a northwest-southeast trending fault block. The Garnet reservoir is mostly comprised of sands within the Upper Ketch Formation with Lower Ketch 2 Formation sands entering the gas leg in the fault-bounded pop-up area on the southwest side. The reservoir section in well 44/27-1 has an average net to gross ratio averaging of 28%, with porosities in the range of 9% - 11%.

The Triton prospect is an untested 3-way and fault, footwall trap of Leman Sandstone reservoir. It is located just 2.5km to the north east of the Perenco operated Neptune Field. The prospect straddles the boundary of all three application blocks.  The best case technical mapping, derived from 3D PrSDM seismic, shows the crest of the structure to be -2840m TVDss. The trap is bound to the SW by a major NW-SE normal fault. Depth conversion is the key geological uncertainty. Velocity sensitivity work shows that closure to the north west is highly sensitive to the depth conversion methodology.  Reservoir quality in this area is good with >95% N:G, 9% average porosity and ~100 mD average permeability observed in the nearby Neptune field. The source rocks are coals concentrated in the Westphalian and are low risk. The reservoir is sealed by the Zechstein Evaporate sequence.

Lead C (Triton) - parallel horst to Neptune Field, but separated from it by narrow graben. Low risk, but poorly resolved through complex faulting in Mesozoic overburden. CoS 30% reduced due to high trap risk - NW limit appears to be limit of interpretation.

trap_type_comment: Simple 3-way dip closure which spills to the NW into Withow, bounded along the western edge by a major NW-SE normal fault. The top seal consists of shales and silts of the Silverpit Formation and eventually the Zechstein salt.
key_evaluation_comment: Reprocessing 90 km2 of 3D seismic data to PreSDM. Following the disappointing results of the spec reprocessing, matching and merging of all the best in-house PreSDM was undertaken and the regional re-interpretation was carried out on this merged volume. Seismic reflectivity data coverage is good over the area of interest however imaging is a challenge beneath a shallow tertiary collapse graben directly above the prospect.  There is considerable depth conversion uncertainty and there does not appear to be a robust structural closure on all depth maps.  GIIP volumes were calculated down to the spill point where structural separation between Triton and Withow was achieved.  The in-place-volumes for the Triton prospect were calculated probabilistically using a Monte Carlo simulation within REP (Reserves Estimation Programme).  Average reservoir properties from Cleeton, Withow and Neptune have been used in the Triton volumetric evaluation.  All five useable depth maps were stacked and run together giving equal weighting to arrive at the final GIIP figures.

The Carnelian Prospect is the only Rotliegendes structure on 47/5f. It is a continuation of the Hyde-West Sole anticline with gentle dip to the northwest.
The overburden shows little variation such that the Time and Depth structure areessential identical. The faulted southwest edge is the weak point. Here the fault scissors upwards, causing the Carnelian structure to lie in a hanging wall.
Although the Zechstein halites remain thick and unbroken, the risk to effective closure is strong. Third parties reviewing the data were dissuaded.

Namurian (and possibily Dinantian) organic-rich shales are mature for gas  generation offshore from the Yorkshire Coast. The strata are not imaged by seismic so the first task will be to acquire seismic to image the play. Despite this uncertainty, the opportunity is considered as a "Prospect Not Fully Defined" The Pilot assumes a directional well from the coastal area penetrating 4-6 km of shales at a high angle. There is the possibility of testing this either close to shore with a land-based directional well or possibly an offshore vertical well.

Organic-rich shales of the Namurian (and possibly Dinantian) are in the gas window and have generated gas which is believe to be trapped in these low permeability shales.  This prospect area overlaps with the Pilot Development Area - it is not the increment reported here but the whole on-block potential.

Up to 2000ft/600m of Namurian Bowland Shale may be present in block 47/6. It is likely that it is in the late oil to gas window and provides an opportunity for shale gas/oil by drilling wells from the Yorkshire coastline out to 5kms offshore. Significant volumes of gas potential is recognise at up to 2.4TCF

Prospect 48/1e-B comprises a series of north-easterly tilted fault blocks, mapped at Base Zechstein, which is on trend with the Cobra gas discovery in the adjoining Block 48/1b to the east. It is very well-imaged on the Reverse Time Migrated data processed by GXT for E.ON and Dana at the end of 2011. For the Mid Case and High Cases the gas-down-to (-3417m) in 48/2-1 is assumed to be the FWL, both cases being dependent on a sealing De Keyser fault to the north-west and a sealing Caledonide-trending fault to the south-west. The low case is based on structural closure above a saddle separating Prospect B from Cobra.  The reservoir is a mixed aeolian and fluvial facies from the Lower Leman Sandstone Formation and is sealed by Silverpit Formation clays and silts.  The reservoir quality is expected to be reasonable and to be gas charged from the underlying Carboniferous Westphalian shales.  Chance of Success:  36%.   (Charge: 100%, Reservoir: 90%, Seal: 100%, Trap: 40%).   .   Probabilistic estimation of gas in place and gas reserves.  Volumes for in-block 48/1e only

The Cobra FWL (-3417m) invokes a sealing De Keyser fault to the northwest and a sealing NW-trending fault to the southwest. The saddle separating the Cobra discovery from the structural extension into block 48/1b is 67m shallower than the FWL in well 48/2-1 and 48/2c-5, suggesting communication across the structure, with the De Keyser providing fault seal. A fault seal analysis also predicted a similar spill point. The structure enclosed by this contour was then broken into risk segments. Though overall reservoir quality is clearly better at Cobra then encountered at Babbage, Babbage flowed better on test. This is primarily controlled by connecting into natural fracture networks. E.ON has developed a geomechanical fracture model over the Cobra structure, to aid in optimal well placement and ultimately maximise production. The dry gas source for the area is the Carboniferous Coal Measures. The Leman Formation is top-sealed by Silverpit Formation clays and silts.

Cobra is an undeveloped discovery that straddles blocks 48/1b and 48/2b. It is located approximately 5 km to the north of PUK's Hoton field. The discovery lies in the northwest of the Rotliegend gas province and consists of a three way dip closure, with a length of 3km and a maximum width of 2km. The crest of the structure is at approximately -10,619ft TVDSS. PUK base case reserves estimates are Cobra is 21 bcf. The reservoir predominantly comprises Aeolian dune sandstones of the Upper Permian Rotliegend with an average reservoir quality range of 12-15% porosity and 0.1 to 10mD permeability.   The Cobra prospect was discovered by the 48/2-1 exploration well in 1969 and is covered by good quality 3D PrSDM seismic data. There is therefore minimal geological risk to this prospect. The remaining uncertainties are the quality of the reservoir, the occurrence of natural fractures and the recovery factor which is very much dependent on a successful well stimulation by hydraulic fracturing.

Cobra is a segmented structure mapped at the Top Leman divided into north-easterly titled fault blocks of generally low relief. 
The structure is ultimately bounded by sealing faults to the northwest and southwest, on which the discovery (48/02-1) and appraisal (48/02c-5) wells prove the presence of gas.

The tightly folded geometry is indicative of a positive flower structure caused by reversal on what was originally a normal fault. The structural spill separating Python from the Hoton Field to the south defines the Mid Case, of which only 40% of the area is within Block 48/1e, whereas the low case is entirely within Block. The reservoir is a mixed aeolian and fluvial facies from the Lower Leman Sandstone Formation and is sealed by Silverpit Formation clays and silts.  The reservoir quality is expected to be reasonable and to be gas charged from the underlying Carboniferous Westphalian shales.  Chance of Success:  45%. The tightly folded geometry of Python is the product of a footwall shortcut fault most likely caused by Alipine stress acting on an unfavourably oriented for reactivation normal fault. Structural spill point has been identified separating Python from the Hoton field to the south. A reasonable independent dip closure defines  the high case. The Lower Leman Sandstone facies range from clean, mature, well-sorted aeolian reservoir sands with the best porosities deposited during drier climatic regimes, to non-reservoir silty lacustrine clays deposited during wetter phases. Python is located further into the main Leman dune best of good quality aeolian sandstone than Babbage or Johnston to the north. It may be possible to enhance flow rates by targeting natural fracture networks predicted by geomechanical fracture modelling.

The reservoir quality is likely to be similar to that in Cobra and Hoton and therefore, the occurrence of natural fractures and the recovery factor is a key risk.

The 49/14a Colorado-NW lead is a faulted four-way dip closure with a column length up to 200m. Structurally this lead is located 15km along strike (NW-SE) from the Caravel field and occurs with a cluster of similar type structures. The Colorado-NW lead occurs in block 49/14a  The Colorado-NW lead is defined on the 2002 Pre-stack depth migrated 3D data set with the closest well 49/14a-2 4 km to the southeast. Structural definition of the lead is hindered by the complex overburden of Zechstein evaporates and lateral variability of Chalk velocities. Reservoir properties are expected to be poorer than well 49/14a-2 due a thicker development of shalier sabkha deposits in the uppermost part of the Rotliegendes, as observed at Carrack. 
Critical success factors for the Colorado NW lead are: 
· Seismic imaging of the complex overburden (i.e. Zechstein) 
· Depth conversion (i.e. Chalk lateral velocity variation) 
· Geophysical support for Direct Hydrocarbon Indicators (DHIs). CoS = 33%

The Colorado prospect is defined on the 2006 Pre-stack depth migrated 3D data set and constrained by the 49/14a-2 dry well (1989) which is outside of closure. The prospect underlies complex overburden geometry of laterally varying velocities in the Chalk & Triassic. Despite the overburden issues there is a flat seismic event in the reservoir section representing a potential gas-water contact.  
Critical success factors for the Colorado prospect are: 
· Seismic imaging of the complex overburden  
· Depth conversion to determine the high-confidence structure 
· Geophysical support for Direct Hydrocarbon Indicators (DHIs).

The Georgia prospect is a stratigraphic trap relying on the pinch-out of Early Westphalian C sands between a Silverpit top seal and a ULWB bottom seal. Reinterpretation of the Top Early Westphalian B horizon resulted in a slightly larger prospect outline in the southwest with respect to the original outline from the application report. Unfortunately, the nearby Monterey discovery (49/8-2) 10 km to the east demonstrates the presence of a thin layer of Lower Leman sandstones. The well log of 49/8-3, 5 km to the east of Georgia, also shows a sandier interval just above the BPU. Finally, well 49/7-1, 4.2 km to the southwest of Georgia contains ca. 30 meters of Lower Leman. Therefore, it is likely that the Lower Leman sandstone is present at the Georgia prospect as well, which will cause the stratigraphic trap to fail.
This risk is considered very high and consequently, no further prospectivity is seen here.

The Dory Deep prospect is a low relief four-way dip structure (Figure 11) which is absent in TWT at Top Murdoch level (structure is only present post depth conversion. Dory Deep was deemed to too high risk to pursue further

The Granby exploration well (49/09-1) tested the Ketch accumulation, which was found to be water-wet with trace shows. The well drilled almost an entire Westphalian B section and may have just tagged the Murdoch sand equivalent unit at td (indicated by a slight gamma ray decrease). The prospect consists of a three-way, fault closed (towards the NE) structure. The Westphalian B section penetrated by the Granby well has been petrophysically analysed for its sealing potential (Figure 24). Although some (probably) isolated water bearing sand stringers are present in the upper part of the section, the middle-lower 300m of the Westphalian B appears to be slightly more homogenous with the occasional clean claystone interval.

Three prospects were identified: Merope, Celaeno and Wren East. Merope and Celaeno lie immediately south of the Wissey Discovery and are bound by WNWESE-trending faults on their southern flanks, and by a large NNW-SSE fault on their western flank. 
Prospect Wren East lies further to the NW and is a fault-bounded, NNW-SSE-trending structure parallel to the Wren Field that lies immediately to the west. All three prospects exhibit a high confidence closure at Top Zechstein, Top Rotliegendes and Top Carboniferous levels. However, each structure has a large throw along the NNW-SSE fault, which potentially results in the juxtaposition of the Rotliegendes section against the Bunter Sandstone. This constitutes a considerable risk to a trap breach and is the main factor behind the decision to relinquish the block.

Re-mapping of the Sycamore Lead also demonstrates that the Triassic Bunter Sandstones in the hanging-wall of the bounding fault locally juxtapose against Rotliegend Sandstones in the foot-wall, as per the Oak Discovery. 
Given that the Zechstein halite is, if anything, thinner at Sycamore than at Oak, the risk of crossfault leakage is considered to be very high. 
The range of gas volumes in the Sycamore lead has been calculated taking into account the possibility (in the minimum / P90 case) of cross-fault leakage, whilst the P10 scenario assumes that the structure is full-to-spill. However, there remains the possibility that the structure could be totally dry as a result of cross-fault leakage.

Stratigraphic trap on Maureen Formation, representing a possible updip extension of the Boatswain prospect i(to be drilled in 2014/15) n Mariner West licence. It is partially covered by the new isometrix survey with the remainder of the prospect defined on 2D of varying vintages and quality. The Tempest structure is formed from an isolated remnant of a Maureen channel, being apparently detatched from the Boatswain sand body. The zone between Boatswain could be due to non-deposition, but is considered more likely to be an area of either depletion (for sand injection into the Heimdal) or erosion. Updip of Mariner this prospect is shallower so likely to be more biodegraded. There is a risk that the oil will be too heavy to produce.

The Admiral and Tempest prospects are both stratigraphic traps comprising a Maureen Formation (Paleocene) sandstone reservoir, and a topseal and lateral seal of Lista Formation shales. Oil is sourced from the Kimmeridge Clay Formation in the South Viking Graben to the east, and is believed to have migrated along a fill-spill pathway through the Mariner Field. Tempest is located to the northwest (up-dip) of the Boatswain Discovery (8/15a-3) and Admiral is located to the west (up-dip) of the Cadet Discovery (8/15-1). 
Detailed mapping of the top Maureen sandstone reflector on new 3D seismic data reveals the Admiral and Tempest fairways in much greater detail than was available prior to application. 
The fairways appear to comprise amalgamated channels and show evidence of later removal of the sand in places.

Several leads (Twin Peaks, Dune, 9/11-10 updip, Giraffe & Lula) remain on the blocks but
these are now considered significantly more risky due to the results of the Sailor well.

Stratigraphic pinchout trap on Heimdal level, virtually unmappable on current 2D seismic but believed to be present by analogy with Mariner Field and wells in surrounding area. At Mariner the Heimdal is very difficult to resolve seismically and its distribution is only becoming stochastically definable in the latest generation of broadband 3D seismic in the area. Of the wells drilled over the Mariner area, only two have so far failed to encounter Heimdal sands (8/15-2A and 9/11-3), so a wide distribution of Heimdal in the area can be assumed.

Possibly on migration route for lighter oil along BCU and may have strat trap capacity. Admiral deep lead is based on the observation of a package developed beneath the chalk over part of Admiral. From observations in nearby wells it has been observed that Mesozoic sediments can be trapped in small isolated basins. Upper Jurassic Piper Formation sandstones are considered to be the most likely potential reservoir in the area, and have been observed over large parts of the East Shetland Platform, but other Mesozoic sediments are also likely to be deposited in the system. However, the poor definition of this feature on the seismic in the area makes it not possible to take the Mesozoic structures further than a lead.
The Admiral Deep Prospect was identified and mapped as a possible Jurassic package within a small graben beneath Admiral.

Central of 3 discrete chennel-like units in the basal part of the Palaeocene section. The easiest to define and most sizeable is Wayfarer Central, defined on three main 2D lines (2 strike and 1 dip line). The structure shows a disturbed bright section sitting immediately above the basement in this area. This is interpreted as most likely a chalk slump, with a clear area of extention and compression on the seismic dip line. A chalk collapse feature is a possible method of generating extra permeability in the sediments allowing the typically highly porous chalk to flow. There is also potential for additional sandy reservoirs to be generated as part of this mass-transport system. Parameters entered cf cp8_14_2

A series of channel features have been identified up-dip of VGL's Dothraki prospect (Block 8/23) using 2D seismic data. The channel(s) are located within the Dornoch Formation, a high-quality deltaic sandstone unit which is overlain by a coal section that VGL believe may be generating biogenic gas. The channel(s) may also provide a differential compaction-induced structural high as is the case in the Dothraki prospect; VGL are keen to investigate the lead with a larger seismic database.

The Lauren lead is a structure identified at Devonian/Carboniferous level and forms the secondary target for exploration within Block 8/22. The lead is formed of a horst structure that is transected by only one seismic line; the nearby 8/27a-1 well indicates that this interval may contain good quality reservoir sandstones below a Permian evaporite seal.

Dothraki is a DHI-supported prospect identified from 2D seismic data on the East Shetland Platform at a depth of around 850m. The  seismic response of the prospect leads VGL to believe hydrocarbons are present in the gas phase.   The prospect is located within the high-quality Beauly sands of the Balder Formation, trapped within a drape over an underlying NW-SE trending Dornoch Formation differential compaction feature. The structure pinches out onto the Dornoch shelf in the north-west.   The prospect is thought to have been charged by the Beauly and Dornoch coals, which were extensively deposited in the area and are currently within the depth window of optimum biogenic gas generation. The large distances between Dothraki and proven mature source rocks/discoveries supports the notion of a locally generated hydrocarbon charge.

Selene was identified by a prominent seismic reflector that appeared to represent a Direct Hydrocarbon Indicator within the Beauly Member of the Balder Formation. 
The 2D HR data confirmed the Selene Main 4-way closure, but with a smaller area, and identified other satellite closures (Selene North and East).
Because the flat spot has been disproven, the case for biogenic gas is difficult to support. Considering the history in the area, heavy oil is now considered the most likely case if hydrocarbons are present.

Dothraki Deep is a differential compaction feature creating 3-way dip closure at Top Dornoch level. The Dothraki prospect is draped over the Dornoch channel, creating structural relief at Top Beauly level. The Dothraki Deep lead is comprised of the same play components as the Dothraki prospect; high quality deltaic sands in close proximity to biogenic gas generating coal beds trapped within a differential compaction-induced high. The trap is less certain as the proposed pinch-out in the north-west is obscured by seismic attenuation that VGL believes relates to the gas-fill of the overlying Beauly reservoir.

Black Argus is an Upper Jurassic stratigraphic trap of Upper Jurassic Hugin/Piper sands that infill a graben on Top Devonian. The mudstones and chalk of the Lower and Upper Cretaceous respectively would act as top seal, with the Devonian tight sands as bottom and lateral seal.

At the time of licence application, the concept behind the Black Ghost and Black Argus leads was that Upper Jurassic Piper Formation-equivalent sands could form traps beneath the Base Cretaceous Unconformity. 
These traps would be formed by either pinch-out or truncation of the sands in an updip direction, with a topseal formed by Cretaceous mudstones and chalks, and bottom and lateral seals provided by tight Devonian or Triassic sediments.

The Scylla Lead is a structural and stratigraphic trap in which the key issues are
uncertainties and risks with trap and migration. On the basis of regional seismic and well evaluation, the main Heimdal Sandstone Member target is likely to be well-developed. Well 9/02-1 encountered a 33 metre thick Heimdal Sandstone whilst 315 metres was encountered in 9/07-1, which lies southeast of the lead but still within the Scylla channel. The trap is dip closed to the southeast but is otherwise thought to be mostly stratigraphic, with possible elements of dip reversal due to differential compaction and locally enhanced by faulting and/or slumping.

The Scylla feature was mapped along its full extent, from P.2149 into P.1976, to a culmination at c. 2,400 ftTVDSS. The shallow nature of the trend, particularly when compared to other heavy oil pools in the area, emphasises the risk to the prospect of the enhanced effects of biodegradation, (i.e. reduced oil quality, increased viscosity / low mobility and concomitant reduction to recovery factor ranges), and highlights the significant risks on both the technical and commercial fronts.

Macduff is a prospect identified in the Upper Jurassic Volgian sands, located in the north-eastern part of Block 9/9f. It is a strati-structural combination trap defined by a north-south trending turbidite deposit visible in seismic amplitudes. 
The well 9/9b-5 encountered about 24m gross conglomeratic oil bearing Volgian sequence, which corresponds to the proximal part or the slope apron of the turbiditic system. It flowed oil at the rate of 16bopd and encountered an OWC at 3924m TVDSS. Macduff prospect is defined as the downdip continuation of the same turbiditic sequence as 9/9b-5 into a lobe complex, but separated from the accumulation at 9/9b-5 by a fault. 
Lateral seal is assumed to be the key risk, as existence of the prospect is highly dependent on the sealing capacity of the fault separating 9/9b-5 accumulation from Macduff prospect.

Maureen Formation: Mermaid up-dip from 9/11c- 13
The Mermaid up-dip prospect represents the up-dip component of the Maureen fairway drilled in 9/11c- 13. The Maureen Fm. thins to the south of the main Mariner Maureen canyon fairway, and in an up-dip north-westerly direction.
An up-dip stratigraphic pinch-out trap is invoked for the Mermaid up-dip prospect, but the extent of the trap geometry and whether it pinches out is uncertain. The Lista Fm. is considered the top seal, but this could be compromised by top-seal breaching by the sand-injectite processes which led to formation of the overlying Heimdal geobodies. Both trap geometry and top seal risks impact the geological chance of success.
Possible extension of Heimdal reservoir on Mariner Field.

The Lista Fm. within the license is relatively thin and shows no indication of the significant jack-up structures or clear seismic reflectivity that characterises the exploitable hydrocarbon-bearing Heimdal Sandstone Member within the Mariner Field (Figure 9 and Figure 10). There are some indications from the seismic data of isolated Heimdal Sandstone Member accumulations, but these are (in general) deeper than the oil-water contact from the nearest wells. 
Indeed, the Heimdal Sandstone Member is present within the two closest wells, 9/11- 3 and 8/15a- 3, at 2 m and 40 m TVD thickness respectively, but both are 100% water saturated.

description: The Kerosene Lead is a distinct anomalous brightening on the map of the top Lower Mousa / Frigg (T9) surface. However there appears to be no structural concordance to this anomaly at all suggesting that it must be stratigraphic or small faults act as local barriers to migration.

The Irresistible discovery (and the Kerosene Lead) are associated with hard acoustic responses at reservoir level. It is possible that the cements may be generated in-situ from excess CO2 derived from the biodegradation of hydrocarbons within the traps, but this link is rather tenuous. The presence of carbonate cements in these reservoirs masks any true fluid effect and thus gives a high degree of uncertainty when delineating the extent of these Eocene prospects and discoveries.

The Irresistible Discovery is located at the northeastern corner of block 9/16. The reservoir is the Frigg Formation turbidites sealed by the overlying mudstones of the Horda Fm. The Irresistible Discovery was made by well 9/16-2, when it encountered a 20m heavy oil (13°API) column. At the time the discovery was made (and at the time of Azinor’s application), the exact trapping mechanism and extent of the accumulation was not completely clear. Initial rock physics modelling for the application indicated that hydrocarbons in the Frigg Formation should result in a further softening of the sandstones and produce a significant amplitude increase that should be visible on seismic data.

Madison is a moderately defined 4-way dip closure on the footwall of the active East Shetland Platform boundary fault. Reservoir is within theMaureen Fm. with claystones of the overlying Lista Formation providing the seal. The Kimmeridge Clay is known to be mature for oil generation in the Beryl Embayment to the East and oil would be expected to migrate into the trap up the East Shetland Boundary Fault zone. An oil gravity vs depth plot relationship derived from surrounding accumulations indicates that circa 18° API oil may be expected in Madison at 5300- 5500 ft.

Pre-drill, the Jock Scott prospect was interpreted as a 3-way downfaulted trap located in a relay ramp setting, with a top seal formed by claystones of the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation and/or shales of the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll Group, and with lateral seals formed by the basin-bounding fault to the west and a stratigraphic pinch-out (and/or downfaulting) to the south. 
The primary reservoir target in Jock Scott were shallow marine sands of the Upper Jurassic Humber Group (Piper Formation equivalent), and hydrocarbons (if present) were expected to be light oil. 
There were no direct (producing) analogues for this prospect concept.

Babbage is a Jurassic sandstone stratigraphic prospect lying in 9/3b and 9/3d.  Top seal is provided by the Lower Cretaceous marls, bottom seal by the Old Red Sandstone basement and lateral seal by the pinchout of the Jurassic reservoir onto the basement.  Evidence for Jurassic pinchout comes from absence of Jurassic in 9/3-4 where Lower Cretaceous lies directly on basement.  Additionally the seismic indicates variable thickness Mesozoic and the pinchout of the Jurassic reservoir has been equated to the limit of seismically resolvable Mesozoic. The Jurassic reservoir has been encountered in three of the Bentley wells and is of good quality with average porosity of 27%. There is good evidence in the form of shows in 9/3-2A and 9/3-1 that oil has passed through the Jurassic and mapping shows a potential migration pathway from the south however hydrocarbon charge and effective sealing remain the key risks. Company CoS = 12%.

The Babbage prospect relied on up-dip stratigraphic seal to the north, northeast and northwest. 
The presence of Jurassic reservoir up-dip to the north in 9/03b-6, has significantly increased the risk on the prospect, to the extent that this play is unlikely to be viable in block 9/3.

Bessemer prospect comprises a series of separated four-way dip closures within the Upper Palaeocene, with slightly different spill points, which collectively make up the Base case for the prospect.  Top seal is provided by the Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales. Bunsen is a four-way dip closed structure located midway between the Bentley and Bressay fields in Block 9/3c. Closure is at the Upper Dornoch formation (now regarded as Lower Eocene age), with top seal being provided by the Eocene Balder tuffs and overlying Eocene shales.  The closing contour is approximately the same as Bentley Field at 3,730 ft TVDSS, which is also the OWC of Bentley; thus it is assumed that Bunsen would be filled to spill. It is considered likely that Bunsen will be charged with oil as the structure lies on the migration route for oil spilling from Bentley into Bressay.  Oil is likely to be of very similar quality to that found in Bentley and Bressay with an anticipated API of between 10 and 11 degrees.  Bunsen measures approximately 1.5 km by 0.5 km, with the structural crest estimated at 3,649 ft TVDSS

The prospect morphology at Camm is similar to that of Chadwick, Cartwright and Clement, in that it is three-way dip closed with lateral seal provided against the East Shetland platform. There are however some differences. Firstly, it is located on an east-west offset of the Viking Graben bounding fault where there is increased structural complexity and some potential fault terraces.
Secondly, the top reservoir structure is somewhat shallower than the other prospects resulting in the top of the closure being close to the top of the platform. The mapped closure represents the top of a potential trap with top seal provided by Upper Cretaceous Chalk and marl and side seal provided by the fault itself. These seals are a major element of risk on the potential accumulation as the top seal is thin and the chalk is prone to fracture near the fault; and directly above that are the Lower Palaeocene sands. The fault itself provides a likely leakage route as it has undergone movement at least as recently as the Eocene, The potential for shale smear is low as both sides contain much coarse clastic material, typically Devonian Old Red Sandstone in the footwall and Jurassic and Palaeocene sands in the hanging-wall.

M Prospect is mapped at the various levels as an anticlinal structure lying immediately to the south and on the hanging wall of the fault which provides the critical southerly closure to the structure drilled by Occidental/Elf Enterprises well 98/13-1. This fault is a constituent part of the overall Purbeck/Isle of Wight Disturbance fault system, as shown on the Kimmeridgian Micrite depth structure map.  The 98/13-1 well, records minor developments of sandy units within the Bathonian Forest Marble and Fullers Earth units and noted weak shows in each.   We have carried out petrophysical analysis of these two intervals using log data which concludes no significant porosity is evident in the Forest Marble.  It is possible that sand units in the Lower Fullers Earth might be better developed on the down-thrown side of major normal faults that comprise the Purbeck/Isle of Wight Disturbance, and may therefore constitute a secondary reservoir objective. Company CoS = 5%.

The Remora lead is a small, faulted four-way closure formed in the transfer zone between two normal faults. Primary potential is in the Triassic Sherwood sandstone. The faults on the structure appear to be old (pre dating the oil migration) with only minor reactivation during the Tertiary structural inversion. The main geological risks are the poor structural definition by sparse seismic 2D data and migration/preservation. Company CoS = 20%,

Remora lies on a small horst block in 98/7b, defined by 2D seismic data and appears to be a transfer
zone between two normal faults. The Lead lies within the same fault block as the Beacon discovery
but is well below the OWC in that accumulation and relies on oil being stranded in this small trap
during the Tertiary tilting. Total relief on the closure at Sherwood level is about 45m and the closed
area is mapped as only 1.0 km2.

The Triggerfish lead is a hanging-wall trap formed against a convex normal fault, located north of the inverted Needles Fault. 
The main fault appears not to have been inverted and may have preserved its sealing ability through the Tertiary structural inversion episode. 
The principal geological risks are the poor structural definition near the edge of the 3D data cube and the migration/preservation of oil.  
The economic viability of such a small feature would hinge on it being developed in conjunction with discoveries of oil in the nearby Stickleback lead. 
Company CoS = 28%.

Triggerfish is a tilted fault block, dipping to the north and defined to the south by an extension of the main Wytch Farm bounding fault. 
It also lies in the same fault block as Beacon, but is significantly down-dip of the OWC and relies on oil remaining stranded during the Tertiary inversion.

The structure is defined by a ~1km grid of offshore 2D seismic lines. The apex of the structure is located some 1200m from the shoreline and the lead could be tested and produced using an onshore rig and a deviated wellbore. The structure appears to be an old one, existing as a high at the time of the oil generation from the source kitchen to the south and southwest. Isopach maps reveal that an oil migration pathway from the source to Steelhead may have existed at this time. The primary target is the Triassic Sherwood Sandstone. Company CoS = 17%.

Faulted 4-way dip closed structure at Sherwood Sandstone level, adjacent to coast. Steelhead is also a faulted anticline downthrown from the NW-SE trending faults that define the northeast margin of the sub-?basin. The closure is poorly defined by seismic data,particularly to the east. There is no seismic tie from offshore to the onshore data. 
Correlations are good at Jurassic levels and there is no clear closure at Inferior Oolite level. Sherwood correlations are made more difficult by the fact that the Triassic sequence is generally thinning to the northeast, as defined by the thin sequence at Lymington-1, and the Sherwood event is not well defined.

The Cloughton prospect has been drilled up by Well Cloughton-1 by Bow Valley and Partners in 1986. The well was targeting a large fault bound Carboniferous anticline imaged on 2D seismic.  DST 2 successfully tested a Carboniferous sandstone interval 7736-7845 ft RKB. This interval is now recognised by Third Energy to be the Skipton Moor Grits. The DST over this interval flowed gas up to 6 Mscf/d without any stimulation. The pressure date from DST 2 did not allow for a reasonable estimation of reservoir pressure and the zone was not regarded as commercial. The sandstones are tight, averaging 7% porosity and saturation was low, up to 35%. The DST on the Skipton Moor Grits flowed  at rates of up to 6 Mscf/d without fracture stimulation. These low flow rates are uncommercial and would require some form of hydraulic stimulation to enhance the flow rate.

The Skipton Moor Grits Derwent Lead is a fault bound footwall anticline plunging to the North. It forms part of a major carboniferous N-S trending antiform which is intersected by younger NNW-SSE faults, which cross cut the structure. The Skipton Moor Grits is a conventional tight gas play, implying that hydrocarbons conform to structural highs. The Skipton Moor Grits are fine to very coarse-grained feldspathic sandstone interbedded with grey siltstone and mudstone. The formation represents the progradation of a turbiditic fronted delta system that migrated from the north to overlay the Bowland Shale equivalent basinal shales.

The Skipton Moor Grits South Derwent Lead is a domal dip closure with a degree of plunge towards the North East. It forms part of a major carboniferous N-S trending antiform, which is intersected by younger NNW-SSE faults which cross cut the structure. The structural configuration of the South Derwent structure is less well defined than the Derwent structure as it is only covered by 2D seismic. The Skipton Moor Grits is a conventional tight gas play, implying that hydrocarbons conform to structural highs. The Skipton Moor Grits are fine to very coarse-grained feldspathic sandstone interbedded with grey siltstone and mudstone. The formation represents the progradation of a turbiditic fronted delta system that migrated from the north to overlay the Bowland Shale equivalent basinal shales.

The West Hose Prospect is based upon two intersecting 2D lines, and lies 3 km north-west of the Long Clawson Oil Field.  A depth structure map of the prospect, at Top Namurian is attached. This places Westphalian and Namurian sands within closure. The closure is based upon a rollover created by a deeper seated fault.  The proximity to Long Clawson Oil Field and to the Kinoulton-1 well means that reservoir presence and quality are low risk.  Additional 2D seismic is required to confirm closure.    An interesting aspect of this prospect is what has been described as a ?flat spot? beneath the closure.  There is possible column height of approximately 170 m from the top of the structure to the base of the ?flat spot?, if indeed this anomaly represents an oil/water contact. Conventional reserve calculations results in 8.2 STOIIP MMbbl and recoverable reserves of 2.46 MMbbl in a maximum case from the Rough Rock sand. Crawshaw, Ashover Grit and Rempstone sands are also possible pay zones.

Yearsley is one of a series of elongate NE-SW anticlines to the north of the east-west trending Flamborough Head fault zone. The structural configuration was defined by isopaching upwards from the deep mid-Asbian seismic marker based on the thickness of the relevant intervals encountered in wells Kirby Misperton-1, High Hutton-1 and Sessay-1. Using this method Top Lower Bowland, Top Upper Bowland, Top Skipton Moor Grits and Top Sabden Shale maps were defined.  Seismic imaging within the Carboniferous is poor on existing 2D data and closure to the south-west needs to be confirmed in any future work programme.

The primary objective in this block pair is the stacked gas saturated sandstones of Namurian and Visean age.  This interval was drilled and logged in several wells in the region, including the Kirby Misperton #1 (which is located about 6 miles north of this block in SE77), a key well for this region.  This area of the Cleveland Basin is the most productive onshore gas province in the UK. Nearly the entire Lower Carboniferous section appears to be gas saturated, similar to areas of East Texas and western Wyoming which are very productive out of stacked, very tight sandstones.   Recent advances in hydraulic-stimulation techniques have made these types of reservoirs attractive targets.  There are a few shale intervals within the Visean section that could also provide secondary targets in the area.  These are seen on the wireline logs of the Kirby Misperton #1 with resistivities averaging 20 ohms; NuTech analyzed these shales and calculated pay for many of them.

The primary objective in this block pair are the tight sandstones of the Millstone Grit seen in all the offset wells in the area.  These sandstones are approximately 80-100 ft thick and are found in the upper Namurian with some additional potential in the lower Westphalian sections.  NuTech petrographic analysis indicates they are tight but HC bearing.  On wireline logs, the sandstones do indeed appear tight (about 10% F), but the mudlogs from the Anston #1 and Warmsworth #1 (which is located in SE50) note gas shows, fluorescence, and HC cut in several of these sandstones.  These types of tight sandstones are productive in many portions of the US, including North Texas and several Rocky Mountain basins, where recent drilling and stimulation techniques have proven effective.  These sandstone reservoirs appear to part of a basin-center type HC accumulation where much of the movable water originally present in the sandstones is driven off and replaced with migrating HCs.

The basin centre tight gas accumulation (BCGA) prospect relies upon deeply buried Carboniferous Westphalian tight sands with low porosity (5-10%) and extremely low permeability (single micro-darcy) to greatly restrict the migration of gas generated from the interbedded coals.  With continued gas generation over time overpressure conditions could be generated to overcome high capillary pressures, and yield high gas saturations and exceed the frac gradient of intervening shales.  Based on analogues (eg Piceance Basin, Colorado) this process of gas generation, over-pressuring, vertical migration and fracturing on a massive scale in the deeper parts of the Cheshire Basin could result in a pervasive fracture system that provides enough reservoir permeability to allow the microdarcy matrix sandstones to be commercially attractive.

In the Widmerpool Gulf the Upper Dinantinan section tends to be referred to the Widmerpool Formation. Source potential appears to be richest towards the top of the sequence. A significant Bowland Shale interval was penetrated at all wells in the block, except in Long Eaton-1 where it is eroded. The Bowland Shales are characterised by interbedded sands and carbonates within the shale formations, which may also present the option of a hybrid play ? the presence of carbonate horizons will also enhance the potential for successful hydraulic fracturing operations due to the inherent cleavage in many carbonate minerals. The Hodder Formation is the only unconventional play to have been hydraulically fractured in the UK.  However, in the Cleveland Basin, the lowermost Carboniferous section has not been penetrated by a well and is therefore unproven.  Within the Craven Basin, the Hodder Formation is of Holkerian age and predominantly grey to dark grey mudstone, with subordinate and variable detrital limestone, siltstone and sandstone.  The formation has not been penetrated by any wells within the centre of the basin, although Well Sessay-1, which is on the basin flank, did penetrate a series of Holkerian mudstones and limestones, that are presumed to be the Hodder Formation.  Seismic data shows that this sequence identified at Well Sessay-1 continues down into the centre of the basin and is located beneath the TD of Wells Kirby Misperton-1 & -8.

The Early Jurassic aged Lias Group is an organic rich shale hundreds of feet thick. Onshore and in the Southern North Sea the Lias is generally considered immature, however there are pockets of Lias that may have been buried deep enough in the past, before being inverted, to generate oil. This area of deep Liassic burial is covered by blocks TA07a and TA08.

We believe that these Blocks are relatively unfaulted and severely Underpressured due to Glacial/Erosional Unloading. Moreover, the Capillary Pressure of such Dry formations can exceed the reservoir pressure, with important implications. The Conventional drilling of the past has therefore been very overbalanced and incurred severe formation damage. The Filter Cake has conveyed a misleading appearance of extremely low permeability and/or an overpressured formation. Proper Drilling and Completion (following the highly successful practices demonstrated commercially in other formerly glaciated areas) can result in wells that may flow 500 Mcf/d. Pad Drilling with four Slant Wells and one true vertical well may achieve production of 2,500 Mcf/d at each Drilling Location. It is well known that Dry formations (such as posited by the BGS for the East England/East Pennines area), although rare can have excellent prospects for deep CBM wells.

The primary target of the Bertha Lead was originally seen as Beatrice Formation A and B sands.
However, reservoir quality of the A and B sands was now anticipated to be poor west of the Beatrice Field, following the results from the 11/29-1 Manuel and 11/30-6 Sybil wells. Since the Bertha prospect lies broadly between these two wells the chance of finding reservoir quality A and B sand reservoir was now judged to be very low. Consequently, the focus for finding commercial volumes switched to the deeper Middle Jurassic Brora Coal Formation and the Lower Jurassic Orrin Formation reservoirs.
The Top Brora Coal Formation structure was re-mapped using the PA Resources 2012 2D seismic data, which covers the western two thirds of the prospect (Figure 22). This structure has been used to serve as a proxy for the deeper Orrin Formation H and I sands. The estimated STOIIP for the Orrin Formation H and I sands is in the range 18 – 46 – 107 MMstb (Low – Med – High) with corresponding reserves of 3.5 – 14 – 43 MMbbls. The overall chance of success for the prospect was estimated to be low.

Due to deteriorating hole conditions and associated logging issues no CPI is available for the 9/14a-15A well. The discovery was appraised by the 9/14a-17Z well, which was a sidetrack from the 9/14a-17B exploration well which targeted the downdip Plantain prospect.

The downdip 17B well encountered 1.8m of net oil pay at the top of a thick water bearing sandstone.

The Tay lead comprises the distal component of the Tay Sandstone Member (early Eocene)on-lapping and terminating on the Puffin High. The trap involves structural and stratigraphic components. Hydrocarbons have been proven at this stratigraphic level in two wells: 29/4a-1A and 29/4a-2. The reservoir sands are thin but may thicken into depositional channel axes. The Eris West Prospect is currently referred to as Aphrodite. Aphrodite is a NW-SE elongate elongated low-relief structure located to the east of the York/Rough fields and to the northwest of the Mercury field. The prospect measures 10km (NW-SE) by 2km at its widest point. It requires hanging wall fault seal at the crest against the Mercury field to the southeast.
The Prospect is defined by faulting on southern, eastern and western sides and dipping to the north side. The crest of the structure lies at the southern end of the prospect where the faulting has limited throw or may not be continuous and so represents a major trap risk
The primary target is the Permian Rotliegend Leman Sandstone Formation comprising aeolian, fluvial and clastic sabkha facies. Carboniferous potential has not been identified in this area due to poor reservoir quality.

The trap at Scutum is a four-way dip closure over a deeper Zechstein salt swell. Both reservoir intervals are interpreted to be thin turbiditic sheet-like sands, which were deposited between positive relief provided by the salt swell and a resistant Maureen marl to the north/north-east. The axis of deposition is thought to have run west-east, causing the sands to thicken to the north, down dip of the discovery well. However, they pinch out towards well 29/7-3, where they are not encountered.

description: The Inner Pear Discovery was made by well 20/8-2 which proved oil in the Upper Jurassic Buzzard Sandstone Member. The proven accumulation comprises a small oil-bearing 4-way dip closure with an unproven combination structural/stratigraphic upside. The discovery has been mapped on reprocessed 3D seismic data where a top and base J62-64 interval have been picked and cut-offs applied to the resulting isopach to define the pinch-out of the Buzzard Sandstone Member reservoir down-dip of the shale prone 20/8-1 well.  The Gross Buzzard reservoir interval encountered at the 20/8-2 well is 102.1m and contains 10.1m net reservoir sands mostly present within two main sand intervals. The upper of these intervals has an ODT at -2,797 mtvdss whilst the lower sand is water-bearing. The ODT within the 4-way dip closure defines the discovery P90 area whilst the P10 case assumes the sands are filled down to the WUT of -2,840 mtvdss in the lower sand of the 20/8-2 well.

The Polly discovery (formerly the Delta Prospect) was drilled by well 12/26c-5 in June 2008 on the western margin of the elongate, tilted fault block structure (Figure 6). The reservoir was 88 ft deep to prognosis with the well finding a 14 ft oil column above a -6,856 ft TVDSS OWC in the A sand (Figure 17). The underlying Middle and Lower Jurassic sands were water bearing. The well TD was in the Triassic at 7,959 ft MD (-7,809 ft TVDSS).
The gross A sand thickness was 59 ft with a N:G of 75%, average porosity of 12% and water saturation of 24%. The average porosity was lower than expected when compared to that of the neighbouring Beatrice Field at 17%. Petrographic analysis of cuttings suggest that porosity has been reduced by diagenetic quartz overgrowths and carbonate cementation. The impact of reduced reservoir quality was seen in the MDT programme which failed to establish pressures in the water leg due to a tight reservoir and seal failures in the oil column
