description:
The Southwest Heather Discovery was made by well 2/5-10 which encountered oil in the Emerald, Brent and Cormorant sandstone reservoirs. The well tested oil at a combined rate of 6,000 bopd across the 3 discrete reservoir zones. 
The discovery was appraised by the down-dip 2/5-11 well (drilled 1km to the north) and the up-dip 2/5-16 well (drilled 1.5km to the west). Both wells encountered water-bearing reservoir sands, limiting the potential size of the accumulation. Seismic mapping shows the Southwest Heather discovery is contained in a small tilted fault block structure and that the up-dip 2/5-16 appraisal well penetrates a separate, more elevated, fault block to the south. 
The lack of oil in the 2/5-16 well suggests the intervening faults are sealing. The down-dip 2/5-11 well tested the same fault block as the discovery well but apparently outside of structural closure.

Licence P2310 contains a single oil discovery, South West Heather, which was proven in 1979 by the 2/5-10 well. Oil flowed on DST from three discrete reservoir intervals within a faulted anticlinal roll-over structure; the Upper Jurassic Emerald Sandstone Formation, the Middle Jurassic Brent Group Sandstone and the Triassic Cormorant Sandstone Formation. 
Following the drilling of the 2/5-11 appraisal well, RFT pressure data established two separate oil-water contacts, one in the Jurassic and another in the Triassic. Between them, both wells have proven up a base case STOIIP totalling 78mmbo within the fault segment of the structure proven by the 2/5-10 well. 
Recoverable volumes are modest, ranging from 15 to 22mmbo, and assume four or five wells (two or three producers with gas-lift, plus two water injectors). The low recovery factor is due to three separate reservoir sandstone layers and two fluid contacts, in combination with a complex array of internal faults, many of which by analogy with the nearby Heather and Broom fields are likely to be sealing.

The Dragon discovery was first drilled by Marathon in 1994 and subsequently appraised in 2005 with well 103/1-2. On Providence's interpretation Dragon extends from Irish block 51/1 into UK block 103/1.
In 2014 the Dragon 3D seismic dataset was re-reprocessed, with the aim of improving data quality to yield higher confidence depth structure maps and to assess the validity of a hydrocarbon related EEI anomaly. Data re-processing and subsequent re-interpretation was completed in 2015. The results of this work yielded improved imaging of the structure of the Dragon field, however quantitative analysis indicated that no direct-hydrocarbon indicator (DHI) was evident. The presence of apparent DHI on the older seismic dataset was attributed to lithological effects. Resultant volumetric calculations show greatly reduced gas-in-place volumetric estimates, and no indication of upside potential as previously indicated by EEI.

The Dee oil acumulation was discovered by well 13/26a-2 and appraised by wells 13/27a-4 and 13/26a-4. The trap is formed by stratigraphic pinchout to west and north, dip closure to the east and fault closure to the south. Mapping on seismic reflection data and acoustic impedance data, calibrated by wells, defines a core development area. Most likely reserves range 8 - 12 mmbbls depending on the mapped trapping configuration. The Dee accumlation is shared by blocks 13/26a (45-60%) and 13/27a.

Dee discovery well, 13/26a-2 was drilled on the SW and crestal part of the structure. It encountered gas in the Lower Cretaceous Punt Sandstone and oil in the Claymore and Ross Sandstones and deeper Permian Rotliegendes Sandstone. DSTs were carried out on the Rotliegendes Sandstone (100-200 bopd), Ross Sandstone (60 bopd) and Punt Sandstone (22.3 MMscfd). The Claymore Sandstone was not tested owing to the low net pay (9ft), but an oil sample with 37 API was recovered. Appraisal well 13/27a-4 encountered 40ft of net oil pay within thinly interbedded, low permeability Claymore Sandstones above an oil water contact at 4750ft TVDSS. During the subsequent drill stem test, the produced fluids were not passed through the test separator and measured accurately. Stabilised flow conditions could not be achieved owing to water influx due to a bad cement job and possible gas breakout within the reservoir. Flow rates of up to 1250 bopd were estimated.

The Palaeocene Balmoral Sand submarine channels are present, with anastomosing features within the Balmoral, but continue until abandonment of the system when discrete depositional fairways can beinterpreted.  The Balmoral thickness varies considerably over the area, however, where channels are present the upper surface shows typical compaction and drape structures which can be highlighted by careful interpretation of the top surface and then illumination of that surface.  Where hydrocarbons are present, whether oil or gas these are normally accompanied by elevated seismic amplitudes and an AVO response.  Most discoveries in the area have had a gas cap over oil of moderate (21-25° API) quality and gas fill will tend to show up preferentially to oil fill.

description:
The Christian Discovery was drilled by Shell Exploration in 1991 targeting the Jurassic anticline approximately 4km from north to south and 2.5km from east to west situated on the western margin of the Western Central Graben. 
The well initially encountered a gross thickness of 135ft sand rich interbedded turbidites within the Kimmeridge Clay formation dated as early to mid Kimmeridgian (J62). 
Petrophysical analysis calculates a NTG of 50%, an average porosity of 13.7% and hydrocarbon saturation of 68%. DST analysis predicts a permeability of around 30-40mD with a skin of 16.5 reflecting how damaged the interval was whilst drilling. 
No contact was encountered, and no water was seen on test leaving an oil-down-to at 13521ftTVDSS. The well still flowed good rates of 6364 bopd and 7.8 mmscfd given the condition of the wellbore. Formation pressures were taken defining an oil gradient of 0.30 psi/ft at 11200psi outlining an overpressure of approximately 5200 psi.

The Christian discovery, proven by exploration well 21/20b-4Y (Shell, 1990), constitutes a HPHT oil accumulation, reservoired in Upper Jurassic “Christian” turbidite sandstones. 
Reservoir pressure was 11,200 psi and temperature 320°F @ 13,475’ss. A DST flowed 6,200 stb/d oil (41.5?API) and 7.6mmcfd of gas. 
The well failed to reach the deeper Puffin sandstone due to mechanical problems.

The Christian oil discovery is an HPHT oil accumulation discovered by well 21/20b-4Y drilled in 1990. The well encountered 137 ft gross of oil bearing Kimmeridgian turbiditic sands, referred to as the Christian Sand Unit. 
These Kimmeridge sands are over-pressured and tested 6,200 stb/d of 42° API oil. No oil water contact was encountered. 
Reservoir conditions are estimated to be 11,220psia and 320°F at 13,475ft TVDSS. Typical shallow marine shoreface Fulmar sands were encountered below the Christian Sand unit. 
The accumulation also extends into Block 21/20d.

The undeveloped Jacqui field tested oil and gas condensate in Upper Jurassic mass flow sands. The different fluid types at different pressure regimes suggest the field is horizontally and vertically compartmentalised due to the presence of multiple sand fans and faulting. description:
The 9/15b-3Z discovery is an oil discovery made at two levels. The shallowest level is within sands in the lower part of the Horda Formation (Frigg Member) and the deeper level is within the Balder Formation. Sands in both of these intervals are interpreted to be injected from a deeper, underlying Hermod or possible Heimdal sand body.
The hydrocarbon are stratigraphically trapped within the encasing shales of the Horda and Balder formations respectively. Pressure data from the well is relatively poor quality but could support a single hydrocarbon column extending from the Frigg sandstone into the underling Balder Formation sand.

description:
The Alpha Prospect comprises of a stratigraphic trap with the reservoir formed by an Eocene sand injectite mapped as being sourced from a series of underlying Odin sandstone 'pods'. These pods are tested by wells 9/9d-17 in the north and 9/14a-6 in the south and both contain water wet Odin Member sands. Top and lateral seal is provided by thick encasing shales/mudstones of the Horda Formation.
The injected sands are interpreted on modern 3D broadband seismic data and display a similar Class 2 seismic AVO response to the hydrocarbon-bearing Frigg sands in the 9/14a-15A well.

Both the Alpha and Alpha East prospects are injectite wing features within the Eocene Frigg formation host shale.
Both wings straddle the 9/9f and 9/14d block boundary. These injectite prospects appear disconnected on lithology inversion datasets although a small possibility remains that these units connect to one another via sub-seismic sands. 
Both prospects are near to the 9/9d-17 exploration well, drilled in 1997, which found wet Balder sands and did not encounter sand in the Frigg injectite target interval.

description: The Nave basement is a 149 km2 4-way dip closed buried hill composed of Lewisian Gneiss Complex granite. The large areal closure and thickness suggests a large HC. accumulation with an estimated Pmean STOIIP of around 1800 mmbbls of oil. The prospect is situated about 160 km from Sullom Voe, 19 km from Schiehallion and 28 km from Cambo.

description: The Scalesia Prospect is a fault bound terrace, situated between the upthrown Hutton and downthrown NW Hutton Fields.  The throw along the terraces bounding faults is variable, although there is offset, there is Brent ? Brent juxtaposition on both the Eastern and Western faults.  This highlights the key risk on the prospect, containment, due to this apparently unfavourable juxtaposition relationship.  However local data in the NW Hutton field identifies that seismically mapped faults with this juxtaposition relationship are capable of holding 100?s ft of column height and can act as sealing compartment bounding faults.  Fault seal analysis will be a key component of this applications work programme for the Scalesia Prospect. No wells penetrate the terrace, but two key exploration wells in the region, 211/27c-12 and 211/27-7 encountered a full Brent sequences with good reservoir quality and as such provide controls on the stratigraphy and properties likely present within the structure.

description: The Bennett structure lies beneath the north western limb of the Gordon Field near the southern margin of the block. It forms elongate structure approximately 9Km long by 2Km at the crest of a northerly dipping rotated fault block under a NW-SE trending salt swell. Regional information from Cavendish suggests that the principle reservoir is the Westphalian A shoreface sands which are overlain and sealed by the coals and shales of the Caister formation. A secondary reservoir may exist in the Namurian Kinderscoutian as seen in the offset Kepler and Copernicus discoveries . A simple migration path from beneath is expected, as the Gordon Field above is charged via the adjacent Tertiary dykes. Imaging of the lead is moderately good, although depth migration is required to properly position the rotated fault block and faults. Sand quality is expected to be very good with porosity and permeability above the regional Carboniferous average.

description:

The Lead is currently mapped in the 2D seismic and saddles Block 44/7 and 44/6. The lead is defined on the Near Scremerston top, calibrated from the 44/6-1 well.

Data quality is not good enough to map any faults that may exist within the structure or to map any particular event with lot of confidence. Reprocessing will surely improve the interpretation and help define closures at other stratigraphic levels. This is part of the work program.

• Lead A is the largest structure and its 3-way closure is mapped / interpreted based on 2D seismic coverage. The Scremerston is the main closure interval (along with more shale prone basal Yoredale) and a smaller 3-way dip closure at BPU
• Closure to east is confirmed by 2D strike line (Figure 14) as a compressive anticline against major E/W fault
• Yoredale strata is progressively eroded at the BPU towards the crest of the structure
• Top seal: The top of the Scremerston and base of the Yoredale sections are shale prone
• Fault seal: Major fault with later compressive phase. Scremerston juxtaposed against older Scremerston/Fell and Cementstone

description: Camomile is an Upper Jurassic (Fulmar) interpod lead located in UK CNS block 29/6 and 19 km from the Bittern oil field production platform. There has been little exploration of the interpod play in the Bittern area, but the discovery of Centurion provides evidence of a working play concept. Camomile is a 3-way fault and dip trap with top of structure at 7,800ft. Key analogues used for volumetric calculations are Centurion, Howe and Bardolino. The main risk is lateral seal

Camomile: The most promising lead given its proximity to the graben; however, the basin model suggests that the Kimmeridge Clay Formation would only be relatively immature here due to the lower throw of the WCG Fault tipping out towards the south. Charge access to the basinal source rocks is likely impeded by a Smith Bank pod and the Zechstein evaporites towards the south and the retreating thrust front of the Centurion complex towards the north. Migration from mature areas deeper in the basin would likely be directed towards Centurion, Curlew, and Kyle structures, thus limiting the volumes. On the updated BCU map, Camomile could be made up of three very small 4-way structures; however, if so it would be connected to dry well 29/6a-6, which was water bearing in Fulmar (some shows in the chalk were noted); however, if not connected, the remaining two anticlines combined GRV would be below economic threshold.

description:
Chai is an Upper Jurassic (Fulmar) interpod lead located in UK CNS block 28/10 and ~16 km from the Bittern oil field production platform. 
There has been little exploration of the interpod play in the Bittern area, but the discovery of Centurion provides evidence of a working play concept. 
Chai is a 3-way fault and dip trap with top of structure at 5,400ft. 
Key analogues used for volumetric calculations are Centurion, Howe and Bardolino. The main risk is charge access

In order to get hydrocarbons this far inboard from the West Central Graben (~15km to Chai; ~17km to Earl Grey), it would require Fleetwing to fill to spill and 
potentially Challenger before filling and spilling from Silverstone. From there Earl Grey would be preferentially charged before Chai (which, was mostly located outside of the licence extent). The charge risk was therefore considered too high to pursue, and the volumes of either lead were not large enough to warrant further maturation without first testing one of the Greeves prospects (likely Fleetwing) for proof of charge in the Jurassic interval on the platform.

description: A low risk, diapir flank trap sealed against Zechstein salt and prospective at Cretaceous/Danian chalk and Palaeocene sandstone levels. Diapir flanks are challenging to image seismically, with common seismic processing/interpretation pitfalls, and the Isolde trap is not imaged on most 3D data. Analogue calibration data coupled with an up-to-date structural model have been used to generate a top Palaeocene depth map with c. 1500m of relief. The map has been structurally validated and is supported by partial imaging on dual azimuth 3D, thereby reducing trap risk. 23/26-17, some 900m down-dip, found oil shows in Palaeocene sandstones and by analogy with similar fields is interpreted to lie a short distance below the OWC. Leakage of gas and oil is proven by shallow well 30/1-7 and since leakage is ubiquitous over analogous fields, is not a significant risk. All 13 of the analogous CNS diapirs hold hydrocarbons in flank traps.

Curlew A was discovered by 29/7-1 in 1977. It comprises two thin oil bearing sands in the Balder and Sele formations within a four-way dip closure over a non-penetrating salt diapir. The distribution of the sands around the closure is poorly understood and the thin nature of the sands (c. 25ft) means that they are difficult to immage on seismic data. An isochron of the lower part of the Tertiary exhibits a thickening to the south of the closure but whether this is due to thicker sands is uncertain.  The above volumes were generated using REP software and are probabilistic.  .   The chance of success is dependant upon the development of thicker oil bearing sands elsewhere within the closure than at 29/7-1. Due to the Lower Tertiary isopach thickening to the south, this has been assessed at 60%.

Re-evaluation of the petrophysics for the 29/7-1 and 3 wells in the Tertiary to better define net pay and net sand intersections in the wells. Review of the FIT pressure data quality in 29/7-1. description: Curlew A was discovered by 29/7-1 by Shell in 1979. 13 metres of Odin and Cromarty deep water sands were intersected in the well and oil recovered by FIT at three intervals, no DSTs were undertaken. The structure is a simple salt induced anticline, mapped at top Balder level with the sands intra Balder and below Balder. Maximum closure for the trap is 21.6 square km. Sand presence and quality across the structure forms the main uncertainty together with prognosis of the OWC. Previous operators have relinquished with appraising the discovery as a result of these uncertainties.  If reservoir and oil are present across the mapped trap then a substantial resource could be present with a Pmean recoverable volume estimated at 46 mmboe.

The prospectivity presented in the licence application was focussed on the Curlew-A stranded
discovery.

description:
Curlew A was discovered in 1977 by well 29/7-1. Oil-bearing sands were discovered in the Lower Palaeocene section, in the Cromarty and Odin Members of the Sele and Balder Formations respectively.
The trap at Curlew A is a four-way dip closure induced by the underlying Zechstein salt movement. Both reservoir formations are interpreted as thin, sheet-like turbiditic sands, with high porosities but low net sand thicknesses and hydrocarbon saturations. The sands cannot be imaged on seismic, even in the high quality reprocessed 2006 PSDM volume. 
As Curlew A lies in a distal and marginal position with respect to the fairway axis, these sands are assumed to have a sheet-like geometry, thickening down dip from 29/7-1 in response to the seafloor topography during diapir movement. The sands thin and then pinch out in the direction of well 29/7-3, as they were not encountered in that location.

description: The Drumdurno trap comprises a three-way stratigraphic pinchout with dip closure to the north. In the south-east crestal part of the prospect the Dirk Sandstone may extend up to the faulted margin of the Renee Ridge, in which case downthrown trapping may be required against Middle Jurassic or older rocks. Such trapping configuration has been proven to work in the surrounding basin. The resource estimates have been generated using the updip pinchout, with different closing contours based on relative complexity of the trap and reasonable column heights.
Drumdurno is an Upper Jurassic Dirk Sandstone member lead which straddles block 15/29c and 15/30c. The trap is a combined 3 way stratigraphic/hanging wall and 1 -way dip closure

description: The Triassic lead is a series of small accumulations on the flank of the salt wall/ salt collapse feature on block 44/7 and 44/7. It forms elongate structures along the margins of this feature.  The principle reservoir is the Bunter sands which are overlain and sealed by the Solling Claystone and Rot Salt. Well data suggests the sands would be poor to absent but a number of small basins exist, formed by early salt withdrawal, where better quality sands may have been deposited. Migration path is expected to be through the adjacent touchdown in the salt collapse feature.
Closure to N poorly constrained; long-range migration from S required.

description:

43/2-1 encountered some weak gas shows within the Carboniferous (C1-C3).

The most likely source would be Carboniferous in age and we believe that the most likely hydrocarbon type would be gas although an oil source cannot be completely ruled out therefore. However, only gas resources have been estimated for this high risk lead.

Structural integrity is a significant risk for this lead primarily due to the potential for leakage across the bounding faults into the younger, sandstone bearing Scremerston Formation. Furthermore, the topseal has to carry some degree of risk because of the potentially sandy nature of the overlying Scremerston Formation.

description: The crest of the prospect at 3,700m ss is centred on an anticline with formed during the Cretaceous due to salt mobilisation at depth within the area of greatest thickness of KCF. The play concept is a hybrid play within the KCF with the potential for natural fractures within the tight limestones and sandstones within the KCF within the anticline, and the wider area away from the anticline where fractures may be persistent or they can be introduced with the aid of modern fracking techniques. The KCF is considered at an optimal depth for an unconventional oil play.

The Base Upper Jurassic depth map indicates the prospect is a structural-stratigraphic closure on a broadly NE plunging ridge. The ridge is downthrown to the N along several NW trending faults. Maximum relief on the structure varies from 150-400 ft with the low case corresponding to the independent structural closure and the high case being a potential structural-stratigraphic closure. The primary risk for the prospect is cross fault seal against either Zechstein salt or Smith Bank which provides the upside stratigraphic potential. Another risk is whether the Fulmar reservoir section is entirely absent from the crest of the Manhattan prospect given that it is absent in the two nearest wells (22/13-6 and 22/14-3) to the prospect. However 22/14-5 Huntington discovery, l5 km to the N, encountered 130 ft Fulmar sandstone which may be equivalent to the section seen at Manhattan. The oil down to of 12,900 ft sub sea seen at Huntington coincides with the structural spill point into the Manhattan prospect. Ties to wells with a preserved Fulmar section and the 3D seismic character suggest the Fulmar may be present at Manhattan.

description: Mapped on PGS reprocessed data (Mega Survey Plus) at Up. Jurassic, Fulmar Fm. level as a stratigraphic pinchout trap, developed within an interpod setting. The P.1420 partnership (operated by Nexen) drilled the 22/13b-9 well in 2015 to test the Manhattan prospect.
The well was abandoned as a dry hole.
Manhattan was defined as a stratigraphic trap at Top Fulmar level that also contained a small structural closure.
The primary goal of the exploration well was to test for economic volumes in the stratigraphic closure but it also
targeted the smaller structural closure. The well encountered 76ft of water bearing Fulmar sandstone 86ft deep
to prognosis, and the well TDed in poor quality sandstones of the Skagerrak Formation. No hydrocarbon shows
were seen throughout the well. Post-drill analysis suggests that the well penetrated the Fulmar outside of the
structural closure, therefore the most likely failure mechanism is the lateral seal/containment in the stratigraphic
trap.
An alternative explanation for the failure of the Manhattan well is that the structure is charge limited which sets
up the possibility of two smaller stratigraphic prospects up-dip of the 22/13b-9 well: Manhattan Coronado and
Manhattan Stratigraphic. Given the results of 22/13b-9 it is felt that these are high-risk leads, and are
sub-economic considering that they only partly extend onto P.2183.

description: The Achaduin lead is a tilted fault block, comprising of an U Triassic Joanne Sandstone Member reservoir (Stacked fluvial sand and channels and crevasse splays of the Skagerrak Fm. ) . The trap has a dip-closure element to the southwest and is fault bounded to the north and east. Analogue structures within the same block of U Triassic reservoir age are the Gylen prospect and the Janus structure.. Achaduin is separated from the water wet Janus structure by a collapsed graben. failed lateral cross fault seal, or failed charge mechanisms are both potential failure mechanisms for Achaduin. Gas/condensate fill is predicted and can be sourced from either the U Jurassic kitchen to the south-west, which would rely on a down charging mechanism or, from a kitchen to the northwest that relies on cross fault charge from Jurassic into the Triassic. The top seal is the Jonathan Mudstone Member. Lateral seal to Achaduin comprises the U Jurassic marine shales of the Kimmeridge and Heather Formations.

east and dip closed to the SW. The structure is similar to Janus and the play consists of

description: The Edinburgh Prospect forms part of a large tilted Mesozoic fault block, whose trap is defined by dip closure against a large bounding fault and a salt diapir/wall. Within the Mesozoic section there are a number of potential reservoirs of Triassic through to Jurassic age. The prospect spans a number of blocks, as well as the UK/Norway boundary The Edinburgh Prospect relies in part on lateral seal against salt.  This trapping mechanism has been demonstrated as successful in the Oda Field which lies 50km northeast of Edinburgh and has an Upper Jurassic reservoir. As such, the Edinburgh Prospect illustrates the potential in drawing on knowledge and experience from both UK and Norway to move exploration forward in this cross border area

Edinburgh is a fully matured large structural trap forming the southeast end of the J-ridge, to the north of the Mid North Sea High. 
Edinburgh requires a number of key trapping and sealing elements including salt seal, fault seal and dip closure. 
Reservoir intervals of the Triassic and Jurassic are found at depths of 13500ft Tvdss to 20000ft Tvdss. 
Top seal in the prospect is provided by the Kimmeridge Clay and Heather Shales, as well as the CromerKnoll Gp and Chalk and the Jonathan mudstone in the case of an independent Triassic hydrocarbon column. 
The marine Kimmeridge Clay is the main source rock for hydrocarbons in the Edinburgh basin, with additional contributions from the Heather shales and Pentland. 
Basin modelling predicts the Edinburgh structure to be gas condensate bearing.

The trap relies on a combination of cross-fault seal against these older Palaeozoic rock units, as well as pinch-out of the reservoirs onto an N-S trending structural nose to the west. The lack of hydrocarbon shows or fluid inclusions in the upper sand of the 21/1-10 well suggest this unit to be in a migration shadow, whilst the lower sand did contain hydrocarbon inclusions. The dry hole analysis of the 21/1-10 well concluded that lateral containment was the most likely reason for failure, either through leakage of the predicted down-thrown fault to the north (juxtaposition against the Rattray Volcanics), or potentially through lack of stratigraphic containment within closure to the east.

description: Ferrobustamite is a large, very uncertain 3-way dip closed structure against the major Rona Ridge bounding fault. It sits in a large basement embayment which is likely to have been a favourable position for sediment deposition. Seals are likely to have formed within the Early Cretaceous and Jurassic, creating potential for three separate columns defined at K60, K40 and Top Jurassic. Volcanic sills, significant burial depths and a gap in the 3D seismic in the middle of the lead mean that the lead is poorly imaged and largely model driven. Gas is assumed to be the most likely phase, in which case the traps are thought to be limited by column height, and much smaller in area. Key risk is Reservoir Deliverability or quality.

Commander Deep is a Triassic Skagerrak prospect, located north of Shearwater and southeast of Aragorn. The Jurassic on top of this structure has been drilled by well 22/30A-16, containing hydrocarbons, but with poor reservoir quality. A different accumulation is expected in the Triassic, since the Heron shale is expected to be separating the Jurassic from the Triassic hydrocarbon column. Good Skagerrak reservoir is expected, not having suffered from the processes that affected the Jurassic. Seal forms the key risk, since a direct connection northward through thief sands (like Aragorn) and juxtaposition and possible lack of fault seal appears possible. description: The Glenapp lead comprises an Upper Sele Sand stratigraphically trapped with an AVO anomaly. These turbidite sands were transported from the west of 22/29d, within a basin floor fan system in an easterly and south-easterly direction . A consequent well defined channel feeder system, highlighted by a significant AVO anomaly, forms the Glenapp lead. The 22/29-6 well and its sidetracks were drilled and found 8.5? of Rogaland sand. But the channel and its associated AVO anomaly, appear to bifurcate around this high penetrated by 22/29-6 . The charging mechanism for the Glenapp lead is thought to be vertical migration from a Kimmeridge Clay kitchen. Analogues are Marconi and Hurricane.

Glenapp: The Tertiary prospect is a closure within a turbiditic fairway in a distal location at the Tay formation (Eocene). 
The Juno well side-track encountered 2-3m of hydrocarbon column while the initial up-dip borehole was entirely water bearing. The hydrocarbon pocket could be caused by a thin shale bed in the upper section of the Tay formation disconnecting the two wells. The remaining up-dip closure within the low angle fold is nevertheless poorly defined with very small resources.

description: The Godet Prospect is located in the northern part of Block 14/28. The target reservoir is the Piper Fm sandstone, analogous to the productive reservoirs in the Renee, Ivanhoe, Rob-Roy and Hamish fields. The trap is formed across a broadly N-S trending structural nose that is highly faulted resulting in the potential for significant compartmentalisation. The Piper reservoir appears to be completely eroded off the very crest of the structure resulting in a stratigraphic element to the closure. The trap is dip-closed to the east with a combination of fault and pinch-out closure to the north and west. The top and lateral seals are provided by the overlying Kimmeridge Clay Fm. A strong ?Class 2P? reflectivity response at Kilgour has the expected phase change between near and far offsets, anomalously decreased Vp/Vs (i.e. Vp/Vs <1.7) and associated hydrocarbon attributes (Hydrocarbon Projection & Ji-Fi Facies) that are similar to those of Columbus. opportunity_comment: Diapir flank structural lead.
key_work_comment: Firm work is to obtain/interpret a minimum 20 km2 of existing 3D and conduct structural geological studies of diapir bulb geometries. Combined with 2D gravity modelling this should constrain shallow salt body dimensions and avoid the common pitfall of excessive salt in the velocity model. Discrete element modelling of diapir bulb evolution will also be scoped. Further work is to secure funding for the contingent Phase A/C work programme via farmout of a majority interest and/or equity capital injection into Soliton. Contingent on encouragement from the technical work programme and on securing funding, reprocess a minimum 20km2 (full fold fully migrated) 3D dual azimuth data through anisotropic PreSDM (reverse time migration) with full waveform inversion. Despite the small area this will be a lengthy reprocessing with extensive testing, utilising the diapir geometric models in this Application and developed in the firm work programme to apply realistic constraints to the velocity model.
description: A low risk, diapir flank trap sealed against Zechstein salt and prospective at Cretaceous/Danian chalk and Palaeocene sandstone levels. Closest analogues are Machar, South Pierce and Mungo fields. Diapir flanks are challenging to image seismically, with common seismic processing/interpretation pitfalls, and the Isolde trap is not imaged on most 3D data. Analogue calibration data coupled with an up-to-date structural model have been used to generate a top Palaeocene depth map with c. 1500m of relief. The map has been structurally validated and is supported by partial imaging on dual azimuth 3D, thereby reducing trap risk. 23/26-17, some 900m down-dip, found oil shows in Palaeocene sandstones and by analogy with similar fields is interpreted to lie a short distance below the OWC. Leakage of gas and oil is proven by shallow well 30/1-7 and since leakage is ubiquitous over analogous fields, is not a significant risk. All 13 of the analogous CNS diapirs hold hydrocarbons in flank traps.

description: ?Linnhe Field Linnhe? (LFL) targets an undrilled closure beneath the Linnhe Field. The Linnhe formation fluvio-deltaic sands are the target reservoir. The structure is a 3-way dip closure with its SE margin eroded by a major unconformity in the same style as the overlying Beryl formation accumulation and adjacent Beryl Bravo field. The mapped closure depth is ~50 to 100? TVD above a wet Linnhe formation penetration (by 9/13-40z) which was cored and found to have excellent oil shows. LFL is analogous to the Beryl Bravo field where intra-formational seals allow formations beneath the Beryl formation to have differing OWC?s and (post production) pressures. It is conceivable that the LFL prospect has the same OOWC as the adjacent Beryl Bravo field Linnhe formation.

Untested structural closures exist below the developed Beryl formation reservoir in the Linnhe, Nansen and Eiriksson formations. Upside is limited in the Linnhe formation by the presence of wet Linnhe sands in the 9/13-40 and 40z wells. A full section of Nansen/Eiriksson has not been penetrated in any of the original wells due to faulting.

description: ?Assynt J40? is an Upper Jurassic 3-way dip closed structure with its up-dip trap being formed by the major north-south trending F1 fault system. The targeted structure sits to the east and in the hanging wall of the F1 fault system. This fault system demarcates two broad pressure cells with Pre-Cretaceous reservoir being normally pressured west of the fault and over pressured to the east. The Assynt J40 prospect targets Callovian age (J40 sequence) sands. These turbidite sands were deposited as a result of region wide erosion of the emergent East Shetland Platform and through local footwall degradation of the major Beryl Field rotated fault blocks. The prospect is up-dip from the 9/14-15a wet well drilled in 2014 by MPX testing a larger Upper Jurassic concept, although this well did not drill deep enough to test the J40 sequence.  The Assynt J40 prospect can likely be stacked with the Assynt J60 and Ard prospects.

The migration path into the Lapworth Prospect is via fill and spill from the Horne prospect to the northeast.

description: Ferrobustamite is a large, very uncertain 3-way dip closed structure against the major Rona Ridge bounding fault. It sits in a large basement embayment which is likely to have been a favourable position for sediment deposition. Seals are likely to have formed within the Early Cretaceous and Jurassic, creating potential for three separate columns defined at K60, K40 and Top Jurassic. Volcanic sills, significant burial depths and a gap in the 3D seismic in the middle of the lead mean that the lead is poorly imaged and largely model driven. Gas is assumed to be the most likely phase, in which case the traps are thought to be limited by column height, and much smaller in area. Key risk is Reservoir Deliverability or quality.

Agnes, in particular, has a high reservoir risk and lacks AVO support, but detailed reprocessing of seismic data (viewed as currently insufficient to address this uncertainty), along with targeted geotechnical studies, will address this risk prior to a well proposal. description: Rustumite is a 2-way dip, fault and stratigraphic pinch-out trap that is poorly imaged on current 3D datasets due to the presence of volcanic sills. It is similar to the prospect known as Audacious, described by DONG Energy who previously held the acreage. Early Cretaceous marine fans coming down a relay ramp from the northern end of the West Shetland Basin wrap around the plunging end of the Rona Ridge, which forms a structural nose, and onlap onto basement. The phase here is very uncertain. An oil case has been assumed based on the oil found (confirmed by geochemical extractions) in 209/12-1 to the North East. The key risks are bottom seal due to the likely eroded and weathered basement, and trap due to the up-dip edge being under sills.

The geological concept proposed in the application for the 27th Licensing Round has been reviewed based on results from the recent data and work. The Lower Cretaceous shallow marine sandstones (K70.2 - K10 from Ichron biostratigraphic sequence) are the main target and they are believed to have resulted from local reworking of Devonian - Early and Middle Jurassic successions from the northern extension of the Rona Ridge, named Rona-Yell ridge complex and from the Shetland Platform.

description:
The Johnnie Prospect has been defined by mapping the top basement across the Rona Ridge. The seismic pick is well defined on the modern, high quality AMR and NSR11 2D seismic datasets. Well 208/27-2 provides a robust seismic-to-well tie for the basement reflector.

The structure represents a culmination of the Rona Ridge associated with the relaying of the main fault that defines the western margin of the Faroe-Shetland Basin. In that context it has a very similar structural setting to the Clair Field and Lancaster-Halifax discoveries to the south-west which have clearly demonstrated the potential of the basement play in recent years. The prospect straddles blocks 208/23, 208/27 and 208/28, with the spill point of the structure being mapped to be towards the south-west in the direction of the Johnson Prospect.

description:
Statfjord South is a Middle Jurassic discovery (Statfjord Group) drilled by 211/29-10Z and appraised by the 211/29-D73. Well 211/29-10Z gives a gross oil column of 29m, 211/29-D73 proved at least a 15m column.  Estimated average properties: NTG of 85%, porosity 21% and oil saturation 71%. Oil is trapped in a tilted fault block and sealed by the Dunlin shales. The structure is at the southern extent of the main Statfjord field, with a 28m step down of OWC from the main field to Statfjord South. 

The Statfjord reservoir is charged from Kimmeridge Clay Formation in the Viking Graben and East Shetland basins to the south.  In addition, lateral migration in a fill-to-spill manner is likely to have occurred along the axes of the ridges (e.g. via the Brent Field to the southwest). Most of the producing fields in the Statfjord area are situated on fault block ridges of tilted fault blocks.

description:
The Cross Prospect is located predominantly in Block 15/18c although the southern extent extends off the block into 15/18a. The target reservoir is the Forties Sandstone Member.
The trap is formed by a compaction-related four-way dip closure at top Forties Sandstone level. There is a potential secondary four-way closure to the east which forms part of an overall P10 closure. The 15/18-1 well appears to be drilled just to the east and likely outside of the main P90/P50 structural closure.

The Cross Prospect is located predominantly in Block 15/18c although the southern extent extends off the block into 15/18a. The target reservoir is the Forties Sandstone Member.
The trap is formed by a compaction-related four-way dip closure at top Forties Sandstone level. There is a potential secondary four-way closure to the east which forms part of an overall P10 closure. The 15/18-1 well appears to be drilled just to the east and likely outside of the main P90/P50 structural closure.
A review of the nature of the overburden on seismic data reveals that the Sele Formation top seal is downlapped by the prograding wedge of the Dornoch Formation. The key risk associated with Cross Prospect is seal integrity, as it is possible that the progradation of deltaic clastics across the top of the structural closure may have partially scoured or had a detrimental effect on the sealing ability of the overlying Sele Formation shales.

description:

The reservoir target is Upper Jurassic Fulmar equivalent sandstones. Detailed work on seismic inversion lithology products using Apache's proprietary 2015 PSDM volume corroborates the interpretation that reservoir quality sands are present at the South Zell am See opportunity.

Lead 2 is located on the rim of a shallow syncline overlying Rattray Volcanics and consist of Upper Jurassic Fulmar equivalent sandstones stratigraphically trapped against Rattray volcanics. The reservoir is predicted to be overpressured. 
Reservoir presence and charge access are critical risk factors with the charge access risk being higher in Lead 3 than in Lead 1 and Val D’Isere.

description: Rennick is a fault enhanced stratigraphic trap. The western and southern edges are defined by stratigraphic pinch-out of the Lower Cretaceous deep water turbidites of the Britannia Sandstone reservoir towards the Pre-Cretaceous North Forties High and edge of GDE defined fairway. The northern limit utlises a proven fault seal which separates the Leverett accumulation from the Brodgar field. The eastern limit is dip closed. The 21/3b-5 well on structure found a 12ft thick Britannia sandstone with strong shows and recovered oil samples on RFT. The RFT data also shows a 200 psi overpressure from the Brodgar field. The Britannia sand encountered by the well is older than the producing reservoir interval in Brodgar Field, the sand packages in this field have intraformational sealing shales which form top seals for oil accumulations below the gas condensate column. One of these shales separates the two accumulations and supports the overpressure difference between the wells.
The Firecrest Prospect is located at the southern margin of the regionally developed Kopervik fairway.

key_work_comment: The key is to understand the distribution of hydrocarbons within the structure and explain the different contacts encountered in the wells. The work program outlined below is aimed at achieving this, and moving to an appropriately targeted horizontal well: Purchase and detailed mapping of existing seismic data. Application of techniques to identify and discriminate thin sand-bodies, including spectral decomposition. Rock physics studies will be undertaken to ascertain validity of using the seismic data to identify reservoir presence and fluid-type. description: Talbot is a Paleocene discovery in the Mey Sandstone in block 30/13 on the Josephine Ridge. It has been penetrated by Wells 30/13-1, 30/13-2, 30/13a-9 and 30/13a-11 and 11z. The reservoir is part of a turbidite sequence (sourced from the NW) contained in a 4-way dip closure. Differing ODTs and fluid contacts have been observed in the wells: 30/13-2 has an ODT 9446 ft TVD, 30/13a-9 had an apparent OWC at 9422 ftTVD, while the deepest oil was encountered at 9759 ft TVD in 30/13a-11Z. The average permeability is low at 14md and the distribution of pay is variable across the structure. The key element in progressing Talbot is in understanding the different fluid contacts encountered and defining the distribution of reserves across the structure.

description: Scaramanga is an Upper Jurassic Fulmar interpod, analogous to the Howe and Bardolino discoveries. Fulmar reservoir is sourced locally from exposed Skagerrak highs. Top seal and side seal are provided by the Kimmeridge Clay and Triassic pod material respectively.

description: The Fyne Discovery is a sizeable 4-way dip closure within the Main Tay Sandstone.  The Discovery was made by Well 21/28a-2 that encountered oil with an OWC of 4583ft SS.  There has been a total of 6 wells and 3 sidetracks drilled to evaluate the structure. The overall structure of the Fyne Discovery results from the movement of the underlying Zechstein salt which has created a broad four way dip closure at the Base Tay (Top Palaeocene) level.  The crest of the structure is at 4485ft SS. The Main Tay sandstone comprises relatively thick sand units and are interpreted as mass-flow sandstones, deposited from high-density turbidite flows ponded within topographic lows. Sandstone beds are typically 10-20 feet thick, less commonly up to 36 feet thick.  Fluid samples were taken from several of the wells showing an oil gravity range from 21 to 26 Ã‚Â°API.

In Well 206/11-1, over 400 m of sandstones were penetrated from 3,500m TVDss, with a DST flowing 1.65 MMSCFD gas from the upper section. Should this well prove to be successful, the structure could form part of a far larger accumulation within a stratigraphic trap against the Rona Ridge.

description: The Wherry NE lead is based on RMS amplitude extractions and detailed seismic extraction. The main risk is that the structure is shallow and whether the faults to the NE are sealing, however the Wherry updip faults have proven sealing capabilities. If faults are breached, migration will pass updip. Trapping mechanisms involve a rotated normally faulted block with a dip closure to the SE, a 3D dataset for the North of block 48/24a will have to be acquired to accurately define the trapping geometry. De Keyser lineaments compartmentalise the Wherry field into West and South, this lineament can be traced through the NE-SW fabric, so it is highly probable that potential leads are limited within that rotated block. With the reservoir compartmentalised, the lead can be sub-divided into Wherry NE and Wherry East

description:
Benriach is a Lower Cretaceous trubidite, mixed stratigraphic / structural trap. The structure pinches to the east against a combination of Jurassic, Triassic and Palaeozoic strata of the Rona Ridge, creating a 3 way dip trap geometry. 
The reservoir is Albian aged Royal Sovereign Fm which consists of deep marine, prograding sandstone turbidites shed from the Shetland Platform to the east.
The overlying Edradour field is analogous in terms of reservoir age, depositional style, trapping mechanism and fluid expectations. The expected fluid is gas condensate. Other analogues include the Brae fields of the Fladen Ground Spur, North Sea.

description:
Skua was developed by Shell as part of the Heron cluster which is a subsea tie-back to the ETAP platform. There are two exploration / appraisal wells (22/24b-7 and ? 9) and one development well, S01s1.  Skua was on production from 2001 to 2006.  The licence was relinquished by Shell in 2016, but the subsea infrastructure remains in Shell ownership.  The development well has integrity issues and will need to be abandoned by Shell

BP?s overall objective in securing the sub-area of 22/24f covering the Skua field is to reach an FDP or drop decision for a Skua redevelopment within 4 years of being awarded the licence. This will encompass the facilities upgrades required and potential two-well redevelopment comprising a central Skua attic producer in the same fault block as the original Shell S01s1 well, and a southern producer in the Upper Skagerrak in the same fault block as well 22/24b-9.

opportunity_comment: The Johnson Prospect is located directly beneath the Victory gas discovery (207/1-3), where good indications of oil in the basement has been recorded in at least three wells.

description:
The Johnson Prospect is defined by mapping the top of the basement across the Rona Ridge. The trap is structural in nature.

The seismic pick is well defined on the modern, high quality AMR and NSR11 2D seismic datasets. All wells drilled in Block 207/1 provide robust seismic-to-well ties for the basement reflector, and the tie provided by 208/27-2 is consistent with the regional tie. The structure represents a separate culmination of the Rona Ridge to the Johnnie Prospect and lies directly beneath the Lower Cretaceous Victory gas discovery. It has a very similar setting to Lancaster-Halifax discovery to the south where a shallower gas discovery in Lower Cretaceous sandstones was also made (Well 205/23-2, Bombardier gas discovery), before the potential of the basement was recognised.

opportunity_comment: The Paddy Prospect is a smaller, hanging wall closure of the Devonian-Carboniferous Clair Group against the basement structure of the Buzz Prospect. The structure straddles blocks 206/11 and 206/16.
key_work_comment:
The Paddy Prospect has been mapped on the best possible dataset currently available over the area. However, the definition of the downthrown fault seal is still only modestly imaged. A 2 year Phase A work programme is planned to de-risk the remaining uncertainty by reprocessing part of the Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey. In addition the reprocessing will further enhance the image of the faulting & fracturing networks within the reservoir with the use of detailed seismic attribute analysis. Experience from the Clair Field demonstrates that this will be critical for the positioning of an inclined exploration well into the structure. 

Following the completion of a successful Phase A work programme, an exploration well would be drilled during a subsequent three year Phase C work programme. Spark Exploration does not see the requirement for further geophysical data to be acquired as part of a Phase B work programme.
description:
The Paddy Prospect has been defined by mapping the top of the Devonian-Carboniferous Clair Group within the West Shetland Basin, and towards the south-western flank of the Rona Ridge. The seismic pick is reasonably defined on the modern, high quality Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey, and also the AMR and NSR 2D seismic datasets. 
The crest of the trap is at 2,800 mTVDss. The spill point of the structure is mapped to be towards the north-east towards the analogue Clair Field.

The reservoir is a continental Devonian / Carboniferous clastic reservoir as found in Clair.

description:
The prospect has been defined by mapping the top of the Commodore Sandstones tied to Well 206/11-1. The seismic pick is well defined on the modern, high quality Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey, and also the AMR and NSR 2D seismic datasets.

In Well 206/11-1, over 400 m of sandstones were penetrated from 3,500m TVDss, with a DST flowing 1.65 MMSCFD gas from the upper section (3,522 to 3,531 mTVDss). Oil and gas was also observed seeping from fractures in the core taken, and gas shows were noted continuing down to 3,880 mTVDss. At the time of application, Well 205/15-1 (Craster Prospect) was being drilled approximately 5 km to the north-west of Well 206/11-1 to possibly explore for a deeper contact reliant on a stratigraphic trap against the Rona Ridge to the south-east. Should this well prove to be successful, the Screwball Prospect could be demonstrated to form part of a large stratigraphic trap.

The trap comprises a rotated fault block structure and is charged via the Kimmeridge Clay Fm which directly overlies the reservoir. Boa shares some dependency with the forthcoming White Bear exploration well in terms of trap (top seal given Jurassic pressures and fault sealing potential).  Estimated Chance of Success of 13%

description: Carver is an Upper Jurassic Fulmar interpod, analogous to the Howe and Bardolino discoveries. It is currently mapped as being an isolated interpod, bound on all four sides by Triassic pod material (akin to the Bacchus field), but may have a thin connection to the interpod network to the south. Charge is provided by downward migration from the overlying mature Kimmeridge Clay, which also acts as the top seal. Fulmar reservoir is ubiquitous in surrounding well penetrations (22/7-1, 22/7-2RE and 22/8a-4), and modelled to be sourced from local Skagerrak highs. Top seal and side seal are provided by the Kimmeridge Clay and Triassic pod material respectively.

Faulted anticline with closures at Triassic level. Reservoirs in the Joanne and Judy are fluvial deposits with a variety of amalgamation and continuity. Sourcing is provided by juxtaposition to the Kimmeridgian clays over the large eastern fault. Seal is provided by intermediate shaly levels in the Triassic. A probable closure at Pentland level could trap hydrocarbons. Positive results at Horne Forties could prove a strat. trap which is required to make adjacent Peach discovery economic. Company CoS = 20%.

The Jenkinson Triassic prospect is located in Block 30/08 to the northeast of Calloway discovery (30/08-3). This is a 3-way dip closure trapped against a major NW-SE trending fault system. The crest of the structure is formed by a ridge defined by an easterly throwing major extensional fault at ca. 15,200ft TVDss. The crest of the ridge is either fault bounded or is eroded by the BCU, both of which are thought to provide effective containment. Structural spill for the proposed dominant Joanne Sandstone Member reservoir section is defined as -16,900ft TVDss, providing ca. 1,700ft of vertical relief. There is also a valid closure at the Judy Sandstone Member level; however this is deep and likely to be ultra HPHT.  The Jenkinson structure is along strike from the Calloway discovery to the south, and is confined in a different structural fault block.

description: The Horne (Joanne) Prospect is located 5kms to the northwest along strike of the Pentland discovery at Callaway. The crest of the structure is at 4,450m ss with a mapped vertical relief of approximately 300m. The cross fault seal is the mature Kimmeridge Clay Formation which provides a direct migration path into the Prospect. The Joanne reservoir is anticipated to be approximately 450m thick (as encountered in the 30/8-3 well). The Joanne Sandstone was good quality in the 30/8-3 well and is the primary objective of the proposed Horne exploration well.

key_work_comment: In addition to fully interpreting the North Calloway prospect using newly acquired BroadSeis DAZ seismic data, the North Calloway prospect would also benefit from further analysis to ascertain whether charge can access the structure via the basin bounding fault to the east of the structure. Further technical work understanding the likely properties of the reservoir from surrounding analogues, integrated regionally with the seismic data, may also help to mature the prospect towards drill-ready status.
description: North Calloway is a fault-bound dip closed structure 6km north west of the Calloway discovery well. North Calloway is targeting Triassic prospectivity, as Calloway was initially. Calloway proved up a good quality reservoir, but appears to have lacked access to a Kimmeridge Clay/Heather Formation reservoir. North Calloway appears to be more optimally located to access large volumes of hydrocarbons, whilst also appearing to posses the same high quality reservoir within structure.

The main prospect identified on the license at the time of the 26th Round application was Horne, a structural trap with a 3-way dip closure against a NW-SE trending fault. 
It lies on a terrace to the east of the J-Block horst. Triassic Skagerrak sediments are considered to be present over the entire structure. Based on seismic correlations and surrounding well control, Joanne (crest 4770m) and Judy (crest 5120m) sandstone members are targeted within this structure with closures defined by their spill toward the SE, at 5030m for the Joanne and 5500m for the Judy.

The key risk is thought to be trap effectiveness, attributed to the sealing capacity of prospect bounding faults.

opportunity_comment: A tilted fault block with a well-defined closure at Top Pentland Sandstone. Mapped as connected in the P10 upside case with the Pentland Sandstone reservoir in the Callaway Discovery.
key_work_comment: The work programme will focus on developing within the first 6 months a detailed well design, well evaluation programme, environmental pre-permitting and costings using the Company?s well management company, Fraser Well Management. Additional geological work will be undertaken on the Pentland reservoir in Block 30/8 to ensure that the data gathering from the proposed Horne well (e.g. coring) is maximised. Pre-well work will include a review of the diagenetic history of the Pentland using the core data from 30/8-1 and cuttings from 30/8-3. There would be new petrophysics project on the 30/8-1 and 30/8-3 wells. Particular emphasis will be placed on predicting the pressures for the well, particularly for the Pentland given the unexpectedly high pressures encountered in the 30/8-3 well and its impact on the drilling.
description: The Horne (Pentland) Prospect is located along strike 5kms to the northwest of the Pentland discovery at Callaway. The crest of the structure is at 4250m ss with a mapped vertical relief of approximately 200m. The cross fault seal is the mature Kimmeridge Clay Formation which also provides a direct migration path into the Prospect. The Pentland reservoir is anticipated to be approximately 270m thick (as encountered in the 30/8-3 well) and so should hydrocarbons be trapped they are expected to be filled to base. The Hydrocarbon-Down-To observed in the 30/8-3 well was 4,696.4m ss which is deeper than the mapped closure at Horne. The Callaway Discovery is assumed to be fault bounded and not in communication with the Pentland at Horne. However the P10 case assumes Callaway and Horne accumulations abut each other across the fault bounding the Callaway horst.

key_work_comment: In addition to fully interpreting the Turnbull lead using newly acquired BroadSeis DAZ seismic data, more detailed interpretation to understand the seismic character of high N/G Pentland sequences vs low N/G Pentland sequences may assist in furthering understanding of the Turnbull lead. If North Calloway is progressed to being drill-ready, Turnbull could easily be tested at the same time; this would only require a short-sidetrack into the reservoir, or possibly even with one deviated borehole.
description: Four-way dip closed structure at Top Pentland level, adjacent to the Calloway discovery. Calloway encountered a fully oil-bearing, low N/G Pentland section, lending encouragement to the chance of technical success at Turnbull. Key risk relates to the presence, quality and connectivity of the reservoir; a high N/G Pentland section would likely represent an attractive exploration prospect.

opportunity_comment: Stratigraphic up-dip pinchout with well 214/29-1 further updip.
key_work_comment: Petrophysical analysis, rock physics, seismic re-processing, Ji-Fi analysis, structural mapping, geochemistry (fluid inclusions), reservoir modelling.
description: The Ghost Prospect is located in the southwest of block 214/29 on the stratigraphic interval below the Nymeria Prospect. The Ghost prospect is identified by a strong amplitude reflector in seismic. The Prospect has a stratigraphic up-dip pinch-out, and is not found within the 214/29-1 Well, but can be correlated to the 214/28-1 well where a Gas saturation has been indicated at 40%.

key_work_comment: Similar to Michael and Tick Tock, Tiny Tim shares dependency with the P2318 "Great Expectations" (former "Pirate Bay") prospects with respects to AVO reservoir and fluid responses. Success with the "Pip" (former "Hook") well, to be drilled in 2018/2019, will de-risk these prospects and determine whether they will be matured to drill-ready candidates.
description: The Tiny Tim Lead is a combination structural-stratigraphic trap updip and to the east of Copperfield. The AVO responses are as expected for Quartz sandstone reservoir, and with a change in AVO character as expected for an oil-water contact, conform to structure at 2250m. It has the same Upper Jurassic reservoir and source play elements as Copperfield. The main risks for Tiny Tim are trap seal and source migration.

"Anchor" Lead in PanCanadian's 20th Round application for Block 15/18. No risking parameters in report. Stratigraphic entrapment of Galley Sandstone, pinching out to NE. Piper Sandstone secondary target. No map for SW part of lead in application report. Underlying KCF likely to be immature.

opportunity_comment: Fully evaluated.
key_work_comment: The main work programme items are 3D seismic reprocessing and G&G work. The reprocessing aims to improve the seismic imaging of Upper Jurassic reservoir interval. Agnes, in particular, has a high reservoir risk and lacks AVO support, but detailed reprocessing of seismic data (viewed as currently insufficient to address this uncertainty), along with targeted geotechnical studies, will address this risk prior to a well proposal. Trap seal is the highest risk to the Copperfield prospect, and additional geotechnical studies are aimed to further the depositional understanding of reservoir, along with progressive accommodation space development (through faulting) through time.  This will facilitate better understanding with regards to faulting and stratigraphic trapping.
description: The Traddles prospect is a 3-way dip-closed trap on the down-faulted terrace juxtaposed to the west of Copperfield. It has the same reservoir and source play elements as Copperfield although the trap risk is higher.

The Kaja lead is situated along a clearly defined proximal lower Balmoral sandstone channel and exhibits a strong AVO response, analogous to the Dumbarton and Lochranza fields, with some structural conformance.  Source/Migration: 90%.   Reservoir: 80%.   Trap: 50%.   Seal: 80%.   .   Overall CoS: 29%

key_work_comment: Uriah and Bitzer are considered secondary targets; given Upper Jurassic exploration success, these Palaeocene leads would be matured to prospects.
description: The Uriah Lead is a Paleocene combination structural-stratigraphic trap to the east of Copperfield. The reservoir has a strong AVO anomaly, with migration focus along deeper Jurassic faults.

Two small Paleocene leads, Uriah and Bitzer exist in the western part of the P2365 licence(Appendix E). They are combination structural-stratigraphic traps thought to encompass deepwater sandstone of the Balmoral Formation (Mey Sandstone Mbr) known to have good, producible reservoir quality in the nearby Lochranza and Dumbarton fields. The volume potential of the Uriah and Bitzer leads has been estimated using a very simple, direct estimation approach using the lead outline areas and calibrated with relevant discoveries in the area. 
No risk review has been undertaken.

Detailed depth conversion to confirm the connectivity of the oil discoveries in the south and the northern extension of the feature.  If the mapping is ambiguous then move to phase B, if not then move straight to Phase C including kicking off a 12mth EBS baseline to benchmark against the East Brae EBS from Marathon's Decommissioning Environmental submissions. 
Carry out a reservoir deliverability study and Initial Well Design & Geomechanical Operating Limits scoping. 
Phase B
Purchase 200 sq Kms of ther PGS 2013 Geostreamer data and carry out a seismic inversion of the data to identify the sand distribution in the Shelterstone discovery

description: The Maureen Field ceased production in 1999, having produced 54.5% of a STOOIP volume of 398 mmbbls. Consequently, the remaining oil in the reservoir is about 181 mmbbls. A redevelopment of the Maureen Field could recover between 10-40% of the remaining in-place oil, the high end being dependent on advanced EOR.

The Maureen field is an oil accumulation reservoired principally within Palaeocene age sandstones at the crest of an antiform formed in response to localised halokinesis within the Zechstein salts. The salts have not yet formed a true diaper, causing only doming within the overburden stratigraphy. Exact timing of the halokinesis is uncertain but early movements were contemporaneous with Palaeocene sediment deposition, evident from the distribution and stacking patterns of the individual Maureen fan sandstones across the structure.

Whitbeck is a complexly faulted, 3-way, dip-closed trap. The discovery well passes through the reservoir section from hanging wall to foot wall. The structure appears to be dip-closed, bisected by the N-S striking fault encountered in the well. The overlying seal is a mix of conformable, impermeable mudstones and halites of the Mercia Mudstones on the Ormskirk Sandstone. Whitbeck appears to be a combination trap, with the discovery well encountering a fault, having reservoir at virgin pressure in the hanging wall and partially depleted reservoir (by ca. 500 psi at the time of drilling in 2009) in the footwall, implying a sealing fault. An alternative interpretation is that the Centurion Mudstone is acting as a barrier to communication between the upper and lower reservoirs (i.e. no fault in the well), and only the lower reservoir is in communication with one of the producing fields nearby (possibly via the aquifer) and is therefore depleted.

Glein is an undeveloped Tight Gas discovery, reservoired in the Leman Sandstone, adjacent to the West Sole field.  The structure is formed of two areas.  Glein West is a well defined steeply dipping fault block sealed by juxtaposition against Zechstein evaporites.  Glein East is a lower relief, structurally complex area which is poorly imaged on existing seismic data.  The discovery contains 161-210bcf GIIP in an elongate NW-SE steeply dipping fault block and is penetrated by 2 wells.  Development is considered to have been hindered by the low permeability reservoir, complex faulted  structure and small volume of gas initially in place (GIIP).  Appraisal uncertainty remains on the GIIP on the eastern flank of the discovery which is structurally complex and poorly imaged on 3-D seismic data.   Reducing uncertainty on this GIIP range would allow a field development feasibility decision to be made.  The envisaged development would be a 3-well tieback to the West Sole Alpha platform.

description: Pegasus East Deep is an undeveloped Carboniferous Discovery which is interpreted to form the easternmost extent of the Greater Pegasus gas accumulation. Two gas bearing reservoir sandstones are present, (stacked fluvial channel complexes) one in the Kinderscoutian and one in the Alportian. The regional top seal is the Silverpit formation, but locally an inter-Carboniferous seal is also required and assumed to be a thick shale in the lower Marsdenian. There is a well defined structural trap which is  easily mappable on 3D seismic data.

Well 43/13b-4, Pegasus East discovery well, was drilled by Lasmo in 1991 in a fault bounded anticlinal structure. 
It lies primarily in the licence P1727 but extends into licences P1724 and P2457 and is located about 11km east of the 43/13b-7 well. The well encountered gas-bearing sandstones of Namurian A and B age (Chokerian and Kinderscoutian) with gas shows within poor reservoir quality sandstones. Three unsuccessful DSTs were attempted across the Namurian B (Kinderscoutian) and the well was plugged and abandoned. 
Pegasus East is a structural closure with faults bounding the Eastern and Northern extents. At the location of the 43/13b-4 well, the Westphalian has been fully truncated however there is potential for Westphalian gas downdip, which has been evaluated as the Pegasus East Flank prospect. As the 43/13b-4 well was drilled in a downdip position on the Pegasus East structure, it is possible that the Alportian is gas bearing updip and prospective volumes have been computed for this interval.

description: The Avalon Channel prospect is located nine kilometres up-dip and along trend from the Avalon oil discovery having been initially identified as a far-angle amplitude anomaly within a clear channelised fairway.  The reservoir lies at approximately 3450ft TVDSS and is comprised of Dornoch Formation sands. Reservoir thickness is prognosed to be approximately 40ft TVT. The trap is predominantly stratigraphic with lateral and top seal provided by intra-formational shales, and the overlying Balder Formation and Hordaland Group. The closest offset well to the Avalon Channel prospect is 21/6-2 located 3.5km to the south. This well found 18° API oil in poor quality Upper Dornoch Formation sands, from which 5 gallons of heavy oil was produced during a DST.

The pre-award prospectivity for the Avalon Channel prospect was based on a reflectivity anomaly that correlated with a channel system up-dip of the Avalon discovery.
Studies indicated that the Avalon Channel was likely to contain gas within a small 4-way dip closed structure within its westerly up-dip extent. Unfortunately, the down-dip oil leg of the prospect was found to consist of a predominantly water wet response with only sporadic indications of hydrocarbons possibly indicative of a hydrocarbon migration pathway, residual saturations or possibly gas in a low-quality reservoir.
The Phase A work programme proved effective in evaluating the Avalon Channel prospect and provided a clear result that indicated a significant decrease in likely in-place volumes.

The discovery was attributed as a heavy oil accumulation (<18o API with high viscosity) and therefore sub commercial which resulted in Mobil abandoning the licence.

Freya and Fulla both are situated on the Rona Ridge 20km to the north-east of the giant Clair Field.
The main reservoir units for Freya are the Clair Group Carboniferous/Devonian sands. These sit atop the basement Rona Ridge. The trap mechanism for Freya is a three-way dip closure, with the west bound by the main Freya fault. Cretaceous shales form the seal both above and at the fault.
Hydrocarbons are sourced from Jurassic Kimmeridge clays from the Foula sub-basin to the west.
The giant Clair field to the South-east, of which Freya could be considered an extension, is the best 
analogue field.

The Skye discovery lies in Block 211/23b, was drilled in 1994 by Amerada Hess. The field was not taken to development due to the marginal economics of a single well subsea tieback. The 211/23b-12 well drilled on Skye found a 60ft oil column in thick, high quality Tarbert sandstones on the flank of a tilted fault block. The structure is analogous to the Dunlin SW structure further to northeast. Fairfield has calculated a range of STOIIP volumes for Skye (12-22-30mmbbo). Under current mapping all of the STOIIP resides in 211/23b (already licensed to the operatorship) although given the seismic vintage, and some of the issues identified elsewhere in the dataset, new 3D seismic data could suggest extension of Skye into 211/23e. Interpretation of Fairfield reprocessed 3D seismic across the area of Block 211/23e has shown additional small fault block closures within the 211/23b and 211/23e blocks. The closures are called the Skylarks and Fairfield estimate STOIIP range of 2-17-70mmbbo.  The work programme is designed to address uncertainties in fault mapping, reservoir presence, trapping geometries and hydrocarbon fill. The work will be based around the acquisition and processing of latest generation seismic data utilising PGS Geostreamer technology to achieve a wider seismic bandwidth at improved signal to noise. This data will be acquired in 2012, with processed products taken to PSTM and pre-stack inversion early in 2013. Subsequent interpretation and mapping will lead to the generation of structural models to be used to development a full understanding of the reservoir and trap potential. The geological modelling will also be taken into dynamic reservoir modelling to assess the range of recovery from the area that can be derived from a development tie-back to the local Dunlin platform.

Faraday is a gas condensate accumulation in the Jurassic Heather turbidites; it was discovered in 2011 with the drilling of the 30/1a-11 well. The discovery well encountered 90ft of hydrocarbon bearing sandstone with good reservoir properties; however, due to wellbore complications neither fluid samples nor pressure data for the accumulation could be collected. Extrapolation of pressure from the underlying Fulmar sandstone suggests the accumulation to be HPHT with estimated temperature of 375°F and formation pressure of 15,750psi. 
Faraday is a tilted fault block system. Faraday is a combination sub-unconformity trap and fault bound trap at Heather Formation level. The overall structure dips to the south-west with up-dip truncation by the Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) to the north-east. The north-eastern limit of the Heather reservoir is constrained by the 30/1f?8 well, which penetrated thin, ratty, Heather sands. To the east, the discovery is separated from the Oakwood discovery by north-east to south-west trending faults.

The Oakwood discovery is a Heather Formation sub-unconformity trap comprising a thick Upper Jurassic wedge which thins out to the north and is eventually truncated by the BCU. To the south, the Upper Jurassic wedge thickens against a Zechstein salt wall whilst to the east and west, various elements of fault seal are required to form an effective trap over the entire structure.
A series of north-east to south-west trending faults bisect the structure and were active in the late Jurassic, with some inverted during the Lower Cretaceous. The main control on the spill point is the western fault separating Oakwood from the Faraday discovery.

The HPHT Calloway discovery is located in block 30/08 to the east of the Judy Field and north of the Jacqui discovery. The 30/08-3 discovery well was a near vertical well, with a total depth of 18,445ft TVDss in the Judy sand of the Skagerrak Formation. The well encountered oil in the Pentland Formation prior to TD in the Triassic. The Calloway prospect is interpreted as a high relief pre-Cretaceous structure and is clearly defined by a major NW-SE trending faults down throwing to the west, and by a southerly throwing fault at the southern margin of the structure. Whilst the main reservoirs are sands within the Pentland Formation, the distribution, connectivity and quality of these sands remain uncertain. Net pay was encountered in the Heather, Jacqui, Pentland and Josephine sections, however the underlying Skagerrak is wet. An ODT was established at -15,469ft TVDss in the Josephine sands. description: The prospect was drilled by the 30/8-3 well in 2006 by BG, discovering gas condensate in sandstones of Jurassic Jacqui Formation, Jurassic Pentland Formation and Triassic Josephine Formation. MDT samples were recovered from the Pentland at measured depths of 4,485.8m and 4,657.6m, both containing oil. A fluid gradient of 0.21 psi/ft can be determined from the limited number of pressure points. The reservoir quality within the Pentland and Joanne are good considering the depth of burial. The minimum hydrocarbon column (filled to base) seen in the Pentland in the 30/8-3 well (271m) exceeds the closure on the structure map (160m) defined by the bounding faults to the horst. It is assumed that the bounding faults are sealing with charge from mature KCF on the eastern boundary.

The Peach discovery lies within a NW-SE trending structure, having both dip and stratigraphic closure of deep marine sandstones encased within basinal mudstones. The structure dip closes to the North and East and relies on stratigraphic pinch out of the Forties sandstone onto Lista shales to the South and West. Peach Extension relies on the same trapping mechanisms as the Peach Discovery although with the stratigraphic pinch out of the Forties sandstone occurring further to the SW.

Kerloch is a series of faulted blocks situated within an area of interplay between 3 significant fault zones, approximately NE 8-9km from the North Cormorant Platform and around 9km SE of the Eider Platform.
The Kerloch prospect was first drilled in 1976 by 211/22-1 and proved a working hydrocarbon system with Middle Jurassic Brent reservoir overlain by Upper Jurassic Heather and Kimmeridge Clay formations. 211/22a-10 was then drilled in 2007, targeting an adjacent fault block and encountered a different oil gradient, and also different OWC from the 211/22-1 well. Geophysical interpretations of the previous seismic vintages highlighted the structurally complex nature of the field. The Osha Lead is a Paleocene Vaila Fm. Reservoir within the T20-T30 sands in the blocks 208/19 and 24. The sands are confirmed within the 208/19-1 well and show excellent reservoir properties sources from the Shetland platform. The lead has a stratigraphic trap, charged by the Kimmeridge clay Fm. directly through Mesozoic faults. In AVO analysis, the prospect appears bright in Far, and Dim in Near AVO, and therefore is indicated as a gas condensate. An analogue for this prospect is the Cragganmore gas discovery, which similarly has a long-distance migration route observed in a number of discoveries within the area.

•Stratigraphic trap depending on updip and lateral pinch-out

The Blackpool prospect is mapped on 2D seismic data as a three-way dip-closed and faulted structural closure within the Triassic Ormskirk Sandstone Formation. The prospect is dip closed to the north, south and east with a fault closure on the western margin which offsets Ormskirk reservoir against Mercia Mudstone Group. The reservoir is likely to be characterised by a high N:G succession of aeolian sandstones with minor fluvial sandstones and playa lake mudrocks. The top seal is provided by the Mercia Mudstone Group mudstones and halites. The source is Carboniferous Namurian shales and Westphalian coals.  Parameters listed above are probabilistic. An inert (nitrogen) percentage of gas in place is applied based on comparison with Marram and Ormonde fields such that inert percentages are P90-60, P50-45, P10-30. Recoverable volumes (bcf) minus inerts are therefore estimated as P90 - 22, P50 - 36, P10 - 49..   .   Risks are estimated as follows; Trap - 47.5%, Reservoir - 90%, Seal - 70%, Charge - 77.5%. The overall Geological chance of success is estimated as 23%.

The Linnhe Field is an abandoned sub-sea development ~6.5km NE of the (Apache operated) Beryl Bravo platform in block 9/13f of the UKCS.
The field was discovered in 1988. The reservoir fluids were not sampled at the time of discovery and were assumed to be similar to the Bravo East fluids. First oil was produced on 24th October 1989 via an un-insulated subsea flowline back to the Beryl Bravo platform. Production was from one producer, the 9/13-40z wellbore, and injection occurred into one down flank well, 9/13-44z (Table 1). Production from the field ceased in December 1991 and the subsea facilities have subsequently been removed and pipelines decommissioned. A final well test prior to field shut-in showed production at 1,174 bopd, 6 MMSCF/D gas and 0% WC. The field had produced 0.77 MMBO and 3.5 BCF of gas or 1.35 MMBOE prior to cessation of production.
