Eris West is an NW-SE elongated low-relief structure to the west of the Eris Field. There is also an additional potential pop-up structure within Eris West, that has a higher relief and was once linked to the Mercury gas field, orientated WNW-ESE and approximately 4km long by 1km wide. The principle risk for Eris West is the ability of the present seismic dataset to accurately define the continuity of the faulting and closed structural trap between it and the Rough Gas Storage Field, combined with the fact that most of the top reservoir structure is deeper than the surrounding fields. Eris West is a low risk prospect, but it does lie down-dip and below the GDT of the Eris field. The principal risk is therefore really associated with the size of closure and whether there is sufficient independent dip reversal to materially separate Eris West from the main Eris field.

description:
Cragganmore was discovered by DONG (Operator), Engie and Dana Petroleum (E&P) Limited (Dana) in 2012 and is located in the North Flett Basin, West of Shetlands, UK. The reservoir at Cragganmore is comprised of turbidite sands of the Lower Vaila formation (Lower Paleocene age), which were derived from the east off the West Shetland Platform. The presence of gas filled reservoir is characterised by a Class III AVO anomaly on 2015 reprocessed 3D seismic data, which defines a 3-way stratigraphic pinch out and 1-way dip closure. Based on the seismic amplitude shut off, the gas-water-contact (GWC) is estimated to range between 11,940ft TVDSS and 12,300ft TVDSS. 

The 208/17-3 discovery well encountered relatively dry gas (estimated CGR ? 10 bbls/mmscf), 96.5ft of net sand, 14.5% average porosity, Sw of 45% and permeabilties of 0.5-8mD. Due to the relatively low permeabilties, the primary objective of the appraisal well is to test the deliverability of the reservoir with a DST and to recover representative fluid samples.

The Aumerle Prospect is a seismic amplitude and AVO-supported stratigraphic trap mapped at Top Forties Formation, lying on the northwest flank of the Arran diapir, down-dip of the Arran North field. 
The Aumerle amplitude anomaly lies along the same northwest-southeast trending turbidite fairway as the Banks discovery, and its similar characteristics and magnitude suggests a similar good-quality reservoir with a condensate and/or gas fill. Aumerle is dipclosed to the west, with a hydrocarbon-water contact inferred from amplitude cut-off at around 2870mSS. However, the Aumerle trap requires an up-dip stratigraphic pinch-out to the east, a fault or stratigraphic seal to the north, as well as fault separation from the Arran diapir to the south.

description: Prospect is a combination trap on the southern flank of the Halibut Horst. Trap boundaries are defined by stratigraphic pinch-out to the north, dip closure to the west and south and a fault to the east. The target reservoir interval comprises Lower Cretaceous-Upper Jurassic sandstones of the Scapa and Birch sandstone members. It is envisaged these sandstones were primarily derived from the Halibut Horst and deposited in submarine fan settings. Charge is invoked from down-dip, mature Upper Jurassic source kitchens via Lower Cretaceous-Upper Jurassic sandstone carrier beds. Potential top and bottom seals are provided by background shales of the Valhall Formation and Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Examples of analogue fields include Buzzard and Scapa.

Thundercat Shallow is an extensive combination trap on the southern flank of the Halibut Horst, a major structural high in the Moray Firth trending approximately east-west. The prospect boundaries are defined by stratigraphic pinch-out onto the Halibut Horst to the north; a short, faulted boundary against the Horst to the east; and dip closure to the south and west. The trap has a shallow crest at 2800ft TVDSS and closing contour at 4200ft. The top and base of the gross target reservoirinterval - Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous ‘Scapa-Birch’ turbiditic sandstones- have been seismically mapped across the trap area and tied down-dip to the closest offset well 14/28a-5Z. Although dry with no significant shows, this well encountered a thick (>700ft), high net-to-gross reservoir section.

description:
Prospect summary:

Trap: Stratigraphic trap (Fig 2.1) 
Reservoir: Mid Eocene turbidites (Fig 1.11,2.1 and 2.1)
Source rock/charge/migration: Potential Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous oil-prone source rocks (Kimeridge Clay Formation) have not been proven in the Rockall Basin. However, there is the presence of rotated fault blocks (Fig 1.9 and 1.10). Also Early Cretaceous shales are proposed to be a potential source rock. The Ariel Prospect is 1.5km from the Benbecula gas discovery which indicates the basin has a working hydrocarbon system. 
Seal: Overlying Eocene and younger mudstones (Stronsay Group) provide a regional top seal (Fig 2.5 and 2.6).
Key risk: The principal risks concern the presence of source rocks and the validity of a migration route through the thick Cretaceous-Paleocene mudstones and Paleocene volcanics from the deeply-buried potential source rocks.

key_work_comment: Detailed mapping of the prospect will be done on new 3D broadband data (unclear when this will be shot). This should clarify the actual geometry of the prospect, including key information like length of stratigraphic pinchout-line, location of apex and potential geomorphological features (scours, channels etc.) that might compromise the sealing components. Dalwhinnie straddles blocks 209/11a and 12 on the original licence. The Dalwhinnie prospect was identified on Dong proprietary 3D merged seismic data and was the primary driver for the initial 27th Round Licence. The potential reservoir target at the time of the application was the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridgian turbidite sands, mapped as a seismic thick showing an amplitude response. The sand was initially mapped on the DN09M1 data as a soft event, but the later TGS broadband seismic represented the feature as a hard event. This was interpreted to be either an igneous event or a cemented sand. Reinterpretation of the TGS Non-Exclusive 3D survey (Northern Lights 2014) seismic had concluded that it was highly likely that the Dalwhinnie amplitude event was of Upper Cretaceous age and not Upper Jurassic as previously thought. description: Block 3/12b contains the Unst prospect. This is an Eocene Frigg feeder channel recognised on 3D seismic, exhibiting a strong amplitude anomaly at the proposed top Frigg sandstone reflector. The anomaly appears to conform to depth structure suggesting that it is representative of a fluid filled closure. The proposed fluid type is gas based on the down-dip occurrence of gas at the Nuggets fields in Block 3/19. An oil leg is also considered possible, but the magnitude of the 'soft' seismic anomaly is suggestive of a compressible fluid and most likely gas. The prospect appears to be structurally controlled with spill likely to the north and north west related to the amount of counter regional dip created by the differential compaction of the sands. The lateral controls appear to be sand limit either as channel or over-bank with surrounding facies mud dominated. To the south the sands are likely to continue basin-ward towards the Tryfan minor gas discovery made by Apache in 3/17-2.

Channelised Tay Sandstone lead with potential DHI. Combined structural/stratigraphic trap.  EnQuest define the geological probability of success,(Pg), as getting on to the predicted the range defined by the P90 - P10 distribution.
Trap: 100%, Seal: 100%, Reservoir: 50%, Migration: 100%, Total: 50%.
EnQuest uses a probabilistic method for the calculation of resource estimates in exploration targets. Usually input variables are entered as normal distributions, except GRV which is entered as log-normal, and except where offset data indicates otherwise. These are primarily based on the P90 (downside / Min) and P10 (upside / Max) estimates of each input parameter, whilst ensuring P99 and P01 values as reality checks. If the base case is quoted in this application it corresponds to the Pmean value of the distribution.
It is to be noted that the volumes calculated in the required DECC 'Part 4' prospect summary sheet will therefore be different from the volumes will be carried internally within EnQuest.

description:
Upper Jurassic interpod developed on a long lived salt wall.  Kimmeridge Clay Formation can be identified and mapped based on seismic response.  Thin Fulmar is known from nearby interpod targeted wells.  Reservoir presence and quality is a key risk and uncertainty.

Hydrocarbon migration from the Central Graben at this stratigraphic level remains an unknown in the area due to patchy reservoir development.

Tiberius is a prospect within the Upper Jurassic Fulmar play within block 28/3. There is a long lived NW-SE trending salt wall present which gives some optimism on the migration route into the area.
Upper Jurassic reservoir preservation (or deposition) is not well understood this far west on the shelf, but is generally thought to be a significant risk. However, there are notable
exceptions to this trend and local tectonics may be more influential than regional trends. The prospect is four-way dip closed structure which is enhanced into a three-way dip closure against the SW margin of the interpod. 
A high case is recognised where the entire NW terminus of the salt wall is oil filled, down to a spill point in 28/4.

The lead is a structural closure bounded to the north by an E-W trending fault with dip closure to the south and is shared with Block 98/11  reservoir 63%; seal 80%; trap 65%; charge 34%; OVERALL 11% or 1 in 9.   Oil volumes estimated by Monte Carlo statistical estimation (MIN=P90; MAX=P10)

description: Colter East is a rotated fault block containing Sherwood Sandstone reservoir sealed by Mercia Mudstone, charged from Liassic oil-prone source rocks in the Wessex-Channel Basin to the south of the prospect. Migration occurred by face-loading of mature Liassic with Triassic Sherwood sandstone in footwalls. Effective Mercia Mudstone caprock preserved trapped oil through a period of inversion and tilting during the mid-Tertiary.

description: Block 98/11b contains the Ballard Point discovery which was drilled by Gas Council Exploration in 1984. Well 98/11-2 flowed 9.6 million standard cubic feet of gas per day with 170 barrels of 45oAPI condensate from Triassic Sherwood Sandstone. The appraisal well 98/11-4,4Z drilled in 1987 tested oil at low rates (c.180 bopd equivalent) from just above the oil-water contact in the Sherwood, and gas at low rates (25,000  50,000 scfg/d) also from the Sherwood. This well appears to share the same fluid contacts as 98/11-2. Rotated fault block trap with Sherwood Sandstone reservoir. Charged by Liassic oil-prone shales, mature into gas window in the deep basin immediately south of the structure. Reservoir has low porosity; the structure having been inverted during the Alpine compressive event but has good permeability for gas.

The Ballard Point discovery is a rotated fault block trap with Sherwood Sandstone reservoir, charged by Liassic oil-prone shales, mature into gas window in the deep basin immediately south of the structure. description: The Calypso Prospect is an Upper Jurassic (Fulmar) fault terrace play straddling blocks 30/27 and 30/28. The Propect is defined by two major NNW-SSE trending faults which downthrow to the east and coalesce to the south. The trap is completed by dip closure to the north. Hydrocarbons would be sourced from the Kimmeridge Clay within the Central Graben with migration through the eastern bounding fault. Although requiring a distance of 30km, good oil shows are observed in the 30/28-2 well on the next terrace down to the east of Calypso, and the Iris accumulation, reservoired in Fulmar sandstones, is only 10km further east. The crest of the structure is at 2,450m TVDss with maximum closure at 2,700m TVDss.

The depositional system is a deep water channel system with sand input from the Dornoch Shelf immediately to the west. The seismic amplitude extent is larger than the structural closure so a stratigraphic component to the trap is postulated.

description: The Garderhouse lead is based on the possibility of an oil leg beneath the seismic amplitudes associated with gas and proven in the Nuggets producing fields where high porosity, permeability Frigg Formation sands are encountered. An oil leg is observed at Nuggets N2 (well 3/19b-2). In Nuggets N1, the API is reported as 19 deg. The depositional system is a deep water channel system with sand input from the Dornoch Shelf immediately to the west. Conceptually, sand isolation points may exist on the Dornoch slope in Block 3/17 and these would provide the up-dip seal to the channel system in Block 3/18.

Buttermere is up-dip of the Nuggets 2 gas field (Total operated) and is comprised of a small gas anomaly (class 3 AVO response) surrounded by a larger AVO anomaly which sits within an Eocene age Frigg Formation basin floor channel/fan system. The results of the simultaneous inversion also indicate the Buttermere lead to be hydrocarbon bearing. The hydrocarbon anomaly exists outside any structural closure and is therefore interpreted as a small stratigraphic accumulation of oil (with a gas cap) within the Frigg Formation channel sands.

description: Vaila is an amplitude defined prospect. The amplitudes conform with structure, but there is a stratigraphic element of onlap and pinch out of the reservoir onto the FuglÃ¸y Ridge to the west, the Pilot Whale anticline to the north and the Brendan's Dome to the east. The  amplitude anomaly exhibits similar phase characteristics to gas in the Strachan Sandstone at Tobermory in Block 214/4, 50 kms to the southwest of the prospect. The interval of higher amplitudes associated with the Grouse Sandstone have the polarity expected at the top (soft - trough) and base (hard - peak) for a gas-filled sandstone. It is considered possible that the gas-water-contact of the structure, as defined by the edge of the amplitude anomaly, is at a sub-sea depth of approximately 2,300 m, represents the fracture limit for the top seal. In the area of the FuglÃ¸y Ridge the elevation above the ?contact? is approximately 300 m, which is within 50 m of the estimated maximum ?fill-to-spill? (the P10 fill case).

description: This prospect is defined within the Zechstein Z2 hauptdolomit in P2331 as a large structural 4-way dip closure with upside stratigraphic potential. The majority of the prospect (ca. 80%) is located within licence P2331 with the remaining portion within blocks 38/22 and 38/23. The hauptdolomit reservoir is well developed in the area and overlies sulfate platforms that can relatively easily be mapped out on seismic data. The hauptdolomit has good inter- and intragranular porosity and fair permeability with additional fracture permeability. Effective side and top seal is provided by anhydrite. Gas (and possibly minor condensate or oil) is provided by Lower and Upper Carboniferous coal-bearing strata mature for gas generation south of the prospect. Analogue fields have been found in the UK Central Graben (e.g. Auk and Argyll), as well as in the Netherlands and Poland.

description: The Sissy Jupe Extension is located to the north of the Sissy Jupe Main Prospect, and involves an age equivalent intra-Kimmeridge Clay Fm. reservoir in a combined stratigraphic-structural trap setting.  The prospect is almost entirely covered by the AH981214 and Moray Firth PT06 3D seismic surveys, although the data quality of these 2 legacy data sets is challenging for detailed stratigraphic and structural interpretation. In addition to the 3D data, 2D seismic data in the east and west of the prospect has been used to define the stratigraphic pinch-out edge within the Upper Jurassic isochore thick.  Since the legacy seismic data is regarded as poor and intra-KCF reservoir intervals cannot be directly mapped, thinning of the gross Upper Jurassic Isochore has been used to define the inferred reservoir pinch-out: a minimum thickness of 1100m of less of Upper Jurassic section defines the pinch-out edge.

Four way dip closed Balmoral and Maureen sandstone prospect, on trend with thick Balmoral Sandstone section encountered in south of block 21/29  EnQuest define the geological probability of success,(Pg), as getting on to the predicted the range defined by the P90 - P10 distribution..   Trap: 80%, Seal: 80%, Reservoir: 40%, Charge: 80%, Total: 20%.   .   EnQuest uses a probabilisti method for the calculation of resource estimates in exploration targets. Usually input variables are entered as normal distributions, except GRV which is entered as log-normal, and except where offset data indicates otherwise. These are primarily based on the P90 (downside / Min) and P10 (upside / Max) estimates of each input parameter, whilst ensuring P99 and P01 values as reality checks. If the base case is quoted in this application it corresponds to the Pmean value of the distribution. .   .   It is to be noted that the volumes calculated in the required DECC 'Part 4' prospect summary sheet will therefore be different from the volumes will be carried internally within EnQuest.

description:
Mesozoic flower structure creating Jurassic and Triassic sequence repetition underlying the Wick prospect in blocks 11/24b and 11/25b on Wick Detachment. Wick structure results from late Jurassic and early Cretaceous compression, enhanced by Alpine inversion and shearing. Stacked low angle thrust sheets, repeating Jurassic and Triassic section. Fracturing may extend into the Devonian creating conduits for oil migration from Devonian source and fracture storage capacity.
For estimating of potential fracture and storage volumes in the Wick and Alpha  inversion features, the Lancaster Field West of Shetland provides a useful analogue. Well 205/21a-7 flowed at 10,930 bopd using an ESP with all the flow coming from the large fractures at the top of the basement. Porosity range for the main fracture zones is 2/5/8 percent with average fracture zone porosity 4.8 percent.  Net to gross for the fractures is 100 percent and water saturation is very low with oil saturation of 90 to 98 percent

Directly underlying the Wick prospect, the Wick Detachment feature remains undrilled in 11/24b and 11/25b.
The prospect is interpreted as a Mesozoic flower structure created Jurassic and Triassic sequence repetition underlying the Wick prospect in blocks 11/24b and 11/25b on Wick Detachment. description:
The structure is created by a mapped left-stepping jog on the right-handed shear system which cross-links Helmsdale and Great Glen Faults. The side-step is some 4 km wide. This step is a compressional structure comprising a zone with at least 4 main reverse faults, all dipping to southwest and all northeast-vergent, operating to drive the brown-shaded sub-thrusting block obliquely under the hanging wall. Associated with these is a fold which is Alpha Prospect, indicated by the dotted green contours. Alpha is expressed only in the sub-thrust footwall.
In the monocline hanging-wall the shears created a small dome which was tested by 11/24a-2 (Knockinnon), it traps a minor oil pool in Callovian, the well terminated in a described repeated section in mid Jurassic sediments. In the footwall, however, a large compressional fold is mapped with 75 msecs dip and fault closure down to 1725 msecs, covering around 5.5 square km.

description: Dunrobin forms part of the Central Ridge structural high. The high is a focus for migration out of the Beatrice / Great Glen sub-basin. Effective charge and trapping is indicated by the presence of a DHI at the crest of the structure. Reservoir is present and charged in a separate structure downdip, where well 12/27-1 tested gas from an oil-stained Beatrice sandstone. High quality sandstone of the Dunrobin Bay Group is also present in 12/27-1. Reservoir can be mapped with confidence from 12/27-1 to Dunrobin on high quality 3D seismic. Both formations are expected to be argillaceous in the area surrounding the Dunrobin Prospect

description: The Raiden lead is a shallow 3-way dip, fault bounded BPU/Devonian closure that is covered by 3-4 2D lines from the PP162DGOGA survey. The BPU gradually deepens in all directions and is significantly down-thrown to the South by a large East-West trending fault which juxtaposes the Devonian reservoir onto upper Cretaceous Chalk. The Devonian lies on a seismically opaque basement with little reflectivity. Raiden has a clear migration pathway from the East Orkney Devonian kitchen to the Northeast. In addition, there are bright amplitudes less than 10km from the crest of the structure that may indicate the presence of hydrocarbons.

This is a prominent horst block that dips to the east and west and is defined by large throw faults to the North and South which juxtapose the Devonian reservoir against Palaeocene shales. Furthermore, the lead is most likely internally faulted by smaller normal faults. However, only one available seismic line directly crosses this lead therefore the exact nature and extent of the closure to the East and West is uncertain. 
Similarly to the Raiden lead, this structure is very shallow and the Palaeocene top seal has been incised by a large glacial canyon.

description:
The Wick prospect is a fault bounded structural high, immediately up-dip of the spill point of the Lybster oil and gas discovery at the Beatrice reservoir level. The Lybster discovery contains oil and free gas cap in the Middle Jurassic Beatrice sandstone interval. The field has produced oil and gas via an extended reach development well drilled from onshore to offshore. Only c.100,000 barrels of oil were produced at the field prior to the field being shut in. Unexpectedly gas was produced with the oil in volumes not anticipated in the development plan and production was shut in as there was no export option for the produced gas.
The Wick exploration well is targeting a P50 prospective recoverable resource of 3.3mmboe on 11/25b with a total of 17 million barrels of oil equivalent, (mmboe) with an upside (P10) possible outcome of 58 mmboe rec for the combined blocks 11/24b and 11/25b. The technical chance of success is high with an estimated 36% probability of encountering moveable oil.

The Wick exploration well targeted a P50 prospective recoverable resource of 17 million barrels of oil equivalent, (mmboe) with an upside (P10) possible outcome of 58 mmboe recoverable. 
The technical chance of success predrill was estimated 36% probability of encountering moveable oil.
The key risk was considered to be containment of hydrocarbons, as the prospect is an Alpine related compressional fault trap requiring downthrown fault sealing against Devonian meta sediments for an upside outcome. Seismic reprocessing had been recently undertaken to improve imaging, and this resulted in recognition of an independent upthrown core to the trap, further improving the chance of success. However, the lack of hydrocarbons in the well proved that the cross-fault sealing lithologies that had been anticipated predrill, did not seal in the up-dip location of the trap. This outcome combined with the noticeably sandy section encountered in the regional sealing Uppat mudstone section has had a negative impact on much of the prospectivity for the licence.

The Knockinnon Discovery is located ~8 km off the coast of Scotland, 15km north-west of the Beatrice Field and 7km south of the Lybster Field. It was discovered by well 11/24a-2 and its sidetrack 11/24a-2z, drilled in 2000 by Talisman. The Knockinnon structure is located on the eastern edge of the Sutherland Terrace immediately adjacent to the Great Glen Fault. The principal reservoir targets are the Beatrice A and B Sands, though hydrocarbon shows were also encountered in the overlying Volgian and Brora Sands. It consists of a complex, faulted and steeply dipping pop-up feature surrounded by a more gently folded structure.The fault delimiting the prospect in the north dips to the SE and defines the area of closure outwith of the drilled area. If this fault does not seal, it is possible that hydrocarbons may have migrated up-dip across the fault towards the Lybster Field.

description: The Sarclet discovery was made by well 12/21-3 operated by Britoil in 1983. The well was targeting an upthrown rotated Beatrice fault block target, which was dry, but the well intersected a younger spiculitc sandstone of Oxfordian age described as the Alnes sandstone. The sandstone is a clean quartz sand but contains Rhaxella sponge quartz spicules which have precipitated quartz cements throughout the reservoir greatly reducing the original fabric poroperm. A petrophysical review of the discovery has been used as input to a volumetric assessment, combined with mapping of the available 2D seismic data. The petrophysics suggests that the intersection may be oil on rock and that the entire fault block could be full to spill, resulting in a significant oil in place estimation. Success at the applicants Wick well may have a bearing on appraisal and potential development of Sarclet.

The Sarclet discovery well 12/21-3, was drilled by Britoil in 1984 and encountered an oil down to at 8,550ft tvdss within the Alness Spiculite Sands. The well was drilled on a simple tilted fault block closure trending WSW to ENE and fault bound to the south.
The Alness Spiculite is composed of altered Rhaxella sponge spicules with dissolved spicule material occupying what was the pore space at the time of deposition. The preserved moldic porosity resulting from the dissolution of the spicules is between 20% and 30%. Despite the high porosity, the reservoir has very low permeability (typically less than 1mD). The measured low permeability in core is corroborated by the test results from offsetting wells 12/21c-6 and 12/22-2, where they recovered completion fluid only, and the lack of inflow with the test of well 12/21-3.

description: Within the East Orkney Basin, there is a Northwest-Southeast trending mound-like feature within the Devonian section that is easily mappable on several OGA 2D lines. This feature has no structural closure but thins to the East and West within the basin. The mound itself may contain reservoir that stratigraphically pinches out either side, however, the application area is out with the Devonian kyle limestone reef trend identified on the Mid North Sea High (MNSH). Alternatively, if the Zechstein is deeper as suggested by Richardson et al, 2005, the mound could be salt with pinch outs on the salt flank trapping hydrocarbons from the basin. Stratigraphic pinch out plays may exist within blocks 13/3 and 13/4 as seismic packages can be seen to thin to the West as the basin shallows. These features cannot be mapped with any confidence, but a denser 2D grid or a 3D dataset might be able to identify stratigraphic closures.

description: Andromeda North is defined as a tilted fault block along the northern edge of the Cavendish-Murdoch fault zone. It is robust footwall 3-way dip closure, reliant on a combination intra-carboniferous-BPU seal. The reservoir target is a stacked sequence of deltaic sands of the Lower Westphalian to Upper Namurian as tested by Pegasus West (43/13b-7) and the Cavendish field to the East. Two sand types are known in the area - a poorer quality fluvial channel sandstone characterised by thicker individual units with poor permeability (typically 1-10 mD) and tidally reworked sandstone which are thinner, cleaner and exhibit much higher permeability and connectivity (typically 100mD to 1D). Anticipated hydrocarbons are dry gas similar in composition to gas encountered at 43/13b-7.

Well 43/12a-3 (Andromeda North) is the most recent well drilled on the Greater Pegasus structure and penetrated a gas-charged lower Westphalian A sand package (W1-40). Additional sand packages (W1-30, W1-20 and N5-20) were present in the Lower Westphalian A and uppermost Namurian section but were encountered below the contact in the well. 
The Andromeda North discovery is a small three-way dip closure, lying entirely within the licence P2128, and the top seal is assumed to be within the Langsettian (Westphalian A) shales above the reservoir.

Mistral is a stratigraphic lead related to an amplitude anomaly associated with a seismic marker interpreted to be near Base Forties / near Top Lista. The anomaly is interpreted to be a deep water Forties age sandstone that is partly overlain by the Topper lead and intercepted close to its seismic limit by well 21/1b-17. AVO modelling suggests that the high amplitude event is not indicative of oil bearing reservoir quality sands. Analysis of the 21/1b-17 well suggests that calcite cemented sands at Forties level could be responsible for the high amplitude seismic response. As with the Topper Lead, Sele Formation shales are interpreted to provide top and lateral seal. Hydrocarbon migration into the Tertiary could be vertically, via faults, or by longer distance migration. There is a risk of biodegradation based on the relatively shallow depth of the target reservoir interval.

The Te-10 lead is identified at Palaeocene, Forties Sandstone Member stratigraphic level, located south east of the Buchan field, as a distinctive amplitude anomaly on the seismic. From the amplitude anomaly and the polygon shape, Te-10 appears to be a meandering feature. However, the limit of seismic signal does not allow confident confirmation on this. The rock physics analysis demonstrate that the sandstone seismic response is hard.
Well 21/01b- 17 has been drilled downdip of the lead to the east and encountered water bearing sandstone in the Forties Sandstone Member with no resistivity kick and no shows.

A J63 to J64 reservoir interval is proposed, with the top, lateral and base seal by claystones of the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation (KCF).

The key risks for Zermatt prospect are perceived to be reservoir presence and trap efficiency.

trap_type_comment:
The Joanne segment of the Isabella prospect is a fault bounded stratigraphic (truncation) salt flank trap on the northern limb of the Jane Salt Diapir (Figure 1, 2). Top seal is provided by Upper Jurassic to Lower Cretaceous shales unconformably overlying the Top Triassic; base seal is the Julius Mudstone mb of the Skagerrak Fm. The Jane Salt Diapir plus the main bounding fault to the J Ridge act as lateral seals. The Upper Jurassic Heather and Kimmeridge Clay fms also constitute the source rock that is proven present and mature in the Harrier Graben. The Joanne sst is truncated by the Mid Cimmerian Unconformity along a ENE trending line north of the Jane Salt Diapir, and is absent to the south of the diaper. Consequently, the underlying Julius mdst and Judy sst members have a shallower crest than the Joanne sst up against the diaper, and the Judy spill point is controlled by the saddle between the Jane Salt Diapir and the J Ridge. Seismic data and data from the analogue Triassic fields on the J Ridge suggest that the Julius mdst is a more than 70m thick competent shale unit that provides an effective Joanne base seal. Thus most of the Triassic analogue fields nearby have separate Joanne and Judy columns. Main risk for the Joanne main objective is considered to be lateral seal towards the J Ridge.
As the Judy sandstone mb is believed to carry a very high risk it is only considered as upside potential. Main risk is on migration as migration would rely on indirect charge from Joanne via fault juxtaposition from a limited number of faults west of the main prospect area. Further, because of the relative shallow position of the Judy crest and the steep limbs up against the salt a material Judy HC accumulation carries a high top seal risk (pressure analysis indicate relative high risk of blown trap). The Judy Segment is a 4-way dip closure against the Jane Salt Diapir limited by structural spill to the J Ridge. Top seal is the Julius Mudstone and base seal is the Triassic Smith Bank Fm. The Jane Salt Diapir acts as lateral seal.
key_evaluation_comment: Since Total take over of P1820 operatorship in December 2018 the prospect mapping and geological model has been revised, including risking and volumetrics. Main objective is now being only the Joanne Sandstone mb of the Skagerrak Fm) and as a consequence of the revised geological model a new target well location has been agreed on in the partnership (Figure 4). A new depth conversion model has been prepared and the propsect model updated accordingly. Pore pressure prediction is curently being updated. Further a new site survey and geotechnical boreholes has been completed (data analysis and reporting ongoing). Well planning is ongoing, drilling rig (Noble Sam Hardly) has been contracted, and spud is expected in Q3 2019.

The Val d’Isere exploration well, 21/10b-11 was drilled during the Initial Term of P1998 and together with the new seismic data, fulfilled the Initial Term Licence commitments.
Val d’Isere was identified as a stratigraphic pinch out of the Fulmar sandstone against a Rattray high. The prospect is located adjacent to the Forties-Montrose paleo high comprised of Rattray volcanics.
The well did not encounter Fulmar reservoir quality sands, which was a failure mechanism that had been identified as a risk pre-spud.

Val D’Isere comprises Upper Jurassic Fulmar equivalent sandstones stratigraphically trapped against Rattray volcanics on the NW edge of the Forties high. 
The top seal is provided by Kimmeridge Clay and the lateral/bottom seal is formed by juxtaposition to Rattray Volcanics. Locally sourced, early maturity oil is predicted as the hydrocarbon fill. 
The target reservoir is predicted to be overpressured. 
Reservoir presence and charge access are critical risk factors.

description: Kessog (Triassic) is situated at the SW end an elongate NW-SE orientated tilted fault block with a total area of approximately 30km2. The structure has been heavily influenced by salt remobilization. The structural crest of the field is at approximately 13600ft TVDss. A HCWC is not seen in the existing wells, and the structure is dip closed at approximately 15000ft TVDss. 30/01c-9 encountered residual oil at 14935ft which, when the depth uncertainty is considered, suggests the discovery is filled close to the spill point and has a column height of approximately 1400ft, lying in the range of offset fields Hudy, Jasmine and Jade. The Triassic Josephine Sandstone reservoir represents deposition at the distal end of a terminal fluvial distributary system in response to the late Norian humid climatic phase and was deposited on a playa sandflat by thin, poorly-confined channel fill deposits and sheet flood sandstones. The discovery was tested by 30/01c-5A at 3683 BOPD/7.6mmscf/d.

The Kessog South is a NNW-SSE trending fault block generated by salt movement.
The Kessog South compartments (C4, C5, C6 and C9) are hydrocarbon bearing in Jurassic Pentland and Josephine sandstone.

description: Kessog South (Jurassic) is situated at the SW end an elongate NW-SE orientated tilted fault block with a total area of approximately 30km2. Erosion of the Pentland Formation at the crest forms a stratigraphic trapping mechanism, with three-way dip closure likely downflank. The structure is complex due to the effects of salt-mobilization and late Jurassic rifting.  Kessog (Jurassic) was discovered by 30/01c-4, drilled by BP in 1986, and tested at 4418bopd / 8.8mmscf/d. Subsequent appraisal wells tested hydrocarbons across the majority of the reservoir section. The Pentland Formation is subdivided into three members which record evolution of the depositional system from lacustrine delta and sheetflood environments towards incised-valley fill deposits, crevasse splays and coal horizons. There are no other examples in the CNS of fields producing from the Pentland Formation as the primary reservoir, only Franklin as a secondary reservoir.

description:
Jolene is a late Jurassic (Oxfordian, J52) Franklin Sandstone Member discovery made in well 30/01c-9 by Total in 2007. 
A distal lower shoreface expression of the Franklin Sandstone was encountered and cored at this well location. The Franklin Sandstone is absent in the other appraisal wells in the underlying Kessog disovery, but regional mapping suggests the possible development of a shoreface system fringing the J-Block structure to the south. 
The trap is closed to the north by erosion of the late Jurassic section, and to the west and south by dip or stratigraphic pinch out. To the east, faulting may control the extent of the accumulation. 
The extent of the accumulation is ~15km2, with a potential column height of ~1000ft. 
The Franklin Sandstone consists of a thin basal turbidite channel fill overlain by shoreface deposits.

The Mussel lead comprises stacked shallow marine and deep-water sandstones within the Late Jurassic Heather Formation (J46-52 and J56) and fluvial sandstones of the Middle Jurassic Pentland Formation. Analogous reservoir intervals are preserved in the Jade Field flank wells and in the up-dip section in Kessog Field. 
The trap is a hanging wall, three-way dip closed against a fault structure which relies on fault seal to provide trap integrity.

The Kessog South is a NNW-SSE trending fault block generated by salt movement.
The Upper Jurassic Fulmar sandstones are hydrocarbon bearing in the C9 compartment.

Sunset prospect is an average energy anomaly It is located on the flank of a salt diapir . In this respect, Sunset is similar to the Fram Field in block 29/3. The north side of the Sunset diapir is hydrocarbon-bearing as seen in the 29/10-2 well. The anomaly exhibits reasonable conformance to structure with the anomaly terminating around the 9,250 ft depth contour at the Forties level. The anomaly also lies in an isochron thick for the Balder to Chalk interval suggesting the section may be sand-rich. The reservoir objective at Sunset appears to be in the Andrew or possibly the Maureen. The primary technical risks are reservoir thickness and quality.

The Holder prospect is a seismic amplitude anomaly sitting within the Tor/Hod Formation of the Cretaceous chalk. The chalk is known to be a commercially viable reservoir at the nearby Stella & Kyle fields and is currently under development at Harrier. The prospect has been intersected by 29/10-2, in which gas peaks of 6% and 15% were observed at 9750 and 9790 ft respectively. Correlation with offset wells places the shows in the uppermost section of the Hod Formation, at a significant kick in the sonic log. The interval was tested, and following acidization of the reservoir, flowed 140 bbls of oil to the surface.

Glengorm prospect is an inversion-modified extensional fault block (footwall closure) at Upper Jurassic levels, with Fulmar and Heather Formation reservoirs likely to be present. The prospect requires fault seal against the inverted fault system in order for the hydrocarbon column to be protected from overpressure-driven breaching (i.e. Glengorm is protected as it is contained within the Bramley 22/21-7 pressure cell). 22/21-7 encountered shows in sandstones at both Fulmar and Heather levels. 22/21-2 to the west also encountered a sand in the Upper Jurassic at TD, believed most likely to be a Heather Sand. Within the Glengorm area, both reservoir sand intervals were deposited prior to the J62 flooding event. Glengorm and other mapped Upper Jurassic opportunities are believed to be protected from the blown trap at the 22/21-7 well because the crest of the structures are positioned deeper and pressures modelled to be within safe distance to the fracture gradient. For the Fulmar level, the maximum hydrocarbon column height down to closure of 1550ft is considered viable. Some uncertainty in depth of burial exists with respect to the Top Heather turbidites at Glengorm.

Eden prospect is the downthrown, hanging-wall segment to the south-east of the greater 22/21-7 / Campbell rotated horst block. Reservoir targets are Fulmar & Heather sands. The top seal integrity is considered fairly robust due to deeper burial than other nearby prospects and in this respect the trap is considered to be 'protected' pending no lateral or vertical leakage along faults. The trapping mechanism relies on fault seal closure to the northeast and north west and is the key prospect risk. Eden is located on a more easterly oil migration fairway and is connected to a smaller, more local kitchen than other prospects. Modelled expulsion rates from this kitchen indicate sufficient hydrocarbons are generated to fill Eden to its mapped spill point. The trapping  mechanism relies on fault seal closure to the northeast and north west and is the key prospect risk.

description: The Shinoi prospect was identified initially by its obvious diapiric structure close to numerous relevant analogues. The diapir sits within the Tay and Forties sand fairway, with the stratigraphy on the north to north-eastern side of the diapir estimated to be the thickest and best quality for both Forties and Tay reservoir intervals. While the Maureen may provide a lateral seal to the chalk in some locations, it is likely that the interbedded sands would create a connected hydrocarbon column with the Forties.

The Walnut prospect is comprised of remobilised Nauchlan Sandstone which is encased in the Alba Formation shales. It is seismically defined using the Qeye Labs 2014 Poisson's Ratio data, which shows that there is connectivity of the Walnut Nauchlan Sandstone to that of the up-dip water leg of the Alba field (Figure 5.2). This connectivity puts considerable constraint on the Walnut prospect definition; limiting it to a small four way dip closure with a pitch out element, separated from the Alba water leg by saddle. The depth of this saddle limits the deepest Oil Water Contact (OWC) and maximum Stock Tank Oil Initial In Place (STOIIP) that can be contained within the Walnut prospect (Table 5.1).

description: Bowmore is an elongate fault and dip-closed gas-condensate discovery mapped at Base Cretaceous level with a crest at approximately 13,800ftTVDSS, bounded to the N by a fault and to the S and SW by dip-closure. Bowmore is proven by the 15/24a-4 and 15/24a-9 wells. An easterly thinning of the Upper Jurassic across the structure results in pinch-out of Upper Jurassic Claymore and Galley turbidite sandstones onto the underlying tilted fault block, overlying deeper shoreface Piper Sandstone. Wireline log analysis confirmed all three sandstones as hydrocarbon-bearing.  Logs indicated that the Piper Sandstone was hydrocarbon-bearing down to 14,520ftTVDSS in the 15/24a-4 well, proving the extent of the discovery at this level. However, on DST the Piper did not flow, confirming low permeability, poor-quality reservoir. Mean recoverable reserves for the Piper Sandstone are calculated at 19mmbbls condensate and 67.2bcf gas.

Seismic mapping and interpretation of various attributes provide strong evidence for the presence of an anomalous body here. 
Rock physics modelling, seismic inversions and geological analogue work has been completed in order to try and discriminate the lithology within Griffon North (reservoir sandstone versus a non-reservoir, mass-transport deposit) but has failed to do so. As a result, reservoir presence remains a high risk for the prospect. The likelihood for stratigraphic trapping to the north and the relatively shallow depth of the prospect also means that charge to the structure from the mature parts of the Cromarty Sub-Basin is another high-risk factor.

Tay Lead H - small 4-way dip closure within late Tay channel sand. CoS 20%. RF cf. Guillemot. Same as Antrim's Mask prospect in their 2013 relinquishment report. Mask Prospect shows a thickened Upper Tay section, with apparent differential compaction
emphasising the dip closure in an east-west sense. The prospect also exhibits an apparently channelized Lower Tay section. Both of these reservoir targets should be sand-prone. Neither anomaly shows the classic features typical of injected sands. The likelihood of there being a seal between the Upper Tay and Lower Tay is thought to be low, hence only the Upper Tay is considered lower risk, but a single well could test both target levels. This anomaly (at both levels) would need to be sealed through onlap or bypass/erosion/truncation of sands to the northwest along the channel axis trend as there is minimal independent dip in that direction. To the west and east, the side seal would be provided by the apparent channel morphology at the deeper level and with  three way dip closure and shale-out at the Upper Tay. Without direct seismic evidence of hydrocarbon presence, the predominant risk at 21/24b-Mask is the stratigraphic closure/shale-out to the NW to secure a trap.

Wade is a four way dip closed prospect with a Tay Sandstone Member reservoir. Amplitude extractions reveal a sinuous channel crossing the Wade trap and offset wells, such as 21/24-5, contain sand at this level. Occasional faults dissect the reservoir and top seal, which perhaps pose a risk for seal integrity. Wade is considered to be oil prone given that the amplitude response is not as bright as that expected with gas. In fact, Wade does not appear to have any amplitude response which would point to the presence of hydrocarbons. This may suggest there is a significant charge and migration risk, which could be corroborated by the lack of shows in the Tay sands at updip well 21/24-5 and there being no evidence of hydrocarbons having migrated into this particular channel system in any other wells.

A small structural closure can be mapped within the Eocene Tay Member play. This is on trend with a channel like feature visible on regional seismic attribute maps.  In seismic cross section the channel like feature is clearly visible although the bright seismic amplitudes form only part of it.  It is possible that there is a small hydrocarbon accumulation within a narrow sand rich slope channel complex similar to that seen in the neighbouring producing fields albeit on a smaller scale. Reservoir is expected to be similar quality to that of the Tay in the producing fields as Tay Member sandstones where encountered are generally good quality reservoir with up to 30 pu porosity and 1 Darcy permeability.  An alternative interpretation is that the bright channel-like feature is only defining part is the sand feeder channel.  The bright amplitudes could be a basal lag or gravel and the sand may be more extensive than the amplitude map suggests.

description: The Bancroft Lead is a Fulmar Sandstone stratigraphic target in the Upper Jurassic, located adjacent to the Kittiwake Oil Field. The trap is sealed up-dip, to the south by the onlapping Fulmar sands onto older Middle Jurassic and/or Triassic claystones. Side seal for the lead are the younger claystone filled channels incisions, possibly of Volgian age.  The events can be mapped seismically and are interpreted to intersect vertically through the reservoir interval and create the potential for lateral seals to the north and south of the Lead. The crest of the target is ~3,500 mSS and the P50 resource is 20 mmbbls.  A number of wells intersect the reservoir adjacent to the lead with numerous oil discoveries. Reservoir presence, effectiveness and charge are considered low risk.  The critical risk is the trap and specifically the presence of a lateral seal that are sufficient to hold a commercially viable quantity of hydrocarbons.

description:
The primary level of prospectivity is the Z3 Plattendolomite interval, tested in the analogue Endeavour undeveloped field (discovery well 41/25a-1) and with reported gas shows in several offset wells. 
The Z2 Hauptdolomite carbonate interval, analogue to the Crosgan discovery, the Pensacola prospect and fields onshore UK, the Netherlands, Germany and Poland, and Early Carboniferous sandstones are secondary objectives. 
The Plattendolomite reservoir objectives are locally thickened shelf/slope carbonates in structural traps, sealed by either salt-facies and/or diagenetic-control. Traps have been formed or enhanced by late stage compression during the Alpine orogeny and presumably resulted in significant secondary fracturing of the dolomitic carbonates. Charge is anticipated from the Carboniferous (Westphalian/Scremerston) via faults or fractures across the Werra Anhydrite, laterally from the east onto the shelf, or alternatively via Cenozoic dykes.

The 22/15-4 well targeted another low-relief four-way dip closure at Top Forties Formation, along the northwest-southeast trending turbidite fairway roughly half-way between the Banks discovery and the Everest field. The highest part of the structure has a crest at around 2615mSS and coincides with strong amplitudes on 3D seismic. However, any AVO effects are subdued. 
The well encountered a 24m oil column within thickly-bedded, moderate net-to-gross Forties Sandstone. 
The oil accumulation is sealed by the overlying Sele Formation shales.

The Esperanza discovery well 22/15-4 proved a high net-to-gross channel fairway of Paleocene age Forties sands draped over a broad structural closure.

Deep purple is a small salt cored dip-closure in the Upper Jurassic at c. 3535m TVDSS with stratigraphic upside in an inter-pod pinch-out against the Triassic. Uncertainties regarding reservoir development and quality and the location of lateral seals (and therefore the shape and size of the trap) due to problems imaging the Upper Jurassic on available seismic, make Deep Purple a high risk play with poorly constrained volumetrics for the upside case. Upper Jurassic reservoir quality in adjacent block 22/15 wells is very poor, but this is considered to be primarily facies and not depth related. 
The Mortimer discovery (23/16d-6), which lies along structural trend 22km to the south-east, had high quality Gyda reservoir development at similar depths, with porosities averaging more than 20%, but the presence of similar clean middle shoreface facies reservoirs across the Deep Purple prospect is unproven. 
The Brynhild discovery in nearby (25km to SE) Norwegian blocks 7/4 and 7/7 provides the best field analogue. Brynhild has 40° API oil in a pinch-out trap at the northern end of Jaeren interpod at 10,760-11,000 ft.

key_work_comment:
Although the Bader structure is well delineated, further work is required to better understand the top seal and to position the exploration well and orientate the contingent inclined well to improve the chance of success and ensure maximum recovery of petroleum. 

The proposed 2 year Phase A work programme is designed to address these issues.
- reprocess the post stack 3D data to undertake detailed attribute analysis to further delineate the fault and fracture network within the structure, 
- studies to address the top seal risk will include using satellite imagery to detect possible oil seepage on the ocean surface, and 
- detailed sequence stratigraphic analysis of the top seal lithologies in the uppermost Cretaceous, Palaeocene and Eocene sections.
description:

Seal: The presence of an effective top seal is a key risk for the Bader Prospect. The extent to which the Upper Cretaceous and Palaeocene shales onlap the basement and form a robust top seal requires considerable further analysis and work. 
Trap: the structural definition of the Bader Prospect is well constrained on modern, good quality 3D seismic data. 
Migration: The position of the Bader Prospect in relation to the mature hydrocarbon kitchen to the north-west is very similar to that of the Lancaster-Halifax and Clair fields. It is therefore highly likely that the Bader structure has received abundant hydrocarbon charge. Fractures within the basement appear to form high effective conduits for hydrocarbons to accumulate at the top of the ridge.

MapThe Humphrey Discovery contains gas in the Lower Ketch 2 with potentially some gas in a poor quality overlying Lower Leman Sand. The structure was interpreted as having a 4-way dip closure at Leman level, sealed by the Silverpit shale. Below the BPU, Humphrey is a combined structural and stratigraphic subcrop trap typical of the Quad 44 Carboniferous. In the application, volumes were attributed to the Leman with the key risk being reservoir deliverability and to the Lower Ketch 2 with the key uncertainty being the position of the BPU and therefore the presence of Lower Ketch 2 subcrop across the remainder of the discovery. The Kepler discovery in Kinderscoutian sandstones represents the largest resource, although only 37% of the volumes are located in Licence P2272 where the crest of
the structure lies.

At the time of the licence application, Kepler, a Namurian aged (Kinderscoutian) reservoir was already discovered by well 43/20b-2, which was drilled in 1988 by Premier Oil. Copernicus is a NW-SE orientated anticline including 4-way closures and truncated to the SE by a major WSW-ENE normal fault. The crest of the anticline is eroded below the BPU. The NE bounding fault, a NW-SE striking inverted normal fault, cuts the BPU and elevates the hanging wall in the SW relative to original footwall in the NE area. Other NW-SE minor faults in the Carboniferous follow the strike of the fold, but do not cut the BPU. A series of en echelon WSW-ENE faults cut across the anticline giving a series of tilted fault blocks and grabens. The crest of the structure at top Kinderscoutian reservoir is 4100m TVDSS with vertical closure of around 200m. The fluvio-deltaic Namurian Kinderscoutian reservoir is of poor to fair quality.

The Triton structure, located 30 km SE of the Cygnus field, is very analogous to the McAdam field, which almost perfectly duplicates the details of the trapping geometry. It is a complex saddle-shaped trap, having structural culminations at its Northern and Southern edges, and limited and crossed by many faults. Definition of the western side is poor, mainly due to the poor imaging below the N-S oriented salt ridge covering half of the prospect. Top seal is provided by Westoe Formation shales. Side seal across the southern bounding fault is uncertain and critical to the trapping configuration.

The Caister prospect comprises a large structural closure mapped at Base Permian and Top Caister Sandstone levels. 
There is a complex overburden that is particularly sensitive to the Jurassic interval, (velocity modelling issue), and the Zechstein, (imaging issue), with the Caister play demonstrating no closure in time but with a prominent structural closure evident when mapped in depth.

The Lucius prospect is a large N-S oriented faulted Brent structure straddling blocks 211/11b and 16b. Lucius is a complex feature being in part both an upthrown and downthrown trap. In the north, Lucius is a hanging wall trap with the Brent reservoir juxtaposing Triassic across a NNE-SSW trending fault with cross-fault seal provided by Triassic shales and siltstones and clay smear generated along the fault plane. In the south Lucius is an up-thrown tilted fault block with the Brent reservoir juxtaposing and sealed by Heather Formation shales across the NNW-SSE trending down to the west fault. In the central area where Lucius transitions from an upthrown to a downthrown trap, the Brent reservoir section juxtaposes a narrow horst where Brent is absent.

description: Podlie Craig Prospect is a 30.4 km2 4-way dip closed structure at the crest of a horst block with a gentle tilt to the west. The prospect is located in the westerly splay of the Corona Ridge mostly in block 213/26a. The reservoir is predicted to be the Rona Mbr., of the Kimmeridge Fm., which can be tied on the existing 3D seismic to well 213/27-1Z (Lochnagar), where the Kimmeridge Fm., was 155 m thick and the Rona Mbr. was 149 m thick (gross). At Lochnagar there was 8.6 m of net pay in the Rona Mbr. (27║API oil), which was significantly underfilled, probably due to a breached seal resulting from Paleogene uplift. The Rona Mbr., displays a very poor correlation of porosity with depth (R2=0.2) regionally, which is due to the variable facies exerting control. The source rock is the Kimmeridge Fm. claystone, which is directly overlying the prognosed reservoir and is in the oil window presently.

description: Lamb Rock Prospect is a 4-way dip closed structure at the crest of a gently tilted to the west horst block, which is part of the westerly splay of the Corona Ridge. The prospect represents a new play in the area, as the stratigraphy has not been drilled nearby. The reservoir is proposed to be early syn-rift deposits of the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll Grp., which we do not subdivide into the recognised formations at this stage,although we recognise that the Lamb Rock location is distal from the sediment input (in the east), so the more marine Commodore Fm. is more likely. The Cromer Knoll Grp., shows a weak correlation between porosity and depth (R2=0.5). At depth, the marine sediments can preserve remarkably high porosity (e.g. Edradour) approaching the theoretical maximum. . Seal is likely to be the overlying Upper Cretaceous post-rift claystones. The underlying Kimmeridge Fm. is presently in the oil window.

description: Prospect 205_P-A was mapped on PGS Megasurvey Plus and part of ST12003, the prospect is defined by Horizon N, which is Colsay 1 Unit, where it is drilled by wells.  The extent of Horizon N is limited to the west, where the reflection picked terminates shortly into the Faroes Islands acreage, which represents the depositional limit, providing stratigraphic trapping potential. The prospect is defined by a 4-way dip closure of 16.3 km2, which may be related to inversion of the underlying Corona Basin against the Corona Ridge (e.g. Podlie Craig). The reservoir is hypothesised to be Colsay 1 Unit, which can be tied on the existing seismic to 205/01-1 (Rosebank)  and 204/05b-2 (Blackrock) which both discovered oil in the unit (Figure 27-30). Colsay 1 Unit is a fluvial to estuarine sandstone deposited in a fairway running approximately SW to NE (see Appendix 9.5) and the NTG is influenced by proximity to this fairway. Seal is claystones and volcaniclastic sediments.

description: Prospect 205_P-B is mapped on PGS Megasurvey Plus and ST12003 where seismic Horizon L can be picked and tied to 205/01-1 (and other Rosebank wells) and 204/05b-2 (Blackrock). At Rosebank, Horizon L represents the Colsay 3 Unit reservoir sandstone, but at Blackrock a disconformity surface at the top of the RLV is represented; both instances show oil at this level. We consider the 204/05b-2 well to have drilled the Colsay 3 Unit prospect (Redrock) up-dip of the pinchout of Colsay 3 unit and that and Prospect_205-P-B is on the fairway. The reservoir is proposed to be the Colsay 3 Unit similar to Rosebank, a fluvial-estuarine sandstone with good reservoir properties. Evidence from Rosebank suggests that if present porosity should be excellent. The seal is proposed to be similar to Rosebank, with Colsay Mbr., claystone and volcaniclastic sediments providing topseal. The source is the Kimmeridge Fm. claystone.

description: Rossini is a 34mmboe (Unrisked P50) lead targeting a proven and locally prolific shallow marine shoreface depositional system known as the Fulmar sandstone. Situated nearby the Romeo 30/11c-6 well which discovered hydrocarbons within the Fulmar and Skagerrak Fms.  This target forms a combination trap created by salt wall collapse/updip fault closure and defined by a seismically mapped wedge between the BCU and TTU with a crest at -8,800ft tvdss, a spill point around - ft tvdss and a maximum relief of 500ft.   Hydrocarbon generation and regional migration is proven in the area, although the Rossini structure is towards the edge of the mature Kimmerdige clay source rock. Upper Jurassic Fulmar targets carry a number of shared risks specifically reservoir presence and quality, however for this target the most significant concern/risk  is mechanical top seal failure given relatively shallow depth to crest and potential for high overpressure.     The geological chance of success (Ps) is 9%

The prospect 29/15-C is a rotated fault block situated updip of well 29/15-2, which has residual oil in the Fulmar.  The structure relies on lateral closure against faults to the west, east, south, and dip-closure to the north. This prospect is located entirely in block 29/15.  The main reservoir is the Upper Jurassic Fulmar Sandstone, which is the producing interval in Fulmar, Clyde and Halley Fields. Well 29/15-2, encountered 70ft of Fulmar sands with 67% N:G and 14% porosity but low permeability.  It is anticipated that the reservoir quality for this prospect would be better because it is located in a more proximal setting. Well 29/15-1 located directly to the south-east, penetrated a thin Jurassic section with no reservoir. The lack of reservoir sands in the 29/15-1 fault block is due to either non-deposition or erosion. Based on current seismic interpretation, accommodation space exists for the Upper Jurassic sands in the downthrown fault block, where Prospect C is located.

The Scarinish prospect was interpreted as an east-west elongated anticlinoform structure rotated over a major east-west north dipping salt body. The primary reservoir objective was the Fulmar (mid-Oxfordian to Kimmeridgian) shoreface sandstone stacked in a wedge expanding during an Upper Jurassic syn-sedimentary salt withdrawal and Rotliegend basement tectonics.

This prospect is a downthrown 3-way fault closure, which straddles Blocks 29/15 & 30/11, and is located updip of well 29/15-2, which has residual oil in the Fulmar. The structure relies on lateral closure against 2 faults. It is juxtaposed to the east against Kimmeridge and Chalk and to the south against Rotliegend and Devonian (tight sands). Based on current interpretation, accommodation space exists for the Upper Jurassic sands in the downthrown fault block south of 29/15-1, where Prospect D is located.The seismic demonstrates that there is an increase in the gross Upper Jurassic thickness from well 29/15-2 to Prospect D. Based on the current interpretation, an improvement in reservoir thickness and quality can be expected as we move from 29/15-2 to the updip location of Prospect D. Well 29/15-1 located directly to the south-east, penetrated a Jurassic section with no reservoir. The lack of reservoir sands in the 29/15-1 fault block is due to either non-deposition or erosion.

description: The Romeo discovery well, 30/11c-6C, was drilled by Suncor in 2012 jointly on behalf of the P1666 (30/11c) and P1816 (29/15a) licensees to test a four-way dip closure at BCU and Top Fulmar levels. Oil columns were encountered at three different stratigraphic levels: low net-to-gross sandstone within the Kimmeridge Clay; poor quality, lower shoreface, Fulmar sandstone; and low reservoir quality Triassic Skagerrak sandstones. The Fulmar sandstones were significantly poorer quality than prognosed due to a combination of a more distal depositional environment and pervasive siliceous and carbonate cements.

The well encountered between 60-250ft of oil column within the Fulmar Sandstone but failed to meet P90 volumes due to poor quality reservoir.
The Fulmar sands encountered in the well comprise low reservoir quality offshore transition/shelf to lower shore face sands and silts ( less than 5mD permeability). The sands contain abundant evidence of siliceous sponge spicules (Rhaxella).
The well encountered c. 200ft of oil column within non-marine, low reservoir quality sands of the Triassic Smith Bank/Skagerrak Formations.
The well encountered a potential 400ft+ oil column within a very low NTG (net-to-gross) Kimmeridge/Heather Formations interval.

This target forms a 4-way dip structure draping over a Jurassic fault block with a crest at 12,840ft TVDSS and spill point at 13,200ft TVDSS. Shirley sits within the middle of the Britannia sand fairway, however reservoir properties are inferior to most of the Britannia field wells. description: Bowmore is an elongate fault and dip-closed gas-condensate discovery mapped at Base Cretaceous level with a crest at approximately 13,800ftTVDSS, bounded to the N by a fault and to the S and SW by dip-closure. Bowmore is proven by the 15/24a-4 and 15/24a-9 wells. An easterly thinning of the Upper Jurassic across the structure results in pinch-out of Upper Jurassic Claymore and Galley turbidite sandstones onto the underlying tilted fault block, thereby providing a combination stratigraphic-structural trap, overlying deeper shoreface Piper Sandstone. Wireline log analysis confirmed all three sandstones as hydrocarbon-bearing.  Core from 15/24a-4 indicated modest but effective Claymore Sandstone quality. This was confirmed by a DST which flowed 3024bbls condensate per day. A hydrocarbon down-to (HDT) at 14,602ftTVDSS was observed in 15/24b-9. Mean recoverable reserves for the Claymore Sandstone are calculated at 19mmbbls condensate and 67bcf gas.

description: Bowmore East is an undrilled elongate WNW-ESE trending fault terrace located immediately E of the Bowmore Discovery. As per Bowmore, the structure is fault closed to the N and dip closed to the S. The Upper Jurassic Piper Sandstone reservoir is interpreted across the structure, the crest of which lies at a depth of approximately 13,200ftTVDSS. For volumetric calculations, a base-case hydrocarbon-water contact at 14,520ftTVDSS has been extrapolated from the hydrocarbon down-to observed in the Piper Sandstone Galley Sandstone in 15/24b-4. However, the failure of the DST to flow means that this prospect has high reservoir quality risk. There is additional risk on trap definition. Seismic data imaging is poor, and it is unclear as to where additional cross-cutting NW-SE faults may be present to separate the structure from the Bowmore Discovery, and to close the structure to the E. Mean recoverable reserves for the Piper Sandstone are calculated at 35.3mmbbls condensate and 125bcf gas.

description: The Dapperling Lead is an elongate low-relief, three-way dip-closed footwall structure on the southern margin of a W-E trending fault, mapped at Upper Jurassic Top Piper Sandstone level. The structure was penetrated by the 15/24a-7 well which encountered the reservoir at just below mapped closure.  The well encountered a 75ft gross interval of clean quartzose sands with a blocky log character at 13,687ftDDBRT, overlain by 120ft of poorer quality silty sand with cleaning upward log character, suggestive of a stacked shoreface system. Fluorescence was observed throughout, and log analysis suggests that these sands are hydrocarbon bearing. However, on account of burial diagenesis, reservoir quality is poor, with average core porosity of 9% and average permeability 0.1mD. Dapperling is estimated to contain 3.5mmbo mean recoverable reserves. The key risk is reservoir effectiveness.

description: The Charmer Lead is an elongate fault and dip-closed structure mapped at Upper Jurassic Top Piper Sandstone level. It is located on the same W-E trending fault and ridge lineament that forms the northern margin of the Bowmore structure and is also controlled by a NW-SE cross-cutting fault which downthrows the Piper interval to the east. The structure was penetrated by the 15/25a-4 well, which encountered the reservoir within the mapped structural closure at 12,738ftDDBRT. The well encountered a 47ft gross Piper Sandstone interval, and wireline log analysis suggest that a bona-fide oil column was present. However, only one good RFT point was obtained indicating that the reservoir is of low permeability. This was confirmed by core analysis which indicates average porosity of just 10% and average permeability of around 1mD. Charmer is estimated to contain 4.2mmbo mean recoverable reserves. The key risk is reservoir effectiveness.

description: The Gingertail lead is an Eocene combination structural and stratigraphic trap mapped at Grid Sandstone level. Up-dip to the NW, the trap requires a fault offsetting the potential reservoir interval against sealing mudstones. The lead stratigraphically pinches out in other directions. Evidence for the potential of the Gingertail Lead is seen in a number of nearby wells that contained thin but high porosity oil-bearing Eocene sandstones, most of which were drilled outside the mapped high amplitudes. The well tested at rates of up to 1080 bopd 41 degrees API but none of the tests produced a stabilised flow rate. Following evaluation of the well results the discovery was deemed sub commercial. The Womack prospect is a Jurassic Emerald sandstone structural / stratigraphic trap located on a fault terrace between the 3/11-1 Oulton discovery and the Cheviot field to the north. Success of the Womack prospect is dependent upon stratigraphic pinch-out of the Emerald reservoir section in the north of the prospect, trapping oil and preventing oil migration up-dip to the north into the Cheviot field. Whilst this trapping mechanism does present risk to the prospect, interpretation of the 2D seismic data set supports a pinch-out of the sand. Additional support for a stratigraphic separation from Cheviot comes from the significant difference in crude properties between the downdip 3/11-1 Oulton discovery and the updip Cheviot field. The prospect is estimated to contain P50 recoverable resources of 14.6 million barrels of oil, and is considered similarly to Oulton as a future candidate tie back opportunity to nearby infrastructure should it prove to be an exploration success.

description:
The Oulton West Frigg gas target is related to the Eocene age sandstone formation that is intersected by well 3/11b-4 at 2940-3020 ft measured depth. This sand is thought to be part of the early Eocene age Frigg formation that is occurring at the basal part of the Hordaland group.  The seismic morphology and 3/11b-4 well data confirm sands, with geometry suggesting a channel complex. These channels are thought to be terminated in the high-quality reservoir sandstone distal turbidite lobes of the Nuggets field. Based on analogues from the Nuggets field and the Frigg field, and based on the well data from the 3/11b-4 well, the reservoir is anticipated to be of excellent quality. Seal can be provided by Horda Formation mudstones. 
A small structural closure was identified within the channel complex from the seismic interpretation. A larger up-dip stratigraphic or structural trap might also be possible, but the up-dip section extends off the edge of the seismic data coverage toward the NW.

A secondary target overlying Oulton West is the Eocene age sandstone formation that is intersected by well 3/11b-4 at 2940-3020 ft measured depth. 
This sand is thought to be part of the early Eocene age Frigg formation that is present at the basal part of the Hordaland group.

Juniper is a high risk amplitude supported stratigraphic prospect.  
The play concept consists of an up-dip stratigraphic pinch-out of the Eocene age Frigg sandstone.

description: The 214/30-1 well made the Laxford gas discovery in 1984 in the Palaeocene, Vaila V3 Sand. The well was drilled on an AVO anomaly on the Flett Ridge and the accumulation is trapped by an up-dip pinch out to the south east and down-thrown fault to the northwest. The find is located 9km from the Glenlivet field. A gross thickness of 35m was encountered with 17m of pay present in the Vaila formation with an average porosity of 19% and a hydrocarbon saturation of 49%. The reservoir had an average permeability of 19mD and tested a maximum constrained flowrate of 17.5mmscf/d on DST. The accumulation was considered sub-commercial at the time of discovery, however a number of factors mean there is upside which has not been fully described.	A gas down to was encountered with no water seen in the wellbore meaning that potential exists down dip. Also, 3D seismic shows a pinch-out to the SE which could constitute upside potential in the  area.

description: The Laxford discovery well 214/30-1 drilled by BG in 1984 targeted a Palaeocene primary objective on a structural nose mapped on 2D seismic data draped over the part of the Flett Ridge. The well intersected gas bearing reservoirs in the Vaila Formation distributed in 3 zones. The reservoir is developed within a low net/gross system and consists of sandy lobe or channel deposits in a submarine fan setting (interpreted from logs). New Corallian regional mapping of the Vaila Formation supports the depositional environment at Laxford being a system of deep-water channels, with fan lobes recognised down dip to the north and to the west at the Scourie prospect. The discovery well intersected a reservoir gross thickness of 36m, with a net to gross of approximately 40%, average porosity 19% and high calculated water saturations of average 51%.  Updip of the discovery a series of channel forms have been mapped on the available 3D seismic data.

description:
Block 214/29b contains the Scourie prospect, a Palaeocene Vaila Sandstone target exhibiting a seismic amplitude anomaly similar to that seen at the Glenlivet gas field located directly south of opportunity. 
The Scourie prospect contains an estimated Pmean prospective recoverable resource of 107 bcf and 1 million barrels of condensate. 
The prospect is mapped as an amplitude anomaly observed west of Laxford. The anomaly is thought to represent a deep-water fan lobe outboard of the Glenlivet system. A recognised feeder channel appears to cut into the Glenlivet reservoir, and the resulting clay plugged scour appears to be non-reservoir bearing, compartmentalizing the Glenlivet field. This provides evidence of up-dip sealing for the channel and the Scourie prospect.

The Laverda Prospect is a Lower Tay turbidite channel stratigraphic prospect identified on seismic by the distinct bright soft amplitude and AVO response sealed by Upper Eocene shales. The channel has a WSW-ENE trending orientation. The soft top reservoir amplitude response shuts off to the east of the prospect (OWX?). To the west, the updip seal is believed to be stratigraphic (shale slump scar). Reservoirs are predicted to be Lower Tay drilled in previous discoveries in Block 28/9 with thickness varying from 3 to 20m with porosity of 30-35%. Key risks are sand distribution and updip sea.  Volumetric estimates are probabilistic, Min = P90, ML = P50, Max = P10..   .   COS for the Laverda prospect is 65%, with the key risk on Reservoir and Trap, 80%.

The Vespa Prospect consists of Eocene aged Middle Tay sandstones. The prospect reservoirs were deposited in a Tay channel system with a WSW-ENE orientation. The prospect relies on dip closure to east, with stratigraphic seal in all other orientations.  The reservoir is expected to be of high quality, with porosities ranging from 28-36% and thickness ranging between 1.5-16 m. The most likely charge mechanism is through the same migration route associated with Catcher, Varadero and Burgman. Key risk is reservoir connectivity and hydrocarbon biodegradation.  Volumetrics computed used probabilistic methodology. MIN = P90, ML = P50, MAX = P10.   .   The net pay for the prospect has been calculated by a function of the amplitude support observed over the prospect, hence it is not possible to supply a net reservoir P90 - P50 - P10 distribution..   .   COS for this prospect is 64%

description: The Laverda discovery lies almost entirely in Licence P2070, Block 28/4a.  It was discovered by the 28/4a-4 well in 2016.  This well was drilled in an up-dip location to test both the Laverda Prospect and the underlying Jurassic Slough prospect.  Laverda comprises a series of discrete sand bodies in the Tay Formation, mapped as a series of laterally disconnected oil accumulations, with OWCs stepping progressively deeper east from the discovery well.  This is demonstrated by pressure and seismic amplitude data around the discovery well, and amplitude data from further east in the accumulation.  A development of Laverda would focus on the eastern portion of the accumulation (not proven by a well, demonstrably not connected to the discovery well) where the highest resource density is mapped.

description: Cougar is a string of three seismic anomalies immediately northwest of the Varadero field and the Rapide accumulation also being applied for as part of this application. Its seismic form and amplitude response are identical to the Catcher area fields and discoveries where hydrocarbons have been found in all wells drilled to date. The primary reservoir will be the Tay Member injectites sandstones that are the main reservoir in the producing Catcher, Varadero and Burgman fields. As encountered across the Catcher area, porosities are upwards of 30% with permeability between 3-8 Darcies. Cromarty Member sandstone will be present below as the parent bodies to the injectites and as the aquifer. To develop Cougar will require drilling for a new template location in a similar development concept to the Laverda/Catcher North development that Premier Oil will execute in 2020. In this scenario Cougar would mostly likely be developed with Rapide.

Chadwick is a combination structural and stratigraphic trap. Lower Palaeocene Maureen sands, proven in adjacent wells and clearly defined on seismic, onlap against an embayment in the Viking Graben fault to the west, northwest and southeast with dip closure to the east completing the trap geometry.  Top seal is provided by Upper Palaeocene shales known to be present in adjacent wells, with lateral seal in the footwall of the bounding fault being basement.  Adjacent wells demonstrate excellent quality reservoir.  The prospect appears to be on a hydrocarbon charging route being located between known fields in the Viking Graben and the East Shetland Platform heavy oil provence. description: Medusa is an Upper Jurassic (Fulmar) interpod prospect located entirely within block 29/20 to the west of the Auk Field and identified on the PA Resources 29/20 3D seismic survey. Structurally it comprises a small four-way dip closure with a crest at 2175m.ss but the larger trap relies on lateral seal against Smith Bank pods to the north and south and dip closure to the east. The prognosed Fulmar reservoir is penetrated by well 29/20-1 which encountered 90m excellent quality, water bearing sandstones. Petrophysical evaluation shows that the sandstones have an average porosity of 22% and an average net-to-gross of 96%. This well encountered the top of the Fulmar sandstones at a depth of 2280m TVDss, which limits the maximum possible extent of the trap as the sandstones are water-bearing with no shows.

An independent closure exists at BCU level within the licence area defining a possible Fulmar interpod lead. 
The postulated reservoir is the lateral equivalent of the Fulmar penetrated by well 29/20-1.
The Fulmar interpod lead has a very low chance of success. The greatest risk associated with this lead is migration.

The reservoir interval comprises a 15m thick interval of porous Z2 dolomites towards the base of the Zechstein interval. The reservoir interval is not seismically resolvable and there are no coherent reflectors within the Zechstein package between the strong events marking the top of the Zechstein and top of the Rotliegend

The Andromeda closure is penetrated by a single well 29/20-1 drilled in 1973 by Shell. The well was not tested and was plugged and abandoned as a dry hole. 
The reservoir is Lower Zechstein in age and designated ‘ZC2’.
