The prospect is a series of downthrown tilted fault blocks, which are located to the north of the Auk Field. 
This prospect straddles Blocks 29/15 and 30/11 and extends into Talisman held acreage to the south (Block 30/16N), where the P90 volume for Prospect F is located. 
The structure relies on lateral fault closure at Rotliegend level to the south against the Devonian Formation and to the east against Kimmeridgian shales and Chalk. Reservoir properties are potentially degraded from those seen in the Rotliegend Auk Fm in the Auk Field, particularly as this structure is deeper, however, more technical work is required in order to better understand this relationship. P90 volume is defined by a 4-way closure at the crest of the structure, and the P10 is the mapped structural spill. 
Company CoS = 14%.

description:
The Poseidon lead forms a significant closure with an areal extent of 49km2, comprising a broad fault terrace in the hangingwall to the Auk North accumulation. 
Internally, at least three different fault trends fragment the internal structure into numerous smaller blocks. 
The crest of the overall closure lies at a depth of 2600m TVDss in block 30/16 and the structure plunges northwards with a fault-enhanced closure is at 3800m TVDss.

At the time of the 26th Licensing Round Application, Talisman identified two prospects, 30/11-E and 30/11-F, comprising a series of downthrown fault blocks at Rotliegend level, located to the north of the Auk Field (Figures 2 and 3). The structures rely on downthrown fault seal against Rotliegend and Devonian formations across their respective southern bounding faults, and against Kimmeridge Clay and Chalk across the eastern bounding fault. 
The crest of each of the prospects lies in the adjacent areas of blocks 30/11 and 30/16. 
The geological chance of success for these prospects is estimated at 1 in 7.

The Duran prospect is a well-defined deepwater Forties channel levee deposit along the southern margin of the main feeder channel to the Forties Field. The Duran prospect is supported by a strong AVO response. Relinquishment - 'The prospectivity of Block 21/8b was assessed using CGGVeritas's multi-client CNS-Cornerstone long offset 3D seismic data. Although not part of the original work programme, VGL undertook an AVO forward-modelling study to further understand the strong inversion anomaly (low Vp/Vs) associated with the Duran prospect on CGGVeritas FaciesFinder data (Figures 3 + 5). The results were disappointing and led to the belief that the inversion anomaly observed was due to the presence of good reservoir sands along a well-defined Forties channel (Figures 2 + 4) and not due to the presence of hydrocarbons. This view was further supported by the release of the 21/8-4 and -4z wells which encountered thin water-wet Forties sands at the same stratigraphic level as in the Duran prospect and hence invalidating the belief that a stratigraphic pinch-out may exist to the southwest of the trap. It was anticipated that the Forties sands associated with the Duran prospect would have shaled out at the 21/8-4 well location'.

The Cinnamon trap is defined at the Base Cretaceous Unconformity (BCU) level by three
way dip closure to the north, west and south and by a well defined, steep fault at its eastern margin. This eastern bounding fault is one of a series of linked faults defining the margin of the East Central Graben. Cinnamon is interpreted as a partially grounded Triassic pod, dipping westwards towards the deep source rock kitchen area of the
East Central Graben. A robust 4 way dip closure is mapped down to a depth of 12713ft (3875 m) TVDSS. Beyond this depth down to the spill depth, the prospect is sealed by dip closure to the north and west and by inferred fault seal to the east. To the south, the trap closure is defined by a combination of cross fault seal and against a Zechstein salt wall. The key risk is identified as being reservoir effectiveness.

description: Earn is a dip and fault closed structure at Rotliegend Leman Sandstone level and is composed of a number of tilted fault blocks. Fault juxtaposition mapping suggests that there is potential for fault compartmentalisation at Earn, therefore the prospect has been separated into four segments, North, Central, South and West. GRV?s for each segment have been calculated stochastically. Each segment has been assigned its own GWC range and built using area vs. depth pairs (top and thickness method), a thickness range, and then rolled-up. The prognosed reservoir thickness distribution has been guided by offset analogue fields and wells, such as Cleeton, Tolmount, Mongour and the 42/27a-3 well.  The same reservoir distribution has been applied to each segment. The minimum, maximum and mode of the distributions of reservoir properties (NTG, porosity and gas saturation) are controlled by and reality checked against offset field and discovery values.

opportunity_comment: The Ginger Prospect is a large and combination structural/truncational closure of the Devonian-Carboniferous Clair Group beneath the Base Cretaceous Unconformity sitting directly on the Lewisian Basement. key_work_comment:
The Ginger Prospect has been mapped on the best possible dataset currently available over the area. However, the definition of the truncational relationship of the proposed Devonian-Carboniferous reservoir section is still only modestly imaged. A 2 year Phase A work programme is planned to de-risk the remaining uncertainty by reprocessing part of the Rona Ridge (RR13) 3D survey. In addition the reprocessing will further enhance the image of the faulting & fracturing networks within the reservoir with the use of detailed seismic attribute analysis. Experience from the Clair Field demonstrates that this will be critical for the positioning of an inclined exploration well into the structure. 

Following the completion of a successful Phase A work programme, an exploration well would be drilled during a subsequent three year Phase C work programme. Spark Exploration does not see the requirement for further geophysical data to be acquired as part of a Phase B work programme.

The crest of the trap is located within Block 205/20 at 2,000 mTVDss. description: The Aspen Prospect comprises a large Upper Jurassic stratigraphic trap formed by a basin-floor fan deposited into the Cladhan sub-basin. The reservoir is interpreted to be J62 (Ptarmigan) age. This is age-equivalent to oil-producing sandstones in the nearby Cladhan Field. These sands are interpreted to represent the more distal basin-floor fan equivalent of the channel sands which form the cladhan Field reservoirs.

The Thunder prospect is an Upper Jurassic basin floor fan stratigraphic trap. It potentially consists of five individual lobes, encased within the mature Kimmeridge Clay Formation. 
The key risk associated with the prospect is the presence of sand in the basin. The presence of sand in the Cladhan Field at the relay ramp to the west of the Thunder basin and some thin sands with oil shows in the wells on the distal margin of the Thunder basin play (210/30-1, 210/30b-3 and 210/25c-6A) show that sands were being deposited during the Upper Jurassic. Although sands were clearly being deposited throughout the Upper Jurassic, what remains uncertain is the quantity and quality of these sands, if any, in the Thunder basin.

The Thunder prospect lies in the downthrown basin to the SE of the Tern field. 
It is structurally down dip from the Upper Jurassic Cladhan oil field and to the NE of Cladhan. It is contemporaneous with the Cladhan Upper Jurassic depositional system, with Cladhan being the relatively minor mid slope channels and overbank deposits and the Thunder area being the terminal depositional basin. Sediments were sourced from erosion of the East Shetland Platform to the SW and beyond, fed through various erosional features on the platform edge, down though a channelised system on the Cladhan mid-slope and funneled through a developing relay ramp into the Thunder Basin which was undergoing syndepositional development and deepening. 
 The basinal structure at Top Brent suggests 2 separate sub-basins exist which have been used to define ‘Thunder South’ and ‘Thunder North’

It is believed that the Pine Prospect reservoir sands were deposited as a basin-floor fan, likely sourced from a slope channel system to the west that can be imaged on seismic amplitude data and has been penetrated by the 210/29c-5 well. description:
The Willow prospect is located in the Heather sub-basin and forms the oldest of three potentially stacked Upper Jurassic sandstone prospects. The gross reservoir package for the prospect is defined on 3D seismic data by mapping the J66 and J62 flooding surfaces which form the top and base of the reservoir interval. The reservoir is interpreted to have been deposited as a series of massflow sandstones sourced by erosion of the East Shetland Platform to the west and deposited as a series of deep-water channel sandstones and/or basin slope fans. 
The Willow Prospect trap relies on pinch-out of the reservoir sands to the northwest and southeast, dip closure to the northeast and fault seal against impermeable basement rocks to the southwest where they are downthrown against the East Shetland Platform. Ariel is likely to have been formed from the distal pinch out of the Brae Formation slope apron depositional system which has prograded from the western margin of the basin. 
The trap is formed by thinning of the Brae Formation and KCF section but in sediments that are older than the J62 aged fan abandonment mudstone. 
The basal seal is the Heather Formation which forms a thick mudstone unit in 16/18-2 with the overlying Brae Formation reservoir predicted to thin and be overlain by the J62 aged hiatal mudstone. 
The Ariel prospect may also require an element of downthrown fault seal (at the north-westerly extent of the prospect) for the trap to be effective and this assumes that reservoir is present up to the faulted margin and has not already shaled out before the fault intersection.

description:
The Barracuda Prospect comprises an Upper Jurassic oil-prone combination stratigraphic/fault-bound trap within the main depositional basin of the South Viking Graben. 
The prospect has been mapped primarily on 3D MegaSurvey seismic data, with the wider prospect area mapped on 2013 3D Broadband seismic data and reprocessed legacy 3D data (MegaSurvey Plus). 
Definition of the gross reservoir package has been achieved through mapping the top Brae Formation (J60) reservoir and underlying top Heather Formation. 
The Barracuda Prospect reservoir is interpreted to be J66 (Brae Formation) age. This is age-equivalent to the adjacent oil producing sandstones in the nearby the Thelma Field. 
The Barracuda Prospect is sealed to the southeast by the lateral pinch-out of basin-floor sandstones proven by well 16/23-5 where a thin condensed age-equivalent shale prone interval has been penetrated. 
The prospect is fault bound to the northeast and dip closed to the northwest.

The depositional units are most apparent on the relative acoustic impedance data. 
The deeper sands of Ariel and Albion, both of which were identified at the time of application, were penetrated by the 16/18-2 well. 
The three prospects are defined by the three depositional units that make up the thick Upper Jurassic wedge that is derived from the Fladen Ground Spur on the westerly footwall of the South Viking Graben.

The Alcedo prospect lies directly above Aston and is defined by a thickening in the Heather Formation on the downdip side of the flexure. 
The play is purely stratigraphic and relies on the thickening being due to a sand body pinching out in all directions to ubiquitous Heather Formation marine mudstones and siltstones. 
Apart from the thickening, there are no other indicators of reservoir facies. The risk of reservoir presence is considered to be high.

description: The Amberjack Prospect is Middle Jurassic gas condensate faulted 4-way dip closure sealed by overlying Heather Fm shales and located on the western edge of the Sleipner Terrace and adjacent to the South Viking Graben. The prospect has been mapped on 3D MegaSurvey seismic data where a top Middle Jurassic coal marker can be mapped as a proxy to the top Hugin Formation reservoir. The Hugin Formation reservoir is characterised by massive sandstones, coaly sandstones and heterolithics that have been deposited in coastal plain, tidal channel bar, tidal flat, mouth bar, shore face and shallow offshore depositional environments. Charge to the Amberjack Prospect is sourced from gas condensate prone Sleipner Formation and gas prone deep Kimmeridge Clay Formation within the South Viking Graben basin to the northwest. Anticipated reservoir fluids are gas condensate of around 44-47░API having a GOR in the range of 3,800-5,100 scf/bbl based on offset fields (Utgard and Sleipner Fields).

The Albion prospect represents the lateral or distal pinch-out of the J62 (or younger) sandstone section and is located in blocks 16/18a, b, c and 16/23b. It has a wedge-shaped geometry and requires a top, base and lateral seal to be effective. The top seal is formed by younger KCF mudstones or Lower Cretaceous mudstones where the reservoir has been truncated by the Base Cretaceous Unconformity. Lateral seal is formed by an easterly thinning and facies change from reservoir sandstones into solely KCF mudstones. Brae Formation sandstones are absent from the KCF section in all wells drilled up-dip of the mapped trap pinch out/truncation. The lateral seal may also consist of a component of downthrown fault seal, particularly in the northern extent of the prospect. This assumes reservoir sandstones extend to the maximum pinch-out mapped. The basal seal is formed by a significant mudstone unit which is interpreted as a J62 aged fan abandonment mudstone or maximum flooding surface which is well defined in well 16/18-2.

It was then known as ?J7? and was worked up and drill-ready in 1995, but was subsequently dropped as it was deemed too high risk and farm outs were unsuccessful. On our current seismic datasets, the prospect is still considered too high risk to drill but the newly acquired Kinnoull/ Arundel OBC seismic (that borders the application area) has given us confidence that new seismic technology could reduce the risk significantly.

description:
The Conger Lead comprises an Upper Jurassic oil-prone down-thrown fault-bound trap within the South Viking Graben. 
The lead has been mapped primarily on 3D MegaSurvey seismic data, with the wider prospect area mapped on 2013 3D Broadband seismic data and reprocessed legacy 3D data.  Indirect mapping of the top J62 (Brae Formation) reservoir has been achieved by using the top Brae Formation (J66) reservoir. Base reservoir is mapped as the underlying top Heather Formation. The Conger Lead reservoir is interpreted to be J62 (Brae Formation) age. This is age-equivalent to the adjacent oil producing sandstones in the nearby the Thelma Field. The Conger reservoir is interpreted to have been deposited in a more distal environment to the Thelma field and is anticipated to comprise channelised lobe and distal basin-floor fan deposits. The Lead is sealed to the southeast by a normal fault that downthrows the reservoir against Heather shales and is dip-closed to the northwest.

The depositional units are most apparent on the relative acoustic impedance data. The deeper sands of Ariel and Albion, both of which were identified at the time of application, were penetrated by the 16/18-2 well. The three prospects are defined by the three depositional units that make up the thick Upper Jurassic wedge that is derived from the Fladen Ground Spur on the westerly footwall of the South Viking Graben.

The reservoir at Albion is the Brae Formation sandstone in the distal extent of the Thelma fan system. 
The trap comprises of the combination of pinchout of the sandstones to the south, possible fault seal or pinchout to the east and dip closure to the north-west.

The Savannah lead was premised on the observation of a dimming of amplitudes at the BCU level that was interpreted to be due to the presence of Upper Jurassic sands occurring immediately beneath the BCU. Trapping would be effected by shale out or subâ€crop of these sands to the southwest, southeast and northeast. The primary top seal to the lead would be by the Lower Cretaceous shale and lateral seal by shale of the Kimmeridge Clay Formation, also the source interval.

The Sienna prospect is an interpreted stratigraphic pinchâ€out of the Upper Jurassic Brae/ Miller sand sequence, sitting within the mature kitchen area of the Kimmeridge Clay Formation forming both source and seal for the prospect, and relies on an eastward sealing fault. The play concept is recognised from seismic which shows the dramatic thinning of the Upper Jurassic section between clearly defined Base Cretaceous and Top Middle Jurassic seismic events. description: Bennet East is a Carboniferous prospect straddling Blocks 43/15 & 43/20. It is a 3-way closure with fault seal to the south, truncated by the BPU and overlain by the Silverpit Fm. Reservoir is anticipated in several stratigraphic levels, from Langsettian (Westphalian A) to Alportian. The Westphalian interval is heavily eroded in this area and BPU is a relatively flat structure forming the top of the effective reservoir unit. The shallowest defined structural closure in Bennet East is at Yeadonian level.  The Westphalian in this area is interpreted to sub-crop the BPU at an Intra-Langsettian level. The sands were deposited in a low relief, fluvial fan system as channel sandstones, tidally re-worked sands & infilled incised-valley deposits.  These are producing reservoirs in the nearby Cavendish and Trent Fields & the Pegasus, Kepler, Copernicus and Browney discoveries.  The anticipate hydrocarbon type is dry gas, with Westphalian coals being the most likely source rocks.

14/15-2 encountered two oil sands within the Eocene, one 13' thick (top at 2411'KB) and a deeper sand with 61' oil pay on water, top at 2813'KB. DST-1 in this sand (2813-2830'KB) recovered 3 barrels heavy oil plus some formation water and filtrate. An oil column was also  encountered in equivalent Eocene sands in 15/11-3 from 2310-2468'KB, though DST-1 in this section (2361-2440') failed to recover hydrocarbons. The top of the oil-bearing interval in both sands is the same event and is characterised by a very extensive bright amplitude. However, there is no obvious structural closure at this level, apart from a very well developed structural nose at 15/11-3. This certainly appears to be a stratigraphic trap, but the extent is problematic. The nearest updip well is 14/15b-3 which is water-bearing at this level. The major risk, other than definition of extent, is viscosity of the oil, which could be immovable. The deeper oil sand in 14/15-2 is deeper than the OWC seen in 15/11-3 and is therefore a separate accumulation. The oil zone corresponds to a structural low and is therefore also clearly a stratigraphic trap, again problematic in extent.

description: The primary level of prospectivity is the Z2 Hauptdolomite carbonate interval, analogue to the Crosgan and Resolution discoveries, Pensacola prospect and fields onshore UK, the Netherlands, Germany and Poland. The Z3 Plattendolomite carbonates and Early Carboniferous sandstones are secondary objectives. The Zechstein dolomite reservoir objectives are locally thickened shelf/slope carbonates in combined structural-stratigraphic traps, sealed by either salt-facies and/or diagenetic-control. Lower Bunter could act as the ultimate top seal. Traps have been formed or enhanced by late stage compression during the Alpine orogeny and presumably resulted in significant secondary fracturing of the dolomitic carbonates. Charge is anticipated from the Carboniferous (Westphalian/Scremerston) via faults or fractures across the Werra Anhydrite, laterally from the east onto the shelf, or alternatively via Cenozoic dykes.

description: The Charlie downthrown structure represents inverted normal fault associated with Alpine inversion. Fault propagation folds provide a small closure that is unlikely to provide commercial volumes. The positive inversion of the Charlie fault was not sufficient enough to thrust the hangingwall passed the null point and therefore relies on fault juxtaposition or other mechanisms for fault seal. This would require the Silverpit mudstones on the hangingwall to be juxtaposed against the Leman Sst on the footwall and the Leman Sst on the hangingwall to be juxtaposed against the Westphalian Coal Measure shales. Alternative measures of fault seal are feasible, clay smear from the Silverpit mudstones and/or fault catacalasis from fault reactivation from the Alpine orogeny.

description: Mimas, prior to being decommissioned, has produced 36bcf over eleven years. Mimas production discontinued due to the LOGGS pipeline and Theddlethorpe terminal undergoing decommissioning in 2018. Mimas was produced using one well, limiting its drainage radius, suggesting it has remaining potential within that produced compartment. Volumetric analysis by Tangram suggests that the horizontal 48/09-N1 well targeted a single compartment of the structure which is compartmentalised by a De-Keyser lineament; suggesting an additional compartment has not been produced. The 48/09-N1 well DST proved a sustained production at commercial flow rates of 43 mmscf/d without intervention. The volumetric analysis and production data suggests that Mimas met its P87 reserve case and the remaining potential of the produced compartment is ~30Bcf to meet the P50 reserve case. Interpretation of the new survey led to a re-evaluation of the Lochran lead and the relinquishment of the P1741 licence.

Lochran Lead: at the time of application this was perceived as a fault segmented, potentially dip closed structure at BPU level. 3D seismic data was not available at this time and the mapping was based on a broad grid of  vintage 2D lines. The overburden is complex and depth conversion resulted in a significant displacement of the Lochran structure westwards, compared with the TWT mapping. The position and presence of a valid structural closure at BPU level was therefore questionable. A new proprietary 3D seismic survey was acquired in 2012 and processed to Pre-SDM (2013) to address this issue.  
 
Interpretation of the new dataset failed to confirm the presence of a significant closure at BPU level. Consequently, drilling was not warranted and a waiver of the contingent well commitment was sought and obtained from the DECC (26/11/2014).

The HPHT Fiennes Prospect is a 3-way dip closed structure within the untested hanging wall of the main western boundary fault defining the southern extent of the Josephine Ridge. The prospect is situated west of the TR1 structure at approximately 14700ft ss to top reservoir. The primary target is an Upper Jurassic gravity flow system, interpreted as a localised sand-rich submarine fan. The reservoir comprises stacked turbidite sands derived from reworking and re-deposition of earlier Jurassic and Upper Triassic sands on the Josephine Ridge to the immediate east and north. Seismic facies are consistent with stacked channel sequences, which show locally erosive and chaotic seismic facies character. There is upside potential within the underlying Triassic fluvial deposits which is also within closure against the main TR1 bounding fault. The main risk is reservoir presence and connectivity. Maximum structural spill is at 15725ft ss. Parameters entered cf cp30_12_19.

description: Roseisle is a prominent Lower Cretaceous four-way dip target, characterised by bright soft seismic amplitudes. The prospect lies 30km north-east of the North Uist (213/25c-1v) gas-condensate discovery. The estimated mean recoverable resource for Roseisle is 340 mmboe, with gas the expected phase. The reservoir is interpreted to be shallow marine clastics. The Schooner C compartment is a mapped high to the SE of the Schooner field. The prospect consists of several NW-SE orientated horst blocks. The reservoir target is the Ketch Fm sst. The Ketch Fm is a combination of thin isolated sand units and thick amalgamated units up to 50ft thick, interbedded with overbank shale units. The Ketch Fm NTG range from 0.10 to 0.50, with an average porosity of 0.12. Permeabilities 1mD to 1000mD.  A lack of well control in the immediate area makes it difficult to predict the fluvial sand distribution. The sand distribution also affects field productivity as the high NTG improves the connectivity of the fluvial sands. Production and pressure history on the Schooner field to the North West shows generally poor interwell communication due to the low sand body connectivity, with connectivity decreasing in a south easterly direction towards Schooner C. It is therefore unlikely that Schooner communicates with Schooner C or has depleted Schooner C pressure.

description:
Below the tested J62 interval in the 21/20b-4Y well on the same anticlinal structure, a secondary hydrocarbon discovery was encountered in the Late Oxfordian  early Kimmeridgian (J56), Fulmar mbr. A 140ft sequence was logged, an interval limited by a fish which was lost in hole. 
Net to gross was calculated at 50% and average porosity for the interval was 16%. 
Hydrocarbon saturation is calculated at 50% though it likely that it is impacted by the poor-quality density log affected by the washed out hole and the resistivity that is likely invaded by overbalanced water based mud by the time the hole was logged. This interval was again drilled with WBM and at 1500psi over balance in order to try and mitigate against the sloughing and swelling shales. Pressures were taken and the interval was cored and logged, initial indications showed low saturation, so no further tests were carried out by Shell, who in hindsight had not appreciated the impact on hole conditions in evaluating the well.

The 21/20b-4y (Christian) well discovered oil in Upper Jurassic Kimmeridgian turbidite sands (Christian sands) which tested oil at a rate of 6600b/d (41.5°API) and 7.6mmcfd of gas. The discovery is HPHT with 11200psi and 320°F reservoir conditions. 
The Christian discovery is mapped as a 3-way dip closed feature bounded to the north by a NW-SE fault. No water was seen in the Christian sands with oil down to 13601ft TVDss. 
A possible hydrocarbon leg was seen in the upper part of the Fulmar section with poor shows down to 13880ft TVDss. 
At its maximum closure Christian is thought to be one of several culminations of a larger feature which includes the Bligh (21/20a-5) discovery.

description:
The Christian J54 prospect is located on a Jurassic anticline approximately 4km from north to south and 2.5km from east to west situated on the western margin of the Western Central Graben. 
The Top Pentland horizon (which defines the Puffin Sand reservoir) was not penetrated by the 21/20b-4Y well but is a relatively strong seismic event that is tied to the nearby 21/20d-8 and 21/20a-5 wells. The structure is very similar to the overlying Fulmar Sand, but instead of spilling to the west the 4-way closure spills to the east and in doing so can join the Bligh structure. 
In drilling the section in 21/20b-4Y below the Fulmar in attempting to drill to underlying Puffin Sand the well experienced a twist off of the drill pipe which left a fish in the hole. 
The section where the Puffin should have been encountered was not logged and drill cuttings were dominated by barite, added to the mud to maintain weight. 
Gas shows remained high throughout despite the well still losing mud.

description: Bligh is an Upper Jurassic gas-condensate discovery made by well 21/20a-5 and appraised by well 21/20d-8. The reservoir is provided by shoreface sandstones of the Frigate Fm. The discovery well encountered 13m gross thickness Frigate sandstones with 7.8m net pay having an average porosity of 16% and Sw of 41.7%. The 21/20d-8 appraisal well encountered a 21m gross thickness Frigate sandstone with 5.9m net pay having an average porosity of 15.8% and Sw of 50%. A DST on the 21/20a-5 well produced 14.8 MMscf/d gas and 2,750 bcpd of 44.7 API condensate. The DST in well 21/20d-8 recovered gas to surface but failed to produce a stabilised flow, likely due to poor reservoir quality in the well. Neither well encountered a GWC. The discovery can be mapped as an extensive structural closure with 3 culminations which is dip-closed to the southwest, northwest and northeast and relies on fault seal to the southeast where reservoir sands are upthrown against Heather Fm shales.

description: The Bellinii lead is an identified untested closure at BCU. The nearest well control is 21/20a-1 drilled by Amoco in 1979. This well encountered over 1300ft of Kimmeridge and Heather section before finding a high-quality section of Puffin equivalent sandstone albeit water wet. These were directly on top of the Pentland formation like that seen over Christian and Bligh. There is also the potential for the J56 aged Fulmar albeit high risk due to lack of presence in the nearby well. The current understanding of the distribution of the Christian turbidites concludes that they are not likely to be prospective at the Bellini structure.

Mapping has confirmed there is a dip and fault bounded anticlinal structure at Upper Jurassic level. The presence and quality of Upper Jurassic sands are a risk. The closest well to Morgan Deep that penetrated Upper Jurassic sandstones is 21/20a-1 which encountered poor quality Puffin sandstones. Both Fulmar Formation Ryton Sandstone members were not developed. Seal retention is also a risk with both 21/20a-1 and 21/20f-7 demonstrating that Upper Jurassic intervals have breached overlying seals and allowed hydrocarbons to migrate to shallower levels. Given Morgan Deep relies on a significant fault along its north east edge and that it lies directly below 21/20f-7, which has proved hydrocarbons at Tertiary level, there is a high risk that Upper Jurassic intervals are already breached. Given the depth of the target interval. It is also anticipated that any hydrocarbons encountered would be HPHT.

description:
Bucephalus is a Carboniferous prospect on the western edge of Block 43/11. 
The structure is a 3-way closure, which has been truncated by the BPU & overlain by the Silverpit Fm. Closure is anticipated in the Westphalian A; all deeper sub-stages sub-crop BPU to the west of 43/11 & are not in closure here. 
The primary focus and prospect definition is based on the presence of a Langsettian (Westphalian A) interval comprising of sands deposited in a fluvial system.  Proven reservoir rocks occur within Westphalian and Namurian in this part of the basin. These sands were deposited in a low relief, fluvial fan system that covered most of the area, as channel sandstones, tidally re-worked sands & infilled incised-valley deposits.  These are producing reservoirs in the nearby Cavendish and Trent Fields & the Pegasus North & West, Kepler, Copernicus and Browney discoveries.  
The anticipate hydrocarbon type is dry gas, with Westphalian coals & Namurian shales being the most likely source rocks.

description:
Losgann is a follow-up target within the ‘Gamma area’ to be drilled following the drilling of the Gamma 1 and Gamma 2 prospects, the results of which will determine the final planned well path for Losgann. 
Losgann will be side tracked from the Gamma 1 horizontal sidetrack to the northeast where an approximate 2.6 km long horizontal section will test the prospect. Losgann targets  Tertiary sand injectites in the inner dyke area and brecciated zone of the Gamma Injectite structure. The Gamma inner dyke and brecciated zone was previously penetrated by 5 wells with varying amounts of oil and gas pay. Well data available to Apache for 9/19-16 and 24/9-3 and 24/9-4 shows the expected facies are thin dykes, sills and breccia. Recent wells drilled by AkerBP in the same area (Froskelar) have encountered similar facies. Losgann has been mapped on far stack seismic.
Reservoir quality is expected to be excellent (32% porosity, multi-darcy sands) based on offset well data.
The main risk at Losgann is lateral seal and the prospect has a Pg of 90% 
The main uncertainties are the Recovery Factors and NTG encountered along the well.

Skylark A prospect is located south of the Skye and Block 6 discoveries and comprises a fault block with stratigraphic closure to the north and east due to erosion of the Tarbert, dip closure to the south, and structural closure to the west. Anticipated reservoir is Tarbert Fm (Brent) rpograding delta sands, with additional potential in the Ness interval. Charge interpreted to be updip from the basinal area to the west. Key risks are erosion of the reservoir interval and hydrocarbon charge. Company OIP provided; parameters entered cf. Dunlin Field.

These two exploration prospects were identified to the south of the Skye and Block 6 discoveries. They are formed from two adjacent fault blocks with stratigraphic closures to the north and east (due to erosion of the Tarbert) and dip closure against contacts determined from structural closure and offset wells. 
Reservoir is interpreted to be Tarbert as in the Skye prospect with additional potential in the Ness interval as in Block 6.
Charge is interpreted to be updip from the basinal area to the west. Reservoir thickness estimates and petrophysical parameters from the offset wells in the discoveries to the north have been used to estimate volumetrics of 26.3 MMbbls in Skylark A and 29.3 MMbbls in Skylark B.

Skylark B prospect is located south of the Skye and Block 6 discoveries and comprises a fault block with stratigraphic closure to the north and east due to erosion of the Tarbert, dip closure to the south, and structural closure to the west. Anticipated reservoir is Tarbert Fm (Brent) rpograding delta sands, with additional potential in the Ness interval. Charge interpreted to be updip from the basinal area to the west. Charge modelling suggests both Skylarks A and B are likely to be HC-bearing, but recent seismic data suggests uncertainty in reservoir connectivity (and therefore migration) from A to B. Key risks are erosion of the reservoir interval and hydrocarbon charge. Company OIP provided; parameters entered cf. Dunlin Field.

These two exploration prospects were identified to the south of the Skye and Block 6 discoveries. They are formed from two adjacent fault blocks with stratigraphic closures to the north and east (due to erosion of the Tarbert) and dip closure against contacts determined from structural closure and offset wells. 
Reservoir is interpreted to be Tarbert as in the Skye prospect with additional potential in the Ness interval as in Block 6.
Charge is interpreted to be updip from the basinal area to the west. Reservoir thickness estimates and petrophysical parameters from the offset wells in the discoveries to the north have been used to estimate volumetrics of 26.3 MMbbls in Skylark A and 29.3 MMbbls in Skylark B.

Three leads have been identified in the P101 relinquishment area. These are Benbow West, Central and South. Reservoirs are considered to be Triassic Skagerrak sands
trapped within a complex system of faults around the Lomond salt dome. 
The most likely source rock is considered to be Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay in the syn-rift sequence deeper in the graben to the west. 
Migration occurs via carrier beds through a series of toppled Triassic fault blocks. This is the charge model for the sub-economic Lacewing Triassic discovery to the south.

The Camilla lead is a small, Lower Cretaceous level fault-dip trap on the downthrown side of the main Smith Bank Fault, possibly with a small amount of fault-independent closure. 
It is poorly defined on seismic and geological reviews suggest very low GRVs may be encountered in the Lower Cretaceous interval across the lead. 
Volumes have not calculated due to its size and poor definition.

The Jenna prospect is a fault controlled rollover anticline targeting possible attic volume in Upper Jurassic Burns Sandstone on the structure on which 12/23-3a was drilled. 
The eastern part of the closure is bounded by a fault to the north; the western part by faults to the south and west (Smith Bank Fault). 
Fault leakage is a critical risk since bounding faults reach the surface.

The Kate prospect targets Lower Cretaceous sandstones in a small fault-controlled rollover anticline bounded to the north by the Smith Bank Fault. Top seal at KCF level is unlikely to be present due to a predominance of sand close to the downthrown side of the Smith Bank Fault, so a shallower seal is required. Charge and migration is a critical risk since there are no shows in the Lower Cretaceous in nearby wells. Fault leakage is also a critical risk since the Smith Bank Fault reaches the surface.

The Vanna lead targets Lower Cretaceous or Upper Jurassic sandstones in a fault controlled rollover anticline. Fault seal is a critical risk since all faults reach the surface, as is the top seal risk shared with the Kate Lead due to the abundance of sands in the Lower Cretaceous.

North Burrigill is interpreted in the 3D as a three-way dip closure that partially rolls into a NW bounding fault.
It is very shallow (0.25 sec) and there is no brightening in the seismic. Closure against the fault is only partial, and the fault at the northern edge of the prospect appears to propagate to the surface, indicating breach of the structure. Due to this high level of structural risk, Equipoise Solutions Ltd did not quantify the volumetric potential of the North Burrigill lead.

The Polo Lead comprises a linear area of subtle mounding and chaotic character on seismic data within the Sola Formation interval. 
This could suggest the presence of a Britannia Sandstone channel of Aptian-Albian age. However, there is no support for a sand filled channel, either from amplitude studies or from differential compaction in the overburden. 
The nearest well 14/15a-4 did not contain any sand at this level. 
The trapping mechanism is entirely stratigraphic, and the lead is considered to be very high risk.

Reservoir-- Syn-volcanic Colsay and Hildasay (Flett Fm) basin floor fan systems, analogs are Rosebank and Cambo Fields
Geometry-- Low-relief 4-way dip closure

Petrophysical evaluation of well 22/16a-4 shows the potential for up to 14m of net pay in thin Volgian sands with average porosity of 12%. 
The prospect was delineated using a combination of the depth structure map and the Volgian interval isopach map. 
Up-dip from the well the Volgian section is truncated by erosion

This is a small closure on the back of an intrabasinal fault. No further work was done on
this lead due to the small areal extent of closure.

Torrance was drilled in 1992 targeting Jurassic Fulmar/Pentland and Triassic Skagerrak formations in a faulted dip closure. The well encountered non-hydrocarbon bearing poor quality reservoir over these objective intervals. A small 11ft hydrocarbon column was encountered in the Eocene Sele Formation in good quality sands (porosity ca. 25%) although saturations were low. 
Identified as an amplitude anomaly, Torrance comprises channelised sand packages of the Sele Formation and is predominantly a stratigraphic trap immediately south of the Starling Field. 
Despite subsequent re-processing and inversion studies in the area around 2000, Torrance remains a distal and disseminated accumulation with relatively low volumes (ca. 14mmboe).
L and NE ('Maersk') have Upper Cretaceous Chalk (Ekofisk and Tor) objectives, the former in a structural closure, and the latter in a stratigraphic trap defined by seismic amplitude anomalies

Aboyne. It is a small two way dip closure against fault. 
The crest is quite deep at 4450m TVDSS. The Maxi HCWC is located at -4550m TVDSS and was established based of a fill to spill scenario. 
PS of 9% (SR:100, M/T:70, R:90, G:40 & S:60%). The MRR is negligible.

Banchory SW. This prospect is located in the 3/19d block. 
It is a three way dip closure against erosion & faults. 
In most of this area the Brent has been eroded by BCU.

description: The Grassholm lead is a stratigraphic closure with pinch-out of shallow marine Jurassic sands against an old Triassic high. The sands pinch-out to the west, north and south whilst structural closure is provided by dip closure to the east. Structural closure to the southeast is enhanced by a north-south fault. A top sand map demonstrating the closure is shown in Figure 6 and the maximum closure is approximately two sq kms. A geologic model of the trapping geometry is shown in Figure 7 and a seismic section is shown in Figure 8 (PSTM and inversion data). From the detailed seismic interpretation it is anticipated that the Jurassic sands (Fulmar equivalent) will average 20m in thickness and this combined with typical reservoir parameters would give a mean reserves case of around 8 mmbbls of oil with a POSG of 16%.

Block 110/05 lies mostly on the hanging wall of the Formby Point Fault. The Sherwood Group is present over most of the block and is uplifted into a potential hydrocarbon trap on a narrow horst on the western edge of the block. The Permian Collyhurst Formation is found in the same structure, but the porosity of the unit is likely to be low.
The current interpretation of the Longmorn prospect is that it is a stratigraphic trap containing Late Palaeocene sands (T35) which were deposited as locally ponded slope turbidites.

The Balder lobe lead is located just West of the main Frigg field and corresponds to the Eocene Balder stratigraphic unit. 9/5a-3 well encountered 8m oil leg column at the Balder (Forties sand) interval. 
It corresponds to a small 4 way-dip closure, upstream in the feeder channel of the Balder lobe. 
At the 9/5a-3 well location, Frigg channel and lobes do not interact with deeper Balder interval.

The structure is a small scale collapse terrace on the footwall of the East Shetland Boundary fault.
Reservoir may be provided by Emerald or Brent Group sandstones, sealed by Heather or Kimmeridgian formation mudstones or ultimately Lower Cretaceous Shetland Group shales and marls.
The partnership have concluded that this small scale fault terrace is unprospective due to the small scale of the structure and its associated volumes in addition to risks on reservoir presence and fault seal.

Deino and Ogre prospects are Frigg Fm four way dip closures located on the edge of a linear feature trending NW-SE toward Beryl Bravo. 
Estimated STOIP volumes are 2 Mmstb in each. Hydrocarbon charge is likely to be similar to the discovery well 9/13-3a (Goblin). 
However, with the combination of limited structural closure and the absence of class 2 or 3 AVO anomaly, no further assessment was made.

The 9/13-3a discovery well (drilled 1973) tested the four way dip closure, encountering a 40’ net pay section in the Frigg formation sands, down dip of the structural crest. The deepest closing contour and estimated OWC was used at -4150’ TVDss for volumetric calculation. 
One DST was run but it failed to produce oil to surface. One quart of heavy tar like oil, estimated at 10o API, was recovered from below the packer in the DST tail pipe. 
AVO assessment shows significant non-conformance to structure, implying either a complex stratigraphic trapping mechanism or a complex velocity field warping the structure in TWT. This adds considerable uncertainty to the static volume.
The mean reserve estimate of 1 Mmboe is deemed sub-economic.
Recommended for deletion due to remapping (Project 01/9). Deletion agreed by DTI.

The Carna structure is an elongated four-way dip and fault bound closure at the Base Permian Unconformity.
Within the 43/22b block, the Carna structure is cut by a northwest-southeast fault towards its eastern end resulting in a separate structure referred to as the Carna Extension.

The prospectivity in the Forth Approaches Basin is believed to be in the sub-salt Carboniferous package. 
One large prospect, Skywalker, is identified in the hanging wall to the main basin bounding fault. Mature Carboniferous coals source the Visean reservoir with intraformational clays and muds providing a local seal beneath the more spatially extensive salt.

The Vernon Lead is stratigraphic trap within the Lower Cretaceous located between wells 20/10-1 and 3 as shown on the BCU TWT map. A seismic amplitude anomaly within the Lower Cretaceous had been identified within the Lower Cretaceous section which lies up-dip from the well 20/10-1 in which thin sandstone stringers were developed at the same stratigraphic level. 
The observed increase in amplitude could represent better development of these sands.

Around the 42/14b-2 well the Zechstein Lead (named Lead Z) is identified by an increase in the isopach between the Top Z2 Hauptdolomit and the Base Zechstein. 
This Lead forms an oblate shape in area, is thicker in the centre and thins towards the edges. 
The 42/14-2 well lies within this mapped Lead and has gas shows in the Zechstein Z2 Hauptdolomit.

The Camster prospect is located in Block 11/24c immediately east and downthrown against the Knockinnon discovery. 
The prospect is a simple downthrown trap against the Great Glen fault at Upper Jurassic Volgian level. Maximum relief mapped is approximately 600m. The lateral cross fault seal is against Devonian ORS, with top seal provided by Uppat and Heather mudstones.
Anticipated reservoir quality is very good for the Volgian, given surrounding intersections and the proximity of the Forse Channel Fan system indicating significant coarse clastic input into the basin at Volgian times related to shedding of sediment from the Helmsdale fault. 
The deeper Beatrice target reservoir quality is anticipated to be fair to poor, given the depth of the anticipated Beatrice section. 
Hydrocarbon charge is expected to be via the adjacent Beatrice sub-basin.
Given the failure at Wick, the lateral cross fault seal anticipated at Camster against the ORS appears to be compromised. As a result, the chance of success has been significantly downgraded.

The Whaligoe prospect is located in Blocks 11/24b, 11/24c and 11/25b immediately east and downthrown against Wick prospect. 
The prospect is a simple downthrown trap against the Great Glen fault at Upper Jurassic Volgian level north and along strike from the Camster prospect.
Maximum relief mapped is approximately 860m. The lateral cross fault seal is against Devonian ORS, with top seal provided by Uppat and Heather mudstones. Anticipated reservoir quality is very good for the Volgian, given surrounding intersections. The deeper Beatrice target reservoir quality is anticipated to be fair to poor, given the depth of the anticipated Beatrice section. Hydrocarbon charge is expected to be via the adjacent Beatrice sub-basin. The Whaligoe Beatrice prospect has a similar structural style to the overlying Volgian prospect. Similar to Camster above, given the failure at Wick, the lateral cross fault seal anticipated at Whaligoe against the ORS appears to be compromised. As a result, the chance of success has been significantly downgraded.

Falcon was the most encouraging lead to result from the updated technical evaluation due to its strong Class III AVO behaviour. 
Falcon is a Palaeocene Vaila intra T35 lead situated to the north of and down-dip from Foinaven. 
Like many Palaeocene traps it is a complex combination trap, in this case requiring fault seal to the south and stratigraphic seal to the east. 
To the north, fault seal (with possible sand on sand juxtaposition) is also required to separate Falcon from the downthrown Falcon North Lead.
To the north, fault seal (with possible sand on sand juxtaposition) is also required to separate Falcon from the downthrown Falcon North Lead.

The remainder of the Mesozoic portfolio consisted of potential Jurassic and/or Cretaceous sands pinching out against the Westray/Macdui Highs. 
Further seismic interpretation downgraded the lateral and seat seals of these previously identified leads. 
These leads required a Kimmeridge seat seal and/or lateral seal against the Westray High.

The Horsham prospect is a nebulous 4 way dip closed structure at Top Rotliegendes sands recognised in well 49/30a-5. 
The structure is covered by the Western Geco Q49/53 survey and Shell propriety Sean survey. 
Local well penetrations confirm the presence of thick excellent reservoir quality sands in the Rotliegendes with 17-23% porosity and high net sand content. 
The Zechstein carbonates and Bunter shales provide and excellent top seal.

The Reedham prospect is a 4 way dip closed structure tied into the Spilsby sands recognised in well 49/30a-5. 
The structure is covered by a Western Geco survey which shows an early Cretaceous depocentre extending westwards from the well onto the Reedham Prospect. 
The depocentre has been inverted during Tertiary inversion. The Spilsby sands pinch-out to the west and this pinch-out provides further stratigraphic closure on the prospect. 
Early Cretaceous claystones provide a topseal.
Oberon West lies northwest of Oberon and similarly comprises Upper Jurassic Piper sands within a faulted trap.
Lead E is a 3-way dip and fault closed structure at BPU level.
Puck S lead - Brent target, assumed to be in tilted fault block trap. Blob with net CoS (24%) and reserves only provided; CoS entered to comply with and parameters entered cf. B0606052.
It is Brent lead and is a 3 way dip closure against a NE-SW trending fault north of the Don SW accumulation.
Fault bounded terrace with 4-way dip closure. 29/14-4 downdip had HC shows in Rotliegend, but effective migration uncertain, good reservoir.
The Fatty prospect is targeting the Palaeocene Upper Balmoral sands in a 4-way dip closure on the southern arm of the west-east trending channel axis.

The Freddie prospect is targeting the Lower Cretaceous Cromer Knoll sands in a combination trap with part stratigraphic closure and structural fault closure. 
The prospect straddles the 15/9 and 15/14 blocks, all within the P1771 licence. 
The Pg is 19% with mean recoverable volumes of 24.1 mmbbls. 
The key risk is containment, primarily on the fault seal for the northern limit of the prospect, which juxtaposes Freddie against the sand-prone Palaeozoic in the footwall.

The Rowallan prospect was high graded to drillable status based on a robust petroleum system analysis and structural similarities with the Culzean gas field. 
The main Rowallan prospect had two target reservoir intervals; a secondary target of Jurassic Pentland formation, and primary target of Triassic Skagerrak formation. 
Both Jurassic and Triassic targets are located in a robust W-E tilted fault block with faults to the north, west and south – there is an extension to the south called Rowallan south (JX does not have an interest in this extension), where the main risk is fault seal on the most southerly fault.

The Triassic Skagerrak, Middle Jurassic Pentland, Upper Jurassic Fulmar and Heather plays are all proven in the East Central Graben, with discoveries and field in each formation. 
The northern segment was excluded from the prospect analysis at an early stage due to the results of the fault seal analysis on the northern bounding fault of the northern sector.

The Culzean N/NW prospect consists of two stacked prospective reservoir intervals. 
The deeper of the two prospective intervals is the regionally extensive Pentland Formation (mid Callovian-mid Oxfordian in the Culzean area) coastal plain which underlies an Upper Jurassic interval with potential for shoreface and deepwater sand reservoir development. 
The trap for both intervals is a 2-way fault, 1 way stratigraphic pinch out, which in part relies on a salt ridge to the west, and dip closure to the east. The Pentland trap is more extensive than the Upper Jurassic trap. The Pentland interval relies on a base seal of the Triassic Jonathan mudstone interval, a proven pressure seal at the Culzean discovery. 
The base seal for the Upper Jurassic would be intra Heather Formation shales. The top seal for both segments is a combination of intra Heather Formation shales and the Cromer Knoll Group marls. 
The charge route into the prospect is from the Lomond deep to the east where the Kimmeridge, Heather and Pentland Formations are all mature.

A seismic feature named ‘Kranto’ exhibiting high amplitudes in the Lower Lista formation on the PGS Geostreamer seismic, possibly indicating a soft interface associated with Heimdal oil sands observed elsewhere across the East Shetland Platform, has been identified in the north of Block 9/7b. Such amplitudes could represent sands deposited southwards from the Kraken area at the end of the Kraken fault relay zone. 
However this feature cannot be mapped with closure, is situated downdip and lower than the estimated oil-water contact at Kraken and is therefore likely to be water wet and is considered high risk.
The underlying Carboniferous contains a three-way dip closed structure requiring fault seal.

description:
The Crusader prospect, an eastern extension of Tweedsmuir South discovery, relies on sands extending on to block 21/2a from the west. 
Attribute mapping provides weak evidence to identify a sand pinch-out edge, which is inferred to be the eastern lateral seal for the Tweedsmuir South discovery. 
The depositional pinch-out is most likely to be within the adjacent 21/1a block, with little sand, if any extending into the 21/2a block. 
Faulting identified in the deeper structure may be a control on the extent of the Volgian sands; this faulting also supports the supposition that Volgian sand is unlikely to be well developed on the Crusader terrace.
Insch UB is partially eroded by BCU and intra Upper Jurassic unconformity on the eastern part
Insch LB presents a crest at -3940m TVDSS on the eastern side of the structure.

Insch Statfjord corresponds to a faulted block which is located in the block 3/19d. 
The structure has been almost entirely affected by a small throw fault located in the central part; however, it appears not to have an effect on the connectivity since the lower part of the prospect has not been affected by it.

The improved seismic over the Banquo/211/8a-2 discovery has provided a much clearer understanding of the structure. 
The north-south crestal fault (Banquo Horst Fault) is clearly seen bending to the south-east forming a ramp feature separating Banquo (211/8a-2) from Helena. The re-interpretation also shows that two compartments are formed by the Banquo Horst Fault on the crest of the horst. 
The well 211/8a-2 successfully tested the eastern compartment but the western compartment (Banquo Horst Area) remains untested.
Appraisal well 30/2a-11 has down-graded the size of the Forties Sandstone reservoired Audacious discovery (30/2a-6), which is considerably smaller than the Courageous discovery.

The Handcross Deep lead underlies the Handcross South Prospect and is mapped at the T35 level. 
The prospect is isolated in a graben between two West - East aligned faults one to the north and one to the south providing good lateral seals against thick shales seen in the 204/14-2 well. 
A clear pinchout is seen to the east but there is no evidence of lateral seal to the west and this constitutes a major risk to closure.

The Whale and Dolphin Leads are structural closures that rely on a combination of fault-sealing and down-dip closure. 
The reservoir target for both prospects is Upper Jurassic, shoreface sandstones of the Sgiath Mbr.

The Griffon West Prospect is a Lower Cretaceous stratigraphic trap. 
The reservoir is postulated to be the Punt Member sandstone.
The development of an adequate reservoir facies within the Punt Member is considered to be high risk; the adjacent 19/04-2 well has no sandstone developed within the Lower Cretaceous and uppermost Jurassic stratigraphy. Charge to the structure is also high risk for the Griffon West Prospect due to the western Grampian Arch having a tortuous migration pathway from the mature parts of the Moray Firth basin. The absence of shows in the nearby wells support the hypothesis that this area has not been charged.

4-way and 3-way dip closures in the area are characterized by their low-relief nature, commonly spilling in strike direction (NW-SE). 3-way dip closures are bounded by NW-SE trending faults. 
These faults have an offset in the Lower-Zechstein, Rotliegendes and Carboniferous strata, but cannot be seen to extend into Upper-Zechstein halite and Triassic strata above.

This is a weak lead that centres around an apparent Maureen fan that appears to onlap onto the Base Tertiary. 
It is defined on legacy 2D seismic data. The prospective area lies south of the Scylla fairway in the southern part of block 8/5. As shown in Figure 20, the downlap is well defined on a
strike section. However on a dip section, a northerly pinchout is difficult to determine, mainly due to sparse coverage of lower quality 2D seismic. 
No volumes have been calculated. The lead is poorly defined and lacks a well-defined updip stratigraphic trap, additionally a lateral seal in the Mesozoic is also required as the lead lies unconformably on the Base Tertiary.

Lower Macduff is the second Upper Jurassic prospect defined in the Kimmeridge Fm. 
This play is characterized by the Miller-type sandy turbiditic deposits as seen in the downdip well 9/4A-2a well (oil shows). 
Lower Macduff is defined as the strati-structural trap at top J62; it is a 3-way closure against basement or fault escarpment with a spill point to the north at 4750m TVDSS. 
The two wells, 9/4a-2A and 9/5a-4 penetrated alternate sand-shale sequence and thin sand stringers in Kimmeridgian respectively. 
Considering the lack of seismic support for sands presence, the reservoir presence on Lower Macduff is the key risk. 
Lateral Seal is a relatively high risk as all along the trap structure, the juxtaposition of the J62 sands varies from place to place.
Untested four-way dip closure in the Maureen sands to the north of the 9/12-3 well.

At the time of the 27th Round application, the potential upsides in the Galloway P2017 Licence were mapped at Upper Jurassic level and named Structures A, B and C. 
During the latest re-evaluation Structure C was no longer recognized as prospective due to lack of structural closure, but a new lead, Structure D, was identified.

Luna is a strati-structural trap at Upper Jurassic Volgian level.
The trap is defined by the up-dip stratigraphic pinch-out to the West-SW. The prospect is located to the Southwest of the producing Franklin field and Northern down dip of the Puffin discovery. 
The trap geometry is well defined by seismic mapping of top and base of the slumped geo-body. 
The extent of pinch-out of the Upper Jurassic Volgian gravity flows deposit is identified as a major uncertainty on the Luna prospect

At the time of application the Blodwyn lead was poorly defined on legacy 2D data, where structural closures were identified at BCU and Palaeozoic levels. 
With the new 3D seismic this lead matured into a prospect with stacked reservoirs in the Jurassic and Permian similar to the Wyvern concept. 
Both reservoir intervals have clearly defined structural closures, with the Jurassic also exhibiting stratigraphic trapping potential

Theo is an Upper Jurassic Fulmar lead that would target a stratigraphic trap on the Western flank of the Komodo high. 
On the new 3D seismic the pinchout/truncation of the Upper Jurassic package can be clearly mapped, but this does not derisk the presence of reservoir within the structure. Notable changes in seismic character occur towards the crest of Theo, but it has not been possible to attribute this to the presence of hydrocarbons. 
The disruption/brightening seen above the crest could be indicative of a gas chimney, but this would suggest that there is a seal/containment failure, which remains as the key risk for Theo.

Gaian West, Gecko and Icefyre identified during the interpretation of the new 3D data and are small structural traps targeting Fulmar sandstones. 
These structures have all benefited from the petroleum systems modelling that suggests they have received charge. 
Although these prospects/leads are lower risk, they are small shallow structures and any accumulation would be sub-economic.

Soup and Elliott were both defined as complex structural/stratigraphic traps in the Upper Jurassic, with Fulmar sandstones being the prognosed targets. 
These structures are now thought to be stratigraphic traps, but are high risk due to the difficulty in mapping the reservoir units and demonstrating a viable migration pathway.

Piers, Icefyre, Gila and Gecko were all identified during the interpretation of the new 3D seismic and are all structural traps at Top Palaeozoic level with primary reservoir being Permian Rotliegendes sandstones. All four leads appear to be robust structural closures, even Piers which extends south and west beyond the licence area and is therefore not fully covered by the 3D dataset. 
Icefyre and Gecko are favourably placed to receive charge and are below similar Jurassic structures, but even with the benefit of this their volumes remain sub-economic.
Demonstrating migration into Gila and Piers is possible via Dulcy, but again, any accumulation is likely to be subeconomic.

Lee was defined as a structural closure at Top Palaeozoic level with the primary reservoir being Permian Rotliegendes sandstones. 
The original structure was partially defined on 3D data, and this remains the case as the southern part of the lead extends beyond the licence area and is not covered by 3D. 
Given the low relief of the Lee structure, lack of 3D coverage and that it extends beyond the licence area, Lee was not recognised as a viable lead and no further evaluation has been conducted.

Monitor was identified during the interpretation of the new 3D data and is a structural trap in a downthrown fault terrace on the eastern side of the Komodo high. 
Primary target would be Upper Jurassic Fulmar sandstones.
The key risk in Monitor would be containment as reservoir would be juxtaposed against Palaeozoic sediments in the Komodo high, but the lead is also challenged as any accumulation would likely be sub-economic.

The original interpretation of Wyvern had reservoirs in the Upper Jurassic Fulmar sands, Zechstein carbonates and Rotliegendes sands. The prospect comprised two segments, an upthrown three-way fault dependent trap in the north (segment 1) and a downthrown faulted structure in the south (segment 2).
It was always recognised that there was considerable containment risk on the downthrown segment 2, and following re-interpretation on the reprocessed TOMO ML seismic, it was considered that segment 2 was no longer viable due to lack of fault seal. This re-evaluation was also applied to the southern bounding fault of segment 1, which was judged as unlikely to seal below the juxtaposition of the downthrown Jurassic/Zechstein against upthrown Permian reservoirs.
Conwy NW is a fault bounded structural prospect at both Upper Jurassic and Triassic levels located to the north of the Deep Banff gas and condensate discovery.
A small dip closed Ekofisk Chalk prospect was identified in the north of the license above a salt high, but recoverable resources are small.

Cretaceous - Numerous Lower Cretaceous leads over P.2101 were defined by the western most stratigraphic pinch out of the Punt age-equivalent sandstones. 
The up-dip offset well, 19/08-1 contains Punt age-equivalent sandstones that are interpreted to be shoreface sandstones that have been reworked by wave action. 
The key horizons used in these Lower Cretaceous lead evaluations are the BCU and the Top Valhall Marl. The Top Valhall Marl has been identified in the 19/10-1 from a synthetic well tie and was mapped across the P.2101 licence area where it represents an approximate Punt-equivalent age reflector. A thickness map between the Top Valhall Marl and the BCU shows the main westerly pinch-out can be separated into a number of scalloped shaped features, as shown in Fig. 5.7. 
The event at the BCU appears highly erosive in this area and is followed by sediment infill. However, down-dip offset well data does not indicate that Punt age equivalent sandstones are present and as a result has placed a high risk on reservoir presence.

FLETT FORMATION LEADS - The Cumberland are defined at T40 seismically, partially on 3D data but the critical up-dip fault closure is not fully covered by fully migrated 3D. The seismic pick used is the Top T40, which corresponds to the top of the Colsay Mbr., lava sequence, within which is siliciclastic sandstone in 164/25-1z
and 164/25-2. The tie to these wells is on good quality RR14 2D data and is robust.
No direct mapping of the reservoir interval is possible. Siliciclastic sandstone is present down-dip in 164/28-1A in the same seismic interval. Top and base seal is interbedded volcaniclastic claystone and is considered robust. The fault seal is juxtaposition of the Colsay Mbr., sequence and the sealing fault up-dip which is a significant risk, although
sealing faults in such sequences are proven (see Walker et al., 2013). The trap is formed by normal faulting in the Eocene, for which the downthrown block to the west is the Cumberland leads. Tilting from the Eocene to present formed the dip component, which dips westwards. 
Both leads are substantially the same, separated by a ~E-W trending normal fault. Migration is prognosed to be from the NERB to the west, where oil shows were encountered in 164/28-1A. 
There is no mapped stratigraphical or structural break between 164/28-1A and the leads.

The Whale Prospect comprises Lower Palaeocene slope channel “Maureen” sands forming a stratigraphic trap, analogous to those in the Mariner Field. 
The prospect lies on the edge of the East Shetland Platform, above the footwall of the major fault complex separating the East Shetland Platform form the Beryl Embayment to the east.

The Dunnock prospect (20/15 & 21/11) is reservoired within the Lower Eocene Dornoch Sandstone Fm and comprises two segments (North & South) separated by a saddle. 
Dunnock South is a 3-way dip closure with fault seal to the west, whilst Dunnock North comprises the stratigraphic upside to the north with sands pinching out before offset well (21/11-1).

Kessog Central segment is an undrilled segment of the larger Kessog structure. 
Kessog Central segment is a NNW-SSE trending fault block (Figure-7) separated from Kessog
South and North by two NE-SW trending faults .
Kessog Central is also recognised has having potential in Upper Jurassic Fulmar, Middle
Jurassic Pentland and Triassic Josephine sandstone reservoirs
There are also two small potential untested closures at Frigg level below any stand-alone viable economic development threshold.
The Lead A is a poorly defined independent feature very close to well 113/28-1.

A number of large undrilled leads have been mapped within the Carboniferous. 
These are four-way dip closed (and potentially stacked) structures, partially sub-cropping the Base Permian Unconformity (BPU), with Yoredale and Scremerston Formation reservoirs (analogue to the Breagh field). 
Top seal is a combination of BPU and Carboniferous intra-formational seal (analogue to the Pegasus field).

description:
The well 205/10-2B has found a 4m oil bearing sand just above the Base Tertiary. 
The sand is described as a fine grained sandstone, silty and partially calcareous cementation. The sample fluid is a light oil: 46 API, GOR 77m3/m3 according to available PVT Study. 
The oil accumulation penetrated by 205/10-2B well is considered to be limited. 
Although there is a regionally mapped, small 4 way dip closure around the well a review suggests that the discovery is a small, stratigraphically limited, ponded “pocket” of sand on a paleo-slope evidenced by the fact that the four nearby wells (205/10-1, 3,4 & 5) did not encounter sand. A preliminary evaluation of this oil sand indicates resources in the range of 1 to 5 MMboe.

Sleadale is a Royal Sovereign strati-structural trap defined by a 4 way component around its crest (at 5850m TVDSS) and a 3 way component combined with the pinch of the Royal Sovereign on the Flett ridge. 
Spill is at 6230m to the SE towards Craster structure.

The Gasta 4-way structure was subject to detailed mapping and fault picking. The structure comprises a NE-SW trending anticline cross cut by a dominant WNW-ESE to NW-SE fault trend dividing the structure into two tilted fault blocks referred to as North Gasta and South Gasta.

Recent industry activity in the FSB and the testing of the 1974 Lancaster discovery by Hurricane Energy, has highlighted the potential for a fractured basement play in this area. 
Three leads (Lemon, and Lime and Grapefruit (both off-block)) have been identified, mapped and assessed. 
The fractured basement leads are in close proximity to the Lower Cretaceous opportunities and represent possible future upside in case of a nearby economic development.

Selene was identified by a prominent seismic reflector that appeared to represent a Direct Hydrocarbon Indicator within the Beauly Member of the Balder Formation. 
The 2D HR data confirmed the Selene Main 4-way closure, but with a smaller area, and identified other satellite closures (Selene North and East).
Because the flat spot has been disproven, the case for biogenic gas is difficult to support. Considering the history in the area, heavy oil is now considered the most likely case if hydrocarbons are present.

The evaluation of the An01 prospect has shown that there is a very good chance (GPOS: 42%) that the anomalies are indeed related to gas bearing sands. The main risks for all prospects are related to reservoir quality and containment of the gas (seal capacity/fault). For An01 there is a possible stratigraphic seal required as the anomalies may not be fully conformable with the structure which is very flat.
Two out of three An01 prospects (An01-273 and An01-278) are structurally independent, i.e. they do not form any 4-way-dip closures and hence are described as stratigraphic traps.

Towards the basin centre the Haupt becomes thinly bedded and dolomitised carbonate mudstone slope sediments of the ‘Stinkdolomit’.

The Te-3 lead was identified as a NW-SE trending channel feature in Balmoral Sandstone Unit. Spectral decomposition as well as differential compaction evidently show the extent of the sand channel. 
Well 20/05b- 12 was drilled downdip of the lead to the east and encountered sandstone, however with no shows at this interval. Given this interval is sand-rich in this area, a significant risk of lateral seal failure is considered.

The Bruson prospect is located immediately to the east of Hannay field (ceased production) and to the south of Finlay discovery (well 15/26b- 9) which encountered oil in the Upper Jurassic, Sgiath Formation (J52) Sandstone Member. The top of reservoir sandstone is seismically mappable as an amplitude anomaly just above the Pentland Formation coal, analogous to the J2 (well 20/05a- 10Y) and Finlay oil discoveries.

The Ju-1 lead was identified on an amplitude anomaly observed in Upper Jurassic interval, where it is stratigraphically trapped. 
Well 20/05b- 3 was drilled within 1km to the south of the lead and encountered no sandstone in Upper Jurassic interval. Therefore, reservoir presence is perceived a key risk for this lead.

The Ju-2 lead is defined in Upper Jurassic Burns Sandstone Member with a stratigraphic trap. 
The Ju-3 lead is located to the north of lead Ju-1 and ca 2 Km north of well 21/05b- 3. Similar to Ju-1, reservoir presence is considered a key risk for this lead given well 20/05b- 3 encountered no sandstone (apart from minor stringers) in the Upper Jurassic interval and meanwhile, the lead location does not present sufficient accommodation space for sediments as observed on the Upper Jurassic thickness map.

The back-basin lead was originally defined in Upper Jurassic, Burns Sandstone Member, with a three-way dip closure trapped against a north easterly fault close to 20/05b- 3. 
The new PGS 3D seismic data reveals a different fault structures than that originally mapped on the CGG 3D seismic data. On the new mapping, JOG did not interpret a three-way dip closure and therefore, the validity of a trapping mechanism is questionable

The Doughnut lead was originally defined in Upper Jurassic Piper Formation Sandstone forming a ring shape around a mini basin, where it is stratigraphically trapped with a pinch out. In the original imaging, a fault separates the sandstone from that observed in well 20/05b- 12, however in the revised imaging using the PGS seismic, there is no evidence to separate well 20/05b- 12 from the lead area, and since this well is water bearing at Piper Sandstone level, it is perceived hydrocarbon charge represents a significant risk.

The prospect 44/19-3 Upside lies north of the 44/19-3 Discovery separated by an E-W fault. 
The reservoir consists of the Upper Ketch sandstones only. The FWL 3651m is taken equal to the 44/19-3 Discovery. There is a reservoir effectiveness risk for the Upper Ketch.

Two areas of the North Valiant Field were evaluated for remaining potential, the SP Southeast segment and the NW North Valiant exploration area. 
The NW North Valiant exploration lead is a low relief, undeveloped fault block to the northwest of the PD segment and southeast of the Frigate structure, and hence 
outside the P.033 licence but within the North Valiant Field area in P.008. It is separated from the North Valiant Field and the Frigate structure by two NNE-SSW trending De Keyser fault lineaments labelled DKN and DKS.

The SP07/02 well was drilled in 1991 to develop the SP Southeast segment. The well was drilled close to a De Keyser fault, and the near-well region may have suffered 
enhanced diagenesis. 
The well was completed in the poor-quality Zone A and Zone B sandstones. Zone C is below the GWC in SP Southeast.

Victor North East is a small, tilted fault block which is entirely below the Victor Field gas water contact and has an estimated P50 gas-in-place of 53 Bscf unrisked. 
Key risks are fault seal and the possibility of depletion through the aquifer. 
In the low case, the structure could be wet with no gas in place.

The Fell Sandstone target is reliant on unlikely fault-seal to the north, where the Fell Sandstone is juxtaposed against the Fell Sandstone.

The Aurora South prospect is a hanging-wall fault block to the south of the Aurora East horst. The trap requires fault seal to the North against the SCF and is 3-way dip closed to the South, East and West. 
The main reservoir is the Yoredale Fm. which has a top seal partly against the BPU (Zechstein Group) and partly against Upper Carboniferous shales.

It is estimated that the prospect has received charge from the underlying Carboniferous Scremerston Fm. and potentially a minor charge contribution from an intra-Zechstein source 
rock. The key risk associated with the Bonnie Brae prospect is reservoir effectiveness.

Both the Alpha and Alpha East prospects are injectite wing features within the Eocene Frigg formation host shale.
Both wings straddle the 9/9f and 9/14d block boundary. These injectite prospects appear disconnected on lithology inversion datasets although a small possibility remains that these units connect to one another via sub-seismic sands. 
Both prospects are near to the 9/9d-17 exploration well, drilled in 1997, which found wet Balder sands and did not encounter sand in the Frigg injectite target interval.

The Plantain South prospect is an Upper Frigg geobody that shows similar seismic characteristics to the Agar discovery. 
The Upper Frigg geobody is located updip of the Agar OWC and also requires a stratigraphic trap. There are also some Lower Frigg geobodies identified. These are considered higher risk because there is potential for connection to water wet sands updip.

Kinlochaline: A fault bounded structural closure in between the Janus and Gylen prospects. 
The closure exists at the Fulmar and Pentland levels as well. 
Kinlochaline is interpreted to be compartmentalised with internal faults.

Structure X is a smaller ‘sibling’ structure of Callanish and shares the same reservoir and seal characteristics. It is bounded by two normal faults. Structure X sits at a water depth of ~1250m with the crest of the structure at 4430mSS. The structure spills into North-Uist at 5390mSS. The ultimate top seal is a thick section of Cretaceous shales (up to 1800m thickness). The reservoir is considered HP/HT. 
Structure X is located between Callanish and North Uist on the ‘fill-to spill’ migration pathway and so if Callanish was fully charged, hydrocarbons would spill into Structure X. The two structures are fully dependent in terms of risk and volume uncertainty.

The Westphalian subcrops the BPU in a north-easterly thinning wedge. Sediments in the subcrop are considered to be Westphalian A in age. The nearest wells show moderate to poor reservoir quality in thinly interbedded sands, shales and coals. The Westphalian A is very thick but NTG is less than 50% and sand connectivity is likely to be mostly poor. 
A small structural closure exists, at the BPU; the potential for larger closures is limited by continued spill of structure to the NW. Seal potential at the BPU is linked to reservoir development in the Leman sand.

Blue Sky IV is an oil and gas lead, comprised of Sele Sandstone Formation turbidite slope canyon sands in a stratigraphic trap. 
It is seen as a seismic anomaly to the west of Blue Sky III that is separated by a structural spill point and low amplitude zone. 
The extent of the reservoir is interpreted to be defined by seismic amplitudes and inversion lithology prediction. It is possible that the bright far-angle PSTM seismic amplitudes may define the hydrocarbon extent

description:
The Browney North prospect is mapped as a small, faulted four way dip closure to the NW of the Browney discovery. 
The top structure ( Figure 5 2) is mapped as the top of the gas bearing sand in well 43/18-1.  
The top seal is assumed to be within the Langsettian shales above the reservoir.

The Browney North prospect is mapped as a small, faulted 4-way dip closure to the West of the Browney Discovery. 
Browney North forms the north-western, undrilled culmination of the Browney structure. 
Based on the gas water contact observed in the 43/18-1 discovery well the Browney North prospect and the Browney discovery are separated by a saddle point that defines the deepest limit for gas-water contact depth for Browney North.
