description:
Fleetwing is a structural trap to the NE corner of the Greeves interpod in 29/1 and extending slightly into 28/5a. 
The targeted interval is the Jurassic Fulmar shallow marine sandstone reservoir with topseal provided by overlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Oil is theexpected phase with migration up from the West Central Graben to the East.

The Fleetwing structure was interpreted to be the most promising prospect given its proximity to the mature source rocks in the West Central Graben, and comprised a four-way with an additional column upside potential provided by a small fault on its southwest side. Fault seal analysis was performed on the fault, which suggested a 30% chance of sealing; however, the fault is small- tipping out to beyond the limits of seismic resolution within a short distance from the maximum throw and showed a complex interaction with other faults and salt withdrawal-based structuration, so it was unclear how much weight could be placed on this upside.

description:

It has an updip stratigraphic closure against Triassic , probably Smithbank formation, to the South. The targeted interval is the Jurassic Fulmar shallow marine sandstone reservoir with top seal provided by overlying Kimmeridge Clay Formation. Oil is the expected phase with migration up from the West Central Graben to the East.
The Hawkstone structure was entirely a stratigraphic trap, relying on lateral/top seal along the south side of the Greeves Container.

Another infill opportunity is seen in a block east of Amethyst East and west of Medina. 
The block is triangular in shape with strong fault definition on the northern and southern sides but discontinuous fault closure on the east side adjacent to the Medina block. The exploration well 47/15- 2 sits in this block and proves gas at Leman level. A GDT of 2670 m TVDss was used in the P90 case. Should the faults separating this block from Medina not be sealing and a GWC of 2703 m TVDss be used, the East and Medina prospects are joined.

Asland North Deep is a prospect identified in the Pre-Triassic interval, located in the northern part of Block 110/9a. The reservoir is identified as Permian fluvio-aeolian sandstones of the Collyhurst Sandstone, sealed by the Cumbrian Coast Group and sourced by the same Carboniferous shales as the Triassic reservoirs in the area. The structure has been constrained with 3D seismic data and reservoir and seal quality estimation is based on regional studies of the Collyhurst and nearby wells as control points.
Asland North Deep is a small three-way closure on a southern, downthrown terrace of the Deemster Platform, partly within Block 110/9a. It is sealed to the east against the East Deemster Fault. Depending upon the sealing potential of the South Deemster Fault and the depth of the hydrocarbon contact there is a possibility Asland North Deep is in communication with the Kappa-Asland Permian Lead to the south.

A steep to vertical Chalk raft may be present on the northeast flank of the salt diapir.

description:

Review of the development concepts and facilities required makes Ada West unattractive.

This lead is a small but robust 4-way closure on top of the L Jurassic Statfjord Group. 
The main reservoir objectives are Statfjord Group continental clastics and the underlying continental Triassic. 
An adjacent well, 211/2-1, was drilled below the prognosed spill point, but had very low gross sand intervals, which were tight, fine-grained and not massive. 
The calculated volumes are probably too optimistic section with respect to the sand quality, so quality of reservoir is clearly a very high risk. 
The middle Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous shales will be a good regional top-seal, and charge will have a significant risk as the structure may be in a migration shadow, situated as it is behind a spur of the Albert Tryggvason structure.

The apex of the closure is 3802mMSL with a mapped spill point of 3959m, giving a column height of 154m. 
The total area is 7.2km2  and the resulting in-place volumes are significantly larger than the 'A' lead. 
There is again a large uncertainty on reservoir parameters and the same inputs were used as in Lead 'A'.

Seismic mapping on the TGS data revealed the presence of a closure at the Upper Jurassic level, termed the ‘Boatswain’ prospect. The 13/21a-1A well (1990 West Wick exploration well and a dry hole at Jurassic level) is the closest offset well to Boatswain (~100 m from the crest) and plays a critical role in understanding the prospect’s risk profile. Seismic interpretation, factoring in well positional and depth uncertainty, suggests that the -1A well drilled the hanging wall side of the Jurassic fault block (potentially a slumped crestal block), and therefore did not test the Boatswain Upper Jurassic closure. All other wells on the block reached TD in the Lower Cretaceous interval.
Boatswain is mapped as a 2-way structural trap bounded by two faults (Figure 7), located within a recognised Oxfordian shallow-marine fairway which trends East – West along the western extent of the Halibut Horst. The reservoir likely consists of fluvio-deltaic sands of the Oxfordian-age Ross Sandstone Member (a proven reservoir in the greater Captain area), with charge occurring from the Upper Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay Formation.

The structuration of the Orchid discovery is caused by a similar catastrophic slumping of platformal units into the basin as the Centurion complex and thus stands to reason that there is also deeper potential in the Jurassic. However, the seismic facies across Orchid Deep is highly transparent and lacking any notable internal reflections, which tends to be characteristic of the Smith Bank Formation shales, suggesting reservoir presence is a considerable risk. 
Furthermore, well 28/5a-4 on the platform is located just up-dip from where the sediments making up the Orchid deep structure would have initially been deposited, also failed to encounter any reservoir prone intervals, thus increasing the reservoir risk than based on seismic alone.

Similar to the Pegasus West discovery, the Pegasus North flank prospect relies on a combination BPU and intra-carboniferous seal trap. It corresponds to the remanent section of Westphalian A-Upper most Namurian age sediments left following BPU erosion on the flank of the Pegasus North discovery.

Well 43/13b-7, drilled by Centrica in 2014, is the second well drilled by the Joint Venture in the GPA and penetrated a gas charged lower Westphalian A to Namurian C section and a separate Namurian A accumulation within the Pegasus West segment, see Figure 27 and Figure 28. The shallowest three (Westphalian A - Namurian C) gas bearing sandstones, with moderate to good reservoir quality, were tested individually, yielding a combined flow rate of 92 MMScf/d and an estimated minimum connected volume of approximately 50 Bscf. 
These upper three sandstones lie on the same pressure gradient and share a common free water level. 
The trap for the Pegasus West discovery is a tilted fault block forming a truncated 4-way dip closure with an element of fault seal against the Cavendish-Murdoch fault. The trap requires a combination of BPU and intra-Carboniferous sealing in order to retain the gas column observed in the well.
Subcrop closure of basal Westphalian A (Crawshaw Sandstone possible) beneath base Permian. High risk of seal failure, and nearby 43/13b-4 dry.

Similar to the Pegasus West discovery, the Pegasus East flank prospect relies on a combination BPU and intra-Carboniferous seal. It corresponds to the remanent section of Westphalian A and uppermost Namurian age sediments left by the BPU erosion on the flank of the Pegasus East discovery

Additional upside potential exists in the intervals located above and below the Pegasus West discovery:
The well did not penetrate deep enough to test the age-equivalent Westphalian section encountered in the reservoir bearing interval of the 43/13b-7 well, but if the intra-Carboniferous seal lies stratigraphically above the 43/12-1 well sands, they have the potential to be gas-bearing updip and to share the same common contact as the 43/13b-7 well sands.
Gas-bearing sandstones were identified in Alportian age (Secondary Play) sandstones in the 43/13b-7 well.

The Andromeda South Prospect lies within the licence P2128 and is located on the southern side of the CM fault, separated from the Andromeda North discovery by that lineament. 
It is defined as a 3-way dip closure, bound to the North by the CM fault and at least partly traversed by a subsidiary WNW-ESE trending fault that may have the potential to compartmentalise the prospect. Both the primary and secondary play of Andromeda South have been identified as prospective. The main risk element for the primary play opportunity is the CM Fault Zone and whether it provides an effective seal. If the fault is open, such that Andromeda North and South are in communication, no accumulation can exist in the Andromeda South prospect, as the Andromeda North free water level (FWL) lies close to the level of the Andromeda South crest. The secondary play is seen as very high risk due to the lack of gas in the same intervals in the Andromeda North discovery.

description: Pensacola gas prospect is a Permian Zechstein Hauptdolomite off-platform carbonate build up. The 2019 Hauptdolomite Ossian oil-gas discovery (well 42/04-1/1Z) is considered partially analogous.

Thunderstorm is a combination trap situated on a terrace area bounded to the north and south by prominent, approximately east-west trending faults. 
Simple dip closure defines the eastern prospect boundary and a shale-out of the target reservoir interval - Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous ‘Scapa-Birch’ turbiditic sandstones - is invoked as the western trap boundary. 
The trap has a crest of 6475 ft TVDSS and closing contour along its eastern margin of 7670 ft TVDSS.
The depth of the closing contour is limited by the 14/29-1 well which encountered water-wet Scapa-Birch sandstones.
